The Śrīmāheśvaratantra; now, the first chapter.
The venerable Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, ocean of compassion, Śaṅkara!
O Hara, Śambhu, Śiva, Mṛḍ, Lord of creatures, salutations be unto you! 1-1-1.
Salutations to you, the deity of all deities, the Supreme Self;
salutations to you, the wielder of the Pināka bow; O bearer of the Gaṅgā, let there be salutations to you.
Salutations to you, whose body is adorned with ashes, who grants fearlessness to devotees, who possesses a luster as white as camphor, and who has three eyes. 1-3.
Salutations to you, O bearer of the crescent moon, O blue-throated Maheśvara,
whose matted locks are bound by great serpents, O bestower of auspiciousness.
O you whose lotus feet serve as a boat for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra, [I bow] to the one who is without possessions, pure, and the cause of the eightfold perfections beginning with *aṇiman*.
Salutations to the Lord of Yogis, to Yoga itself, and to the Master of Yogins;
salutations to You, the sun within the lotus-heart of yogis, who are composed of the bliss of yoga.

For the purpose of creation you are Brahman, for the purpose of preservation you are Hari himself, and for the purpose of dissolution you are Rudra; O Lord of Gods, salutations to you who possess the form of the Trinity.
Salutations to You, who are to be known through the Vedanta, who consist of eternal bliss, who are stainless, pure, and whose consciousness is being-consciousness-bliss. 1-8.
Salutations to You, who are stainless, free from desire, and without a lord; the Self of all, subtler than the subtle and greater even than the great.
Salutations to you, whose form is eternal pure consciousness, unconditioned by space, time, and the like;
salutations to the sole protector of all worlds, the destroyer of suffering.
"You are Brahmā, you are Hari and Rudra; you are the bearer of oblations and the offering itself.
You are the mantra, the officiating priest, and the deity; you are the sacrifice and the essence of its fruit. (1.11)
Have mercy, O Mahādeva; be gracious, O Supreme Lord!
When you are pleased, the wish-fulfilling trees bear fruit for all the worlds.
I have been assigned half of your body by you, the protector of the distressed;
I have thereby achieved my purpose—what else remains?
Therefore, I wish to ask about a certain supreme secret;
if I am most dear to you, O Lord, then tell me all of it! 1-14.
O Lord, sixty-four tantras have been proclaimed by you; yet in them, the knowledge of reality has not been made manifest. (1.15)
Reveal that, O Lord of Gods, if you deem it fit to speak.
Śiva said:
"O lady of excellent hips, O fair-faced one, this knowledge is not fit to be spoken;
rather, a kingdom may be given, a head may be given, or even all one's possessions may be given."
The knowledge of Brahman must not be given away; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O lady of pure smiles.
O Goddess, whatever sin one might incur by committing thousands of killings of Brahmins, that same sin one incurs by revealing the ultimate truth. 1-18.
The sin of thousands of killings of children, ten thousand killings of women, the evil of killing a hundred thousand cows, as well as that arising from betraying trust—[all these are removed]. (1.19)
O Goddess, whatever sin arises from betraying a friend, betraying a teacher, or betraying a virtuous person, one incurs that very sin by revealing the ultimate truth.
Therefore, a wise man should guard [this knowledge] like the fetus of a mother’s paramour;
since you are my devotee and most beloved, O friend, I speak this to you.
One should understand that knowledge by which the Self shines forth clearly;
it is eternally and perpetually veiled by ignorance in the form of delusion. (1.22)
The state of saṃsāra shall persist as long as ignorance shines forth;
for that long there will be delusion, for that long there will be wandering, and for that long alone there will be fear. (1.23)
The unreal notion of "I" and "mine," forgetfulness, the perception of suffering, attachment to various phenomena, and the longing for the fruits of actions. (1.24)

The distinction between bondage and liberation, as well as the ego-identification with the inert body and so forth—so long as these persist, the state of being a Lord (Īśvara) would be like that of a stone statue or similar objects. (1.25)
The status of sacred sites (tīrtha) and so forth exists only as long as ignorance persists;
once perfect knowledge has arisen, neither this world nor such conceptual construction remains. (1.26)
When the delusion and confusion have ceased, there is neither "you" nor "I," nor indeed anything at all;
the Self alone, by itself, through itself, attains the Self within the Self. (1.27)
Then one becomes absorbed in the essential nature of the ocean of bliss;
O Goddess, an ultimate dissolution will occur at some point. (1.28)
That very Self, the imperishable, remains as the one alone in person;
He is Śiva, He is Viṣṇu, He is Indra, and He indeed is the gods and the demons.
He alone is the yakṣas and rākṣasas, the siddhas, cāraṇas, and kinnaras;
he is the sages beginning with Sanaka, as well as the mind-born sons of Brahmā.
Animals, birds, mountains, grasses, and creepers—he alone is this entire world, consisting of both the gross and the subtle. (1.31)
Just as silver appears in a mother-of-pearl shell due to ignorance, O beloved, so too that silver, O Goddess, dissolves into that very same shell through knowledge. (1.32)

In that same way, O Goddess Śāṅkarī, the entire universe appears within the supreme, imperishable Brahman; it is a delusion caused by something, yet when that delusion is destroyed, [the truth remains].
Only the Supreme Brahman remains—manifest, imperishable, and immutable.
At that time, neither you nor I exist, nor Viṣṇu, Lakṣmī, Brahmā, nor Sarasvatī. (1.34)
Neither Īśvara nor Śiva shall exist as they did before;
O beloved, just as effects produced from clay are of the nature of clay. (1.35)
In that very same way, O Goddess, this entire world shall become one with Brahman;
just as, O Mistress of the Gods, moving waves arise upon the ocean by the power of the wind, yet when that wind is stilled, they become as before.

Likewise, due to delusion that causes the forgetting of knowledge, the world of moving and non-moving beings—which arises from the twenty-four principles—is perceived as real, though it is merely a mental construction. (1.37)
O Maheśvarī, these fourteen worlds are born therein:
seven below and likewise seven above; such is the number, fourteen.
Aṭala, Vitala, Sutala, Talātala,
Rasātala, and Pātāla, as well as Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar above them.
Mahar-loka, Jano-loka, Tapa-loka, Satya-loka, Vaikuṇṭha, Śiva-loka, Devaloka, and likewise those situated within them.
When delusion is stilled, all these will become identical with Brahman;
as long as there is the serpent-like error regarding the rope, O dear one, so long will there be fear. (1.41)
But one who has realized [the rope] as being merely a rope no longer experiences fear;
this proliferation within the non-proliferated arises clearly through delusion. (1.42)
Ignorance bestows fear as long as one does not realize delusion;
it manifests in two ways, three ways, five ways, and again in twenty-four ways. (1.43)
Furthermore, this delusion, which is itself manifold—being single, threefold, and again manyfold—having spread wide, veils the Supreme Lord. (1.44)
Through the conjunction of time, māyā, and portions [of the soul], the Lord created the cosmic egg;
he is the imperishable, all-pervading creator of millions of lakhs of cosmic eggs.
No desire should be directed toward him, for he is devoid of qualities and beyond primordial nature;
nevertheless, like a child at play, he sports with multitudes of millions of cosmic eggs.
This supreme, pure, immutable, and transcendent Person, who is pure consciousness alone, creates and withdraws [the universe] by the mere casting of a sidelong glance. (1.47)
His gross body is the Virāṭ, which arises in fivefold divisions:
Pātāla is at the base of his feet, and Rasātala is in the region of his heels.
In his ankle is Mahātala, and in his two shanks is Talātala;
above the shanks is Sutala, and Vitala is above the hips, O beloved.
At the middle of the waist is the Atala [region], and likewise within the belly is the mortal world (Martyaloka);
the Bhuvarloka is in the regions of the sides, and above that are Svarloka and the others.
The luminaries are upon his chest, and likewise the Great Light (mahas) is upon his neck.
The Janaloka is in his mouth, the Tapoloka on his forehead;
the Satyaloka is in the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), and Indra and the other gods are in his arms.
The quarters of space reside in the region of his ears; sound resides within his hearing;
the two Nāsatyas reside in his nostrils; and Fire is established in his mouth. (1.53)
The sun is situated in his eye, for day and night belong to the Lord of Days; Yama is in his fang, and Māyā is in his smile, O Maheśvarī.
Modesty resides on his upper lip, while greed is on his lower lip;
righteousness is indeed upon his breasts, and unrighteousness is established upon his back.
Indeed, the oceans are in his belly, and the mountains are in the joints of his bones;
the rivers are situated in the region of his veins, and the trees abide upon the path of his body hair.
The clouds are said to be in his hair, and the moon in his heart;
this, indeed, is the gross body of Brahman, the Supreme Self. (1.57)
The *liṅga* of that imperishable one whose self is consciousness is indefinable by measure and devoid of end or limit; for it is indeed Nārāyaṇa. (1.58)
To Hiraṇyagarbha, the Lord of the world, whom the wise call Nārāyaṇa—the sustainer of all, the infinite, the primordial, the cause even of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, and the Sovereign. (1.59)
To Him who is the constituent part of all time, the ancient one, higher than the highest, whose feet are praised by yogis,
and who is the sole cause of Brahmā, Śiva, Viṣṇu, and the rest— from whom the path of the Veda has proceeded.
To that Nārāyaṇa, the God of gods and the refuge of the worlds, they declare his *liṅga*—as long as the *liṅga* does not reach dissolution, nor does his gross body attain rest. (1.61)
Beyond that, the very cause is the body of that Supreme Self; it is indeed delusion.
As long as this delusion does not come to an end, the subtle body (liṅga), bound by its effects, does not perish. (1.62)
O Mother, the primary cause does not attain peace, for it is the seed of all that is moving and unmoving;
nor does that Great Cause, the seed of seeds, reach a state of rest.
O sinless one, this teaching, more secret than the secret, has been spoken to you.
It must not be disclosed before anyone; it is the truth, the absolute truth, O sweet-spoken lady.
Although Hari was entreated again and again, he did not speak to Padmā;
yet, out of affection for you, I have here revealed this matter clearly.
This was not even told to my secret son, Gaṇarāja Nandin; O auspicious one, this which is well-guarded has been spoken by me out of affection for you. (1.66)
Therefore, O blessed lady, this must be kept more secret than even one's private parts on all sides.
Thus has this been fully explained to you; what else do you wish to ask?
Thus ends the first chapter in the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Māheśvaratantra within the Śrī Nāradapañcarātra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī. 1.1.
Now begins the second chapter.
The venerable Pārvatī said:
"O Blessed One, O God, Lord of the gods, Protector of the world, Sovereign of the universe!"
I am blessed; I am favored; my entire life has been made meaningful.
With my mind cooled by the rain of the nectar of your words,
I know no higher good than the discourse on the knowledge of reality.
Of what use is long life to one of evil mind who is like a stone, whose heart is not attached for even a moment to the contemplation of reality? (2-3)
Sacrifices, gifts, austerities, pilgrimages, vows, observances,
and restraints do not approach even a fraction of the value of the singular contemplation on the reality of one's own Self.
The performance of sacrifices and other rites is for the sake of the singular purification of the reality of the Self;
when the mind is purified, O dear one, the manifestation of that reality occurs. (2.5)

O Śaṅkara, if that very [knowledge] is obtained without effort—whether by fate, through the satisfaction of the Guru, or even by means of spiritual practices (sādhana)—[then one attains success]. (2.6)
What indeed remains for him as a further means for attaining his own supreme Self?
Therefore, this contemplation of reality is greater than all else. (2.7)
"I have heard it from you, O Great Lord; speak again according to the truth.
Though that which is to be asked appears in many ways, nevertheless, O Lord, speak of the One."
O ocean of compassion, through the sequence of practice, I ask you once more about that most wonderful secret which was not told to Padmā by Hari;
a doubt has arisen regarding this matter, and you ought to dispel it. (2.9)
That supreme Lakṣmī, who is his eternal companion, that virtuous woman who is as dear to him as his own life—what is more excellent than her? (2.10)
What is the secret, what is the inner self (adhyātmya), which has not been spoken by Hari himself?
O Blessed One, tell that here, if you deem it fit to speak.
To me, there is nothing superior to you, even more so than my own life;
nevertheless, I belong to you alone, since half of my body was bestowed upon you.
"O Lord, you must not keep that secret; it must be kept hidden by you. Having said this, she bowed again and again at the lotus feet of Śiva.
Śiva said:
"Oh, you are blessed, you are blessed, you are blessed in the three worlds!
One would not find a beloved wife, dear as life, equal to you."
Satiated by the nectar of your words, I shall speak; listen to that.
Once, indeed, Viṣṇu was seated in solitude in Vaikuṇṭha. (2-15)
Having fully restrained the group of senses with his mind, he whose intellect served as a charioteer—possessing great splendor and tranquilized by a weight of joy—meditated upon something. (2.16)
With eyes filled by a flowing flood of tears and a body marked by horripilation,
he was like a sea with its waters stilled after remembering the ocean of the rasa of divine play.
The activities of the vital breath, the senses, and the mind are submerged in the path of meditation;
filled with an internal abundance of joy, he is incapable of external perception. (2-18)
And it was truly marvelous that she remained there with her body alone;
for that daughter of Bhṛgu was playing there together with her female companions.
Seeing him with his vital breaths, senses, mind, and intellect dissolved in the path of meditation, and with all external consciousness destroyed, her heart was filled with wonder.
Who is this that is meditated upon with a steady mind by the Teacher of the Three Worlds? I do not see anything else in the world that is more worthy of meditation than him. (2.21)
He who is the cause and the presiding deity even of Brahmā and Rudra,
whose deeds in his incarnations Nārada and others sing— || 2.22 ||
Desiring to attain that state, pure Brahmins—upheld by sacred knowledge, austerity, and virtuous conduct—practice the vow of forest-dwellers and the discipline of ascetics. (2.23)
There is no one else equal to him in this world, so how could there be anyone superior?
For from his opening of the eyes the universe is born, and by their closing it is dissolved. (2.24)
Having concentrated the mind upon that [Brahman], yogis—freed from fatigue—cast off ignorance, the knot of the heart, and attain stainless knowledge. (2.25)
In whosever heart this Lord dwells, that person has achieved their life’s purpose;
oh, this Hari, who is supreme bliss, places His mind within such a one! (2.26)
Thus remaining in doubt, she stood before her friends; then, with great joy, one of her companions spoke to her with a smile. (2.27)
The friend said: "He is the teacher of the Lord of the three worlds; whom else could he possibly meditate upon?
[Not even] the hosts of gods, asuras, humans, nāgas, gandharvas, and apsarases. (2.28)
The Siddhas, the Lords of Yoga, the Rudras, the Ādityas, and likewise the Vasus;
the hosts of Maruts, the Soma-drinkers, the Pitṛs, and also the Cāraṇas. || 2-29 ||
There is indeed nothing in the three worlds more worthy of worship than that which those whose minds are inclined toward devotion constantly revere. (2.30)
The lord of her life has gone into solitude, meditating in his heart upon you alone—his beloved, dear as his own life, devoted to her vows, and whose very breath is her husband. (2-31)
Blessed are you, and fulfilled is your purpose, since Lord Hari has been propitiated by you through constant service with pure devotion.
Unable to endure even a moment’s separation from her,
Hari remains in solitude with closed eyes, meditating upon your form within his own heart.
"Therefore, those women in the world who are the recipients of their husband's love are blessed"—
this she said under the pretext of a joke, yet she considered it to be quite untrue.
Rama said:
"O friend, if it is thus that the Lord of Gods never remembers me at any time on the path of meditation, then these words of yours are indeed meaningless. (2.35)
Detached from me and always fond of those who possess nothing, how can he meditate on me in his heart, being unable to endure our separation? (2.36)
By his constant grace, my great afflictions have been rendered inactive;
I know those of firm vows who worship me throughout the entire world. (2.37)
And whoever in the three worlds, wherever they may be situated, worship them—I constantly behold those devotees within my heart. (2-38)
O friend, though Hari meditated upon him in his heart at that time,
I do not know how [he did so], for you are the knower of all states of being and reside within all worlds.
Therefore, the Lord does not meditate upon me, nor upon Vidhi, nor even upon Rudra Śaṅkara, nor upon anyone else, nor even upon a devotee who is dear to him as his own life.
Who knows what supreme Lord is established within his mind?
Therefore, as he awakens, I ask everything of him without doubt. (2.41)
Having spoken thus, filled with curiosity along with her circle of friends,
she stood before the Supreme Lord with her hands joined in the gesture of reverence.
At that very moment, Hari, having released his meditation, beheld her directly—
standing in the midst of a circle of her friends with her palms joined in reverence.
She was radiant with splendor, adorned with divine ornaments,
and possessed the pure luster of cheeks illuminated by her shimmering jeweled earrings.
She with the beautiful nose, beautiful teeth, and beautiful eyebrows, adorned by the region of her chin;
with a neck like a conch shell, she was enchanting with a radiant pearl necklace upon her heart. (2.45)
She was beautiful with her girdle and waistband, adorned with bracelets, armlets, and anklets;
she was the manifest deity of the three worlds, her eyes cast down in modesty.
Seeing that the lotus-eyed Hari had awakened,
she touched his foot with her head and spoke, filled with humility.
Rāma said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Blessed One, O Compassionate One toward devotees, O Supporter of the Earth! Have mercy, O Lord of the World, and dispel my doubt."
You alone are the creator, destroyer, and protector of all worlds;
you are the deity of all deities, and there is none equal to or superior to you.
Why do you meditate, standing in solitude with your senses and inner disposition dissolved, your body intensely marked by horripilation from the mass of bliss arising from that meditation? (2.50)
My mind is distressed by this, fearing someone other than you;
O ocean of compassion, tell me how I may return to my true nature. (2.51)
Thus addressed by the goddess Ramā with sweet and melodic speech, Hari— the self of all embodied beings— seemed as if he were himself delighting his beloved.
The Blessed Lord said: "O auspicious lady, listen now to the words I speak.
I am the manifest teacher of the world; there is no one else to be meditated upon by me."
I am the Self, the support of all, adored by Brahmā, Rudra, and Indra.
Behold me alone, spread throughout the entire universe of the moving and the unmoving;
behold the universe spread within me. What else do you wish to know? (2.54)
O auspicious one, you are my power, sharing the same nature as I, who am the sustainer of all; you consist of the primordial support of everything and are composed of my own bliss. (2.55)
The gods beginning with Brahmā, the sages firm in their vows, the guardians of the quarters beginning with Indra, and the sages beginning with Nārada—all these [worship] you. (2.56)
O fair-browed one, even those who worship you do not touch even a particle of your grace;
yet you, whose form is supreme bliss, are merged within my heart.
But when I do not see you at all, the world appears to me as blindness;
O Goddess of gods, when you are seen, I see clearly once again. (2.58)
"You went together with your friends for the sake of gathering flowers;
meanwhile, O lovely-faced one, I was unable to endure separation from you. (2.59)
O beloved, staying in solitude with your mind fixed on you, your life-breath centered on you,
and your thoughts intent on you, he meditates on you alone within his heart with eyes closed.
O Lalana, I was meditating through the yoga of meditation upon your charming form, so difficult even for the gods to attain; yet, in that very moment, you have arrived.
"Thus have I spoken to you; know this to be the truth, O lady of virtuous vows.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Lord of Gods, by your grace, the thoughts within the hearts of all [are known]."
O Lord, I know everything according to one's karma and according to one's inclination.
O Mādhava, though meditated upon by you in my heart even during our separation,
I dwell only in you, for I am the witness of your inner mind.
"Oh, how wonderful this appears, O Lord! Though I am situated within you, I do not know that which dwells within you, just as a person whose mind is elsewhere does not perceive their own self."
Your devotees are not to be deceived, for they are exceedingly dear to You;
how else could anyone else in this world worship one who deceives his devotees? (2.65)
If you contemplate even a single devoted person suffering in the three worlds, by your very will, all that suffering shall come to dissolution. (2.66)
Therefore, some other Lord besides you is indeed inferred;
tell me about him, O Lord of Gods, if I am dear to you.
There is no one else dearer to me, nor is there any lord other than you;
filled with curiosity, I wish to know the supreme truth.
Viṣṇu said:
"You should not feel curiosity; find contentment with my words.
Wise and virtuous people do not harbor persistence."
For men possessed by dogmatic attachment, neither dharma nor artha, nor even desire, ever succeeds; indeed, the fruit of wisdom is non-attachment. (2.70)
O beautiful one, whatever is requested—be it my head, cattle, wealth, prosperity, the kingdom, the treasury, the earth, the fortress, or anything else—should be given. (2.71)
They do not benefit those who give up their wealth, lives, and bodies;
rather, they themselves will depart, having been cast off and dragged away by the force of time. (2.72)
By one who destroys the hope of a supplicant, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is destroyed.
Therefore, everything including one's own life and so forth must indeed be given when requested. (2.73)
Since that supreme reality is indeed ungraspable and transcends the world,
therefore, having abandoned stubborn attachment with a serene inner self— (2.74)
"You must conduct yourself, O blessed one, with a desire to seek my favor. Thus addressed then by the powerful Viṣṇu, Lakṣmī was overcome with a slight anger, her eyes turning red.
Holding himself by means of his own self, he spoke these words again:
"A single body is traditionally said to consist of the bodily portions of both female and male. (2.76)
How can you see me as distinct [from him], when I am of one form with his body?
By the poets of old, love has been depicted as existing within the state of matrimony. (2.77)
"O, even though you alone were an expert in the ways of love, you have destroyed it! Fie upon that woman who, being devoid of love for her husband, is disrespected in the home;
and fie also on that deceitful husband who neglects even a virtuous wife. (2.78)
Therefore, O God, how shall I obtain my desired day of merit?
Until you are pleased, I shall perform severe austerity.
"By which [means] the Blessed One, being pleased, will instruct me in that state"—
having said this, and having bowed repeatedly to the feet of the Blessed One and circumambulated him, Ramā departed from Vaikuṇṭha for the sake of ascetic practice.
Although she was being restrained with various conciliatory words and speech endowed with reason, Ramā did not turn back from her resolve. (2.81)
Thus ends the second chapter in the Śivomā-saṃvāda, within the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Māheśvara-tantra in the glorious Nāradapañcarātra. 2-2.
Now begins the third chapter.
Pārvatī said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear [this], for my curiosity is indeed great."
Although he was entreated again and again by the virtuous Rāmā with supreme devotion. || 3-1 ||
He did not speak of the supreme reality; for that purpose she has gone to perform penance.
O God, you ought to explain to me that which is most wonderful of all.
Śiva said:
Listen, O beautiful one; out of affection for you, I shall tell you everything without omission.
Otherwise, O Goddess, this is not to be spoken even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
When Viṣṇu, though entreated, did not speak what was in his heart,
she was shaken by the fire of separation caused by the frustration of her desire to hear [him].
Having reached Ketumāla, he performed a great and fierce austerity that tormented all the worlds, having established a self-imposed discipline for himself.
The virtuous woman fashioned an image of Viṣṇu that was supremely beautiful;
there she attended upon it with love, censuring her own body.
Through bathing at the three times of day, through discipline, and through self-restraint,
that virtuous woman attained purity of heart and remained lying upon the bare ground.
In the cold season she remained immersed in water; in the summer she practiced the austerity of the five fires;
and even during the rains, she stayed on open ground, enduring the rain and the wind. (3.8)
Casting aside feminine fickleness and her abundance of various ornaments,
she constantly lay upon the ground, meditating on Hari within her heart.
In her dreams she constantly beheld the lotus-eyed Hari;
even there, as she made this request, he spoke dejectedly, saying "No."
Having fallen asleep, she woke up right there once more;
thus, her heart having become absorbed in Him, she was utterly helpless. (3.11)
She reproached herself, seeing her desire unfulfilled;
for when the ascetic queen had not attained her heart's wish in this way, she,
being pure in soul, stood upon the earth on one foot.
Placing her husband in her heart and placing her heart in him,
the virtuous woman attained a state of oneness and performed supreme austerity.
The smokeless fire arising from that crest, blazing intensely with smoke,
scorched the entire universe, which was overwhelmed by fear.
Gods, asuras, humans, nāgas, gandharvas, and apsarases; likewise piśācas, guhyakas, siddhas, vidyādharas, and those who move through the sky as celestial wanderers (cāraṇas). || 3-15 ||
Afflicted by the unbearable fire consisting of ascetic heat that blazed forth,
and agitated by grief, they found no happiness anywhere.
Then Indra and the other gods, the Maruts, the Uṣmapās and others,
the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and likewise the Pitṛs— || 3.17 ||
They went for refuge to Brahmā, the irreproachable Grandfather;
they beheld the supreme deity Brahmā upon his exalted throne.
He saw him engaged in breath-control (prāṇāyāma), possessing a bright beard, with four faces,
surrounded by Sanaka and others, and worshipped by Nārada and others.
He was likewise surrounded by the Vedas in embodied form, each seated upon its own separate lion-throne, as well as by the Purāṇas, the Saṃhitās, and the various branches of knowledge.
He contemplates himself as the Supreme Self, beyond darkness,
through the excellence of merit, through dharma, through renunciation, and through the perfection of knowledge.
Where they gather together and sport through self-investigation, celibacy, restraints, observances, and the practices of yoga.

Seeing Brahmā, the primordial and ancient Person, seated upon the supreme throne, those immortals bowed down with eyes clouded by tears of joy; their skin bristling with thrill, they spoke words in faltering voices.
Salutations, salutations to You, the sole creator of the world; salutations, salutations to You, the sole sustainer of the world;
salutations, salutations to You, the sole destroyer of the world—the infinite one whose nature consists of the qualities of rajas, tamas, and sattva. 3-24.
The egg consists of the collection of twenty-four principles; within it, you exist under the name Virañci.
As the refuge of the world, you yourself vomit forth the universe, and thus you are celebrated by the wise as Pitāmaha, the Grandfather.

You are the witness of all, the inner self of the universe, Hiraṇyagarbha, the sole creator of the world; likewise, O God, you are its destroyer and its protector. There is nothing whatsoever that exists superior to you. (3.26)
You are the primordial God, the ancient Puruṣa, the manifest self-luminous one, unborn and the Supreme Lord.
Alas, those whose minds are deluded by your Māyā perceive multiplicity within you, the One Lord! 3-27.
You are the primordial Person, the full; you are infinite and without support.
And by means of your own māyā, through the very elements, you create all beings.
This entire universe, including all things mobile and immobile, was created by you through your own power;
why do you not protect it from this suddenly blazing fire?
"O Lord, this world created by you will go to destruction;
we do not know the cause therein, so let that be investigated. (3.30)
"What is this unprecedented fire that has arisen, blazing on all sides?
Because of it, this entire universe—including gods, asuras, and humans—is filled with agitation. (3.31)
O Mahāmati, devise a means for its pacification, lest the worlds today be reduced to nothing but ashes. (3-32)
Thus, while those gods were uttering their piteous words,
he reflected through the yoga of meditation and grasped this very matter within his heart.
Then the Grandfather spoke these words to the immortals:
"Listen, all you immortals, to the words uttered by me."
"The goddess Ramā, having been personally insulted by her husband, is performing penance.
O Lord of Gods, what supreme reality beyond even Bhava are you meditating upon? Tell me that.
Though addressed in this way, Hari indeed did not speak.
Then, distressed by her persistent efforts and filled with wrath, the goddess Ramā approached Ketumāla and undertook severe austerities.
Viṣṇu’s beloved performs that terrible penance which strikes fear into the worlds; from the region of her forehead, a fire consisting of ascetic power arises.
Because of that, the worlds will be intensely tormented, nearly consumed by fire, and deprived of their senses; they will undoubtedly go to destruction if she does not abandon her asceticism.
Therefore, having gone to Hari’s abode in Vaikuṇṭha,
all of us gods together with Rudra shall propitiate Viṣṇu.
Having thus resolved, they all came to my abode;
with palms joined in reverence, they praised me with sweet speech.
O Goddess, I too have honored those led by Brahmā and headed by Indra; having greeted the Lord of Gods with my gaze, I have embraced the Grandfather.
"O Goddess, having bowed to Bṛhaspati and the others as was appropriate, those immortals were addressed by me with the words: 'Be seated, be seated!'"
Those dwellers of heaven sat down with dejected faces and feverish hearts: "O gods, is all well with you? Does prosperity attend upon you? (3.43)
Welcome, O all you gods! You are exceedingly dear to me.
This world of mine has been seen by you, which remains unseen by those who turn their backs on me.
If you have a longing for this place, then delight yourselves here in the forests and groves;
listen to the beautiful calls of the parrots, cranes, and other birds. (3.45)
Let them smell the supreme fragrance of the most divine creepers, which produce flowers in all seasons and enchant many bees.
Let the yak-tail fans sport unrestrainedly upon golden pedestals fashioned from great emeralds, enjoying the pleasant touch of the breezes from the Ganges.
May all, together with their wives, sport without fatigue in the pleasure-pools that are always filled with nectar and resound with the cries of intoxicated swans. (3.48)
"Whatever is desired by your minds, perform that without indolence.
For what purpose have you come here, led by Brahmā and Upendra?"
"Declare whatever must be done, if there is anything at all.
Thus addressed by me, those dwellers of heaven spoke to me.
O Blessed One, ocean of compassion, you who are affectionate toward your devotees, O Dhūrjaṭi!
What need is there to speak of the welfare of those who are constantly meditated upon by you? (3.51)
We know that very same thing to be unwholesome: the lapse of remembrance of your feet;
yet today, through the arising of your grace, we recognize ourselves as complete. (3.52)
"What are you meditating upon so long, dear father, having restrained the mind within your heart?
You appear as if you have attained bliss, like the very Self of all embodied beings. (3.53)
"O Brahmin, tell us this, if you deem it fit to speak.
Having heard their most excellent words, I, gladdening their minds, spoke to them with supreme utterances. (3.54)
"Listen, all you gods, to what has been uttered by you:
'Father, why do you meditate for so long, restraining the mind within your heart? (3.55)
Even the Self itself appears as if it has attained bliss for embodied beings;
that cannot be described by me, O gods, even in tens of millions of aeons.
Yogis do not reach [the goal] by means of yogic practices, nor by sacrifices, austerities, and the like; nor by knowledge, sacred fords, or dispassion, without the service of the virtuous. (3.57)
This entire universe is mere illusion; in reality, nothing exists at all.
Even the seven worlds, beginning with the earth, have been swallowed up by time. (3.58)
All the worlds, even the gods, though satisfied with the bliss of sense objects, do not attain a mere drop from the great ocean of eternal bliss. (3.59)
For in the Vedas, action is indeed predominant; therefore, the destiny [of those who follow them] consists of action.
Those who are whirled about by actions are like blades of grass by the currents of water. (3.60)
They do not find that reality even in hundreds of millions of kalpas;
some in this world, devoted to heaven, worship with weak understanding. (3.61)
Some have their intellects restrained through the eightfold yoga,
while others do so by means of the rules for castes and stages of life, characterized by their respective conducts.
Some were devoted to eating leaves, while others subsisted on air;
some were naked, and others wore black or red garments.
Some, with shaven heads, are devoted to eating fruits and roots;
others, weak and skilled only in smearing themselves with ashes, desire liberation.
They do not attain liberation at all without the realization of reality;
for this ocean of māyā appears as if it were real, though it is actually non-existent. (3.65)
It is intensely crowded with the bubbles of many millions of world-systems;
it is matted with the network of waves of the principles (tattvas) and is a deep pool of the waters of latent impressions (vāsanā).
Its banks are brimming with sin and merit; it is filled with the mud of delusion;
and its infinite expanse contains the lotuses and water-lilies of good and evil deeds. (3.67)
Constantly frequented by the porpoise of egoism (*ahaṃtā*), the river of worldly existence has the trees on its banks as its objects of desire and abounds with the foam of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). (3.68)
It causes suffering through the stones of the pits of desire, anger, and great greed;
it is terrifying with the serpents of censuring others and harming others. (3.69)
There, where faith is a vast lotus pond and delusion is inexhaustible, many who are exhausted by the thirst for sense objects fall into it repeatedly. (3.70)
Having seen Kamalākara full of passion, someone indeed took delight in him; though he was being served, he was not satiated, like a greedy bee. (3.71)
Indeed, not perceiving the passing of the day, the bee—his soul enticed by greed and his senses unsubdued—would meet its destruction right there out of its longing for honey. (3.72)
Where flocks of swans, having quickly smelled a bed of lotuses and realizing it is impermanent, rest happily in their nests. (3.73)
There, a cow that was sinking and languishing, submerged in the mud and afflicted by thirst, was lifted up by the Great-Souled One and established in the ocean of nectar. (3.74)
There, many elephants sport repeatedly with their female mates, never satiated and constantly intoxicated by the fragrance of lotuses. (3.75)
Where the powerful crocodiles slaughter schools of young fish, there the fisherman quickly seizes them as well. (3.76)
Agitated by the fear of crocodiles and having overcome their thirst,
they do not even drink the water, taking refuge instead in the shade of the lotus plants.
There, a traveler bitten by a serpent and longing for water was revived by a wise physician through the administration of mercury. (3.78)
There, an arrogant courtesan was being served by five actors who were exceedingly cruel and constantly intent upon their service. (3.79)
Thirsty for them, they go toward the actors and indeed bring those [actors] to the actresses;
then, by their command, they sport with speed and according to their own will. (3.80)
If the knowledge and realization that is supremely radiant, like the light of a thousand suns, arises, then [the darkness] dries up; it is not otherwise. (3.81)
But when supreme knowledge has dawned, there is neither "I" nor "you," nor anything at all;
even deities such as myself and others will not attain the supreme reality.

How much more so for others of limited intellect, who are like those dreaming while awake; for they are possessed by such an obsession that [their wives] are dearer to them than even their own lives. (3.83)
In Ketumāla, she practices austerities with a mind no less than that taught [by me];
therefore, I shall by no means speak of the root of my bliss.
"Let whatever task may be suitable for me be announced. Thus addressed, all those immortals looked at one another.
Having heard what Śaṅkara had spoken, they were filled with supreme wonder.
The gods said:
"O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you are the Guru who bestows knowledge upon the worlds."
"O Lord, what you have said is true: the consort of Viṣṇu is performing penance.
By that penance, the entire universe has been scorched on all sides by fire.
O Śambhu, please consider what indeed must be done now. (3.87)
Śiva said:
The goddess Ramā is the power of the universe, auspicious Śivā who consists of a portion of Prakṛti;
she is the wave of bliss of Viṣṇu, by whom the auspicious universe shines. (3.88)
Devoted to her husband, she has abandoned him and speaks of no other; she performs intense and great penance that consumes the world. (3.89)
Therefore, she cannot be won by anyone else except for her own husband, Mādhava;
thus, let us all go today to Viṣṇu together.
Having gone there, we shall report whatever inauspiciousness has occurred in the world,
even though we ourselves are worthy of honor, having witnessed both it and the destruction of the universe.
"He will restrain Ramā from her penance that is so difficult to overcome"—
having heard these words of mine, all the gods were freed from their anxiety.
And I too went with them to the abode of Priya,
where all were dark as a rain cloud and dressed in yellow silk garments.
Wearing a crown and earrings, and bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
the Lord of the World went there and was praised even by the hosts of gods.
Homage to the remover of distress, who strives to protect the world through various incarnations such as the Fish and the Tortoise;
to the kinsman of the world and the remover of bondage; and to the protector who guards [the world] when its destruction is imminent.

O Lord of the gods, when your ancient path of the Vedas is shattered by the fierce and violent arguments of heretics, you then assume a beautiful body of pure essence through your own essence and provide protection.

As if entering this cosmic egg composed of earth, water, fire, air, and ether, you have become renowned as the "living soul" (jīva) within the moving and unmoving world; therefore, there is nothing that transcends you.
O Lord, protect the worlds with your fierce austerity, for they are being consumed by fire and have lost their joy; since you are the Protector, you must be their guardian.
Turn back your supreme, virtuous, and beloved wife, who is dearer to you than your own life;
indeed, householders should never oppose their wives on a daily basis.
In whatever house a woman may be discordant or even treated with contempt, there is no happiness, nor prosperity, nor health, nor the well-being of the progeny in that house. (3.100)
"How could this entire world, which is your home, exist in happiness while you have fallen into conflict with your wife, who shares the same character as yourself? (3.101)
"Therefore, O Lord, be vigilant for the sake of protecting the universe.
Having thus informed him and bowed down to the Lord of the worlds, all the immortals [departed]. (3.102)
With their lotus-like faces withered, they sat silently with their palms joined in reverence.
Thus ends the third chapter in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī, within the Uttarakhanda of the Māheśvara Tantra in the glorious Pañcarātra. 3-3.
Then, in the fourth chapter, Śiva said:
"Now, having heard those words of the gods, which were exceedingly distressed..."
Laughing, he scattered words that reached the hearts of the gods.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Maheśa, O Vidhi, O Brahmā, and you gods headed by Śakra, listen!
The goddess Ramā, the ascetic goddess, is dearer to me than my own life."
Having become separated by quarrel, she went to Ketumāla and performed austerities;
by that fierce asceticism, the entire universe was scorched on all sides.
O gods, she finds no satisfaction except for that which she has resolved for herself;
this is the innate nature of women: their hardness and lack of discernment.
Impurity, cruelty, obstinacy, as well as recklessness, falsehood through greed, deceit, folly, and crying out at an improper time; 4-5.
A family is ruined by a wicked son; a kingdom is ruined by a bad minister;
a Brahmin is ruined by service to a Śūdra; and Sarasvatī [the goddess of learning] is ruined by lack of practice.
Lifespan is destroyed by sleep; prosperity by lack of effort;
virtues by greed; wealth by sins; and happiness is ruined by a bad wife. (4.7)
Where there is harmony between husband and wife, the three aims of life flourish;
through discord they perish, like seeds and sprouts in the heat of summer. (4.8)
The Goddess, having become insistent, would not desist by any means;
for the abundant misery that has arisen for the worlds will thereby be turned back.
"I shall perform a counter-action; go forth, filled with joy!
Having heard these words of the god, the deities circumambulated Janārdana.
Having bowed down, they returned to their respective abodes filled with great joy;
likewise, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa went to Ketumāla.
There that high-minded woman stood with her body motionless, resting on her big toe, her gaze directed upward, and her internal breath restrained.
Indeed, with the flames flashing from the crest of its own nature,
it seems to swallow the cosmic egg in the form of a mouthful, like the crest of fire at the end of an aeon.
And seeing her in such a state, the three of us, Brahmā and the others,
were struck with supreme wonder at the marvelous deed of the Goddess.
Then, having approached her, Hari spoke as if smiling:
"O Goddess, dearer to me than life, why do you grieve in vain? (4.15)
Desist from asceticism, for its fruit here is the result of futile exertion; the performance of ritual action by the virtuous involves great effort yet yields little fruit. (4.16)
"Absorbed in the essence of the bliss of meditation, that mind of his will descend in an instant.
When Hari had spoken thus, consoling his beloved most earnestly, [the mind descended].
He beheld his beloved, seated upon his lap, dark as a rain cloud, four-armed,
accompanied by Virañci and Īśāna, and adorned with a garland of forest flowers.
Rama prostrated herself on the ground like a staff with her palms joined in reverence;
she did not utter a single word, nor did Rama rise again.
Seeing that supreme love for himself, Hari was greatly amazed;
with affection, he spoke to the Goddess while Brahmā and Rudra listened.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Kamalā, honored by the world, you are blessed, you are truly blessed!
For virtuous women who are devoted to dharma constitute half of their own selves for men."
Those devoted to dharma must conquer the worlds with the assistance of women, because all [attainments] become fruitless for one who is without a wife. (4.22)
The female is the root of all phenomena; since she does not exist [for you], how could they exist?
Without them, neither the worlds nor even knowledge can possibly come to be. (4.23)
Fie upon life in this world for one bereft of a wife, which is held in contempt by those who know the Dharma in their assemblies;
for such a man, even the gods, the lords of sages, and guests seem to neglect his house as if it were devoid of wealth. (4.24)
What is the use of wealth consisting of mere riches, or of prosperity devoid of happiness?
What is the use of happiness for one in whose home there is no noble woman who practices the Dharma? (4.25)
A woman of noble birth nourishes a husband who is immoral, ill-behaved, wicked, impoverished, and overcome by old age; therefore, a wife is indeed most venerable.
I consider no friend to be equal to a woman, nor a kinsman, nor a brother;
for those others may be consulted separately, but a woman never at all. (4.27)
Whether in happiness or in suffering, in life or even in death, there is nowhere a friend equal to a woman; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O sweet-spoken one! (4.28)
Therefore, you especially please me as a jewel among women, since you are celebrated as the foremost of those who regard their husband as a deity. (4.29)
For women as well, the supreme duty is the service of their husband;
through body, mind, and speech, there is nothing else whatsoever. (4.30)
That woman in this world who is devoted to her husband, who is dedicated to the duties toward her husband, and who does exactly as he says, enjoys imperishable happiness. (4.31)
Therefore, I am now thoroughly pleased with your austerity. Arise, arise; may it be well with you, O bestower of happiness upon the world through your penance! (4.32)
More than seven kalpas have passed while you have been emaciating your delicate body day after day; indeed, such fruitless exertion is not fitting for you.
Your beautiful body is suffering upon beds of flowers;
how then can she endure the rain of heat from the fierce and scorching sun?
The vine-like body is tormented by cold, heat, wind, and rain;
your hair has become matted locks, and they distress my mind. (4.35)
Your face, with its bimba-like lower lip and the noble radiance of a gentle smile,
does not shine like a winter lotus withered by the frost.
Your cheeks have become darkened by the heat of the fierce sun; deprived of the beauty of pearl necklaces, they do not shine as they did before. (They shine [no longer] as they did before. 4-37.
Whose happiness is there when they behold your eye without collyrium, your forehead deprived of saffron, and your face bereft of betel? (4.38)
"Do not wither your beautiful body with this most difficult austerity;
bowing my head at your feet, I entreat you again and again."
"O Kamalā, as for what you asked me when questioned, 'What are you meditating upon in private?'—
know that it is something which cannot be spoken even in tens of millions of aeons."
Nevertheless, I shall speak, for I have been won by your asceticism;
yet, O Goddess, that must never be uttered directly with the tongue.
Nevertheless, I shall speak; listen to the manner of it, O beautiful one:
at the end of the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age, evil-minded Asuras in the form of kings will strive for the destruction of the path of the Vedas. (4.42)

[He protects] women, cows, Brahmins, and holy men; those who are most righteous; ascetics; the various castes and stages of life; the boundaries [of social order]; and those who follow their respective duties.
When they inflict suffering, then for the protection of the Dharma, for the sake of guarding the Vedas, the Dharma, and so forth, and for the destruction of the evil-minded, I [shall act]. (4.44)
In the palace of King Yadu, born of the lineage of Yayāti,
I shall become Vāsudeva, renowned by the name Kṛṣṇa.
There too, you shall become an excellent woman named Rukmiṇī;
there, certain kings and asuras, weak in knowledge, [shall seek you].
Having conquered those wicked ones in battle, they will come to carry you away;
I shall carry you, who are dear to my heart, there is no doubt in this.
Then, O beautiful one, virtuous women of noble family, possessed of sons and husbands,
shall sing of my deeds for the sake of auspiciousness.
Having heard that through the performance of ritual honors, my heart will become filled with happiness, like the ocean at the rising of the moon.
It is not possible to describe you with words such as "it is like this" or "it is like that";
one experiences it for oneself alone, like the drinking of sugar-mixed milk.
O Goddess, even a single drop from that ocean of bliss does not exist among the gods, such as Brahmā and others; what then can be said of anything else?
One does not know that which has not been taught; it is not taught by means of words.
Only the one who possesses direct experience always knows it as having the form of pure experience. (Alternatively, the reading is: "that which is unfit to be spoken. || 4.52 ||
O God, O Mistress of the Gods, the object of inference can indeed be known through the means of inference by means of its characteristics; it cannot be known by any other means whatsoever. (4.53)
But listen attentively, O beautiful one, as I describe the characteristics:
one who surges with internal bliss and has forgotten all external attachments. (4.54)
The flowing of tears from the eyes, trembling, the breaking out of perspiration, horripilation, and the choking of the throat—these, indeed, they know to be the characteristic signs. (4.55)

O Goddess, by these characteristics you shall know that which resides within my inner heart—that which is fit for meditation and bliss—which is not proper for me to speak of [this is also a reading]. (4.56)
Therefore, O beloved, you must observe that vow as well;
this which I have told you is my entire essence, of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, this alone is the secret of all the Vedas;
this alone is the supreme knowledge, and this alone is the highest ritual action.
This alone is the supreme yoga; this alone is the supreme sacrifice;
this alone is the supreme object of meditation; this alone is the supreme goal. (4.59)
This alone is the supreme object of knowledge; this alone is great wealth;
this alone is total prosperity—this is the truth, the absolute truth, O devoted wife! (4.60)
Thus addressed by Viṣṇu, the devoted goddess Ramā abandoned her distress, just as one afflicted by the summer heat is refreshed by a great rain-cloud.
With her lotus-like eyes blossoming and overwhelmed by a weight of joy, she of pure intent fell prostrate like a staff at the feet of her husband. (4.62)
Praised in many ways by Brahmā and by me as well with words of praise,
she considered herself to have achieved her purpose, having attained the fruit of her asceticism.
Showers of flowers fell, and kettledrums resounded in the sky; the lords of the Gandharvas sang, and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
The seven sages, having approached, praised that woman who was free from malice; the heat of the worlds subsided, and there was auspiciousness everywhere. (4.65)
A breeze blew with a pleasant touch, the quarters of the sky possessed pure radiance, the waters were serene, and the fires blazed auspiciously. (4.66)
The minds of all beings who had lost their composure became serene.
Thus, when this auspiciousness arose, the deities in heaven,
all men on earth, and the lords of the serpents in the netherworld were filled with joy.
Having gone to the world of Brahmā, I am Brahmā; having come to Kailāsa, Viṣṇu has taken Lakṣmī by the hand toward his own abode.
Thus have I explained to you what was asked by you, O blameless one;
the knowledge of reality is not easily obtained, therefore, my dear, it is most secret.
O Goddess, there are only a few rare individuals who are fit vessels for the knowledge of reality;
after examining them over a long period of time, one should reveal it to them. (4.70)
O Goddess, that person of deluded intellect who speaks to another out of affection, greed, or even fear cannot be a knower; he is merely one who fills his own belly.
When turbidity does not arise through long-term cohabitation, service, beatings, or harsh words, he is, in my view, considered qualified. (4.72)
One whose body is bristling with horripilation upon hearing a discourse on reality, and whose eyes are overwhelmed with tears of joy—he, in my view, is considered qualified. (4.73)
Averse to slandering others, free from desire for the wives or wealth of others, without anger, liberated from greed, peaceful, and proficient in the scriptures. (4.74)

One who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras, who is full of faith and free from fear, who delights in virtuous qualities, who is ever-generous, and who is dispassionate toward external objects. (4.75)
He should be afraid of evil, free from hatred, and without greed for sense objects and the like;
moreover, O Goddess, he should be characterized by other auspicious marks as well. (4.76)
He should be known as the qualified recipient; this secret must be given to him.
O Goddess! This is a mystery of the Vedas; one must not reveal it otherwise.
Revealing [the truth] while his own mind is deluded, he becomes a vessel for calamities; alas, neither that teacher nor that disciple attains the perfect realization of reality. 4-78.
O beautiful one, those who are instructed by one who knows reality become knowers of reality themselves;
however, those who are instructed by the unworthy indeed become unworthy as well. (4.79)

O Dear One! Those who teach what is unfit for them, and those who are themselves worthy [of it], yet [teach it] to one who is unworthy regarding Śiva—due to the fault of falling away from both, they go to hell. (4.80)
Through the loss of their duties and their unfitness, there is a fall from the world and a failure to receive the fruits [of their actions];
for them there shall be incomparable darkness as long as the moon, sun, and stars exist. (4.81)
For how could the Buddha awaken one who is asleep if he himself were unawakened?
A gourd can save a stone, yet a stone cannot save another stone. (4.82)
Therefore, having thus resolved, one who has gone for refuge to a true guru—that wise person—should deliver himself from the delusion and confusion of the self. (4.83)
Thus has this been fully explained to me, O beloved, which I was asked by you;
in brief, O Great Goddess! What else do you wish to ask? (4.84)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Śivomā-saṃvāda within the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Uttarakhanda of the Māheśvara-tantra in the Śrī Nāradapañcarātra. 4-4.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Protectors of the World, God, Lord of Gods, Dhūrjaṭi!
This story, which bestows great merit and destroys evil, has been told.
O Lord of Gods, that which the Blessed One, the beloved of her life, did not tell Rāmā directly with his own mouth, he will now speak through dramatic gesture. (5.2)
O Lord, you yourself declare that very reality directly to me;
O God, you alone are such a compassionate one, and no other, O Lord.
By the power of the knowledge of that reality, all enjoyments were disregarded;
though alone, Nandi, wearing the directions as his garment and with matted hair, wanders as a wise man.
You are the teacher of all the world, the instructor in the path of reality;
there is no one equal to you who possesses the experience of the knowledge of reality.
"From the gift of half your body, I know that I am dearer to you than your own life;
therefore, O Lord, you speak that which is the most profound truth."
This is not surprising in you, O Lord, the Great Sovereign and ocean of compassion;
therefore, O Maheśvara, being in doubt, I wish to question you.
As for what you previously stated— that delusion (*moha*) is the form of the cause of the world,
just as leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth arise from a seed— (5.8)
Thus, this world consisting of gods, asuras, and humans has arisen from delusion;
delusion originates from ignorance, and from delusion is born all that is moving and unmoving. (5.9)

Just as [the mother-of-pearl], having covered the pearl-oyster, clearly manifests itself as both a snake and silver according to its own power and in accordance with [the observer's] ignorance (yathājñāna), so too [does consciousness manifest]. || 5.10 ||
Likewise, O Śaṅkara, the supreme Brahman, which is indeed imperishable, creates the universe by veiling itself through its own power alone; ignorance is the cause of delusion. (5.11)
O Lord, regarding that which was spoken by you, I have a great doubt:
concerning that which you have called the Imperishable (akṣara), free from phenomenal expansion and devoid of affliction.
It is faultless, stainless, pure, desireless, and free from attachment.
Self-luminous, beyond the qualities (guṇas), consisting of pure knowledge, equal, auspicious, changeless, eternally shining, and transcending the states of existence and non-existence. (5.13)
Who can say that there is any association with ignorance in Him who is the object of all desires?
How could delusion born of ignorance exist in that Lord whose nature is pure knowledge? (5.14)
If ignorance were to cause obscuration in that which is self-luminous, then how could even darkness not obscure the sun in the slightest? (5.15)
Or how is it that even when delusion has been destroyed, liberation remains?
That the unreal appears as real—this is my great doubt;
O Lord of Gods, O Master, you ought to sever it with the sword of the knowledge of reality.
Śiva said:
Listen with care, O beautiful one, to this most wonderful secret;
out of affection for you, and having been entreated by you with love, I shall speak it. (5.17)
One must not disclose this secret, which is equal to the intimacy between a mother and her son, to just anyone.
O auspicious lady, one should guard it in every way and never dispute it under any circumstances.
The supreme, eternal Brahman is not an object of dialectical reasoning;
those disputants whose intellects are hardened by mere logic are of deluded understanding.
Just as darkness can never be capable of obscuring the sun, so too ignorance can never prevail over that which is self-luminous. (5.20)
Thus, through authoritative reasonings, it appears as if contradictory to those people who, though experts in the means of valid cognition, have arisen from the creation of delusion. (5.21)

O Goddess! How could even wise men, by means of the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), be able to know [the Self], just as a person in a dream cannot know the solitary one who perceives that dream? (5.22)
O Goddess! likewise, one does not know even the means of valid cognition in their entirety;
for within this imperishable Supreme Brahman, there is established an immersion in ignorance. (5.23)
Therefore, one should not employ reasoning that contradicts the scriptures; for the wise consider that reasoning alone to be valid which is in harmony with the words of the scriptures. (5.24)
Just as worldly transaction does not proceed from what is solely real or solely unreal, so too is worldly transaction set in motion by both the real and the unreal. (5.25)
That ignorance is indeed unreal; Brahman alone is the absolute reality.
For a sprout does not arise from husks, nor even from rice grains alone. (5.26)
Just as the expansion of a sprout arises through the union of the husk and the grain, so the origin of the universe arises through the union of ignorance with Brahman. (5.27)

Therefore, no doubt should be entertained regarding Brahman when it is a matter of ignorance; the intellect should not be removed by logical arguments concerning those entities which are beyond the world. (5.28)
The voices of the Upaniṣads declare that one should not apply reasoning to those [matters];
for the existence of ignorance regarding Brahman is not established by worldly experience. (5.29)
This [dharma] is established by the Veda; therefore, the Veda is the authoritative means of knowledge.
That which is non-worldly and contradicts the Śruti cannot be established. (5.30)
How could that which is non-perceptual and worldly, as well as perceptual and non-worldly, be established if it were invalid, based on the words of worldly people regarding what is perceptual? (5.31)
Whatever the king of valid cognitions (pramāṇa) determines, that should be accepted exactly as it is; otherwise, it would be a deviation from its true nature. (5.32)
Both the supramundane and the mundane are contained within this;
yet, if he is turned away from that, he enters a womb consisting of outcaste status.
These—Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—follow the Vedas;
but those who are abandoned by the Vedas and abandon them go to a succession of lower births. (5.34)
Perception, inference, verbal testimony, and comparison—these four, O Goddess of Gods, are the means of valid knowledge; of this there is no doubt. (5.35)
Perception is established as valid in the worldly realm, but it is certainly not so in the non-worldly;
for instance, it is inferred that "the mountain possesses fire because of smoke. (5.36)
By what means can Brahman—the reality beyond existence and non-existence, supreme and immutable—be fully realized here?
Therefore, an inferential cognition of Brahman can never be established.

Due to the absence of similarity in the world, even similarity itself cannot be established. One should understand that [the scripture] is just as the Brahman-proclaimer has described it—[the eternal] Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman) which is beginningless; for otherwise, he would indeed be a heretic. (5.38)
Living beings consist of the radiance of Brahman; "Brahman alone" is the certain conclusion.
For embodied beings, however, there is the notion of "I," such as "I am a human," and so forth. (5.39)
One perceives this insentient body as the self itself;
O blessed lady, this is indeed a perversion and this very thing is full of doubt.
For that which is supramundane and doubtful is resolved by the Veda alone;
without certainty, eternal liberation is never attained anywhere. (5.41)
Therefore, by means of the Vedānta texts, which are the most excellent of all aids, one should investigate the Supreme Brahman; for thus he attains his own Self. (5.42)
The Supreme Brahman transcends sound, yet it is said to be the object of sound;
nevertheless, O beloved, it is known through beginningless words and not otherwise.
The king of means of valid cognition is direct experience, which is superior to scriptural testimony; nevertheless, the experiencer himself teaches it directly through words alone. (5.44)
If that which is spoken by the Guru and that which is declared in the Vedas appear to have one and the same meaning, then the person has achieved his purpose and becomes liberated from doubt. (5.45)
O Goddess, when doubt has ceased and self-experience has arisen, this doubt that "Brahman is ignorance" will come to an end. (5.46)
If that which is consistent with scripture is not contradicted by reasoning and valid means of knowledge, it is not contradictory for the wise, even for those who possess direct experience. (5.47)
This [world] is perceived while awake; in a dream, it is merely apparent (prātibhāsika).
Even when that [dream-world] is sublated in deep sleep, the fundamental ignorance (mūlājñāna) indeed persists. (5-48)
The manifestation delimited by that [body] is perceived as the individual soul (jīva);
for manifestation, being of the nature of cognition, illumines both the external and the internal. (5.49)
But that ignorance, O beloved, having transformed into the forms of the body and so forth, is pervaded therein by the reflection of consciousness; thus it becomes the empirical reality.
O Goddess, this fundamental ignorance which resides within the self—without its removal, O Goddess, living beings exist merely as appearances. (5.51)
O Goddess of the Suras, they are never liberated, neither at any time nor by any means, even through vows, fasts, observances, or various kinds of austerities. (5.52)

Neither by the study of one's own sacred texts, nor by recitations, nor by gifts, nor by pilgrimages, nor by other means of spiritual practice; nor even by the observances of celibacy, forest-dwelling, or mendicancy—[can one cross] this unfathomable ocean of ignorance, which is difficult to traverse and devoid of shore or limit. (5.53)
Surging up and sinking down through states such as divinity and dullness, some have not reached the further shore, and none indeed shall reach it. (5.54)
"Aha! Here is the Supreme Person, the Lord, who is supreme bliss;
O Daughter of the Mountain King, those whom He gazes upon with a glance of grace shall attain [liberation]. (5.55)
In this ocean of the path of ignorance, even we and Brahmā and the others have attained the form of bubbles, set in motion by the wind of His will. (5.56)
O Goddess, just as bubbles subside when the wind is stilled and return to the state of water,
so too will the universe, which is no different from us, pass away.
Just as in a dream, lack of awakening creates a wondrous spectacle, so too, through lack of awakening, the Self brings forth the entire world of moving and non-moving beings. (5.58)
Through awakening, [the world] goes to dissolution, and the Supreme Brahman alone remains;
just as when a snake is dissolved in a garland, only the garland itself remains. (5.59)
"Through superimposition and negation, the Supreme Brahman alone remains;
thus, O beloved, everything that I was asked by you has been explained to you. (5–60)
In brief, O Great Goddess, what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Śivomā-saṃvāda, within the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Uttarakhanda of the Māheśvara-tantra in the Śrī Nārada-pāñcarātra. 5-5.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, ocean of compassion, friend of the distressed, Lord of the universe!
Having drunk in your eloquent speech, great bliss arises. (6.1)
"O Maheśvara! That which was stated by you in brief—that everything from Brahmā down to the stationary beings has arisen from ignorance—" (6.2)
"Expand upon everything again, according to the distinctions of creation and dissolution.
Listen, O Pārvatī, I shall explain to you in accordance with reality that which you ask;
by the mere hearing of it, the Supreme Self is revealed. (6.3)
That which I have called ignorance is said to be neither existent nor non-existent;
for if it were existent, liberation would be utterly destroyed, and if it were non-existent, how could it appear? (6.4)
Therefore, O beloved, they know this root ignorance (mūlājñāna) to be indescribable, the producer of the three qualities (guṇas), destructible by knowledge, and of a positive nature (bhāvarūpa). 6-5.
Ignorance has been described by the wise as being like the horn of a hare, the horn of a man, the son of a barren woman, or a flower in the sky; how then can it be called "existent"? (6-6)
For one would never employ that which is unreal as a cause;
how then could it create the cosmic egg, from Brahmā down to the level of stationary objects?

Nor can its non-existence be established, because that [unmanifest] consists of the three qualities (guṇas), is well-known from the Śruti, and is extended in the form of space and the other elements. (6.8)
O Daughter of the Mountain King, even though primordial ignorance appears as if it were real, it is dispelled by knowledge, just as darkness is dispelled by the flame of a lamp. (6.9)

O Beloved, the awakening to one's own true nature is indeed called knowledge (*jñāna*). O Goddess, delusion regarding one's own true nature is the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) known as worldly existence (*bhava*).
For one whose self is deluded, a great conceptual construction arises even while lying down. (6–10)
For in that very same way, once the Self is attained, even that ignorance is destroyed along with its root;
for that ignorance is twofold, distinguished by the difference between cause and effect.
In the imperishable supreme bliss, the syllable *Mūla* (the Root) is the ultimate cause;
it is of the nature of the effect due to the differentiation of the intellect (*buddhi*), and the intellect is illuminated by appearances. (6.12)
It produces the macrocosm (brahmāṇḍa), which is causal in nature, and the microcosm (piṇḍa), which consists of effects; the wise proclaim the identity of the macrocosm and the microcosm. (6.13)
Just as the sun is reflected between a vessel and its rim, the Imperishable (akṣara), through its own manifestation, is conjoined with cause and effect. (6.14)
Just as the sun is perceived as one when two limiting conditions are absent, so too is the pure, solitary, and imperishable [Self] perceived when two limiting conditions are absent. (6.15)
O beloved, the primary adjunct is pure due to the predominance of sattva, whereas the minor adjunct is indeed impure due to the predominance of tamas. (6.16)
Because it is supreme, because it is pure, and because it is preeminent among sentient beings,
it gives birth to Nārāyaṇa and the others, who are augmented by all-encompassing knowledge.
The *kāryopādhi* (the effect-condition), being base and impure, is characterized by *tamas*;
it extends the creation of individual souls (*jīva*), which is devoid of the qualities of the Lord of All. (6.18)
The creation, beginning with Nārāyaṇa and ending with living beings, exists within the limit of delusion;
yet the Vedas have proclaimed that Brahman is indeed one and without a second. (6.19)
Just as the threefold modifications of the intellect— namely waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—
occur again and again within that which is called the individual soul (jīva), whose nature is mere appearance.
In the same way, ignorance regarding Brahman manifests in three ways;
root-ignorance, which is the locus of dissolution, is proclaimed as deep sleep. (6.21)
That dream which has Nārāyaṇa as its limiting adjunct (upādhi) is called "sleep"; the ignorance consisting of the limiting adjunct of Viṣṇu is designated as "waking. (6.22)
The primordial life-force, the great life-force, is proclaimed by the name Viṣṇu;
he alone is called the life-force of all beings. He perceives within the self of manifestation (ābhāsātman), while the self of manifestation belongs to the Supreme.
Ignorance, manifesting in various forms while situated in the waking state, [is characterized by] gods, asuras, humans, and others, including gandharvas, uragas, and kinnaras. (6.24)

These various [beings], such as cattle, insects, and winged creatures, fashioned by karma and established in their diverse distinctions through the ascent of latent impressions (vāsanā)—[all these he perceives]. || 6.25 ||
The Imperishable One perceives himself through the form of Nārāyaṇa;
waking dissolves into dreaming, and dreaming goes to the state of sleep.
When that [sleep] reaches dissolution, only memory remains here—this is the fourth state (turiya). || 6.26 ||
Just as a dream occurs within waking, and just as waking occurs within a dream, so it is with this phenomenal world, O Goddess; he who understands this is liberated. (6.27)
This imperishable Supreme Self perceives both waking and dreaming;
yet the individual soul (jīva) experiences waking and dreaming as the consciousness of the perishable and the supreme Self.
Both that dreaming and that waking are devoid of objective reality.
The time of approaching the gross object is proclaimed as the waking state;
however, having abandoned the gross, the approach to the subtle object is considered the dream state. (6.29)
Even the non-existence of subtle objects is a state of attachment;
that sleep, O fair-faced one, is indeed ignorance in the form of delusion. (6.30)
One should understand that cause to be fashioned by the Great Cause;
it is extended in the form of effects, gradually differentiated through increasing coarseness.
Therefore, I shall declare that to you; listen with a one-pointed mind.

Ignorance, primordial nature (prakṛti), illusion (māyā), delusion, the unmanifest (avyakta), the primary matter (pradhāna), and the unseen force (adṛṣṭa)—thus do various disputants describe it in many ways.
All that is indeed of one and the same meaning, for the qualities do not contradict reality;
quarreling occurs only over names, never after seeing the actual meaning.
This is because both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* arise from that very source of creation.
The distinction between cause and effect is proclaimed as "non-difference" (abheda), as seen in the case of clay and gold [as causes] and the jar and the earring [as effects]. (6.34)
Alternatively, there would be either difference or non-difference; it is proclaimed that this case is just like that.
That ignorance has two powers, consisting of projection (vikṣepa) and concealment (āvaraṇa). By the power known as concealment, it suddenly veils Brahman. (6.36)
Just as a tiny cloud obscures the thousand-rayed sun,
so too does falsehood obscure the infinite and indivisible Brahman.
Though unobstructed, the full Self is free from attachment and beyond conceptual construction;
yet, following the influence of its own latent impressions, the imperishable Consciousness appears as if its nature were divided.
Then that power of projection, as if externally and yet within,
displayed the vast manifold universe with all its curiosity.
Then he beheld himself established as Nārāyaṇa,
the ultimate refuge of the Vedas, the paths of the Vedas, and the worlds.

The Imperishable One himself beheld [the world] in the form of Nārāyaṇa. That Supreme Deity, whose self is the Veda, thought: "May I be many" (an alternative reading is: "He, the Supreme Deity, whose self is the Veda, thought: 'May I be'"). From that, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) was born; undergoing transformation, it became threefold.
It is indeed threefold: sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa.
From the tāmasa ego (ahaṅkāra), O beloved, the insentient ether (nabhas) was born. (6.42)
O fair-eyed one, sound was his sole quality.
Then the sense organ of hearing arose from the ether permeated by *sattva*;
sound is its object, and the deity of the direction [presiding over it] is the *sāttvika* quarter.
From the predominance of the quality of rajas, speech emerged as the receiver of words;
O goddess worshipped by the gods, the deity Agni was there as the constituent of sattva.
Just as from space arose wind, along with its qualities of sound and touch, so too,
O beloved, from the wind permeated by *sattva* arose the sense organ of the skin.
O beloved, from the wind permeated by the quality of rajas arose the sense organ of the hands;
its function is grasping, and Indra is its presiding deity.
Then, from air, fire arose, possessing the nature of sound and touch;
and from light, when it was pierced by the quality of sattva, the eye arose, which perceives form.
From that in which the quality of rajas predominates, O beloved, the organ of feet arose; Upendra is the deity presiding over it, belonging to the sattvic nature, and movement is its object.
The three qualities—sound, touch, and form—arise from water and fire, with taste being the predominant quality;
from water, which is permeated by the *sattva* quality, the sense of taste arises, as well as the apprehension of that taste.
O goddess honored by the gods, Varuṇa became the deity presiding over the sattvic element;
from the water, which was dominated by rajas, there arose the anus for the purpose of excretion.
Yama was the presiding deity there, and from him the Sāttvika element arose.
From the waters came the earth, possessing the five qualities beginning with sound.
O Śivā, from the earth, which was permeated by Sattva, the sense of smell that perceives fragrance emerged.
The Nāsatyas were the deities there; a sāttvika [nature] arose, O Hā, and the sense organ known as the secret organ (the genitals) was produced from that which was permeated by rajas.
By that, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, the experience of bliss arises;
therein the god Prajāpati is proclaimed to be of the nature of sattva. (6.53)

O Goddess of the Gods, O Śivā, from the elements in which rajas predominates, when they have combined, the fivefold vital breath (prāṇapañcaka), whose nature is the power of action (kriyāśakti), is born.
O Goddess of the gods, from the elements in which sattva predominates, when they have combined,
that which is characterized by the predominance of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) is called the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
The mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and consciousness (citta) constitute the internal self;
the skin, eyes, tongue, nose, and ears are the organs of perception (jñānendriyas). (6.56)
And the organs of action are speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ. (6.57)
The guardians of the directions— Dik, Vāta, Ārka, Pracetas, Aśvin, Vahni, Indra, Upendra, Mitra, and Kāla—
are the presiding deities of the ten sense organs, as have been proclaimed by me.
Brahmā is the lord of the earth, Viṣṇu is the leader of the waters,
Śambhu is the lord of fire, and Īśvara is indeed the lord of the wind.
Sadāśiva is said to be the deity of space; these are the deities of the elements.

The ten sense organs, the intellect, the mind, and the pentad beginning with the vital breath—this is clearly declared to be the *liṅga*, the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*). (6.60)
O Goddess of gods! Listen as I describe the distinction therein:
O Goddess, the pentad beginning with breath, together with the organs of action. (6.61)
That which is known as the sheath of vital breath (prāṇakośa) possesses the qualities of hunger, thirst, and so forth;
that which is joined with the mind and the organs of knowledge is declared to be the sheath of the mind (manakośa). (6.62)
Joined with the organs of intellect and knowledge, it is proclaimed as that which is called "consciousness" (vijñāna).
