O Goddess! these three sheaths, in their individual aspect, are declared to be the subtle body (liṅga).
In that regard, O beautiful one, the individual soul (jīva), consisting of manifestation, goes and comes;
O Goddess, the three sheaths, which are insentient, are set in motion by the manifestation of Brahman.
Just as iron [is moved] by the proximity of a magnet, O Goddess of the gods!
That which is inert is non-existent, O Goddess; that which is sentient is existent, O Beloved! (6.65)
Therefore, O beautiful one, that conscious Brahman is indeed the Truth;
for it is the collection of all signs, O beloved, while that which appears there is but a semblance.
They call him Hiraṇyagarbha, and likewise Sūtrātman.
Thus, O auspicious Goddess, O Maheśānī, I have told you in brief that which I was asked by you; what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Śivomā-saṃvāda, within the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Uttarakhanda of the Māheśvara-tantra in the Śrī Nāradapañcarātra. 6-6.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Pārvatī said:
O God of gods! O Mahādeva! O Śaṅkara, ocean of compassion!
Having heard your words, my mind is not satisfied.
O Śaṅkara! You have described the forms beginning with Nārāyaṇa;
you have explained that the cause for their manifestation is merely the ignorance of Brahmā. (7.2)
The doubt regarding the connection of ignorance with Brahman has been dispelled by you;
O Lord of Gods, tell me specifically the cause for the arising of delusion.
Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess! I shall declare this secret that is hidden in the Vedas;
it must not be spoken to just anyone, but should be told only to one who offers his very self.
O Goddess, out of affection for you, I speak this and not otherwise:
Brahman, which is Being-Consciousness-Bliss, through its aspect of existence (sadaṃśa), is the perishable world.
The Supreme Brahman, whose nature is consciousness, is eternal, imperishable, and immutable;
through the playful diversion of child-like sport, [He creates] multitudes of millions of cosmic eggs.
Although it creates and indeed withdraws [the world], it remains likewise changeless.
Therefore, even beyond that syllable (Akṣara) is that which is beautiful with supreme bliss,
eternally delighting in Vṛndāvana, and an ocean of the essence of various divine pastimes.
It shines within the city of Brahman, beyond the reach of mind and speech,
like the pericarp of a lotus in the midst of eternal Vṛndāvana.
It was adorned with many great gardens, like its leaves.
His own abode is the bliss of rasa, self-luminous and most brilliantly radiant;
there the Yamunā flows, her lofty jewel-strewn banks shining like ten million suns.
It resounded with the cries of various birds, such as swans, cranes, and ducks,
and was filled with circles of bees greedy for the fragrance of the forests of blooming lotuses.
It was adorned with sands consisting of the nine precious gems and embellished by high embankments made of great jewels.
With various divine creeper-thickets radiant with unfading flowers, and made beautiful by the humming of bees attracted by their celestial fragrance; || 7-12 ||
With seventy holy bathing places whose grounds were resplendent with rows of divine jewels, and with celestial pavilions featuring floors shining with gems set above; || 7.13 ||
O Śivā, it possesses shimmering waters of nectar, is garlanded with golden lotuses,
and is frequented by flocks of birds with variegated wings and red-tipped feet.
Fanned by breezes of pleasant touch, with its swaying lotuses and here and there grounds of great emeralds strewn with rows of pearls,
it shines intensely like the sprouts of devotion upon a pure and darkly beautiful heart. (7.15)

There, parrots, cranes, and other birds, perched upon the branches of the wish-fulfilling trees whose beauty of foliage was stirred by gentle breezes, recite divine and excellent tales of wondrous virtues.
Where there is neither sorrow, nor fear, nor death,
and where infinite Time has no power;
having reached that state, the lords do not grieve again.
In the groves, those of pure intent possess bodies that sport with grace.
Possessing the beautiful luster of molten gold and having enticed the Lord with the casting of their side-glances,
they move about like manifest flashes of lightning.
In the dense thickets, the courtyards resounded with the humming of female bees.
The breeze, spreading the suspicion that it was the hundreds of creepers blooming in the groves of full-blown *cāmpeya* flowers,
spread forth a supreme succession of bliss within her slender form.
It spreads [the fame] of those high-browed women who possess the bloom of youth. || 7-19 ||
O friends with eyes like lotuses, resplendent with ornaments, with pearl necklaces hanging upon the high and full circles of your breasts,
you whose garlands of garment-fibers are moistened by saffron water,
surpassing the beauty of the rising orb of the sun.
There, the gods and Siddhas, difficult for others to behold, sport, their cheeks shimmering with golden earrings that quiver as they move. (7.21)

Where the grounds shine with manifest supreme beauty, delightful with the mass of radiance rising from sun-stones (the "jewels of the sky," meaning the sun; *dyumaṇi* = *ambaramaṇi*, the sun; *dyumaṇimaṇi* = sun-crystal), variegated by the rays of clear emeralds, and possessing the passionate splendor of rubies that rival the beauty of moving mountains. (7.22)
From afar, the earth appears as if covered with green grass-blades, because it is flooded on all sides by masses of the beauty of blue mountains rising upwards.
According to their relative distinction, there are two mountains composed of blue flowers;
they are divine, filled with various wonders, and as enchanting as celestial gardens.
There stands the glorious and great mountain of rubies, which illuminates the quarters of the sky with its throbbing garlands of rays.
There, many lakes abound with the nectar of consciousness and shine on all sides, constructed with slabs of great jewels.
Where the garden-creeper channels pour forth sweet nectar,
those bees, playing in groups and filled with bliss, drink from them.
Wherever there were bower-dwellings with smiling faces,
adorned with scattered golden couches and seats,
and featuring pavements shimmering with laughing gems;
The flocks of warbling birds are ever auspicious. || 7-28 ||
The expansive array of shimmering jewels spreads its splendor upon the surfaces of moonstone slabs on her thighs,
while the reflections of light rays from the lotus petals growing along the banks are cast there as well.
In those who have attained [mastery], there arises an indescribable channel of supreme joy.
Here, beryl creepers appear on all sides, in which the dancing of red coral blossoms shines forth;
they catch from afar the faint rays of white pearls.
It imparts a stainless splendor to the radiant Noble One.
Wherever the campaka groves flourish on all sides, utterly abandoned by intoxicated, wandering bees,
there the lords of birds (peacocks) incessantly cry out upon the branches.
Amidst the sounds of singing rising on pleasant breezes.
In days of gloom, the mass of pollen from clusters of fully blossomed lotuses was held all around by the swarms of light rays resting upon the lotus-forest of her dark-bellied luster.
The wind, being driven forth, carries the brilliance of lightning.

The beauty of the lotuses in the pleasure-pool clearly rises up, crowded with swarms of humming bees hidden within the thickets; while from the *kadamba* trees growing upon the embankment, [garlands] hang down, fixed by their cords.
O you whose virtues are as lovely as a thousand swings, O you of vast qualities!
From afar, O daughter of the mountain, the waters of the lotus-pools—
consisting of nectar-like fragrant scents expanding through the force of the wind and masses of rising pollen— [flow].
It delights the lake of the mind; thus it is the state of passion. || 7-34 ||
Possessing the full abundance of enjoyments in pavilions resting upon broad coral thresholds shining in the center,
with thousands of female companions stationed upon the stairways—
The grove was filled with the soft sound of mṛdaṅga drums being struck.
The jewel-moon, whose nature is never to fade, shines eternally, raining down pure nectar consisting of its ever-emerging rays;
it is perpetually endowed within with its own digits that dispel all darkness.
He whose abode is the opposing side to the well-known positions of purity and its opposite.
In that place where the most wonderful Great City shines, situated upon an island radiant with jewels sparkling in the midst of the ocean of nectar—
therein [shines] the supreme wonder.
It was not fashioned from a single radiant gem.
His own abode was a temple of wondrous form, resplendent with great pillars of precious gems,
and [adorned] with many rising suns and moons— its vastness equal to the sky.
Adorned with jewels that radiate light and serve as a rebuke [to darkness].
In which ten exquisite grounds for dwelling in manifold bliss appear—
grounds featuring delightful monasteries, beds, seats, and fly-whisks.
The preparation of the supreme fragrance for the unguent of the deceased. || 7-39 ||
By the excellent, fragrant smoke rising from great incense-burners moving along the paths of the latticed windows,
stirred here and there by the breeze from the pleasure groves;
They were perfuming the abundance of forest flowers.
In some places, it indicated midday with networks of moonlight from the sun; in other places, it revealed the night by means of jewels resembling collyrium.
In one place it was as red as the rising sun, glowing with the luster of rubies; in another, it was like the twilight, suffused with the brilliance of sapphires.
O Mother, the altar is lotus-shaped and square;
at its four corners are golden jars filled with nectar.
Where faces shine with the splendor of jeweled lotuses,
and pearl canopies are formed by the sprouts of light from the gem-studded floors.
"O beautiful one, here they appear split open, displaying various wonderful forms;
and around that great mansion, O lovely lady, there are lotus pericarps. (7.45)
There were twelve thousand rows of palaces dear to him, O Pārvatī, with thresholds of coral, doors of jewels, and lofty arches of pearls— veritable embodiments of manifold wonders.
They were adorned on all sides with various colors and great variegated patterns,
and they shone with jewel-lamps gleaming from the rows of windows.
And with long, winding ponds lined with rows of blooming blue lotuses,
which were constantly entered by groups of adorned female companions.
They were richly adorned with tinkling golden ornaments, beautified by garments of Kauśāmbha silk,
and their eyes were rolling from tasting the flavors of various amorous delights.
I bow to the great gate with its radiant jewel door-panels,
from which the Yamunā river shines clearly in the distance, facing it directly.
That courtyard was slippery with saffron paste,
radiant as a thousand rising suns,
and mingled with the rays of pearls.
Its interior was reddened by the radiance of jewels.
There, the various grounds shine forth as a temple of supreme bliss, strewn with gold and pearls and jewels. (7.52)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, where there are many wonderful mosaic pavements shining on both its left and right sides as well as in front.
There, rows of jewels set upon pillars of Jāmbūnada gold,
possessing unshaken luster, enhance the splendor of that great island-lamp of the earth.
In its center stands a certain palace, surpassing all others, adorned with heaps of priceless pearls and rubies, graced with shimmering banners,
and featuring thresholds fashioned from lapis lazuli and coral.
The glorious pavilion, its splendor enhanced by heaps of flowers. || 7-55 ||
The herds of dancing celestial nymphs, their faces radiant with smiles, dance to the light tinkling of their anklets and the brilliant luster of their armlets and rows of beautiful bracelets.
Without displaying any dramatic gesture, the beauty of his swaying earrings shone forth.
Where, amidst blue lotuses fashioned from sapphire gems,
a swarm of female bees appears to be hovering;
where, seated upon the surface of the ground made of shimmering crystal—
The swans, distinguished by the brilliance of their feet and beaks, took refuge there.

O Daughter of the Mountain, my mind is drawn toward the white Sindhu-horses on a path colored by the tender pollen of the Kalpavriksha trees, where swarms of bees are delighted by the fragrance wafting through the quarters of the sky.
Let Khaṇḍa sink within the interior of the great jeweled pavilion.
On the further bank of the Yamunā, his own abode was established.
O Great Goddess, in another [aspect], however, there is the abode of the Imperishable.
O Īśānī, facing the abode are forests and groves,
as well as a pool consisting of consciousness and bliss, adorned with jeweled pavilions.
There was the Pārijāta grove, radiant with coral and flowers,
shining with various trees that had the appearance of rubies.
With creepers made of beryl, possessing petals of ruby,
joined with clusters of pearls and accompanied by golden sprouts.
Resplendent on all sides with herds [of animals], it is an abode of the delights of various sports—a pure lake extending for a number of one hundred and twenty-five thousand yojanas. (7.64)
A pavilion with a jeweled floor set upon slabs of precious gems, beautiful with stairways fashioned from coral, rubies, and other such stones.
The women staying there sing of their husband’s boundless glory;
some swing in swings while singing with sweet voices.
Some, radiant with the joy of various sports through mṛdaṅgas, vīṇās, and other instruments,
play with great delight, filled with supreme bliss along with their female companions.
There is the Great Lotus Grove, where the lotuses consist of rubies,
and there is a beryl lotus pond shimmering with stalks and rows of leaves made of beryl.
It was enchanting with divine fragrances shining from coral filaments,
and it created a canopy in the sky with dust raised by the wind.
O Goddess, it extends for a hundred thousand yojanas in every direction;
through contact with the bliss of its fragrance, there arises a succession of the bliss of Brahman.
He appears as one who is by no means to be entreated by anyone at any time;
the Blessed One sports somewhere, accompanied by his beloved consorts.
In spring, with water-jets emerging from fountains of saffron-water, adorned with ornaments of spring flowers and shimmering pearl decorations; (7.72)
They played with one another through both secret and open games,
amidst the wafting of various fragrances and the songs of various flocks of birds.
In the rainy season, amidst a sky filled with clouds flashing with lightning, there arose divine, piercing cries that ever increased one's bliss.
In the various stages [of the seasons], he rejoices while being sung of by throngs of friends;
thus, in due order, the Blessed One sports according to the seasonal course.
Once, upon a most enchanting mosaic floor within a jeweled palace,
it was adorned with sixteen great pillars of precious gems situated in the four directions.
Because they are mutual reflections of one another, he shines like the moon in the midst of stars when situated between two beloved women. (7.77)
There the Blessed One, the Supreme Person who is composed of rasa itself, delights in various playful jests and various amusements and curiosities.
The Imperishable and the Supreme Self are designated as the Puruṣottama;
O beautiful one, both are indeed one and the same entity, distinguished only by their playful manifestations.

O Dear One, because he is the creator of the syllable (akṣara), there is no arising of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa) [in him]; and because he is free from deceit and is the very essence of aesthetic flavor (rasātman), there is no other creator of creation.
For there was a desire to see the Imperishable One, O beloved, in order to behold His divine play;
behold the fullness of the love of the Beloved in the radiant Puruṣottama.
Knowing that, the supreme person (Viṣṇu) directed his desire toward his beloveds;
then those [goddesses], accompanied by Śrī and Svāminī, made their request to him.
The friends said:
"O Master, O Supreme Bliss, O Lord higher than the highest!
We are dear to you, and you are dear to us; therefore, do what is pleasing to us."
But as for the Lord, whose nature is the Imperishable, those pastimes which the Master creates—of what kind they are and of what sort we have not experienced them. (7–84)
The desire of us whose minds long to behold that [form] obstructs us;
O treasure of compassion, out of mercy, cause us to experience it. (7.85)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O beloved ones, listen to my words with attentive minds;
you are not fit to be seen, for you abide in the state of eternal bliss."
O sweet-spoken ones, there occurs a complete loss of the nature of bliss through the sight of the pastimes of her who possesses the three qualities. (7-87)
Through the entry of my illusory power (māyā), there shall arise a manifold diversity among those whose nature consists of objective entities;
and you shall never behold me, together with my divine play (svalīlā).
There will be only the experience of suffering and never of happiness;
you will forget me there—what else can I say to you, O sirs? (7.89)
Thus addressed, all those beloved women replied to Puruṣottama:
"Even so, my dear, none of that has ever been experienced by us at any time."
Therefore, act in such a way that [the truth] becomes ascended upon direct experience;
for one who desires pleasure does not turn away from it without seeing its suffering.
"Without suffering, happiness is not perceived in its true nature;
therefore, fulfill our desire by showing us your virtuous pastimes.
When he was thus addressed by his beloveds, he replied, "So be it."
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Śrīmāheśvaratantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. || 7-7 ||
Then, in the eighth chapter, Śiva said:
By his will, he created Nidrā (Sleep), who consists of the three guṇas and whose form is delusion.
Thus, his knowledge having slipped away, the Lord of the World fell into delusion.
O Dear One, that ignorance which is of the nature of delusion possesses two powers;
O Goddess, the first is considered to be obscuration (āvaraṇā), and the other is considered to be of the nature of projection (vikṣepātmā).
Just as a lamp is self-luminous, and just as a covering of clouds may obscure it, so too this [Self],
when concealed, manifests various states once it has conquered them.
Thus, having veiled the immutable Puruṣa by means of its nature as a covering, she then displayed the universe within herself through the form of projection. (8.4)
Those who know it declare that ignorance is endowed with two powers;
just as a sleeping person abandons what was seen while awake. (8-5)
When the intellect is permeated by those latent impressions, one perceives a dream;
just as the Soul of the Universe, O Beloved, beheld the world mounted upon a dream.
Just as a man lying down might become a king in a dream and, by means of that royal body, exercise control over all his subjects; || 8-7 ||
In that same way, the Lord, whose nature is consciousness, assumes the form of Nārāyaṇa;
by means of that form, O Queen of the Gods, he perceives the play of a dream.
O beautiful one, sattva, rajas, and tamas are the earth and the other elements;
O Goddess, O beloved, from these were born the things from which the cosmic egg arose.
Therein these worlds are born, seven above and likewise seven below;
there are seven oceans and seven continents, with Jambūdvīpa situated in the center.
In the midst of that is Bhārata-varṣa; therein is the district of Mathurā.
In the center of that, O beautiful goddess, Gokula has arisen like a vision in a dream.
O Beloved, the entire universe appears as if external while remaining within [the Self] due to sleep;
it is the very existence of Brahman that constitutes its existence, for no separate existence exists. (8.12)
O Goddess of the gods, just as paintings on a wall do not exist as separate from their substrate, so too at that time [the elements] do not exist, even though they consist of fear.
Thus, O Goddess, this manifold and variegated universe rests upon the wall of the Self; it is nowhere separate, yet the unwise perceive it as distinct. (8.14)
O Goddess, this secret of Brahman causes my tongue to grow dull when attempting to speak;
my limbs grow limp and my voice falters.
Nevertheless, overcome by love, I shall tell you just a mere indication.
Once, the Lord known as Puruṣottama himself was seated in a circle of female companions, embraced by his mistress.
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, treading upon the surface of the earth with his feet,
he brandishes a lotus with his hand while his body is firmly supported by his feet.
Delighting in the essence of divine play, adorned with divine ornaments,
wearing a crown of divine rubies, and embellished with divine earrings.
His glossy locks of hair were curved like a motionless swarm of bees;
his face was radiant as an autumn lotus, raining down bliss upon the eyes.
His teeth were like divine diamonds, his lips were like coral shoots,
and he was the festival of curved, creeper-like eyebrows shaped like the bow of the God of Love.
He surpassed the ocean of the essence of sweetness with the sweetness of his smile;
he was enchanting with the beauty of the three lines shining upon his conch-like neck.
His chest was radiant with a pearl necklace, shimmering with the luster of flashing jewels;
he was adorned with a network of tinkling bells set within his girdle and skull ornaments.
Adorned with bracelets, armlets, upper-arm ornaments, and a multitude of finger-rings; possessing a beautiful nose and a handsome face, his lotus-like countenance was graced with a noble smile.
His limbs were anointed with divine perfumes, and he was adorned with celestial garments;
his beautiful form was as cool as the waves of the ocean of nectar.
With sprouts of fine body-hair rising from a deep whorl at his navel,
his mistress sat upon his left side, sharing the same seat.
Adorned with the brilliance of the tips of unswerving lightning flashes as her ornament,
she has a nose as large as a divine *dhātrī* fruit, with pearls dancing upon it.
O Goddess of Gods, with the playful movements of her eyes filled with the sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra-rasa), she seems to plunder the profound depth of her husband’s mind. (8.27)
Her mind, submerged in the ocean of her lord’s life, was surpassed in sweetness by the honeyed play of his speech and drowned in the flood of light from his gentle smile.
Her eyes were startled by the humming of bees greedy for the fragrance of her breath;
the playful movement of her creeper-like eyebrows surpassed the grace of Kāma’s excellent bow.
The female swans were bewildered by the resonance of her jeweled girdle,
while the circles of her anklets were submerged in the mass of light from the moons of her toenails.
Her lotus-face was like a wave surging from the ocean of bliss, and she was enchanting with the weight of pearl necklaces shimmering upon her jar-like breasts.
Resplendent with neck-ornaments, her throat adorned with a *kambu* shell and possessing a pure smile, the friends placed their beloved in front and joyfully spoke to the lord of their lives. (8.32)
The friends said:
"O lord of her life, the great tree of your beloved’s desire has not borne fruit at all; how much less so while you, her husband, are present?"
The frustration of our desires truly agitates the heart of my beloved;
the longing to witness her childhood play and other such pastimes dwells within my own heart and afflicts me.
O Lord, just as between the moon and its moonlight, or between a flower and its fragrance;
just as between sound and meaning, O Master, or between fire and its flame. (8.35)
O Mistress of the Gods, that beginningless non-duality belongs to you, the Sovereign, in exactly the same way;
O Lord, for us as well, it exists in the same way through our Sovereign.
For what reason do you not fulfill that desire?
Perform without delay exactly what resides in your heart.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Śrīmāheśvaratantra, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, within the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. || 8-8 ||
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Śrī Śiva said:
"Then, O beloved, having heard the words of her friend that a vision [of me] was necessary,"
Though remaining silent, he thought in his mind, "May all be so."
All her friends, together with their mistress, stood as if gazing upon that lotus-face of hers; and the Lord likewise remained standing there.

Having departed with portions of their latent impressions (vāsanā), all of them were born as cowherd women in Gokula, each separately in the houses of the cowherds, situated within the district of Mathurā.
Born in the house of Vṛṣabhānu, she is renowned as Rādhikā;
O beautiful one, she possesses even a slight trace of the latent impression of being a mistress in some part of her being.
O Goddess of the gods, their friends have also been born; I shall tell you some of their names—listen with a one-pointed mind. (9.5)
Sundarī, Svarṇavarṇā, Ramyāṅgī, Svarṇamālinī, Lalitā, Citravarṇā, Viśākhā, Vijayā, and Jayā.
Sukuṇḍalā, Kuṇḍalinī, Mālinī, Svarṇamañjarī, Mañjughoṣā, Vicitrā, Devasenā, and Varūthinī. (9.7)
Gaurī, Citrāmbarā, Tanvī, Candralekhā, Manojavā, Ajitā, Jayinī, Śyāmā, Balākī, and Vimalaprabhā. || 9-8 ||
Tārā, Kuraṅganayanā, Kamalā, Vanamālikā, Nityā, Vilāsinī, Tāmrā, Anaṅgā, and Anaṅgamālinī. (9-9)
Anaṅgamekhalā, Mādhvī, Mohinī, Madanāvatī, Puṣpāvatī, Hemalatā, Hemamālā, and Manojavā. (9–10)
Karpūragandhā, Kāśmīrī, Padmagandhā, Vihāriṇī, Haṃsinī, Citriṇī, Citrā, Sunandā, and Bindumālinī. (9–11)
Manojā, Aṅgalālityā, Vaitālī, Vimalaprabhā, Padmarāgā, Vicitrāṅgī, Nityānandā, and Niraṅkuśā. (9.12)
Thus, these lotus-eyed companions are renowned by the millions;
they cannot be limited by any number, for they eternally take refuge in Vṛndāvana. (9.13)
Although their number is said to be twelve thousand,
they were those who resided in the inner apartments and whose minds were united in secret intimacy.
Then all of them, having passed from the waking state into the dream state, beheld their own selves as if they had entered Nanda’s cowherd settlement, with its banners unlowered.
Just as the fragrance of a lotus is carried away by the force of the wind, O beloved, the lotus itself neither increases nor decreases in any way. (9.16)
Likewise, though led there by delusion, they experienced that dream of another's self as a dream, an illusion, and a mental fantasy.
The Supreme Lord, the Soul of all, also witnessed this pastime.
Pārvatī said:
"Those friends of yours who were mentioned by you have arrived at the cowherd settlement of Nanda."
O Śaṅkara, tell me the manner of experiencing the immutable divine play.
How did that Supreme Self, the Blessed Lord, witness the divine play? Of what nature was that play—was it with attributes (saguṇa) or without attributes (nirguṇa)? || 9.19 ||
"Are they impermanent or permanent? Speak according to the truth, O Śaṅkara.
Śiva said:
"Listen, Pārvatī; I shall explain to you these questions that are well-guarded secrets."
O Goddess of the Suras, [this should never be given] to atheists, to rogues, to skeptics,
nor to those who revile the Vedas, nor ever to one who lacks faith.
To one whose inner self is purified by faith in the Vedas, Śāstras, Purāṇas, and so forth;
who is free from censure, pure, and who perceives Brahman everywhere. (9.22)
To the one who is free from greed, peaceful, stainless, O Maheśvarī,
grateful, and whose mind is purified by the performance of ritual acts and right conduct.

O Goddess, having examined him in a hundred ways, one should give [the gift] to one whose form is stainless through bathing, charity, compassion, dexterity, self-restraint, and so forth; never elsewhere.
Whether out of affection, greed for wealth, ignorance, or even fear, the deluded soul reveals [the secret], thereby falling from the state of hell to that of the stars and moon. (9.25)
Therefore, O Goddess of gods, O Sovereign of the Suras, you too must keep it secret so that the vision of the Brahma-līlā may be granted to your friends. (9.26)
I shall describe that manner; listen with a one-pointed mind.
Kaṃsa, the wicked son of Ugrasena, was the lord of Mathurā. (9.27)
Having heard that his own death would come through the hand of Devakī’s son, the evil-minded and powerful Kaṃsa quickly began to kill his sister with a sword.
Though restrained by Vasudeva with both political wisdom and instruction in spiritual science, the wicked and sinful man did not desist; he then devised a stratagem against him.
And she has no fear for you, O hero; if you have fear of your sons, I shall hand over those sons whom she will bring forth.
You should have no doubt, for the Person consists of truth;
when truth is lost, he himself is lost and enters into the great darkness of the unmanifest.
Thus addressed, the wicked one, his mind deluded, released his sister;
by her, in due time, a son was born who resembled fire.
Taking him, Vasudeva went to Kaṃsa and, seeking to appease him,
offered his own son as a gift to Kaṃsa, who was destined to be his death.
But Aṅgirasena, seeing him with a serene inner soul, replied to his son: "O sinless one, I am pleased with you."
"O hero, I have no fear of you; therefore, I do not kill your child.
It was heard by me long ago that my death shall come from the eighth pregnancy of you two."
"Why do you kill children in vain, becoming an object of reproach to the world?
O sinless one, when your eighth son is born..."
Then, having quickly approached me, you must indeed inform me:
"May it be well with you; go in peace for a long time, and by all means do not harbor any fear."
Thus commanded by Kaṃsa, the noble-minded Vasudeva returned, taking his son with him, yet remaining full of doubt regarding Kaṃsa’s words.
Then, his mind deluded by Nārada’s words, that wicked man,
filled with rage, went there once more and slew his son.
He seized both Vasudeva and Devakī with fetters;
that wicked man caused whatever sons she gave birth to to be killed.
The Great Goddess Yogamāyā, commanded by the God of gods, bore the seventh embryo known as Śeṣa, who was exceedingly difficult to endure;
having drawn that embryo from Devakī, she transferred it to Rohiṇī.
The Lord himself manifested within that womb of Devakī,
bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus, with his beautiful four arms.
Clad in yellow garments, dark as a rain cloud, with shimmering crocodile-shaped earrings,
a glittering ruby crown, and adorned with bracelets and armlets.
But Vasudeva, seeing him with eyes wide with wonder, praised him with the words of the Upaniṣads; then, being pleased, he spoke these words:
Viṣṇu said:
"I was indeed gratified by you previously through your difficult penance;
thus, I became your son, renowned by the name Pṛśnigarbha."
Likewise, in my second birth, O delighter of the Yadus, you were the patriarch Kaśyapa, while I attained renown as Upendra.
O Vasudeva, having been born in your house in this third birth, I have now manifested for the sake of granting you liberation. (9.47)
"Lead me to Gokula, where Yaśodā, the wife of Nanda, resides; there Mahāmāyā was born—take her to your own home."
"Let there be no fear for you anywhere from Kaṃsa, even though he is suspicious of me," said the Lord of the Gods in the presence of the couple as they looked on. (9.49)
But when there is a mental modification regarding the Imperishable (akṣara) upon beholding his divine play,
he attains the state of a manifestation (vyūha), consisting of that [divine play] as its limiting adjunct and having it as its mode of existence.
The Lord immediately became two-armed and attained the state of an infant;
into him entered the Lord himself in person, in the form of rasa.
Taking her while she was stupefied by yogic sleep, Vasudeva went to his own home; meanwhile, [the child] was led to Nanda’s house in Gokula. || 9.52 ||
In the morning, having heard the sound of a child, the eager household guards, filled with haste, informed Kaṃsa of Devakī’s delivery.
The wicked Kaṃsa, arriving in haste, violently seized the goddess and dashed her against the surface of the earth; thereupon, she flew up into the sky.
Enraged, she spoke these words: "He who was born from Hari is the destroyer of you;
he who exists for the sake of protecting the dharma of the Vedas and for the purpose of turning back the heretics. (9.55)
For the sake of destroying the Asuras, he manifests through his divine play;
desiring to recover the Vedas swallowed by darkness at the end of the age, the omniscient and omnipotent Lord himself was born in the form of a fish. (9.56)
He who, in the form of a tortoise, supported Mount Mandara upon his back;
he who, desiring to lift up the earth, O fool, assumed the body of a boar. (9.57)
He who, as a treasure-house of compassion, assumed the form of Nṛsiṃha and manifested from a pillar in order to slay the betrayer of his own devotee and to protect his devotees. (9.58)
Having assumed the form of a dwarf for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of his devotee,
the Lord bound Bali and gave the three worlds to Maghavan.
Having seen the Kṣatriyas acting with wicked conduct, he who was born in the house of Jamadagni made the earth devoid of the seed of the Kṣatriyas.
He who, having become the son of Daśaratha, slew in battle the wicked Rāvaṇa— the one who makes the world cry out— was a refuge for others and a destroyer of enemies.
In the Kali age, for those evil-minded Asuras who are about to be born and who have set out upon the path of the Vedas, [there is that which occurs] because of their unworthiness for it.
In order to produce a lack of interest [in false doctrines], the Supreme Lord, having formulated various heretical systems, will bring about their destruction. (9.63)
"O you of deluded intellect, wherever he may be born, death will come for you!
Having said this, Māyā vanished; Kaṃsa, however, remained dejected.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā, within the Uttarakhanda of the Māheśvaratantra in the glorious Pañcarātra. 9-9.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Śiva said:
Then, at the house of Nanda, a great festival took place as soon as morning dawned.
Having bathed and purified himself, the high-minded Nanda summoned Brahmins who had mastered the Agamas and gave them cows, garments, and ornaments.
The cowherd women, adorned with various ornaments and garments, went forth delighted;
they congratulated Nanda on all sides with auspicious blessings.
Having gone to the highly fortunate Yaśodā, the gopīs were filled with great joy;
their minds became intensely eager for a vision of Kṛṣṇa. [At that time, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, in the form of a youth, granted them his own vision. || 10.33 ||
All the gopīs became as if submerged in the bliss of beholding Śrī Kṛṣṇa, their very forms appearing as though they had returned to their own world. || 10-4 ||
In every house there arose a succession of great festivals; bards, panegyrists, heralds, and genealogists arrived in great numbers. (10.5)
To them, the king of cowherds gave costly ornaments and garments;
then Pūtanā, the slayer of infants, was commanded by Kaṃsa.
Slaying the newborn infants, she wandered all around the cow-pen;
those children, being overcome, entered into the interior of Pūtanā.
Having heard of the birth of a son in the house of Nanda, and desiring to kill him,
he assumed a deluding form adorned with divine ornaments.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, and enchanting with her divine fragrance,
she entered Nanda’s house slowly, captivating his mind.
Then, having approached the lying-in chamber with a cruel resolve,
she deluded her [the mother] with words expressive of outward affection.
She took up the lotus-eyed child like a sleeping serpent;
placing him upon her lap, she fondled him in many ways with a pure smile.
Hari placed his breast, smeared with Hālāhala poison, upon Pūtanā’s lotus-like face; Hari drank the life-breaths of Pūtanā that resided within her.
Her body, measuring one and a half yojanas in width,
fell upon the surface of the earth, making the entire region of Vraja tremble with the sound of its impact.
Even by giving her own milk, which was like the deadly poison hālāhala, to Hari, the Supreme Soul, she attained the supreme goal; how much more so, then, those who perform virtuous deeds?
Pārvatī said: "Regarding those infants staying in Vraja who were killed by her—
Hari drank in all those residing in Pūtanā along with her very life-breaths."
"Thus, O Lord, what you have asked—'Who are the children here?'—Śiva said:
Once, at a sacrificial session of Brahmā, there were gods, Gandharvas, and Pannagas. (10-16)
All the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and great ṛṣis assembled there,
as did the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, and Pitṛs.
The fires and other winds were present there, and their great assembly hall was magnificent; the lords of the Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsarases danced. || 10.18 ||
Seized by passion agitated by the sight of the Apsarases, the Grandfather’s mind was altered; even though he strove, he was unable to restrain his heart. (10.19)
His great seed, consisting of ascetic power and knowledge, quickly spilled;
not knowing its location, the Lord offered it into the fire of the sacrificial pit.
Emerging from the midst of the fire, those youths possessed of fiery splendor all bowed down to the Grandfather with their palms joined in reverence.
"O Brahman, you are our father; we are your sons at your pleasure, O Lord. We have been produced by you; tell us, what shall we do? (10.22)
Brahmā said:
"The auspicious seed, consisting of asceticism and knowledge, was cast by me into the fire;
you were born from that, and therefore you are indeed the Agnikumāras (Fire-Boys)."
"O sons, having reached the Daṇḍaka forest, perform austerities.
Having been addressed thus by Brahmā, they all took refuge in the Daṇḍaka forest.
Performing austerities with great effort, they were restrained by their devotion to Brahmā;
then, after some time had passed, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, appeared in person.
Having slain Rāvaṇa in battle and having established the kingdom in the hands of Vibhīṣaṇa,
he ascended an excellent celestial chariot and retired to the Daṇḍaka forest.
Having gone there to the hermitage of Agastya, Rāma paid his respects;
the sage honored him with bulbs, roots, fruits, and other offerings.
The sages, firm in their vows, also beheld Rāma;
honored by the sages, Rāma dwelt there for several days.
Once, O beautiful one, Janaki went to see the auspicious hermitages of the sages out of a sense of friendship toward the wives of those sages as well. (10.29)
He recounted the meritorious stories of Rāma concerning the slaying of Rāvaṇa,
while being honored by the wives of the sages, as well as by the sages and virtuous men.
Having turned back from there, Jānakī went to see the sons of Agni who were performing austerities, full of perfection and surrounded by the daughters of sages.
Having paid homage to those princes who were radiant as fire,
Jānakī sat there for a moment, her gaze fixed upon the beauty of the forest.
Driven by various fates and having committed an offense, those young princes spoke words that provoked indignation.
"O Sītā, this lord is the manifest Īśvara, the master of the worlds;
he has descended upon the earth for the purpose of protecting the Vedas. (10.34)
For whom there is neither self nor other, neither one who is hateful nor one who is dear—Rāma, the lotus-eyed, is true to his promise, patient, and heroic. (10.35)
Clad in matted hair and bark garments, immersed in delusion, he wandered from forest to forest; despondent, he roamed about questioning the lords of the woods.
Thinking "this is my beloved," with his mind utterly deluded by infatuation, he embraces a certain lovely, leafy creeper and finds satisfaction. (10.37)
Though restrained by Lakṣmaṇa, who said, "She is not [your] beloved," he built a bridge across the ocean after forming an alliance with the monkeys.
"O Sītā, because of you, even this lord has been subjected to such mockery;
therefore, women are always embodiments of evil and the sole abode of faults."

"Those who desire happiness should never, under any circumstances, harbor [this] in their minds; thus spoke those wise ones. Having heard these words, the beloved wife of the son of Daśaratha [reflected].
Enraged, with blood-red eyes, she resolved in her mind to utter a curse.
Sītā said: "O young ones, you shall quickly reap the fruit of this insult to me. (10.41)
With your bodies split in two, you who consider yourselves wise shall all fall to the earth; everyone must experience the fruit of their own actions.
When Sītā had spoken thus, the infants, their bodies suddenly split in two, fell upon the earth; the wives of the sages were struck with amazement.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the sages listening there;
having thus cursed those princes, he went to the abode of Sītā.
Then, having heard that unpleasant news, Rāma became deeply dejected in mind; he censured Sītā within his heart, thinking, "What is this [deed] of that ill-behaved woman? (10.45)
"Alas, women of deluded intellect, wicked and cruel-hearted, have here acted without reflection, having lost their sense of discernment! (10.46)
This illusion, fashioned by fate, stands as an obstacle to those seeking the highest good;
for those desiring liberation from saṃsāra, it is itself like a fetter. (10.47)
They are a chest for great delusion, intent on what is harmful for their own sake;
with minds characterized by anger, greed, and falsehood, they are never to be trusted.
One should never place trust in them, for they undoubtedly kill those who trust them;
being evil-minded, they engage in great harm for the sake of a small gain. (10.49)
"A wise man should not fall under the power of a woman; one who has fallen under her power is destroyed.
Having reflected thus in his heart, the Lord spoke to Jānakī.
Rāma said:
"O you of virtuous conduct, why have you performed this censurable act?
This injury to a youth is not a deed worthy of us."
O beautiful one, these men— whose minds are sustained by austerity and knowledge, and who are distinguished by modesty and good conduct—
do not deserve a curse, even if they should kill you.
Having heard the truthful words of men who speak according to reality, those of deluded intellect who become angry—there is no atonement for them anywhere. (10.53)
O Sītā, since those compassionate ones spoke the truth regarding me,
how could such indignation toward them have arisen, which leads to such misfortune?
If even for a very slight offense such a great punishment has been inflicted upon him,
this is not fitting, O fierce lady, for compassionate Kṣatriyas.
Thus addressed by Rāma as "virtuous one," we forest-dwellers living in the hermitages of sages bowed our necks in shame. (10.56)
With her hands joined in *añjali*, awakened by her husband’s words, Sītā said:
"O Lord, a great offense has been committed by me; there is no doubt about this. (10.57)

"O Lord, O treasury of compassion, please forgive my misconduct—even though I have exerted myself against those who were neither deserving of punishment nor guilty, and have indeed performed the restraint of my mind and body. (Note: The root text reads *yanmanyorurdamaḥ kṛtaḥ*. 10.58.
"Bestowing favor upon them, even though they are virtuous ascetics," Rāma said: "O blessed lady, I shall not grant favor to these princes. (10.59)
May liberation come to those favored by me as easily as water merging into water.
May the Supreme Lord, the Paramātman, who is celebrated in the Vedas and Vedāntas, bestow his grace upon them so that direct experience may arise. (10.60)
Therefore, O Sulocanā, these [beings], with only their subtle bodies remaining,
shall dwell within me perpetually for the sake of manifesting at the proper time.
And thereafter, they dissolved into the Blessed Lord Rāma when Hari himself descended directly into the house of Vasudeva.
Those boys who had crossed over in the land of Vraja and were situated within her body—all of them, being in Pūtanā, were destroyed by her. || 10.63 ||
With their vital breaths, she drank [the lives of] the children situated on her right side;
all those who were on her left side became women in the Gauḍa country. (10.64)
Desiring to destroy the enemy's army, he brought the maidens;
Nanda, who was restrained by royal law, arrived at that place.
Thus, O Goddess of beautiful eyes, that which I was asked by you has been told in brief, O Great Sovereign; what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Śrīmāheśvaratantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. || 10-10 ||
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
The venerable Śiva said:
Then, having taken the life-force of Pūtanā along with the child, the ocean of compassion—
He brought down the cart with the effortless grace of a sprouting leaf.
Then Hari struck Tṛṇāvarta as he was carrying him through the air;
at that moment, he was merely yawning after having drunk from Yaśodā’s breast.
The ocean of mercy, while eating clay as a playful diversion in his childhood, displayed the fourteen worlds within his mouth; he thus fashioned for the Kumāras a supernatural physical form.
The Lord himself did not eat earth, nor even curds or milk;
for the sake of nourishing the princes, the Master provided everything else. (11.4)
All the cowherd women residing in Vraja, their hearts captivated by Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes, sought to entice Śrī Kṛṣṇa, saying, "I shall give you milk and even curds. (11.5)
Having said, "The fresh butters are soft," they led him to their own homes;
then, having called him to a secluded place and given him curds and honey, [they spoke].
Though he was but a child to the world, he embraced Kṛṣṇa and kissed his lotus-like face, bringing joy even to Yaśodā and Nanda.
Embracing when being embraced, and kissing when being kissed, he increases the joy of the Gopīs' hearts with his amorous gestures. (11.8)
Perceiving him to be like one who knows the art of love through his amorous gestures, those cowherd girls were so immersed in curiosity that, though eager, they were unable to speak.
She also brought another woman into the house and gratified her with food and drink,
having adorned her with collyrium, cosmetics, and fragrant unguents.
Having placed him upon an auspicious seat and given him a roll of betel, [the preceptor says:
"Play here without fear with these children. (11.11)
"Do not go elsewhere; your mother has been informed and will beat you," so said some cowherd girls who were bound by love for the child of Vraja.
Having taken the son of Vrajeśvara home, the other women said:
"O noble Kṛṣṇa, if you dance, I shall grant your heart's desire."
Thus addressed, he began to dance with impetuous joy,
his eyes filled with a multitude of glances full of emotion.
She requested, "Grant me the desired boon you promised for the purpose of teaching the art of dance. When she had spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa chose his own desired object.
Two excellent balls shine within your heart;
give them to your friends, the sons of cowherds, for the sake of playing. (11-16)
O Goddess, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, renowned by the name Rādhikā, laughed, thrilled with joy upon hearing the words of Kṛṣṇa. (11.17)
The mistress, overwhelmed by love for Śrī Kṛṣṇa, became possessed of latent desires;
she was the one celebrated as having twelve thousand companions. || 11-18 ||
All of them are her limbs; there is no difference whatsoever between their substances.
Kṛṣṇa is the self of the Mistress, and that Mistress is indeed the self of Kṛṣṇa. (11.19)
No distinction exists between these two, just as there is none between the moon and its moonlight;
the Supreme Brahman, whose essence is rasa, is the enjoyer of rasa, as proclaimed by the Vedas. (11.20)
The experts in the science of aesthetics have declared that *rasa* is indeed the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*).
This erotic sentiment is considered to be of two kinds: union (*saṃyoga*) and separation (*vipralambha*). (11.21)
And regarding the two who are united: union belongs to those who are joined, while separation belongs to those who are parted.
Because rasa is eternal, the separation that arises is of the nature of its own parts. (11.22)
This very nature of aesthetic flavor (rasa) consists in being subject to union and separation;
for otherwise, why would such a desire to see [the object] arise even toward the Immutable? (11.23)
And how is it that the flavor of beloved things is likewise of such a nature?
For Brahman, which consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss, has been described by the crest-jewels of the Vedas. (11.24)
Consciousness and bliss, however, reside only in the immutable Supreme Person;
both together constitute Brahman, which is devoid of any distinctions within itself. (11.25)
O fair-eyed one, even in the state of Brahman, which is imperishable, bliss consists of two parts, arising from the similar, the dissimilar, and its own internal aspects. (11.26)
For primordial nature (prakṛti), which has the seeds of biting [suffering] as its root, resides within the imperishable Self;
therefore, there is no persistence of the play of rasa in the Lord, who is immutable, O Maheśvarī, because He is beyond primordial nature and devoid of qualities. (11.27)
In the Supreme Person, who is perfect, whose self is bliss, and who is absolute, there exists a delightful pastime consisting of aesthetic rasa, which remains ever-new at every moment. (11.28)
That internal mental state which desired to behold the Imperishable has now arisen in the house of Nanda through the descent of Puruṣottama. (11.29)
Those whose latent impressions (vāsanā) consist of the desire to behold His qualities, pastimes, and so forth, are the beloveds of Him;
they alone are the beauties of Vraja, and with them the Rasa sports.
Rādhā, the mistress, is herself the Sovereign Lady of Vṛndāvana;
even a separation lasting for but a moment became the very essence of aesthetic rasa. (11.31)
The time required for each leaf of a cluster of lotus petals to be pierced by a fine needle is what is designated as a *lava*. (11.32)
Even here, Hari indeed sports through states of union and separation;
Kṛṣṇa, whose consciousness is overwhelmed by the pangs of separation, [sports] with Rādhā as his own essential form.
He became absorbed in the thought, "How might she be united with me?
And, having formed a friendship with her companion, he spoke of her stories incessantly.
Through constant hymns of praise to Your true nature and descriptions of Your gait and smile,
today’s garment has been made beautiful by Your companions.
Having had their hearts thus revealed, those friends said to Rādhikā:
"O Rādhā, this son of Nanda appears to me to be truly beautiful. (11.36)
This clever lover of Vraja is a match for your beauty;
his speech is constantly filled with talk of you, he is ever your life-breath and your mind, and he meditates on you alone in his heart so that union with you may come to pass. (11.37)
Rādhā said: "O friend, consider where my union with him might take place;
for I too am equal to him in form, beauty, and virtue."
I have been deluded for a moment, yet I do not forget him in any way whatsoever.
I constantly see Kṛṣṇa, the delighter of Yaśodā, in my dreams,
playing with me and drinking the nectar of his lower lip.
O friend, upon seeing whom now there arises upon my limbs a cloak of perspiration and horripilation, or a trembling, or a breaking of the voice. (11.40)
O friend, my mind, submerged in the ocean of the nectar of his beauty, finds no cessation anywhere except through the sight of him. (11.41)
Through delusion, I perceive the form of Kṛṣṇa standing near me;
seeing him vanish in an instant, my soul suffers intensely. (11.42)
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? Before whom shall I lament?
Lead me to Kṛṣṇa, the son of Nanda, who is dearer to me than my own life. (11.43)
My creeper-like body, licked by the great flames of the fire of separation,
will attain peace when drenched by the flood of nectar from Kṛṣṇa’s lips.
"Deliberate within your own heart upon the means for my union;
go to the meeting-place and exert effort for the arrival of Kṛṣṇa."
Having been addressed in this way by Rādhā, the friend went to her lord of life.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā, within the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Māheśvaratantra in the glorious Pañcarātra. 11-11.
Now, the twelfth chapter.
Śiva said:
Having seen her arrive with a mind overwhelmed by joy, Kṛṣṇa—
Having recognized this accomplishment of his task, his eyes shone with joy.
Out of affection, she asked that friend: "O friend, tell me now what was said by Rādhā;
having heard it, I shall attain satisfaction. (12.2)
As many portions of time as have passed since you departed,
so many ages (yugas) were there for me, distressed by separation.
The friend said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, due to separation from you, Rādhā also suffers exceedingly;
she finds no relief anywhere without the sight of you. (12.4)
"Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa!"—this mantra was muttered day and night by her, who was distressed by separation and who considered death to be near at hand.
Her creeper-like body, consumed by the fire of separation, does not shine,
like a delicate lotus plant in winter, withered by the frost.
O Lord, having fashioned an image made of cloth in secret day and night,
she, emaciated by separation, places it in her heart and lies down.
Her bimba-like lips are parched, and drowsiness has settled upon her eyes;
otherwise, how could there be such speech from her mouth? What more shall I tell you? 12.8.
The mental faculty does not apply even the slightest degree of continuous pursuit;
O son of Nanda, this desire of yours is indeed established otherwise.
"Therefore, go near him, having fixed your appointment at the rendezvous.
Having heard what was said by her friend, the Lord rejoiced in his heart. (12.10)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"I shall come there once you have made a firm resolve regarding the rendezvous; bring her there quickly, having disguised her appearance."
O timid one, you must not feel even the slightest fear toward anyone;
I shall deceive all people by means of the arts of magic and the like.
"Go there and offer my salutations to Rādhikā;
you are exceedingly dear to me, even more so than my own life. (12-13)
There is no difference whatsoever between us, even for those whose nature is identical to the vital breath (prāṇa).
O beautiful one, the satisfaction I derive from the remembrance of your name is such that I never experience such satisfaction anywhere else through service to me or meditation upon me.
"Relate these and other such words of mine to Rādhikā.
Then the friend went back and told Rādhā everything exactly as it was.
Having drunk the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s words, which was capable of putting to shame the sweetness of ambrosia,
his heart leaped up like the earth parched by the summer heat.
Then, in the chamber of the secret convention, a bed made of flowers was prepared,
resplendent with rows of blossoms emitting the great fragrance of various scents.
And [the place] was perfumed on all sides by the smoke of burning agallochum,
with divine betel-leaves possessing flavors fit for drink, and with ointments for the limbs.
Honored in that beautiful residence and surrounded by Rādhā’s friends, she went there;
seated upon her throne, Rādhā longed for union with her beloved.
The sky was turned tawny by the radiance of the tips of unsteady lightning flashes;
her well-rounded thighs, hips, and breasts were perfectly formed.
Her mind was enchanted by the nectar flowing from the stream of her sidelong glances,
and she shone with a nose-ornament shaped like a parrot.
The diamonds of her teeth cast doubt upon pomegranate seeds;
the excellence of her own voice, resonant with the sound of the lute, bestows delight;
and she perfumes the quarters of space with the fragrance of camphor-filled betel rolls. (12.22)
The radiance from the jeweled mirror dispels the pride from her broad cheeks,
and her conch-like neck shines with a jeweled auspicious thread.
Her sprout-like fingers gleamed with a multitude of jeweled rings,
and her belly was lovely with the three folds of a waist that shone beneath the weight of her breasts.
Fragrant with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, camphor, and other perfumes,
she had the expanse of her breasts bound by a bodice that stole away the scent of her breath.
She is beautifully adorned by the brilliance of pearl necklaces shimmering upon her breasts,
and she forms a circle with the radiance of her tinkling ruby anklets.
Seated upon the Rādhā-throne, how did she act out of devotion to her beloved?
O friend, consider why the lover has not returned even until this day.
"Are you detained by some beloved woman, or have you been deceived by her?
How can it be known whether her words are untrue or true? (12.28)
"If my beloved does not come, I shall undoubtedly give up my life.
Having spoken thus to her friend, she placed her face in the palm of her hand.

Overwhelmed by the fever of separation, Priyaṃvadā sighed deeply, her breath hot as the flames of the fire of parting; she mentally reviled everything—betel, perfumes, flowers, and all the implements of pleasure—that had been brought before her. (12.30)
"That curved face with its moon-like smile, that expansive gaze,
that speech which has conquered the sound of Kāma’s bow, and that beauty of his— O friend, for one whose soul is thus perpetually intent on meditation upon the most beloved, [what else remains]?"
Why does this consciousness of mine become so bewildered, as if it were kissing the deadly Kālakūṭa poison? || 12-31 ||
At that very moment, Kṛṣṇa arrived at the rendezvous like his own life-breath;
the lotus-eyed Rādhā rose quickly from her seat.
Seated together on the same seat, they were fond of each other’s delight;
their side-glances filled with emotion, they were mutually infatuated.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O beloved, for my body is consumed by the flames of separation from you,
even the sprinkling of the nectar of ten million oceans of ambrosia would not bring me peace.
O Rādhā, in separation from you, even that which is dear became unpleasant;
even the rays of the moon were as harsh as those of the sun. (12.35)
O beautiful one, in separation from you, they wither the vine of their bodies;
their bed, though filled with nectar, is as if strewn with glowing coals. 12.36
Sandalwood ointment on the body causes pain like sparks of fire; a night seems as long as ten million kalpas; a flower feels like the point of a needle;
and even a cool breeze pains the body like the flame of a forest fire. (12.37)
O beloved Rādhikā, day and night I meditate upon you, with my life-breath fixed on you and my mind intent on you, through the recitation of the great mantra: "Rādhikā, Rādhikā. (12.38)
I shall pacify this life-taking poison of the serpent of separation; O beloved, today you have been found by me like a treasure by the destitute.
When the great fuel of discernment, knowledge, discipline, and serenity blazes forth intensely,
doubled by the wind of separation within;
O Gopī, I offer my body into the fire of Smara.
For a moment from here, or for a moment from there,
for a moment in the house, or for a moment on the bed;
likewise, for a moment outside or inside oneself—
The cessation of one seized by a planet has been explained. || 12-41 ||
O Rādhā, how many beautiful-eyed women are not present here who do not delight me,
my intellect being obstructed by drops of rainwater?
Like a bird [flying] near the water's edge. || 12-42 ||
O young woman, even upon seeing your form brought before them by delusion at the very faces of the quarters,
the expansion within their hearts reaches its limit.
Having observed that joy is indeed futile, one should regard sorrow [as equally so]. || 12-43 ||
Samudra and Rudra are renowned throughout the world for their bearing of the Hālāhala poison from the ocean;
I, however, am like the fire at the end of an aeon.
Even though he is consumed by separation, this is not surprising. || 12-44 ||

May you alone be mine in birth after birth—even though my slender body has become an oblation of flames arising from the fire of separation from you—[Note: This is said by Śrī Rādhikā even though Kṛṣṇa, known here as *Akṣarātīta*, has not descended; the distinction is that this was spoken solely to demonstrate the greatness of her own love. May you alone be mine in birth after birth—even though my slender body has become an oblation of flames arising from the fire of separation from you—[Note: This is said by Śrī Rādhikā even though Kṛṣṇa, known here as *Akṣarātīta*, has not descended; the distinction is that this was spoken solely to demonstrate the greatness of her own love. May you alone be mine in birth after birth—even though my slender body has become an oblation of flames arising from the fire of separation from you—[Note: This is said by Śrī Rādhikā even though Kṛṣṇa, known here as *Akṣarātīta
And "a dear friend"—thus did the Creator ordain.
O beloved, the clusters of ketaka buds burst forth along with my heart; the clouds, however, burst forth simultaneously with my eyes.
They scatter profuse showers of water.
This very fire of separation consumes my body in an instant,
since his face is a brother to the rays of nectar—
He does not depart from the path of unshrinking meditation. || 12-47 ||
The winds blow, shaking the rows of clouds flashing with lightning, causing the peacocks to dance, and emitting the fragrance of beautiful ketaka flowers.
My heart is breaking into a thousand pieces.
Clearly bearing the lore that deludes the world, her two eyes have become the arrows of Love, while her two eyebrows have assumed the form of a bow.
Is this knowledge of mine that which brings about liberation? || 12-49 ||
With his lotus-face licked by the rows of light from the teeth revealed by a rising smile,
and with his shimmering eyes as the bees [hovering there].
Bewildering my heart. || 12-50 ||
This lotus-foot of yours is my object of meditation;
this beauty of your form is my song.
No reality whatsoever appears apart from you.
Without you, the world appears as if blind.
Thus consoling his beloved with words imbued with love,
Kṛṣṇa took delight in embracing her firm breasts and other such acts.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Śrīmāheśvaratantra, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, within the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. || 12-12 ||
Now, the thirteenth chapter.
Śiva said:
Once, those maidens performed a vow with concentrated minds.
"Worshipping Kātyāyanī, [they prayed] that Kṛṣṇa might become their husband."
At the end of the month, Kṛṣṇa went to the riverbank to bestow the fruit [of his boon];
having seized the garments left on the bank, he then climbed a *nīpa* tree. (13.2)
Having witnessed the deeds of Kṛṣṇa, the maidens were overwhelmed with love;
with faces smiling with bashfulness, they spoke to Kṛṣṇa, who was standing amidst the Kadamba grove.
"O Kṛṣṇa, give us black garments; we are exhausted by the water.
Having become one esteemed by the elders, you ought not to do this. (13.4)
If anyone should indeed know this, then it would be a great misconduct;
for when the cruel-minded King Kaṃsa learns even slightly [of this], [it will lead to disaster].
"For then this would indeed be a misfortune for us and for you as well.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O beautiful-eyed ones, come here and receive each your own dwelling."

"Otherwise, terrified by the fear of Kaṃsa, I would not give them at all. Hearing his words, the gopīs, their eyes smiling with bashfulness, emerged from the water and said, "Kṛṣṇa, give us our clothes! (13.7)
Kṛṣṇa, with a joyful heart, gave garments to each of them individually.

It should be understood that the Blessed One performed the sport of stealing their clothes solely for the purpose of giving to each of the maidens the specific portion belonging to himself, which was the very nature of his own internal part. Having engaged them all with the portions residing within Himself, Kṛṣṇa, who is fond of rasa, made them fully complete and fit for the experience of rasa. (13.9)
Then the Blessed One, being pleased, granted a boon to the maidens.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Indeed, those nights, which are presiding deities, abide in me; they are dear to me. (13.10)
"Behold, O lotus-eyed ones; I shall delight you there.
Therefore, return home; in due time, your desire will be fulfilled. (13.11)
Then all the cowherd women, having obtained the boon and their desires fulfilled,
went home full of joy, singing the pastimes of Kṛṣṇa.
Arousing the wrath of Indra and making a festival for the slaughter of the cow,
he [the bull] drenched the lord of the earth, Saṅkarṣaṇa, with the waters and food released by Indra.
Kṛṣṇa, dispelling the pride of Puruhūta, gratified him who for twelve years had abandoned water, fruit, and roots.
Once, Kṛṣṇa alone went to the auspicious Vṛndāvana and set his mind on sporting there with only his female companions.
Having beheld the delightful Vṛndāvana, where the trees bow with blossoms and which is enchanting with the echoing sounds of warbling birds, swans, and bees.
Then Kṛṣṇa beheld the full-blown jasmine and lotuses shaken by the gentle breeze, as well as Yogamāyā, who destroys the power of Time’s illusion.
O Goddess, at the end of waking and at the beginning of deep sleep, that which manifests is perceived; for the sake of divine play, Puruṣottama made it such. (13-18)
This [power] is established as twofold: manifest and unmanifest;
it is manifest in the aspect of seeing, and likewise in the concealment of the seen. (13–19)
Just as one cuts off external light and shines within the internal space,
so is that which is renowned as the "Yoga-māyā" of the Lord of the dream-māyā of the waking state.
Time and illusion were swiftly seized by her, whose nature is that very consciousness;
consequently, the entire universe of moving and unmoving beings, consisting merely of their effects, was dissolved.
The Imperishable One beheld that dream arising from the power of yoga,
O Sovereign Lady, which consisted of the elements, the senses, and the qualities, neither deficient nor excessive.
He wore a crown of divine rubies and shimmering crocodile-shaped earrings,
adorned with various ornaments resplendent with divine pearls and gems.
There, the form of Kṛṣṇa appeared, augmented by his yogic power (yogamāyā),
accompanied by a breeze carrying the fragrance of extraordinary, divine flowers from celestial creepers.
The most wonderful and glorious Vṛndāvana is served from all sides by birds,
deer, creepers, trees, winds, the moon, and the stars.
The seasons, the flowers, and the night—all was new, O beloved. (13.25)
She spread forth, emitting [light] and swallowing the universe with her might, dispelling the darkness like the flame of a lamp in the sky. || 13.26 ||
Even the cosmic manifestation of Yogamāyā, including the gods, asuras, and humans, was mentally conceived by Puruṣottama within those [energies]. (13.27)
By means of his power to assume any form at will, he awakened the previously latent desire within their hearts,
so that the longing of the fair-browed women might sprout forth in their minds.
Then, for the purpose of increasing that [joy], he produced the sound of his flute;
the sound of the flute was established in the sky born of his yogic power (yogamāyā).
O beloved, those cowherd women first heard that very sound.
The sound of the flute, moistened by the nectar of the lower lip and accompanied by the wind,
entered through the opening of the ear and intensely inflamed the passion within the heart.
Then, suddenly abandoning their beds, seats, and food—those [energies] renowned as Sāttvikī, Rājasī, and Tāmasī—[they departed]. (13.31)
And maidens in the form of the Vedas arrived, infatuated by the sound, even though they were repeatedly and diligently forbidden by their circles of kinsmen. (13.32)
Just as the momentum of rivers toward the ocean does not cease. || 13-33 ||
Though forcibly restrained, some gopīs, emaciated by separation, gave up their lives;
in an instant, they returned with divine bodies. (13.34)
The women of Vraja entered the supreme yogic circle; it was luminous in front, but behind them it became empty. (13.35)
Twelve thousand maidens have been mentioned, and likewise others;
indeed, they should be known to be as many, having heard the sound of the flute at night.
Forty groups of those women have been declared;
their number is twelve thousand according to their state of union. (13.37)
Māyā fashioned for them a dress worthy of union with their beloved; their ornaments, garlands, and garments were of a kind unlike anything found in the world.
Wearing identical dress and ornaments, all of them of the same age, O beloved, with equal hearts and equal tastes, they went into the presence of Kṛṣṇa. (13.39)
Even while sporting, he remained composed for the very purpose of maintaining the Vedas;
he established the boundaries of conduct through his speech, for speech arose from the Source.
They are not negated in their own nature, nor is their own nature beyond the scope of speech;
otherwise, O Dear One, it would be a contradiction for them to have the nature of rasa while being the enjoyers of rasa. (13.41)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O women, for what purpose have you all come together and met one another? Indeed, traveling through the forests at night is not appropriate."
By suddenly abandoning the dharma of women—the auspicious service of a husband—she certainly destroys both her worldly and her otherworldly welfare. (13.43)
That which brings satisfaction to her husband is the duty appropriate for a woman;
abandoning that, a woman certainly falls, there is no doubt. (13.44)
"Therefore, O women, go to Vraja with your minds restrained by my words.
Having heard those sharp words, which were like deadly *hālāhala* poison, the cowherd girls—
Did they fall to the surface of the earth as if struck by a thunderbolt?
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Guptasāra*, within the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the *Māheśvaratantra* in the illustrious *Pañcarātra*, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. 13.13.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Pārvatī said:
O Lord of Gods, O Supreme Ruler, O Dhūrjaṭi, O Nīlalohita!
O Sadāśiva, tell me what happened there after that.
Śiva said:
Having suddenly heard those harsh words, they were overcome with agitation;
they became as if lifeless, for their beloved had become the very form of their life.
Agitated by grief, their speech choked and their breath suspended, the women of Vraja shed tears from their eyes that were even hotter with their anguish. (14.3)
Resorting to fortitude, those belonging to the mode of ignorance, distressed by separation, said:
"Why do you speak such words devoid of consideration for Kṛṣṇa? (14.4)
In this world, those who speak without having investigated are established as fools;
therefore, one should speak only after investigation, since you yourself are omniscient. (14.5)
O Kṛṣṇa, we gopīs are your maidservants; our minds are fixed on you, you are our supreme goal, you are our very life, and we are composed of you; we perceive nothing else whatsoever.
"Our husbands, sons, brothers, and kinsmen are not our refuge;
we have you as our sole resort, having entrusted our very souls and bodies to you. (14.7)
"For those women whose conviction remains fixed in the thought, 'I am a wife and this man is my husband,' this which you teach is their supreme duty. (14.8)
One should never abandon that duty for which one has authority;
otherwise, how could renunciants not perform [their duties], let alone householders? (14.9)
O Lord, we have transcended the body, transcended the cave of the heart, and transcended the world;
having come to you alone for refuge, how could we be worthy of worldly things? (14.10)

The delusion "I am" arises with respect to modifications such as son, wife, wealth, and so forth; through the force of that superimposition, they possess the status of being subject to the attributes of the body.
For when one has entered upon the path of qualification, that wicked person who violates the Dharma certainly falls, without a doubt, because of his latent tendencies (vāsanā). (14.12)

This persistent attachment, rooted in the thought "this is mine," which resides toward one's husband, children, and so forth, has been destroyed along with its root; how then can you urge me toward that?
There is nothing that can obstruct love; the state of love is supernatural.
Drawn by love, we have arrived here in the middle of the forest at night.
Like one who is ignorant, why do you, though knowing that [truth], prattle thus—
having abandoned the paths of the world and the Vedas along with their roots, like one in the middle of a forest?
At night we women approached you, yet even those were abandoned by you; thus the way of love has been destroyed and treachery has been acquired.
But we shall not go; having renounced all possessions, we will offer our bodies as an oblation into the fire of separation and come to you—of this there is no doubt. (14–17)
Therefore, O Govinda, accept us; we gopīs are not to be neglected.
Abandon this reserve, O Kṛṣṇa, and take refuge in the way of love.
Having heard these words of the cowherd women as they were truly reported,
he gladdened their hearts with streams of nectar-like speech.
With a sweet smile and a glance, Kṛṣṇa spoke these words:
"O gopīs, you are blessed, most blessed; you are as dear to me as my own life-breath."
Never shall they be restrained by my life-force, which is centered in you;
nor shall any prohibition arising from the play of words ever be applied toward me. (14.21)
"I know clearly that you are indeed bound to me by love; this refusal of yours is merely for the sake of desiring to hear my words, and not out of any real feeling. (14.22)
For those seeking knowledge, this definitive determination of Dharma has been clearly delineated and rendered free from doubt:
that the supreme scripture is service to the husband, for I myself am the husband in embodied form. (14.23)
Because he is not perceived through any other means, he is understood as mere meditation;
therefore, I alone am your eternal husband.
Having spoken thus, he who stood among them took his pleasure accompanied by those lovely women;
embracing each of them individually, he drank the nectar of their bimba-like lips.
Making them laugh and laughing himself, Kṛṣṇa amused them with various playful diversions;
pulling at the waist-knots of some and even drinking from the mouths of others.
Leaving one woman, he embraced another; even while embracing one, he drank the nectar of another's lips, and with his eyes, he bit [the faces] of yet others.
With their eyes half-closed, the gopīs uttered sighs of pleasure;
thus the Lord Kṛṣṇa, overcome by rasa, took delight within that circle.
Perceiving Kṛṣṇa to be utterly overwhelmed and fallen under their control, all the cowherd girls thought so; that very state of mind was the essence of the Rāsa dance.
This very aesthetic flavor (rasa), when fully transformed, is certainly determined to take the form of pride;
this is the boundary of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) as defined by the treatises on rasa.
Listen also to the reason for that, which must not be spoken of in any way:
it is the desire to behold the Imperishable, which is required for the sake of fulfillment. (14.31)

And even there, pride arose as the cause for his disappearance. Then, beholding those women full of pride, the Lord, in the form of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), dissolved into their very hearts, as if to dispel their pride. (14.32)
Furthermore, her mental activity, established in the Imperishable and free from worldly absorption,
having attained its proper place, became perfumed by the latent impression of the *rāsa*-pastime.
Having gained knowledge through her, he contemplated the one situated in the maṇḍala;
thus the Blessed One beheld the great glory of the Rāsa-play.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Māheśvara Tantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. || 14-14 ||
Then, in the fifteenth chapter, Śiva said:
"When supreme bliss has become internalized, it manifests in two ways within the heart and the maṇḍala."
Not seeing their own lord, they suffered, distressed by separation.
When his mind was filled with bliss, consciousness clearly manifested within the creepers, trees, and other plants; thereupon, he questioned the trees and the creepers.
Those who did not offer a reply were censured by those of firm resolve;
having attained the state of Kṛṣṇa through Kṛṣṇa’s possession, they declared, "I am Kṛṣṇa. (15.3)
Thus performing various kinds of pastimes while distressed by separation,
they all then united together at the instruction of Tāmasī.
They imitated the pastimes of Vraja as a means for attaining that state,
beginning from the slaying of Pūtanā up until the binding with the rope.

The manifestation of the pastimes of Vraja became manifest to the mind of the Supreme Self (the Lord). [An alternative reading is *cittago*. [At the conclusion of the Rāsa-līlā, following the water-sports, the Blessed One was seated in a pavilion on the bank of the Yamunā amidst His friends. When He remembered the disappearance that occurred in the midst of the Rāsa and saw that the circle of friends had vanished, He was informed by them: "I have fully performed the pastimes of Vraja. At that very moment, He caused the entirety of the Vraja-līlā to ascend the path of His memory. Thus speaks the gracious Navaraṅga Svāmī.]
This eternal and indivisible pastime of Vraja has been described in the Vedas.
Then, as if possessed by the movement of the syllables, he emerged from the circle of his friends with a wide, lotus-like face full of wonder. (15.7)
Clad in garments of lightning-flash radiance and resplendent with necklaces of pearls, they seem to soothe him with the nectar-like garlands of their shimmering side-long glances.
Upon seeing him, though overcome by separation and having fallen into ultimate sorrow, they were indeed once again immersed solely in a flood of bliss. (15.9)
With his hand, Acyuta wiped the faces of the weeping women, which were soiled by streams of tears, using the hem of his own garment.
The Blessed One performed the great festival of the play of rasa with them through embraces, kisses, and various displays of amorous gestures. (15.11)
And that sorrow which was experienced by her friends during their separation has, alas, been dissolved in the ocean of the nectar of bliss! (15.12)
Then she engaged in water-sports in the pure waters of the Yamunā;
thereafter, the gopīs, standing on the bank, again began their disputes.
"O sinless one, thus has this state of the Rāsa-līlā been described to you by the Blessed One, who is absorbed in meditation and overflowing with supreme bliss. (15.14)
Śiva said:
And in order to fulfill the remaining desires of his companions,
Puruṣottama again manifested that Māyā of Time.
The Imperishable One beheld that dream as a manifestation of Time and Māyā;
having slept in the house of Nanda at dawn, he was certain that "I have awakened. (15-16)
And he saw all his friends who had risen from the cowherds' houses;
yet these were not at all impressions of the immutable Self due to its entry into the body, but rather [the impressions] of the kūṭastha itself. || 15–17 ||
Various [manifestations] blossomed forth, appearing like a great wonder;
