so too did the female tortoises and the Śrutis, which follow the expansion of Time and Māyā. (15–18)
Due to the onset of an exceedingly intense separation, even Uddhava, through his own instruction,
[found himself] within the heart of the Immutable One, in the ocean of the nectar of the manifest pastimes of Braja.
Like rivers, they remained there, their hearts touched by that nectar;
then Akrūra, commanded by Kaṃsa, went to Gokula.

When Kṛṣṇa had departed with him, the cowherd girls, distressed by separation, passed their days in sorrow through the recitation and other forms of discourse concerning him. (Note: An alternative reading is *tatkathākhyāpanādibhiḥ*, meaning "by the proclamation and other means of his stories.")
Having slain Kaṃsa, Cāṇūra, and Muṣṭika in a wrestling match,
he stood with his loincloth tucked up, grey with shimmering dust and marked by blood.
While all the worlds looked on, he reached the prison-house,
where Devakī and Vasudeva remained full of longing.
Overwhelmed with affection, he prostrated at the feet of his mother and father;
with palms joined in reverence, he said this to them: "May you forgive me. (15.24)
Having propitiated his father and especially his mother, Kṛṣṇa then bathed in the Yamunā and put on pure, divine garments.
Having slain Jarāsandha and the others, and having married sixteen thousand one hundred and eight beautiful-eyed women, [he lived]. (15–26)
Having slain the burden of the earth consisting of the Asuras, the Blessed One, desiring to remove the remaining burden augmented by the Yādavas, cast a curse upon the lineage.
All the Yādavas, their intellects consumed by the curse, perished among themselves;
meanwhile, the Blessed Lord remained there in secret at Prabhāsa.
Four-armed, with eyes like lotus petals, wearing yellow garments, his form adorned by the Kaustubha gem,
and bearing the Pāñcajanya conch, the lotus, the discus, and the mace.
Hari shone forth, possessing the quality of bold song. || 15-29 ||
Touched by an arrow from a hunter while suspecting him to be a deer, the lotus-eyed Hari himself went directly to Vaikuṇṭha. || 15-30 ||
Those who were present as the root-counts, their limbs seized by the illusion of Time (Kālāmāyā), also assumed various forms within that dream-like play. (15.31)
O beloved Śivā, when those latent impressions (vāsanās) have dissolved into them, the immutable one attains awakening; this is the great dissolution (pralaya). || 15-32 ||
Upon the destruction of delusion, all these shall become identical with Brahman.
Thus, O Śivā, that which I was asked by you has been fully explained to you.
O sinless one, this teaching, more secret than the secret, has been spoken by me;
it must be guarded with great effort, like the embryo of one whose husband is alive.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Māheśvaratantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. 15.15.
Now, the sixteenth chapter:
O Lord of Gods, O Blessed Śambhu, having heard that which you have spoken as being extraordinary, my heart today sinks into an ocean of wonder.
"In this regard, O Lord Śaṅkara, you have said that those who were the beloveds of the Blessed One have arrived here for the purpose of experiencing the remainder of their karmic desires. (16.2)
O Lord, how was the remaining desire experienced by them, or how could they be recognized by their characteristics? Please tell me that.
O Maheśvara, having gone to the world of mortals, you have become the spiritual preceptor of the wives of Kṛṣṇa; that which you spoke in secret, [is as follows]. (16.4)
Yogis, men of knowledge, devotees, those established in action, and those whose wealth is austerity—
you alone are their primordial Guru, for you are the instructor of each respective reality.
Those wicked ones who proceed with their own actions while disregarding you do not achieve success even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
You alone are the creator, the speaker, and the protector of all dharmas;
indeed, through devotion to you alone does the perfection born of action arise for men.
"By your word, those dear to the Blessed One shall attain awakening on this earth;
for you, O Śaṅkara, are the guru for those who have entered mortal bodies. (16.8)
Therefore, O Lord, this must certainly be taught; out of compassion for me as well, you should surely reveal this wonderful secret. (16.9)
Śiva said:
"O Goddess of the lords of gods, O Lalitā, you are blessed; your words are supreme.
Having heard them with a delighted heart, I shall relate this auspicious narrative. (16.10)
I am the manifest teacher of the Dharma and the spiritual preceptor of the three worlds;
how can those fools who revile me ever attain success? (16.11)
Established through various dharmas and with true devotion to diverse deities, I am the teacher in each of those places; yet the vulgar revile me. (16.12)
What do those fools not do, since the Māyā of the Great Lord is so powerful that it deludes only those who deserve to be deluded, and not others? (16.13)
Those for whom the eternal Dharma exists will indeed attain its fruit.

However, those many moderns of deluded intellect, asserting that "heaven is happiness" and "hell is suffering," do not believe that there are separate locations for heaven and hell elsewhere; that is incorrect. Among the fourteen worlds, above this world is the third, Svaḥ (Heaven), and below is the seventh, the world named Pātāla. It is true that within that very region, in the southern direction, there exist various hells. They do not disparage the gods, the Dharmas, the Vedas, or the philosophical systems. (16.14)
Those devoted to the doctrines of heretics and who revile the Vedic dharma fall into hell; they do not return at any time.
O Goddess, this very same characteristic applies to those who have entered the mortal world;
both Puruṣas—the Imperishable and the Supreme Self—are distinct from one another. (16.16)
O Beloved, both the Śabdabrahman and the Parabrahman are indeed non-dual;
O Beloved, the dharmas such as ritual action and knowledge arise from the Śabdabrahman.
If all of them, though free from desire, were intent on their own self-enlightenment, then by censuring those who practice the Dharma, it is the Dharma itself that has been censured. (16–18)
In that regard, by censuring the Dharma, one censures the Śabdabrahman itself;
through that censure, the Imperishable Supreme Brahman would become reviled. (16–19)
For when the two syllables [of his name] are reviled, O Goddess, Puruṣottama is reviled;
and when one's own husband is censured, O Goddess, what destiny can there be for those who are dear to him? (16–20)
One should not, in thought or speech, revile the auspicious teachings of the Vedas, nor Brahmins devoted to their duties, nor cows that yield the milk of desire for the sacrificial oblation. (16–21)
Therefore, all such things as these should be understood in their true nature through the mind;
free from censure, hatred, and the like, one should worship the Supreme Person. (16–22)
O Goddess of the gods, one should recognize her as the beloved of Kṛṣṇa himself;
having understood that everything is born from the Imperishable through a state of non-duality. || 16-23 ||
One should bow to Him with mind and speech; O Goddess, they call this devotion to the husband (pātivratya), which consists of perceiving nothing other than Him. 16.24.
He alone existed here in the beginning, and even later he is exactly the same;
who else indeed could there be, O Goddess of Gods, when one observes through the vision of reality?
Therefore, this devotion to the husband of the wives of Kṛṣṇa has been declared by me;
[it is for those] who do not know even the mere understanding of such devotion to the husband.

O Goddess praised by the gods, there is certainly not even a trace of latent impression (vāsanā) in her regarding this dharma of a devoted wife, whether acquired from a true teacher or from the scriptures. (16.27)
Having heard this, she attained steadfastness in that; they call her the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
Some fools, however, say that wifely devotion is otherwise than this.
Only one husband is to be served; no other should ever be honored.
By serving another in this world, a woman becomes fallen. (16.29)
O Goddess, this devotion to a husband is worldly, not transcendental;
for a worldly husband is one who lacks lordship, is limited, and is subject to defects. (16.30)
That woman likewise [attains such status] in the world through her devotion to her husband;
for the Lord is the all-pervading one, the manifest soul of the universe, whose very form is the universe. (16.31)
He alone has attained renown through all forms and names, having realized that the eternal Brahman is the true nature of all names. (16.32)
O Goddess, with an impartial vision she perceives everything everywhere.
O auspicious lady, this is what I have told you regarding this virtuous devotion to one's husband. || 16-33 ||
Thus, due to ignorance regarding this definitive conclusion, they wander about, utterly deluded:
"The six systems of philosophy are my limbs—the feet, the belly, the two hands, and the head. (16.34)
Whoever should create a division among them is indeed a cutter of my own limbs;
thus, having correctly understood the dharma of a devoted wife from the mouth of the Guru. (16.35)
They call him a beloved of Kṛṣṇa who serves his husband;
they call him a beloved of Kṛṣṇa whose body is marked with horripilation upon hearing conversations about Kṛṣṇa, and whose eyes are filled with tears of bliss. (16–36)
Śrī Pārvatī said:

For what reason does one perform action appropriate to their caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama) while being free from desire and intention—[that person] whose will is devoid of desire and intention? (16.37)

O Lord, even a child does not act without aiming for a result. Since the latent impressions of Brahma’s creation reside within these supreme living beings, why would a soul that has entered this world engage in activity in vain? (16.38)
Arising from the creation of delusion and infatuated by the fruits such as heaven, they engage in ritual action; this is not surprising, O Maheśvara. (16.39)

"O Śaṅkara, those who are dear to Kṛṣṇa and are of the very form of Kṛṣṇa have come together through their latent impressions (vāsanās)—or according to another reading, 'through their desires'—how then do you enjoin them to fruitless action? (16.40)
Śiva said: Whether unawakened or awakened, one should always perform beneficial action; however, for one who desires liberation, O proud lady, action performed with desire is censurable.
The person who performs action is the best; he easily crosses the ocean of worldly existence.
Those in this world who are devoid of action appear to me as fallen from dharma.
O Lord, O Beloved, out of compassion for those who lack faith in the teachings, the wise will not impart the meaning of the scriptures to them, just as one does not sow seeds in barren soil. (16.43)
And the determination of reality does not arise for one who is devoid of scripture;
therefore, having abandoned the definitive scripture, any other means is in vain. (16.44)
Just as one who wishes to cross the ocean might grasp a dog's tail, so too, without the definitive determination of reality, even doubt does not cease. (16.45)
O beautiful one, in a heart stained by the mire of doubt, the reflection of the sun of love cannot appear, by which Kṛṣṇa might shine forth. (16.46)
Therefore, it is certain that neither knowledge nor devotion arises in its true form within a human being who has fallen away from the conduct of the castes and stages of life. (16.47)
Therefore, one should perform the daily (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites without hesitation;
however, one should abandon from afar those actions performed for specific desires (kāmya) as well as those that are prohibited (niṣiddha).
Neither the obligatory nor the occasional rite ever binds one with the fruit of action;
however, by the mere non-performance of them, a transgression arises. (16.49)
There is no fruit in performing [rites] other than the purification of the mind; those embodied beings who perform rites for the sake of desired objects and the like are born again and again. (16.50)
Therefore, having abandoned that which is performed for desire, the wise person should perform the obligatory rites,
O beloved, whether in the state of being unawakened or even when awakened.
One's innate duty must be performed; one should not be overcome by obstacles therein.
Listen now to my definitive conclusion regarding that action which is performed even by one who is awakened.
Knowledge through mere report is not true awakening;
O Goddess of gods, when there is direct awakening, the body dissolves instantly.
Therefore, this verbal awakening does not exist as the ultimate reality;
for verbal cognition is indeed incapable of destroying the delusion of saṃsāra. (16.54)
Darkness never departs by the mere report of a lamp;
rather, it is only when the body has fallen, set ablaze by the fire of separation.
Then one should know that self-realization has been attained; otherwise, it remains merely verbal.
Through mere verbal awakening alone, one should abandon both obligatory and occasional rites. (16.56)
He should be known as one who incurs transgression; he shall not attain awakening.
For as long as there is identification with the body, so long indeed does the sense of "mine" persist. (16.57)
For as long as there is attachment to the body, action must indeed be performed;
one should perform the action prescribed by the scriptures for the sake of ceasing improper action (vikarman).
Since the inclination toward improper action (vikarman) is innate to human beings, by the power of such improper action, embodied beings [undergo rebirth] again and again. (16.59)
O Goddess, O virtuous lady! The daily and occasional rites, when performed without the desire for fruit, purify the mind; they do not result in [the accumulation of] physical karma. (16.60)
"O Goddess of gods, what loss is there for men in performing actions without desire?"—thus, out of ignorance regarding this definitive conclusion, the deluded consider themselves wise. (16.61)
Those with sinful minds, abandoning the practice of purification, indeed wander about;
they are attached to worldly pleasures and claim, "I am a knower of Brahman. (16.62)

One should abandon like an outcaste that person who has fallen from both ritual action and Brahman, who is attached to the pleasures of the body and senses, and who says, "I am a knower of Brahman. (16.63)
I do not consider him a man of true knowledge who, while prioritizing the doctrine of Brahman, remains bound by the regulations of caste and stage of life—like a donkey adorned with jewels. (16.64)
Subverting all sacred rites, they are indeed the destroyers of the world; for in the Kali age, the discourse of Brahman will exist in every house and among every person.
Then, in that time, there will be the destruction of righteous deeds;
for those devoid of righteous deeds who devote themselves only to evil.
For those asura-beings, there is no turning back from hell;
therefore, having thus reached a firm conclusion, one should be devoted to righteous deeds.
I consider those who serve Kṛṣṇa alone to be beloved by Kṛṣṇa;
thus, O Goddess, have I described to you the characteristics of latent impressions (vāsanā).
For by knowing which, the realization of one's own self arises indeed before long.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the glorious Pañcarātra, in the glorious Māheśvara Tantra, within the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī. 16.16.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Pārvatī said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, the definitive conclusion is well-esteemed by the virtuous."
This purifying characteristic of the conduct of the virtuous has been described for the sake of men.
For those who are devoid of righteous action, who have abandoned good conduct, and who are defiled and wicked, the realization of Brahman does not arise. (17.2)
Just as one might gradually leave behind the steps while descending into water step by step,
so too should that wise man gradually relinquish his attachments to the body.
When the identification with the body has dissolved and one’s own Self is known by itself,
one attains a state of being equal toward stone and gold, remaining poised in equanimity.
When the experience of one's own bliss arises toward those who are indifferent, enemies, or friends,
there is no further need for ritual actions at that time, just as a sovereign emperor has no need for begging.
Just as one who is satiated by nectar has no need for food, so too, when the bliss of one's own Self has arisen, there is no need for ritual action. (17.6)
What need is there for a palm-leaf fan when the breeze from the Malaya mountains has been obtained?
Once the dawning of the bliss of one's own Self has occurred, what purpose is served by ritual action?
Pārvatī said:
"O Lord, O Master of the Bhāgavatas, what you have spoken is excellent;
yet, with my mind agitated by doubt, I wish to know the ultimate truth."
In the Kali age, the discourse on Brahman will exist in every house and among every person for the purpose of destroying righteous action; of this there is no doubt.
Regarding that which has been spoken by you, I have a great doubt;
there is nothing whatsoever as pure as this discourse on Brahman.
Austerity, charity, ritual action, yoga, self-study, observances, and restraints—
all these culminate, O Maheśāna, immediately following the arising of the knowledge of Brahman.
O Mahādeva, for those great-souled ones who are solely devoted to the knowledge of Brahman,
everything— both that which is obligatory and that which is occasional— attains a state of constant perfection.
If even one who has destroyed the entire universe were liberated through the knowledge of Brahman,
there would be no loss of karma for him, just as a lotus is not affected by water.
The Kali age is exceedingly evil, characterized by darkness and impurity;
it constantly delights in unrighteousness, by which the people on earth are afflicted.
Where heretics shall arise as the cause of the destruction of Dharma,
and where there shall be a confusion of castes among those who plunder their respective duties.
There were twice-born men who sold their daughters and sold the Vedas;
they delighted in the customs of the Mlecchas in this world and were experts in the Mleccha languages.
Their limbs nourished by the food and drink of barbarians, they reviled righteous deeds;
devoid of the utterances *svāhā* and *svadhā*, they were devoted solely to their genitals and bellies.
In the Kali age, all people will be devoted to fallacious reasoning for the sake of coveting the wives and wealth of others, and they will be devoid of all righteousness.
"O one worshipped by the gods, this discourse on Brahman—which in the Kali age appears in every house and among every person—seems to me almost impossible, yet it is so. (17–19)
Even in this Kali age, so full of great sin, the glorification of Brahman has begun;
how then could it lead to the loss of dharma for people? This is my wonder in this matter. (17–20)
"Having reflected, speak to me, O God, out of compassion, O ocean of mercy.
Śiva said:
"O blessed lady, you have asked well for the sole benefit of all the worlds. (17–21)
Therefore, I shall declare that to you; listen with a one-pointed mind, for by the mere hearing of it, faith in the Dharma arises. (17–22)
Formerly, during a twelve-year drought when there was no water,
and when the abundance of forest roots and other provisions had been utterly consumed by forest fires and the sun.
Some beings, overcome by hunger and thirst—and some even reading *kṣut-tṛḍ-bhyāṃ ca parītāpaiḥ*—took refuge in mountain caves;
emaciated by disease, they perished while devouring one another. (17.24)
In the beautiful hermitage of Gautama, situated on the bank of the Tapatī, certain Brahmins arrived, afflicted by hunger and desiring to sustain their bodies. (17-25)
They beheld the sage Gautama, surrounded by a multitude of disciples, blazing as if with fire through the power of his Brahmanic splendor. || 17-26 ||
Having produced food through ascetic penance and nourishing a multitude of disciples,
all the brahmins bowed down to him with their hands joined in the gesture of reverence.
The Brāhmaṇas said:
"Save us, save us, O Sage, O giver of refuge to those who have come for protection!
We are all twice-born ones tormented by the fire of the stomach. (17–18)
In a region of the earth devoid of water, roots, tubers, and other such provisions cannot be obtained;
consequently, the rites enjoined by the Vedas simply do not proceed here.
Food is indeed the life-breath of living beings; he who gives food bestows life itself.
Therefore, by the gift of food, you, our father, have become the giver of life to us. (17.30)
On one side are all dharmas, sacrifices with the gift of one's entire possessions, fierce austerities, and even very many gifts and vows. (17-31)
O Sage, indeed there is no measure that can equal the gift of food;
hunger and thirst are the very laws of life, for by hunger the body is emaciated. (17.32)
Indeed, when the body becomes emaciated, the sense faculties become weakened;
with the functions of the senses and mind languid, one falls into a state of helplessness. (17.33)

When the mind withers, there is a dissolution of the intellect, and from that, meditation ceases. O Lord, for one who is thus distracted by contemplation, how can there be the experience of one's own Self? (17.34)
Therefore, there is no gift equal to food in the three worlds for one whose sense faculties and mental functions have withered and who is tormented by hunger. (17.35)
O Sage, by one who has provided satisfaction to living beings through the longing for food,
everything has been given, offered in sacrifice, recited, austerity performed, and auspicious merit accomplished.
It has indeed been heard by us that the earth filled with jewels was given by him to a twice-born man, and for that very reason, he attained perfection in knowledge.
O Lord of Sages, what else remains to be made known to you, who are omniscient?
Therefore, O dear one, act swiftly so that our lives may be sustained. (17.38)
For food is indeed the root of the body, and this physical form is the root of Dharma;
yet, regarding the purification of the mind, Dharma alone is specifically the cause. (17.39)
Devotion, knowledge, dispassion, and the purification of the mind—these arise for one whose mind is purified.
Therefore, this body is called the means for accomplishing all goals. (17.40)
Again and again one obtains a village, again wealth, again a field, again a house;
again one performs auspicious and inauspicious karma, but never again this body. (17.41)
The wise must by all means exert themselves to protect the body;
for even those afflicted with leprosy and other such diseases do not desire the abandonment of their bodies.
That [wealth] should be protected for the sake of Dharma; Dharma is for the sake of knowledge alone;
and knowledge is for the sake of the yoga of meditation—by means of that, one is liberated without delay. (17.43)
"Relying on the power of your asceticism, protect us miserable ones here"—
hearing these words of those brahmins, the one whose wealth is penance [replied].
Hearing [the cries] of the wretched who were afflicted by hunger, he became compassionate.
Gautama said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly wise ones! These words of yours are indeed just. (17.45)
The body is said to be the means for achieving dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
therefore, O lords of sages, the body must be protected with great effort. (17.46)
Those devotees and practitioners who do not desire the abandonment of the body—though smeared by great sins and the like, and having desisted from all ritual actions—[attain liberation]. (17.47)
Indeed, that very body which has become a burden to the earth must be cast off—provided it is one that has performed great merit through service to the ancestors, the gods, and guests. (17.48)
And since he is fit for the yoga of meditation on the Lord, how can he deserve renunciation?
If the body must be nourished here even by means of prohibited action, [then what need is there for renunciation]? (17.49)
Having burned those [karmas], he indeed leads one to the supreme state;
as long as the body remains in this world, one should practice what is wholesome.
Since this body is as fragile as a water bubble and destined for destruction, one should practice the eternal Dharma with this transient physical form. (17.51)
Seeing everything as consisting of Brahman, one is liberated from the distress of delusion;
therefore, being that very person through ascetic power, I shall accomplish what you desire.
"O Brahmins, may you be free from feverish distress and remain diligent in your respective duties;
for at the door of the fortunate man who has performed meritorious deeds, seekers of wealth arrive. (17.53)
Therefore, they should be honored even at the cost of one's life and wealth;
for this body, composed of the five elements, is impermanent and fragile as a moment.
Fame and dharma will inevitably perish; they do not endure in every way if one abandons malice toward living beings and fails to maintain compassion for them. (17.55)
The true Dharma was not acquired, nor was fame spread upon the earth;
neither was the self examined for its purity by those who know the Vedas and by the virtuous. (17.56)
That birth is for the sake of bearing the burden of the earth; for he who lives is indeed as good as dead.
Therefore, O lords of sages, I am here for you who seek [my help], at the expense of my own ascetic merit.
"I shall perform service here so that my body may be sustained.
Having said this, Gautama [honored] them indeed with gifts, honors, worship, and other such offerings. (17.58)
Delighted by his arrival as a guest, he honored him accordingly.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā, within the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the venerable Māheśvaratantra in the glorious Pañcarātra. 17.17.
The eighteenth chapter.
Śiva said:
Thus were the sages then honored by that sage.
They lived happily in that spacious and auspicious hermitage.
[Alternatively, there is the reading *prātarutthāya*. Those seeds sown in the morning that had reached maturity by midday, and others in the afternoon—by means of those, the Sage sustained them. 18.2
Satisfying the gods with oblations (havya) and the ancestors with ancestral offerings (kavya), those lords of sages then spent many series of days subsisting on the remaining nectar.
Then, at the end of twelve years, there was a most beautiful rain;
the earth, along with its sprouts and its waters, became once again as it was before.
Those subjects, who formerly dwelt in mountain caves, took up their respective places;
O beloved, due to the lack of food and other necessities, dharma perished and [adharma] began to prevail.
The earth was filled with food and other necessities, and the entire world was most auspicious;
then, after some time, the lords of sages desired to depart.
Bound by love and unable to endure separation, he visited the Brahmins every day;
thus, those lords of sages remained for several months that had been forbidden [for travel].
Again, out of eagerness, they asked him regarding his departure for his own hermitage;
Gautama, however, being deeply pained by the grief of separation, said "No" to the brahmins.
Then, having made a secret agreement among themselves, some of those brahmins spoke to one another as to how the abandonment of the sage might be accomplished.
Bound by the power of affection, the sage will not abandon us of his own accord;
therefore, act with diligence so that he may be abandoned by us. (18.10)
Deliberating thus with one another, they conceived a plan in their minds:
"Having cast a curse upon the sage, we shall go as we please. (18.11)
Struck down by fate, they all consulted with one another;
then, at some point at midday, they went to perform their midday rites.
Surrounded by hosts of sages, he went toward Tapatī,
[toward] the cow created by the munis, who was aged and trembling excessively.
Seeing her sinking into the mire, the compassionate Gautama felt pity;
having approached the side of Surabhi, the sage touched her. (18.14)
At that moment, the illusory cow suddenly fell down, having met its death.
Seeing this, the sages said, "Fie, fie upon your deed, O Gautama! (18.15)
"A cow has been harmed; she was weak—what could be more blameworthy than this?
From this day forward, men seeking even water shall not find it at your door. (18.16)
"They ought not to remain; what can we do? We shall depart from there.
When he had spoken thus, the sage reflected and perceived the harm that would result from their presence. (18.17)
Enraged, like a blazing fire, he spoke these words:
"By your own actions, you shall become outcasts from the Vedas and ungrateful. (18.18)
In the Kali age, you fools will become devoted to censuring the Vedas, the Brāhmaṇas, cows, and mantras, while pretending to be devoted to the discourse on Brahman.
Corrupt within yet pure without, devoted to the doctrine of causality, they turn their backs on dharma and ritual action out of the conceit of being knowers of Brahman. (18–20)
Those who are experts in restating that "Brahman is truth and the world is false" [ask]:
what would happen to auspicious and inauspicious karmas because of the falsity of the world? (18–21)
Thus, these deluded nihilists, ill-intentioned revilers of the Veda, [speak] with words born of the playful display of Brahmanical doctrine and filled with pride in their own sentiments. (18–22)
Merely concealing their evil deeds behind the guise of a virtuous appearance, through formal precepts, and by means of nectar-like pleasant speech and the like— these serve only as a curtain.
Proclaiming yourselves to be possessors of knowledge in this world, you who are evil-minded shall indeed become cat-like hypocrites in the final age.
"But true knowledge shall never arise for you"—thus was it said to those cursed by Gautama when they attempted to destroy the Dharma. (18-25)
The latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of those who acted against Gautama became established;
then, endowed with those impressions, they became deceitful in the sinful age of Kali.

Having descended to the surface of the earth, [having heard these words: "O Brahmasṛṣṭis, having set aside service to the illustrious Pūrṇapuruṣottama and instead relying on the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) and other matters prescribed by the Vedas, the path to your own abode must never be abandoned here; for it is seen that there is transgression (*pratyavāya*) from abandoning service to one's husband. Therefore, for the Brahmasṛṣṭis, service to their own husband, who is Pūrṇapuruṣottama himself, is the supreme duty. Those who have taken refuge among the Brahmasṛṣṭis, being base people, practice here things that are indeed contrary to the Vedas and the Śāstras. (18–27)
They hate right conduct, faith, sacrifices, vows, and austerities;
having encountered one another, they act with hostility, their knowledge lost and their minds bewildered. (18.28)
Those who are intent on seizing the property of others, harming others, and approaching the wives of others—
through their association, the creation of Brahmā will fall into impurity.
Just as a crystal appears soiled due to its connection with impurity, even so this creation of Brahman appears as such because it rests upon Him. (18.30)
Therefore, those who desire to know the truth should truly abandon reliance on such hypocrites;
for they are described as those who maintain the guise of performing virtuous religious acts.
There are also other heretics who have resorted to a demonic nature;
those most sinful ones likewise revile the ancient Vedic dharma. (18.32)
I shall tell you that in brief; listen with a one-pointed mind, so that heresy may never delude the intellect of those who hear it. (18.33)
Formerly, during the war between the gods and the asuras, when the asuras had been defeated,
all these who were appointed to oversee heresy were created by the Self-born One.
While all the Asuras were performing austerities seeking victory,
Viṣṇu, urged by the gods, assumed an exceedingly difficult-to-penetrate illusion.
The Lord, whose soul is yoga, deluded them for the sake of creating obstacles to their asceticism;
that high-minded one spoke to those fools in the form of a Buddha.
"All the gods can be conquered by you through [your] views";
having thus established themselves in the Buddhist Dharma, they became capable [of doing so]. (18.37)
He said to them: "Become my Arhats, like me; those who possess the Dharma together with knowledge are remembered as 'Arhats'. (18.38)
The Buddhist śrāvakas, the Nirgranthas, and likewise the Siddhaputras—all these should be known as Arhats who act with malice. (18.39)
To those whom he told, "Live on, having completely cast off the affliction of the triple Veda," they became known as the Jīvakas,
excluded from all religious duties.
Those who, having become like the sun in the sky, indeed expound the dharmas, are also called Kāpilas; for Kapila is the Sun himself.
"Practice this, my command of exceeding splendor," he said to them;
those Carakas should be known as deceitful practitioners of unrighteous conduct. (18.42)
It is said that "long practice" refers either to the subtle form of the Dharma;
because you have been told, "Practice the Dharma," you are those who possess long vision.
Wearing blue rags and thus being clad in bark, they said,
"Take refuge in this dharma which is exceedingly pure and stainless."
Viṣṇu spoke through his illusory power (māyā): "For they are proclaimed to be pure, even those who eat excrement and who have skulls as their ornaments. (18.45)
Likewise, all other evil-minded ones—the deities of the Asuras, the Buddhist Śrāvakas, the Nirgranthas, and similarly the Siddhaputras—[shall be destroyed]. (18.46)
All proponents of selflessness are nihilists; they are born again and again among those who abide in unrighteousness. (18.47)
Having reached hell through those very actions they cultivated, there are those men who wear matted hair in vain, who shave their heads in vain, and who go naked in vain. (18.48)
These and others are heretics outside the Veda, practitioners of evil deeds;
by the word "pāśa" (bond), the dharma of the triple Veda is meant, for it is remembered as such because it protects the world. (18.49)
Because they fragment that [truth], for that reason they are called *pākhaṇḍas* (heretics).
For if their status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) were not stated with due respect, [they would be rejected]. (18.50)
Thinking that it is simply impossible, others may come to hold an impartial view toward those who are absolute adversaries of the established path of the Three Vedas. (18.51)
Without rejecting all of them—the heretics, those who persist in improper acts, the cat-like hypocrites, and likewise the sophists—purity of dharma is not attained. (18.52)
One should not honor, even with a mere word, those who follow the conduct of cranes (hypocrites), nor those Smṛtis that are outside the Veda, nor any false doctrines whatsoever. || 18.53 ||
All those are fruitless after death, for they are remembered as having darkness as their ultimate end;
so too are the Purāṇas, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and likewise Pāśupata.
The customs of countries, castes, and families, as well as other even greater dharmas, are all authoritative provided they do not contradict the Vedas; otherwise, they would not be so. (18.55)
Whatever Smṛtis are outside the Veda, and whatever false doctrines there may be—all of them are fruitless and, moreover, are causes of sin. (18.56)
Therefore, O Goddess, worshipped by the Lord of the Gods, with every effort one should abandon all that is contrary to the Vedas and take refuge in the Veda alone. (18.57)
The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and the Dharmaśāstras, together with the Vedāṅgas—these fourteen are the seats of knowledge and of dharma. (18.58)
Just as the Vedas, so too is the Tantra for the purpose of determining the Dharma;
by practicing what is taught therein, O Goddess, one is liberated from the bonds of worldly existence. (18.59)
Know those fools of sinful intellect who act otherwise than this to be Asuras, who were deluded by Viṣṇu in ancient times. (18.60)
Those who are eloquent in discussions of Brahman while being solely intent on the destruction of Dharma—one should turn one's gaze toward the sun upon merely looking at their faces. (18.61)
Merely by his touch, one should enter the water along with one's clothes;
in the Kali age, they will proclaim the doctrine of Brahman among every person.
Thus, O Goddess, that which was asked by you, the most excellent, has been told to me in brief, O Great Goddess; what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Śrīmāheśvaratantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. 18-18.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
Śiva said:
Now, O Śivā, listen to the determination of the desires of those who are dear [to you].
By the mere hearing of which, detachment from the body and the home arises.

And that desire which existed regarding the sight of their beloveds during the Rāsa dance—having been shown there, it remained for the most part unfulfilled and was thus distinguished [as a source of longing]. (19.2)

O Goddess, for the sake of enjoying those [pleasures] again, all those beloved ones who had departed from the rāsa dance entered the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), which consists of time and māyā, together with him. || 19-3 ||
O Goddess, having arisen in the land of Bhārata, they did not remain in one place due to the influence of delusion, which was created by Īśa and is difficult to overcome. (19.4)
Having lost their connection with the self, they became dear to the Blessed One,
just as a person in a dream whose memory has been cast off by sleep.

Just as one who has obtained an elephant in a dream considers himself to be that elephant, so too, having assumed a form acquired through delusion, one identifies with it due to the state of self-absorption. (19.6)
They wander in various ways through high and low wombs;
therein, they are defiled by the contact with karma arising from the conceit of a body. (19.7)
From that, a bondage of karma arises which leads further and further into births such as those of dogs, crows, owls, cats, donkeys, vultures, and so forth. (19.8)
Wandering again and again among humans, being born and dying over and over, there is no end to their cycle. || 19-9 ||
They have experienced again and again the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the intense suffering of childhood, and the suffering caused by the abandonment of the body. (19.10)
In one place there is dharma, in another grief; in one place passion, hatred, and the like;
in one place bondage, in another liberation; and in yet another, the beating of the king. (19.11)
Driven anywhere by the desire for food, even though they were poor, their senses and facial expressions became withered, and they fell into a state of wretchedness. (19.12)
Having encountered extraordinary suffering arising from the loss of sons, friends, wives, and so forth, they indulge in torments, crying out "Alas! Alas! again and again. (19.13)
Just as the devoted wife of the royal seer Bṛhatsena, deluded regarding the proper rule, fell asleep with unwashed feet and while still impure from remnants of food. (19.14)
A certain yakṣa, wandering at night, carried her off while she was asleep and brought her to a great island in the ocean created by the power of the yakṣa's illusion.
She beheld a divine city with celestial watchtowers and gateways; then the Yakṣa vanished from her sight, as she was utterly deluded by his possession.
The young woman wandered through the city from house to house, deprived of her senses;
wherever she went, she was terrified by the people there.
Wandering in the darkness of the Tāmiśra hell with a bewildered mind, she was there forcibly stripped of her garments by adversaries somewhere. (19.18)
With disheveled hair, stripped of clothing, and her body grey with dust,
she wandered alone day and night through the city like a female ghost.
Weeping piteously and dejected, being repeatedly beaten by the people, her mind agitated by hunger and thirst, she seemed to leap from person to person. (19–20)
Exiled from the city by the great multitude into the forest,
her mind was terrified upon hearing the terrifying roar of tigers and lions.
Upon seeing them, the virtuous woman hid herself once more within the clusters of trees;
bitten by serpents dwelling in the hollows of the trees, she became helpless.
Her mind reeling from poison, she lay upon the ground;
bitten in all her joints by scorpions and other creatures that had emerged from beneath the earth.
Thus the queen of the king endured various kinds of torments in the great forest, her lotus-feet pierced by gravel and thorns.
"Who are you, and to whom do you belong, O lady of beautiful thighs? Thus questioned by the Seven Sages, she replied:
"I know neither myself, nor my father, nor my mother, nor a husband. (19–25)
"I am submerged in an ocean of suffering and extreme misery," she declared, having been severely tormented and repeatedly reviled by wicked city-dwellers. (19–26)
Indeed, my clothes, ornaments, and other possessions were stolen by wicked thieves;
overcome by hunger and thirst, I was banished from the city by those most sinful men. (19–27)
She went to the great forest and wandered about, agitated by the fear of tigers and lions;
her inner being was afflicted by the poison of cruel serpents and scorpions.
I wander day and night, knowing neither the cardinal nor the intermediate directions;
therefore, O merciful ones, grant assistance to me who am without a protector. (19–29)
When this was said by that virtuous woman, who was deeply afflicted by compassion,
the lords of sages sprinkled the Yakṣa with the water from their water-pots.
When the illusory power (māyā) had subsided, he regained his own self;
he then remembered his mother, his father, and likewise his husband, Bṛhatsena.
Ashamed and with her face cast downward, the young woman addressed the lords of sages:
"Of the wise Bṛhatsena, born of the Solar dynasty... (19.32)
"O brahmins and gods, I am beloved; having gone to bed while still impure from food, I was brought to the shore of the ocean by someone, overwhelmed with fear. (19.33)
There I beheld a single, divine, and most wonderful city; in it wandered alone a woman distressed, who endured the suffering of the world day and night. (19.34)
Then, driven out by the citizens, she reached this great forest;
her self-knowledge having vanished, she wandered upon a path filled with suffering.
"By you, our ignorance has been destroyed, like darkness by the rays of the sun;
through your favor, we feel as if we have recovered a lost self. (19.36)
And I see my body, with its garments, ornaments, and finery, just as it was before, like one who has awakened from sleep after a dream has vanished.
"O most blessed ones, by your grace we have crossed the ocean of suffering.
Having said this, she bowed again and again at the lotus feet of the sage.
Then the best of sages, consoling that virtuous lady, said:
"Do not fear, O auspicious one, you who are devoted to your husband. (19.39)
The universe originates from ignorance; in reality, nothing exists at all.
As long as ignorance resides within the self, so long does it manifest fear. (19.40)
O beloved of the royal sage! Just as even a false dream causes fear, so too does this world, though false, cause fear to those who partake in such [delusions]. (19.41)
Just as a rope, when unknown, appears as a snake and causes fear, so too is this phenomenal world (prapañca) a transformation (vivarta) of Brahman, conditioned by ignorance (avidyā). (19.42)
When it is not recognized as being one's own self, that which constitutes a portion of it is terrifying;
however, when it is recognized as one's own self, it no longer brings about fear. (19.43)
The Self is pure, imperishable, subtle, all-pervading, eternal, and stainless;
yet, veiled by its own māyā, it perceives a dream within itself. (19.44)
Just as water might be covered by mosses arising from it, so too is the absolute, imperishable Brahman concealed by its own māyā. (19.45)
The Supreme Brahman, veiled by Māyā, again entering the dream-mansion as the witness of the dream, quickly assumes the name Nārāyaṇa. (19.46)
From his navel there arose a lotus, and upon it was born the four-faced one,
the preeminent among those who know the Vedas and the seed of the tree of worldly existence.
O beautiful lady, we have all been born there as mere dream-creatures;
impelled by our past actions, we wander upon a path composed of dreams and illusion.
O virtuous lady, you have indeed experienced this illusory manifestation of the Yakṣa;
now that it has withdrawn, you have regained your own self as before.
In the same way, all we living beings are composed of the reflection of Brahman;
upon the dissolution of the portions that are effects of Māyā, we shall become of the nature of the Imperishable. (19.50)
While the effects of illusion persist, suffering, grief, fear, and lamentation exist;
likewise, dharma and adharma, merit and demerit, and even truth itself are perceived. (19.51)
Therefore, having firmly realized in your heart that suffering is unreal,
O beautiful lady, remain forever free from sorrow and free from fear.
Having spoken thus, O beloved, those best of sages, by the power of their yoga-māyā, brought her home in the twinkling of an eye, separated from him by but a single ghaṭikā.
The king’s beloved wife, too, having reflected upon that event again and again, overcome with great curiosity, reported everything to the king. (19.54)

Thus, O Goddess of the gods, those beloved ones of the Blessed One indeed possess a deluded understanding of the nature of the self; they are like a magical illusion or a dream of the Supreme Self (or, according to another reading, "by the Supreme Self"). || 19.55 ||
O Goddess of gods, those whose minds are deluded and who have fallen away from bliss wander again and again through various wombs within this world, O beloved, even though it is unreal. (19.56)
In their own abode of great bliss, no appearance of suffering exists;
nor is there ever any experience of suffering for those residing there. (19.57)
There was no meanness, no suffering, no agitation, and no discontent at all;
for she considered that request made by her beloved to be a persistent insistence, O Daughter of the Mountain King.
The mind, through its connection with the dream-state of the immutable [Self], produced these mental objects (or "appearances," according to the alternative reading *bhāvaḥ*).
O Great Goddess, although this dream is non-existent, it is a source of great suffering. (19.59)
For even now, the remainder of desire arising from one's own latent impressions continues to be indulged in.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the Śrī Pañcarātra, in the Śrī Māheśvara Tantra, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. 19-19.
Now begins the twentieth chapter.
Pārvatī said:
"O God, O Mahādeva, O Supreme Self, O Supreme Lord!"
Having heard this which you have spoken, my mind is exceedingly agitated. (20.1)
Even though the Lord, the immutable Supreme Self, is devoid of effort,
a desire to see arose within him to behold his secret play.
For those who dwell in eternal bliss and are dear to the Supreme Self, the desire to see has arisen solely upon witnessing suffering. (20.3)
O Maheśvara, this appears to me as a great marvel;
O Lord of Gods, dispel that dart in my mind which causes great agony. (20.4)

But for the Perfect One whose desires are fulfilled, [these exist] merely through the observation of divine play; indeed, those beloved ones who constitute His limbs are equal to Him, the Supreme Self. (20-5)
How could one who desires suffering find pleasure in those [women] whose very form is absolute bliss? For no fool anywhere ever delights in the sight of suffering. (20.6)
"Tell me this, O Blessed One, having shown compassion toward me.
Śiva said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim a most wonderful secret. (20.7)
"O beloved daughter of the mountain! That which is most secret in the Vedas, Āgamas, and Purāṇas, I have never spoken of to anyone from this day forward."
O Goddess! Out of affection for you, I shall speak this and not otherwise;
indeed, it must be kept secret by you from both Skanda and Gaṇeśa.
One who steals what has been revealed takes away dharma, as well as fame, fortune, and happiness,
just as a common prostitute misappropriates the Vedas, Shastras, and Puranas.
This knowledge is a great knowledge (mahāvidyā), to be guarded like a woman of noble family;
well-guarded, this great knowledge brings about the attainment of wisdom for men. (20.11)
Just as revealed property falls into the hands of thieves, so too does revealed knowledge fall into the hands of the uninitiated. 20.12
Therefore, this knowledge that reveals Brahman must be guarded with effort;
for mantras, medicinal herbs, ritual actions, and dharmas indeed bear fruit only when kept secret.
I shall tell you even that which is inexpressible; listen with a one-pointed mind.
Bliss that falls within the scope of calculation exists only in the Imperishable (akṣara).
The Teacher, whose senses are fully restrained, who rules over the earth consisting of seven islands—healthy, without rival, young, and honored by the lords of kings. (20.15)
O Queen of the Gods! That [bliss] is indeed called human bliss;
a hundredfold human bliss is said to be the bliss of the Gandharvas. (20.16)
A hundredfold joy of the Gandharvas is declared to be the joy of the Pitṛs; indeed, a hundredfold joy of the Pitṛs is said to be equal to one joy of the Upadevas. (20.17)
A hundred Devānandas is proclaimed as Upadevānanda;
O Goddess! A hundred Devānandas is called Vairañcyānanda. (20.18)
The hundredfold bliss of Vairañca is known as Vaiṣṇava-bliss;
the hundredfold bliss of Vaiṣṇava is said to be Rudra-bliss. (20.19)
Described by a hundred Rudrānandas is the great Īśānanda;
described by a hundred Īśānandas is that known as Īśvarānanda (an alternative reading is *īśvarānandasaṃjñakaḥ*); while Śaivānanda is absolute. (20–20)
O Goddess! By a hundredfold of that, there arises the supreme bliss of Prakṛti (Prakṛtyānanda).
A hundredfold of the bliss of Prakṛti is called the bliss of Puruṣa (Puruṣānanda). || 20-21 ||
The hundredfold bliss of the Person is called the bliss of the Imperishable; the Imperishable is the Supreme Brahman, and from that, the bliss of Brahman is traditionally known. (20–22)
The universe consists of the bliss of Brahman; no diversity exists therein.
Due to its association with the limiting adjunct of Māyā, it is perceived as manifold. (20–23)
But when that cognition is dispelled, only the Supreme Brahman remains;
O Goddess, its Māyā is Prakṛti, which is eternal and possesses the same nature as Him.
For she is preeminent in pure sattva, stainless, and consists of the nature of gnosis; therein appeared the reflection of the imperishable Supreme Self. (20–25)
O Goddess, those who propound the conclusions of the Vedas call him Puruṣa;
he alone, in the form of Time (Kāla), is the agitator of Prakṛti. (20–26)
From him was born Nārāyaṇa, who is designated as the Praṇava;
the wise call him Hiraṇyagarbha as well. (20–27)
Those who know the scriptures declare that he alone is composed of the Śabdabrahman;
therefore, O beloved, the Vedas proceed from that Śabdabrahman as their very self.
In the beginning, the universe consists of sound, and from that it becomes composed of objects;
sound is of the nature of *prakṛti*, while the object is of the nature of *puruṣa*. (20–29)
This phenomenal world is of a dual nature; therefore, it assumes the forms of male and female.
So too do you and I, as well as Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī, Brahmā and Sarasvatī. (20–30)
The sun is Sañjñānala, Svāhā; Puruhūta is Pulomajā;
the ocean is Maryādā, and the tree is Pallavinīlatā. (20.31)
Whether it be great or even very small, all that consists of these two natures;
for both of these—the eternal Prakṛti and Puruṣa—reside within the Imperishable.

O Goddess, disputants here contend that both [the waking and dreaming states], which undergo transformation as the phenomenal world through their distinction as waking and dreaming, are eternal. (20.33)
"O Goddess, some proponents of deluded intellect, under the influence of egoism, claim that the phenomenal world is either eternal or indeed non-eternal. (20.34)

They do not understand the eternal and the non-eternal due to the fault of grasping their own position [or, as another reading has it, due to the fault of grasping their own doctrine]. Or rather, because the cause is eternal, let there be eternality even in the stream [of effects]. (20-35)
Since the destruction of what is produced is established by scripture, what harm is there even if it is impermanent?
O Goddess, it is only those of base intellect who thus dispute between duality and non-duality.
Those who know the truth understand that the individual soul (jīva) is distinct from the Lord (Īśvara);
it is Brahman itself that is proclaimed as the "soul" due to the power of ignorance. (20.37)
The proponents of non-duality do not know the individual soul (jīva) in the ultimate sense;
yet this is not contradictory, O Goddess, because of the distinction based on the limit of ignorance.
But when ignorance is destroyed by knowledge obtained through the grace of the Lord, O beautiful one, the waking state dissolves like the witness of a dream. (20.39)
Only the one eternal Brahman alone remains;
for thus say the proponents of non-duality who rely solely upon the Śruti. (20-40)
The Supreme Brahman is indeed one; there is nothing manifold here at all.
Just as clay alone is real, so too are name and form merely modifications.
Thus, non-duality has been proclaimed in manifold ways by hundreds of scriptural texts;
yet even those devoted to the doctrine of duality [cite] the statement "two birds" [from the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad].
For they indeed praise duality alone; non-duality consists of devotion.
O beloved, those who stand upon the steps below the level of non-duality are merely situated on the lower rungs. (20.43)
Among them, Nārāyaṇa is the manifest Supreme Brahman according to the Vedic revelation;
the individual souls consist of the reflection of Brahman and are dependent upon the qualities of their minor limiting adjuncts.
O beloved, they also say that those who are dependent and subject to others are eternal;
yet even such "eternality" is unimpeded only when rooted in delusion.
"For those who have attained sleep, sleep itself remains stable for a time"—those who dispute this without knowing the heart of the scriptures [speak thus]. (20.46)
In this investigation of duality and non-duality, they would not attain the ultimate reality;
therefore, with every effort, one should seek the singular certainty of all the scriptures. (20.47)

O Goddess of gods! having understood this, they worship it as the embodiment of the fruit, free from doubt, disregarding the various differences in scriptural statements due to the affliction of the intellect and the ego. (20-48)
These very ones proceed as if pierced by thorns and fallen from their fruit;
yet Brahman alone is non-dual, appearing as two through the distinction of its playful manifestation (līlā). || 20-49 ||
Both engagement and withdrawal are established within the differentiation of divine play;
for withdrawal is indeed designated as happiness, and happiness is of the nature of bliss.

O Goddess, O lady of excellent hips, through the consequence of primordial nature (prakṛti), its manifold activity proceeds; for those who do not understand it, it exists in the form of suffering. (20.51)
That [divine play] is said to belong to the Imperishable (akṣara), whose nature transcends all else;
yet even a trace of the play of worldly activity (pravṛtti-līlā) does not exist in the Supreme Self (parātman), who is beyond. (20.52)
O Goddess of gods! For one who possesses desire, there shall always remain but a mere fraction—a mere trace—of that great ocean of eternal bliss, even while he maintains his eternal form. (20.53)
He who can take any form at will is eternally blissful; a fraction of his desire is said to be a mere trace.
Therefore, O Goddess, in that very Imperishable One, there is indeed eternal desire for the vision [of him]. (20.54)
Therefore, O Pārvatī, that desire to see which arises from that very syllable does not have a single agent; for it consists of both the supreme and the non-supreme.
In the Imperishable, which consists solely of the essence of knowledge, desire does not arise spontaneously;
nor does the Supreme Person, the Full Self, directly impel [it]. (20.56)
Therefore, those who know the scriptures declare her to consist of *sāmarasya* (perfect equilibrium).
Through this *sāmarasya*, she is the abode of bliss, having abandoned the grasping of her own side and of objects. (20.57)
But having completely abandoned the possessor of the limbs, it crawled intensely into the limbs themselves;
consequently, a desire to see [the suffering] arose even in the mistresses regarding the sight of that misery.
But she pervades both and is the cause of all causes (or, according to another reading, "the cause of all causes").
From her proceeds the activity of effects, which is bound to the qualities of the cause.

Having become of the nature of both female and male, she created Nidrā (Sleep) by her will through the various distinctions from Brahmā down to a blade of grass; that Nidrā also was born as having a dual nature.
Consisting of knowledge, inherently pure, and devoid of external activity, it creates delusion through sleep; for that [delusion] is indeed both conscious and unconscious.
That which is conscious in nature is the cause of an effect that possesses consciousness; yet it is also the cause of the insentient, because this [effect] is itself devoid of consciousness. (20.62)

He alone is said to be both knowledge and ignorance; hear the reason for that as well: for this [Self] is the knot of the conscious and the unconscious, yet it exists solely in the form of consciousness. (20.63)
O Goddess! when it undergoes transformation, they know that as "vidyā" (knowledge);
but when, having veiled consciousness, it assumes solely the form of delusion—|| 20-64 ||
Obscuring the cognition of the living self (jīva), it is sung of as ignorance (avidyā); casting off darkness and impurity, it is characterized by pure goodness (śuddhasattva). (20.65)
O Dear One, it is said that Māyā is that which creates the distinction within the intellect of the individual soul; having cast off its sāttvika portion, she remains as pure consciousness alone.
They know that knowledge which makes [Brahman] directly manifest as the "knowledge of Brahman" (brahmavidyā).
Therefore, O lady of excellent complexion, I have described that knowledge to you in three ways.
From that, the three qualities (guṇas) were born; they too are of such a nature, O Śivā!
Know sattva to be consciousness, and know tamas to be unconsciousness. (20.68)
Because it possesses the nature of both [rajas and tamas], that rajas consists of both the conscious and the unconscious;
the five elements were born from it, and they too are of such a nature.
And because they possess a twofold nature— as that which is to be presided over and as the presiding agent—
the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) arose from them, assuming both forms.
All this that I was asked by you has been told, O Śivā!
In brief, O Maheśānī! What more do you wish to hear? (20.71)
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the glorious *Pañcarātra*, in the glorious *Māheśvaratantra*, within the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī. 20.20.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
Śiva said:
"Listen further, O Goddess of gods, to another supreme secret."
It should be guarded with great effort and must not be shown to just anyone. || 21-1 ||
This should be spoken to one who has been thoroughly tested through beatings, threats, and the like;
for without a worthy vessel, this knowledge never remains. (21.2)
When the syllable has manifested, there is a most auspicious power called *icchā* (will), which, upon seeing the longing for the separation from true love, envelops the limbs. (21.3)
Then she conceived a passion for Puruṣottama;
filled with longing, she joined her mistress and entreated him.
Though forbidden with many kinds of words, all those beloved women, deluded by desire, did not heed them and entreated him every day.
O beloved, when their prayers were accepted by the Imperishable One in the past, she then returned to sleep and fell into deep thought once more.
The conscious self, the Puruṣa, being directly agitated by sleep consisting of delusion,
lies upon the auspicious couch composed of the five Brahmans.
O beloved, as soon as he was reeling with sleep and had forgotten his true self,
that other [consciousness] indeed sported within the pericarp of the lotus of his heart.
O Goddess! She divided her own form into five parts by herself:
Udgāriṇī, Pālikā, and likewise Saṃhārikā; || 21-9 ||
Viśālā and Vyāpikā—these are proclaimed as the five powers (śaktis). || 21-10 ||
She who removes [impurity] with rajas as her predominant quality is considered Pālinī;
she who has tamas as her predominant quality is Saṃhartrī; and she who is pure sattva is Viśālikā. || 21-11 ||
The attributeless, all-pervading power, known as Will (icchā), is said to be fivefold. O Goddess, these very powers arise in the waking state, as well as those that are natural (prākṛta).
On that bed made of desire, there is a faultless couch; upon the shoulders of the two nurses, Udāriṇī and Pālikā, rest his two feet. (21.13)
Her two hands rest upon the region of her broad and captivating neck;
Vyāpikā stands as a support, serving as a couch-like plank. (21.14)
Within the five [elements], there was a reflection of the imperishable conscious self;
for that consciousness which is reflected therein indeed gives rise to her. (21.15)
He manifested that which is the extremely extensive limiting adjunct (upādhi) consisting of the Vedas and so forth;
and within that reflection of consciousness, O Śivā, there is that which protects.
He manifested a very extensive adjunct consisting of the four-armed form and others;
and that consciousness which is reflected therein is indeed the power of withdrawal (saṃhāriṇī).
O most beautiful one!
That consciousness which is reflected in the limiting adjuncts such as Indra and others—within that [reflection], there is a certain vastness. (21.18)
And he manifested merely the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the eight arms;
that consciousness which is reflected therein is considered to be all-pervasive.
And from that, O beloved, Brahmā created the ten-armed one who possesses five faces and other attributes, as well as Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. (21–20)
Having attained a fivefold state, she eternally sustains the supreme [Lord] and [carries out] creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace.

Those who have the form of the presiding deities of the elements constantly perform [their functions] for the sake of accomplishing the triad beginning with creation; they enjoy a portion of the three [gods]. (21–22)
The wise know that concealment (*tirodhāna*) and grace (*anugraha*) reside in the two feet of the bed;
through the fivefold division of powers, the Supreme Will itself is *Sumaṅgalā*.
She assumes the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, possessing various natures;
however, the form of the Imperishable (Akṣara) is twofold, due to the distinction between Puruṣa and Akṣara.
Nārāyaṇa himself was born from Puruṣa, beheld by him in a dream; O beloved, Nāda and Bindu were born as Śiva and Śakti from Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa exists in three ways by virtue of consisting of sound (nāda) and the point (bindu):
Saṅkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. || 21–26 ||
Viṣṇu alone is said to be fourfold, indeed appearing in manifold ways through his various portions;
O Īśvarī, I am Rudra, whose self consists of eleven divisions.
O beautiful one, there are hundreds and millions of divisions of my own self;
yet these two, Sadāśiva and Īśvara, are devoid of such divisions of the self.
O Maheśānī, Nārāyaṇa arose in two ways through the division of the Vedas and the Praṇava; he was indeed the Sound (Nāda) resulting from the contemplation, "May I become manifold."
O beautiful one, no division exists within the drop, whose nature is indivisible.
O auspicious lady, this is the Great Principle (mahattattva), which is the mind of Nārāyaṇa.
When the mind thought, "May I become many," from that ego (ahaṅkāra) was born; having issued forth, it attained the state of a drop (bindu).
The *bindu* should be known as being of the nature of emptiness; therefore, the universe is devoid of objective reality.
This very *ahaṅkāra*, though pervasive, is seen within the manifestation of Brahman. (21–32)
The radiance of Brahman is changeless, free from conceptual proliferation, and stainless; it neither acts nor is it tainted, like a lamp that illuminates.
O beautiful one, the agency and the state of being the enjoyer belong to the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra);
likewise do merit and demerit, virtue and vice, as well as bondage, liberation, and so forth. (21.34)
It would be divided by the ego through the arrangement of various distinctions;
because of its identity with the ego, it is clearly perceived even within a mere appearance. (21.35)
As long as this knot consisting of egoism is not torn asunder, even though it does not exist, transmigratory existence nevertheless does not release one. (21.36)
O Goddess, just as the redness of a crystal produced by contact with a hibiscus flower does not depart without the removal of that flower. (21.37)
In the same way, O Goddess of the Gods, as long as there is no falling away from the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), the cycle of transmigration does not cease for the living being,
even in tens of millions of billions of kalpas.
O Pārvatī, this ego (ahaṅkāra) is said to be threefold according to the distinction of the qualities (guṇas);
this very ego is twofold: as "I" [the cosmic] and as residing in the individual soul (jīva).
The principle of Mahat is said to be threefold, according to the divisions of the internal (ādhyātmika) and so forth;
that which has the form of the mind of Nārāyaṇa is called the divine (ādhidaivika).
That which is the mental form of living beings is called the "internal" (ādhyātmika);
that which exists in the form of the body of Brahman is called the "physical" (ādhibhautika). || 21-41 ||
Established in Nārāyaṇa as his presiding deity (or, according to another reading, "established in Nārāyaṇa as the form of the inner self"),
he manifested through the distinctions of phonemes by way of the very nature of the Vedas.
O Goddess of gods, that which is living exists in the form of the mind,
conjoined with the vital breath (prāṇavāyu) moving within the suṣumṇā.

O Goddess, joined with that [vitality], the wind is again struck at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) by means of the palate, the lips, the nostrils, and so forth, O Supreme Mistress—[some read "by means of the body" (dehena)]. 21-44.
The essence of phonemes manifests through the distinctions of prose, verse, and so forth;
for that which is the cause of the three worlds exists as the body of Brahman. (An alternative reading is *tal loka*).
From that, O Goddess, the world was born—the gods, asuras, humans, and serpents. Thus has this most wonderful secret been declared to you. (21–46)
To one devoid of faith, to the wicked, to the ungrateful, to the evil-minded, to the atheist, to the undisciplined, and to one who has turned away from the Vedas and the scriptures; || 21-47 ||
O Goddess of gods, one should never show [this] to one who is untrustworthy.
When the king, however, [offers] his entire property, his army, his treasury, the earth, and his elephants—
One who desires to know should announce this; then he should reveal it to him.
Otherwise, there will be a loss of accomplishment; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. || 21-49 ||
Therefore, you too must indeed guard this with every effort.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the Śrī Nāradapañcarātra, within the Śrī Māheśvara Tantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī. 21-21.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
Pārvatī said: "O Lord of the gods, O Lord Paśupati, that which was spoken by you, O Master—"
Having entered through the cavity of the ear, it becomes consciousness-bliss within the heart.
The supreme among sacred fords, the highest among forms of knowledge, the ultimate among yogas, and the most excellent among dharmas. (22.2)
Of all things that ought to be heard, this alone is indeed the supreme thing to be heard;
and of all things that ought to be known, this is said to be the supreme thing to be known.
I have heard this especially with its underlying reasoning;
nevertheless, my inner self does not attain lasting satisfaction. (22.4)
Therefore, O Dhūrjaṭi, I ask you about the distinction therein;
tell me that, O Mahādeva, and be most gracious.
In this manifold world of dreams and illusions, the dear friends of the imperishable Supreme Self have come into being through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). (22.6)
The time for their ritual actions has passed since they departed;
for how long will they all remain here, deluded? (22.7)
O Supreme Lord, how will they attain awakening? Who will be their awakener? Will they proceed simultaneously or separately? (22.8)
O Mahādeva, please explain all of this out of your grace; O Śaṅkara, dispel my great doubt today.
Śiva said:
Listen, Pārvatī, I shall explain your questions in their entirety. You are dearer to me than my own life; therefore, I shall speak according to the truth.
Formerly, there was a creator named Aṣṭavaktra, the son of Viriñci-Brahmā,
whom those who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedānta call Śabdabrahman.
At the conclusion of two parārdhas, O Maheśānī, there occurs the great Brāhma kalpa; this dissolution is said to have Prakṛti as its limit.

And the remaining single primordial nature (prakṛti)—for that is indeed presided over by the Puruṣa—O Goddess, according to the sacred tradition (śruti), the world remained empty for some time thereafter. (22.13)
From that, the power of sleep (nidrā) manifested within the imperishable Supreme Self; from that, the Great Principle (mahat-tattva) arose, and from that, the ego-sense (ahaṅkṛti) was born.
And he himself was born in three ways according to the distinction of the *guṇas*, O beautiful one;
from the *sāttvika* [aspect], the mind was born, as well as those ten deities. (22.15)
From Rajas the sense organs arose, and from Tamas the elements came into being;
from those, O Goddess, an egg was formed, wherein Nārāyaṇa resided.
[In this regard, there is also the reading *tatra*. From his navel there arose a lotus, upon which Brahmā himself came into being;
and his supreme lifespan is said to measure two *parārdhas*. (22.17)
O Maheśvarī, within this cosmic egg, indeed in Jambūdvīpa, in the region known as Bhārata, the latent impressions of beloved objects reside. (22.18)
O Maheśvarī, in this second half of the first Parārdha,
he manifested his divine play at the persistent request of the Svāminīs.
Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the supreme bliss, appeared in the house of Nanda;
thereafter, his beloveds manifested themselves in the guise of cowherd girls.
To fulfill their desire, Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama),
performing the Rāsa-līlā, delighted those beloved ones.
Through the immersion in the power of yoga (yogamāyā), as he was destroying the effects of māyā,
even when the dissolution of Brahmā occurred, this world became just as it was before.
Then everything—from Brahmā down to the stationary beings—is born again;
due to the non-fulfillment of desires, latent impressions remain within the midst of their effects.
They move about according to the time, according to the place, and according to their inclination;
but when two parārdhas have passed away and all things mobile and immobile have perished.
When Virañci has attained liberation and the beloved Akṣara has indeed awakened,
those latent impressions (vāsanās) will awaken and become absorbed into its own reflection.

And due to the manifestation of his divine play at the end of the Dvāpara age in the Kali Yuga—[in some manuscripts, verses 26 and 27 read: "Kṛṣṇa appeared for the sake of showing his beloveds the play of suffering; and among them was one supreme, most fortunate, and beautiful beloved who would awaken them all by declaring the final verdict"—such a variant reading appears]. He could not endure witnessing the play of suffering of his own beloveds. (22–26)
And among them, he will most thoroughly awaken one who is supremely fortunate, beautiful, and dear to him,
by declaring the final decision.
Then, according to that tradition, all those beloveds of the Blessed One,
overcome by separation from their own husbands, abandoned their bodies belonging to the phenomenal world.
They shall attain their station in the Bhagavān’s Lokavaikuṇṭha in groups,
sporting with Padmā according to the prescribed manner for the enjoyment of time.
Even having abandoned their divine bodies, they will become absorbed into one's own form;
O Supreme Goddess, even the Imperishable One experiences this as if in a dream.
His intellect having achieved its purpose, he will become immersed in supreme bliss;
at that time, O beloved, all his divine sports will take on an eternal form. (22–31)

O beautiful one, although the Blessed One is the Self of the world and possesses a divine nature, he appears thus due to the connection with a trace of ignorance, even though he is the imperishable Supreme Self. (22.32)
Because even a portion of their sleep remains, they will stay for some time;
O Goddess, all of them shall go simultaneously to their own abodes.
O Goddess of gods, there can be no separate course for them in any way;
O beloved, this is due to the similarity and the state of oneness with the realm of dream. (22–34)

And because of their lack of aversion despite the diversity [of the world], and due to the absence of any distinction in their love for their Lord, they do not depart separately; therefore, they abide in Vaikuṇṭha. (22-35)
O Goddess of the gods, by means of gradual practice, all shall undoubtedly attain [liberation].
Therefore, O Goddess, one's own husband is especially the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
For one must always be devoted [to the path] in accordance with the Vedas and Shastras; O Parvati, ritual actions bring about the end of the inherent nature of the body and the senses. (22-37)
The meditation upon, hearing of, and chanting of the Supreme Brahman, as well as all actions—whether good or bad—arise entirely from the nature of the self. (22.38)
From the abandonment of the true and attachment to the unreal, there arises wandering through various wombs;
for one whose self is forgotten due to the afflictions arising from mental anguish, physical disease, and poverty. (22.39)
O Goddess, for one in whom tamas is predominant, there can never be anything auspicious;
therefore, one must certainly perform here that which brings about the end of the body.
At the end of the body, there will never again be any connection with karma, for the purpose of ceasing transgression and avoiding the performance of undesirable actions. (22.41)
One should abandon obligatory, occasional, and optional ritual acts;
O Goddess, he who conducts himself in this way attains success without obstacle.
He who, greedy with desire, acts by transgressing the injunctions of the scriptures,
attains no success in this world, nor the supreme goal in the next.
All this that I was asked by you, O beloved, has been told in brief, O Maheśānī. What more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Śrīmāheśvaratantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. || 22-22 ||
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
Pārvatī said:
"O Sadāśiva, I desire to hear further; tell that to me."
On the surface of the earth, the wives of the Blessed One were situated within various wombs.
In various places, diverse deeds were also performed:
in some places pilgrimage, in some places charity, in some places fire-offerings, and in some places recitation.

In some places there was the performance of sacrifices and other rites, as well as the practice of Vedic study; in others, the worship of ancestors and gods, and the honoring of Brahmins and the virtuous.

In some places there was the practice of reviling others, while in others there was the honoring of gods, brahmins, and guests; in some places there was the misappropriation of gifts, and likewise the seduction of the senses. (23.4)
Speaking untruth, backbiting, harming living beings, stealing gold and so forth, and the consumption of liquor and meat. (23.5)

Likewise, treachery, envy, violence, and the various types of ripening [of karma], as well as the transgression of the conduct prescribed for one's own caste and stage of life, and acting according to one's own lustful desires. (23.6)

O Lord, proclaiming one's own virtues, breaking the ranks [of the assembly], performing useless actions, revealing the secrets of others, eating the food of barbarians, and living anywhere at all—[these are to be avoided]. (23-7)
O Lord, the practice of what is forbidden, the transgression of prescribed conduct, and likewise the sale of cows, land, elephants, horses, daughters, and so forth—O Master. (23-8)
The selling of the Vedas, likewise the terrifying of living beings, the abandonment of duty through laziness, and likewise even the presence of egoism; 23-9.
O Lord of Gods, these karmas—whether they be existent or non-existent, and whether they are great—are indeed of three kinds:
those already begun (prārabdha), those accumulated (sañcita), and those currently being performed (kriyamāṇa).
I do not see their end, even in hundreds of millions of eons,
regarding both that which has been accumulated and that which is being performed, merely by means of the knowledge of their own nature.
The destruction of *prārabdha* karma is nowhere established by the scriptures;
for no action is exhausted without being experienced, as the destruction of actions occurs only through their fruition. (23.12)
Thus, the established doctrine of the scriptures has been declared by you in every respect;
for, due to the continued existence of *prārabdha* karma, even while remembering one's own true nature, [the body persists]. (23.13)
How can going to Vaikuṇṭha be within the range of one whose karma has been cast off—or, according to another reading, one whose karma has been consumed?
For if those [beings] go there while leaving their karmas unexhausted, [then how can it be accessible to one who has abandoned them]? (23.14)

"Even those [actions], O Lord, do not remain for even a moment without a connection to an agent—or rather, without a connection to an object (karma)—[this is also a reading]. You ought to sever this doubt of mine. (23.15)
Śiva said:
"Well asked by you, O blessed lady, is this most wonderful secret, by the mere hearing of which one is liberated from the bondage of karma. (23-16)
