Both his accumulated merit and that which is currently being performed perish entirely, for his body has become nothing more than an oblation in the fire of separation. (23.17)
Having cast off their elemental bodies born of the elements and having assumed a fiery form, they proceed to the world of Brahmā accompanied by their *prārabdha* karma alone. (23.18)
And when the beloveds of the Blessed One ascend upwards from the world of Brahmā and reach the vicinity of Vaikuṇṭha, a powerful wind indeed blows downwards. (23.19)
Then, possessed by that [power], the friends cause their vine-like bodies to tremble;
and, O Goddess of Gods, by that trembling of the body, the rows of *prārabdha* karmas [are shaken]. (23–20)
Like flowers falling from trees, they gradually discharge [their bonds];
free from the connection of karma, these radiant ones go to Vaikuṇṭha.
O beloved, listen as I describe those actions, both existent and non-existent, which have flowed from the body and constantly take refuge therein. (23.22)
Those who have composed hymns of praise through acts such as service and prostration, or those who have rendered assistance by bestowing wealth, grain, and garments; || 23-23 ||
Delighted upon hearing of his virtues and distressed by his censure, they shared his meals, his dwellings, his vehicles, and his seats. (23–24)
O Goddess of the gods, there is no doubt that virtuous deeds take refuge in them;
whereas for those who have caused them suffering through censure, harshness, and backbiting, [the opposite occurs]. (23–25)
Taking away what belongs to him, proclaiming his very faults, speaking groundless slanders, as well as beating and threatening him; (23–26)
Indeed, all unwholesome actions take refuge in those wicked ones;
for the connection with actions belongs to the body, and never to the self. (23–27)
O Goddess of gods, both praise and blame concern the body and do not pertain to the Self;
therefore, O Pārvatī, neither by the praise nor by the blame of the body [is the Self affected]. (23–28)
They undoubtedly attain his merits and demerits;
having thus destroyed their own merit and demerit, they sport in Vaikuṇṭha.
Those who are sattvic and dear to the Lord shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu;
indeed, at the conclusion of two parārdhas, they will all go there simultaneously.
The quality of passion leads to enmity, and the quality of darkness leads to my abode;
O daughter of the mountain king, there is no distinction in the manner of their operation regarding the destruction of karma.
And all go to a destination corresponding to their virtues; of this there is no doubt.
Listen now to the specific manner regarding that journey to Vaikuṇṭha as well.

The mark of these [subtle elements] is their latent impression (vāsanā); at the end of the body, they enter the earth. Having remained there for some time, they become joined with the earthly sense organs.
O Goddess, having served the earthly realm, she enters the water;
after remaining there for some time, she obtains the sensory faculty of taste. (23–34)
Being served by that which is exceedingly divine, she enters the principle of fire (tejastattva).
Having remained there for some time, she becomes endowed with the fiery sense organs.
Having reached the object, which is form (rūpa), it then enters the wind-element (vāyu-tattva).
Having remained there for some time, it becomes endowed with the sense-faculty of touch (tvag-indriya).
Experiencing divine touch as its object, she would enter the sky;
after remaining there for some time, she would then regain the faculty of hearing.
Having reached the object of sound, one then enters the *bhūtādi* [tattva];
having abandoned the *tāmasa* *bhūtādi*, O beautiful one, one goes to the *rājasa* [state]. (23.38)
Then, having attained that which consists of pure being (satva), he rejoices for a long time in Vaikuṇṭha;
by this sequential yoga, the beloved ones of Hari shall go there.
This account of your journey to Vaikuṇṭha and so forth has been fully related to you;
it must not be told to just anyone, yet it has been revealed out of affection for you.
Indeed, you too must keep this truth secret; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
Even by giving it to an unworthy son, one would incur sin.
All this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Māheśvara Tantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. 23-23.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, Maheśāna, Dhūrjaṭi, Nīlalohita!
Furthermore, I desire to hear the definitive determination of Your eternal pastimes.

How could there be play (līlā) in that which is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa)? If there is play, how can it be devoid of qualities? Or how could there be play in that which possesses qualities (saguṇa), since [play] consists of qualities and is eternal? || 24-2 ||
That which is unimpeded throughout the three periods of time is declared to be eternal.
Or perhaps this play occurred in the past, or it will occur in the future. (24.3)
Alternatively, this [world] may never have arisen, nor shall it arise again;
for if Līlā has now arisen, the effect that is the creation perishes.
O Lord, how can it be said by a wise person that she is eternal, if her play has attained eternity within the heart of the Imperishable? (24.5)
"O Lord, since eternity did not exist previously, how could there be its persistence? You ought to sever this doubt of mine now. (24.6)
I see no one other than you who can dispel my doubt;
for there is nothing unknown to you, since you yourself are omniscient.
Śiva said:
Listen, O Pārvatī; out of affection for you, I shall speak in its entirety that by the mere hearing of which supreme realization arises. (24.8)
Even in that which is devoid of qualities and transcends the imperishable, what contradiction is there in divine play?
However, that play which belongs to the one possessing qualities is described as being itself possessed of qualities. (24.9)
Whatever play there may be in the attributeless [Brahman], that play must be attributeless;
I shall now state the definitive conclusion regarding that play of Brahman. (24.10)
Brahman exists in the form of aesthetic flavor (rasa), as it is sung in the Vedic sciences;
that flavor consists of union and separation, and is thus twofold in nature. (See 11.21–22, p. 122) || 24.11 ||
Union occurs when they are joined, and separation when they are apart;
therein, their eternal play consists of various states of being. (24.12)
"O beautiful one, because Brahman is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and because it is eternal, this sport (līlā), being both eternal and devoid of qualities, is not contradictory. (24.13)
Some say that play (līlā) is not at all applicable to the one devoid of qualities (nirguṇa);
rather, it belongs to the one endowed with qualities (saguṇa), who is characterized by play due to the presence of a connection with Māyā. (24.14)
Those whose minds are deluded by māyā describe that which is beyond qualities, supreme, subtle, and inaccessible to speech or mind, as having divisions. (24.15)
Fearing a contradiction with scripture, the application [of the senses] was treated separately;
yet, being deluded, you do not perceive the contradiction with the scripture concerning rasa. (24.16)
O beloved, the Śruti texts negate any material form;
the scripture concerning Rasa venerates a form consisting solely of bliss.
Otherwise, O Goddess, this [method] consisting of two parts, established by scripture and pleasing to the ear, is never suitable for the Formless One. (24.18)
There are hundreds of idle chatterings for those who do not understand scripture and reasoning;
the mind of the discerning connoisseur of essence finds no delight in them. (24.19)

O Goddess, such is the flavor that is experienced through the divine pastimes; therefore, it is remembered that the flavor consists of the essence of the pastimes, and the pastimes consist of the essence of the flavor. (24.20)

Because of identity and because of having a single form, the divine play (līlā) consists of Brahman; the states conducive to that play are the determinants (vibhāvas) and the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas). (24.21)
O beloved! Even those objects of perception and experiences are of such a nature:
the moon, ornaments, decorations, garlands, unguents, and breezes. (24.22)
Long ponds, groves, gardens, seasonal trees, and creepers;
clothing, drink, and food; and the warbling of bees, parrots, and cuckoos—these [are the enjoyments]. (24.23)
For that collection of factors which produces rasa is itself known to be of the nature of rasa;
therefore, the objects employed for aesthetic play are likewise of the nature of rasa. (24.24)
The state of rasa is twofold: that which has become liquefied and that which has become solidified.
The liquefied state resides in the beloved, while the solidified state is within the range of vision. (24–25)

Therefore, this aesthetic flavor (rasa), which has become liquefied, whose substratum is the beloved, and whose essence is the state of the beloved, manifests by itself those states that are dear and desired. (24–26)
O Beloved! They maintain that even from that which has become condensed, the rasa does not truly manifest if it is devoid of a beloved object as its basis. (24-27)
In the mirror of the beloved, one may perceive one's own self as if it were a reflection;
yet, just as when the mirror is removed, the face is no longer perceived. (24–28)
In the same way, rasa deprived of its limbs does not find its own experience;
for rasa is indeed bliss, and therefore it consists of the two petals of the pleasant and the unpleasant. (24–29)
That causal totality is of the nature of bliss; its essence consists of all existence.
O Beloved, there is never, at any time or place, any contact with the qualities of Māyā.
That which is of the nature of rasa, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), sporting eternally in its divine play,
non-dual, the supreme Brahman known by the name Puruṣottama.
O beautiful one, this [Līlā], though past, future, and even present, should be known as eternal; this Līlā is indeed imperishable. (24.32)
Thus has this been told, O Goddess; now listen to another question, by the mere hearing of which doubt is dispelled.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the Śrī Nāradapañcarātra, within the Śrī Māheśvara Tantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī. 24–24.
Then, in the twenty-fifth chapter, Śiva said:
"Since eternity did not exist previously, how could there be its persistence?"
"O Goddess, regarding that which has been spoken by you—[there is also a reading 'pṛṣṭham' (the question)—] hear my definitive conclusion [on this matter]. (25.1)
Whatever does not exist will never manifest;
for only that which already exists in every way can manifest, my dear. (25.2)
Therefore, O Goddess, the phenomenal world is described from the perspective of its positive aspect;
for when it is said that "the jar does not exist," the existence of the jar is nevertheless implied. (25.3)
O Goddess, in the same way, the phenomenal world (prapañca), though non-existent, is perceived as existent through false hearing;
its state of being immediate or mediate is declared by the scriptures regarding existence and non-existence.

Likewise, this play of manifestation and this play of aesthetic flavor are of that same nature; indeed, all of them should be understood as eternal by those who follow the teachings of the Vedas. (25.5)
Just as the prior non-existence of a jar is conceived in the clay, its subsequent origination from the clay is then figuratively attributed to it. (25.6)
Furthermore, O Goddess of the Gods, its non-existence is not characterized as absolute;
for just as a mango tree, though residing within the mango seed, becomes manifest from it. (25.7)

O Goddess of gods, if that which is truly non-existent were indeed to manifest, how could there ever be the manifestation of a *chudchuda* tree from the seed of a mango? (Note: There is also a reading: "from the seed of a mango, of a *bhrava* tree. 25-8.
O Goddess, those who are skilled in the meaning of the scriptures should know that existence is threefold: the empirical, the ultimate, and the apparent. (25.9)
In the case of "silver in mother-of-pearl," this existence would be of a phenomenal (prātibhāsika) nature;
or likewise, the great wealth consisting of elephants, horses, and so forth, would be of a dream-like (svāpnika) nature. (25–10)
This empirical [existence] remains awake for the sake of worldly transaction;
but the existence of Brahman, O Goddess of Gods, is proclaimed as the ultimate reality. (25.11)
O Goddess, it is said that the reality of the divine play exists by virtue of the existence of Brahman;
O Sovereign Lady, no one is capable of bringing about the non-existence of that which is real. (25.12)
Therefore, O Goddess, it is said that her manifestation through divine play occurs at the proper time, specifically in every twelfth year of the Mistress, O Beloved. (25.13)
This divine play manifests repeatedly and eternally;
indeed, throughout this entire duration of time, within the imperishable Supreme Self.
In the world of secret delight, she becomes Sumaṅgalā;
from that, she is born among beloveds, and from that, the expansion of her divine play arises. (25.15)
That play resides within the nature of the syllable (akṣara), and from that it may become unstable;
for that, O Goddess, is indeed mere memory and never a direct perception.
O Supreme Goddess, when the twelfth year of her mistress had passed, she appeared once again through the power of her own yoga as a portion of Kāma. || 25.17 ||
O Goddess, desire arises within the immutable Supreme Self;

and from that, O Beloved, threefold play manifests at the proper time. (Note: This threefold nature of play was explained very clearly by Śrī Śiva to Śrī Pārvatī in the Sundarītantra and the Ālamandārasaṃhitā.)
The shadow of Śvetadvīpa is established in Mathurā,
and likewise, O beloved, the reflection of Vaikuṇṭha is in Dvārakā.
But Vraja, O Goddess of gods, is the direct reflection of Goloka;
it is likewise stated in the first chapter of the Purāṇasaṃhitā:
"Thus, within Brahman, who is pure consciousness, devoid of qualities, and free from duality..."
"I have heard that Kṛṣṇa sports in the realm known as Goloka. (25.54)
There is nothing higher than this, even according to the Vedas and the Āgamas;
nevertheless, the Veda indeed declares that there is one who is higher than the Imperishable (akṣara).
The Lord who dwells in Goloka is said to be beyond the Imperishable (akṣara); who is that one who is even higher than Him, and who is eternally celebrated by the Vedas? (25-56)

In the *Pādma* as well, the superiority of this *līlā* over the *līlā* of Goloka is proclaimed: "And this *līlā*, O Śivā, consists of the bliss of aesthetic rasa. (25–20) [The reading is also found as *līleyam*.]
O Goddess of gods, she indeed manifests at every opportune moment (samaya). I shall explain that opportune moment; listen with a one-pointed mind. (25.21)

Two atoms (paramāṇu) constitute one minute particle (aṇu); three of those constitute a mote of dust in a sunbeam (trasareṇu). And by three such motes of dust, there is a unit of time known as a *truṭi*. (25.22)

A hundred of those [tālas] constitutes a *vedha*; three *vedhas* are known as a *lava*. A *nimiṣa*, O Goddess, consists of three *lavas*, and a *kṣaṇa* should be understood as consisting of three of those.

Five *kṣaṇas* constitute a *kāṣṭhā*, and ten such *kāṣṭhās* likewise [constitute a *nimeṣa*]. A *laghu* should be known as consisting of five *kāṣṭhās*, and ten *laghus* [constitute a *muhūrta*]. (25.24)
One ghaṭikā should be known as a muhūrta, and two ghaṭikās as a [single] muhūrta;
seven ghaṭikās constitute a prahara, and by four of those, a day is remembered [to be measured]. || 25-25 ||
Furthermore, four watches are said to constitute that day and night. || 25-26 ||
With ten, five, and again with fifteen [days], the first fortnight is bright (śukla) and likewise the other dark (kṛṣṇa); that constitutes a day and night for the ancestors (pitṛs).
A month is said to consist of two fortnights; those two together are known as a season (ṛtu).
Three seasons are proclaimed to constitute a southern course (dakṣiṇāyana).

They say that three [such days] constitute a day and night for the gods. O Goddess, a year is said to consist of two solstices (ayana). A hundred of those years is defined as the maximum lifespan of human beings. (25–29)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, the four yugas— Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali— consist of twelve thousand divine years.
A thousand cycles of four yugas is said to be one day of Brahmā;
his night is of equal duration, during which the three worlds are dissolved.
Fourteen Manus are born during the day of Brahmā;
O Goddess, in each Manvantara there are seventy-one Yugas.
O Goddess, in every Manvantara, there is the descent of Viṣṇu upon the earth,
as well as the deities beginning with Indra and those who are the Seven Sages.
Indeed, they become distinct according to the divisions of the Manvantaras:
Svāyambhuva, Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, and Raivata. (25–34)
O Ambikā, six Manus, beginning with Cākṣuṣa, have passed away;
the seventh, named Vaivasvata Manu, is now currently reigning.
Twenty-eight cycles of the four ages have passed, O beloved;
in this twenty-eighth Kali age, O Goddess, this divine play has arrived. (25–36)
The first half (of the aeon) has passed, and the second is now proceeding;
even therein, the ninth month of the first year is said to have occurred. (25–37)
Today, O Goddess Priyaṃvadā, it is indeed the sixteenth day, the second watch of that [day], and the third muhūrta is currently proceeding. (25.38)
In this manner, O beloved, a day of Brahmā is said to consist of his own days and nights; and through the divisions of fortnights and months, it extends up to a full year.
In this manner, a hundred such years would constitute the dissolution of Brahmā;
by the closing of Viṣṇu’s eye, the entire lifespan of Brahmā passes away.

Starting from a mere blink of an eye and proceeding through the divisions of moments (*lava*) and instants (*kṣaṇa*), up until a hundred years of Viṣṇu, may it become a single blink of my own eye. (25.41)
Even that which takes as long as a hundred years by the measure of a human blink is but a single blink for the Lord; and by the measure of His blinks, [the world-cycle proceeds].
A period of one hundred years constitutes a single blink of Śiva’s eye;
and by that same sequence of blinks, there extends a period of one thousand years.
The flickering of the corner of the mistress’s eye during Kṛṣṇa’s amorous play lasts for twelve years by the mere measure of its blinking. (25.44)
Then, after twelve years have passed, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, desire may arise once more for the sake of beholding her divine play.
The eternal manifestation of Līlā is said to occur repeatedly; it is that very portion of desire which is established within the heart of the Imperishable (Akṣara). (25.46)
Through union with that [divine power], His desire to see [the world] arises at its respective time;
thus, that pastime is eternal, consisting of aesthetic flavor (rasa), and is as dear as the Beloved herself.

That rasa which has been described through the two petals known as union (*saṃyoga*) and separation (*vipralambha*), when it occupies the petal of separation (*vipralambha*), [is called the erotic sentiment]. (25.48)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, that very same play manifests when it remains pervading the entire field of conjunction. (25.49)
O beloved, when the aesthetic flavor (rasa) reaches the juncture of union and separation, then Līlā becomes manifest as Kṛṣṇa himself within his own abode.
Then the time for awakening is near for those whose minds are fixed on Kṛṣṇa, through the true lineage of the Guru and in accordance with the meaning of the scriptures. (25.51)
"Therefore, O auspicious one, you must proceed with the means for the sake of attaining the Self;
thus have I explained to you that which I was asked, O fair-eyed lady. (25.52)
In brief, O Great Goddess, what more do you wish to hear? || 25-53 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Śrī Nāradapañcarātra, within the Śrī Māheśvara Tantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī. || 25-25 ||
Then, in the twenty-sixth chapter,
Pārvatī said:
"O Maheśa, I desire to hear the definitive determination of the means of accomplishment (sādhanas)."
By the mere hearing of which, indeed, everything becomes fruitful. || 26-1 ||
Śrī Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the definitive determination of the practice (*sādhana*). It is more secret than the secret itself; it must not be spoken of directly to just anyone. (26–2)
This meaning of the Tantra, which is a secret meaning hidden within the Vedas, was obtained by me from Īśvara; it was received by me from Sadāśiva.
Seated upon a couch made of wooden planks extending for a hundred thousand yojanas,
Sadāśiva, stationed above the peak, heard this.
O Goddess of gods, that which was described by me in secret through the power of will—that has been told to you, O virtuous lady; listen further to what follows.
Once, while I was dwelling in solitude, a thought arose in me as I remembered my beloved:
"I alone am the lord in this world, or perhaps there is someone else besides me. (6)
O Goddess, while reflecting in this manner, I indeed maintained my meditative absorption;
O beautiful one, five thousand yugas passed away during that time.

[The Samādhigīta (variant reading: *i0 pā0*)] O Goddess of the Gods, while established in samādhi, I heard the speech of the Lord. Having heard that, O Goddess, my heart became free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*). 26-8.
O Goddess of the gods, from that time forth, remaining in seclusion, I have meditated upon this divine play through the yoga of meditation with a mind free of conceptual construction.
Since this tantra was spoken by me, the Lord of Samādhi, it has therefore attained the renown as the Māheśvara Tantra. (26.10)
O Pārvatī, sixty-four tantras have been spoken by me alone; they are for the purposes of deluding, driving away, subjugating, and killing. (26.11)
They produce immediate conviction through various mantra-based means, and they delude the world by means of such arts as the magic of Indra’s net (indrajāla). || 26-12 ||
O Goddess! Those have been explained to you in detail; yet, O Sovereign of the Gods, not even the slightest bit of ultimate reality (paramārtha) exists within them.
All that has been described by Māyika is for the use of those who live in illusion;
this *Māheśvara-tantra*, however, is what was heard by me during meditative absorption (*samādhi*). (26.14)
"It is my conviction that this is the means for awakening to those things that are dear;
otherwise, there is no other purpose for this knowledge of the Lord (Īśvara). [The readings "tanmaheśvaravikhyātam," "tanmayeśvaravikhyātam," and "tanneśvaravikhyā" are also found. || 26-15 ||
Furthermore, O Queen of the Gods, there are Vaiṣṇava tantras known as the Pañcarātra,
which were spoken by Viṣṇu and number twenty-five.
The *Hayaśīrṣa-tantra*, the *Ādya-tantra*, the *Saṃmohana-tantra*, the *Vaibhava-tantra*, the *Pauṣkara-tantra*, the *Prahlāda-tantra*, the *Gārgya-tantra*, and the *Gālava-tantra*. (26.17)

The Nāradīya, the Śrīpraśna, the Vaiṣṇava, the Pauṣkara Tantra, the Prahlāda, the Gārga, the Mānava, the Nāradīya, the Śrīvatsa—[or alternatively, this reading], the Śāṇḍilya, and likewise the Īśvara;
the Satyokta, the Śaunaka Tantra, the Vāsiṣṭha, and the Jñānasāgara. (26–18)

The Svāyambhuva, the Kāpila, the Tārkṣya, the Nārāyaṇīyaka, the Ātreya [or, according to another reading, the Nārasiṃhākṣa], the one called Nārasiṃha, the Ānanda [or, according to other readings, the Ādākṣa or Āṭṭākṣa], and likewise the Āruṇa. || 26-19 ||
O beautiful one, such knowledge is called "celestial" (vaihāyasa) and "universal" (viśvokta);
it is intended for those people who have utterly strayed from the path of the Vedas. (26–20)
The paths such as the Pañcarātra and others are beneficial only for a limited time;
O Goddess of Gods, there exist very many Buddhist Tantras as well. (26.21)
All of those were proclaimed by Viṣṇu in the form of a Buddha; there is not even a trace of dharma in them, for they are intended to delude the wicked-minded. (26.22)
"But in the end, they will surely lead to hell; of this there is no doubt.
Pārvatī said:
"For what reason was [this] done by Viṣṇu, the God of gods, who is the embodiment of goodness? (26.23)
Alas, even by one who is compassionate toward the world, deception has been practiced!
O Lord, falsehood can never exist in a person who is faultless. (26.24)
Impelled by whom did Hari compose the delusive scripture?
Tell me this, O Omniscient One, for the removal of my doubt. (26.25)
Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the cause of this delusive conception.
Once, both Brahmā and Viṣṇu had their inner minds enveloped by self-conceit.
Constantly disputing with one another, those two, both full of pride, countered each other, saying, "I am Brahman, not you! (26–27).
O Goddess, with both their minds enraged, the two of them reviled each other.
Brahmā said:
"Since you, disregarding me, hold yourself in such high esteem... (26–28)
"You shall become unworthy of worship in the worlds; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard this terrible curse, Madhusūdana [reflected].
Enraged, he returned the curse: "You too shall become just like this.
Having thus uttered curses at one another, they were both deluded by destiny.
Both of them, with their faces withered, sought refuge in me alone;
however, O Goddess, I established a specific condition for their curse.
I shall speak to you that which was proclaimed by Brahmā; listen to it.
The word of Brahmā or Vaiṣṇava never becomes otherwise at any time. (26–32)
Therefore, you shall indeed become unworthy of worship in the worlds;
however, no curse shall attach to you regarding the worship of the five deities.
Indeed, it is only a curse that would obstruct your worship;
O Hari, assume a single body as the object of this curse.
"Let your curse remain only upon that very form of being, and not at all upon the embodiment of pure existence (sattva). When this was said by me, both of them departed for their own abodes.
In the meantime, O Goddess, a great battle between the gods and the asuras took place; in that conflict, the enemies of the gods were defeated by the gods. (26–36)
Seeking the means for victory, they performed most intense penance;
the Lord himself went there in the form of a Buddhist to create obstacles to their asceticism.
Having composed Buddhist tantras, he showed them to the Daityas:
"There is no self other than the body, and there is no liberation beyond death. (26–38)
Neither gods nor ancestors exist; they have been shown by the Veda in vain.
The scripture was fabricated here by the Brāhmaṇas solely for their own livelihood. (26-39)
O lords of the asuras, in no way should [the self] be maintained as being valid;
thus have you been deluded by the tantras, primarily those that propound the doctrine of selflessness. (26.40)
The Asuras, their intentions captivated by the Buddha’s illusion, engaged in battle;
from that time forward, Hari attained a state of being unworthy of worship in that form.
O Supreme Goddess, the grasping of the Buddhist teaching [and also the reading "of him born in the house of Śuddhodana"] has arisen;
therefore, the tantras spoken by them are devoted to nihilism (nāstivāda). || 26-42 ||
O Goddess, in the investigation of dharma and adharma, these [other systems] are not to be grasped by the wise;
this Tantra of Maheśvara is the most excellent among all Tantras. (26.43)
Having heard that which was uttered according to the true state of reality by Śakti through the desire for their essential unity (sāmarasya), Sadāśiva became the seat of the Imperishable (Akṣara).
O blameless one, I have related this to Īśvara exactly as I heard it;
O Goddess, Īśvara told it to me during his meditative absorption exactly as he had heard it.
Out of affection for you, my dear, I have spoken this and not otherwise;
indeed, you must keep it secret and never speak of it to anyone at all.
"For not everyone is qualified to understand the meaning of this Tantra.
Pārvatī said:
"Even if one who is devoid of qualification should engage in this [practice]... (26.47)
Becoming free from doubt and fear, and endowed with love and devotion, one should contemplate the eternally blissful Supreme Person as one's own Lord within the heart. (26.48)
"O Lord of Gods, please explain to me clearly: what state does one attain who casts off a body withered by the flames of separation from Him? (26.49)
Śiva said:
If some individual soul, consisting of the appearance of Brahman, wanders about, [he may attain liberation] through the powerful accumulations of merit perfected over many births. || 26-50 ||
O Goddess of gods, through association with the virtuous, one may attain this knowledge—having conquered the senses, being free from sense-objects, and endowed with love and devotion. (26.51)
Upon casting off the body, he attains that very state which young maidens reach; his dissolution does not occur like [the merging] of water in water, but rather in the Imperishable.
Since he has become separated from her who sports in eternal pastimes, he likewise does not see Him who sports in eternal pastimes. (26.53)

O Parameśvarī, because it is merely the manifestation of the syllable within oneself, therefore, O Goddess, in Vṛndāvana—which is the immutable and heart-pleasing (there is also a reading: "in the syllable that is heart-pleasing")—it is the heart-pleasing one who abides as the peak-syllable (kūṭastha). || 26-54 ||
"One should remain experiencing divine play (līlā), remaining free from rebirth;
thus has the conclusion been declared for you, O beautiful one, regarding those who lack [spiritual] qualification. (26.55)
Henceforth, I shall state the definitive conclusion regarding devotion; listen to it.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Māheśvara Tantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. 26.26.
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter.
Śiva said:
[This concerns] those who delight in eternal bliss and are dear to the Supreme Lord.
O Goddess, one must by all means indeed perform service to one's own husband.
Good conduct, which is a limb of devotion, must be practiced for the purification of action;
those devoid of good conduct will not attain perfection even if they were already perfected. (27-2)
The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of right conduct; austerity does not purify one who is devoid of right conduct.
Holy fords do not purify one who is devoid of right conduct, and for one devoid of right conduct, there is no spiritual success whatsoever. (27.3)
Right conduct is the primary dharma; right conduct destroys inauspiciousness.
One attains purity through right conduct; therefore, one should always practice it. (27.4)
Through improper conduct, the intellect becomes defiled;
when the mirror of the intellect is soiled, there is no capacity for perceiving the play [of reality]. (5)
Right conduct has been declared by the virtuous as being always present in all dharmas;
for a dharma devoid of right conduct is indeed reckoned as non-dharma. || 27-6 ||
Therefore, O beloved, one must protect one's conduct in every way;
conduct is said to be of two kinds: external and internal. (27.7)
The wise know that the purification of one's inner being alone is the internal conduct;
for the sake of its accomplishment, external practices such as physical cleansing, which are to be performed by means of the body, are prescribed. (27.8)
O beloved, the state to be attained is the goal, while the means are the purification of the body and so forth;
I shall explain that conduct by which the mind is thoroughly purified. (27.9)
One should not speak to it, nor look at it, nor listen to it in any way;
one should not touch it, nor smell it, nor eat anything that is considered impure.
When speech, having expanded, strives to describe the qualities of the Lord, then evil pierces it; thus pierced, it speaks with discordant words.
O beloved, when one desires to behold the Lord in embodied form,
then the eye, pierced by evil, sees what is disagreeable.

When the sense organ of hearing desires to hear the qualities of the Lord, one should know that at that very moment it has been pierced by evil, and one should understand it to be in a state of doubt.
When one strives for sensory gratification with food that has been offered [to others], at that very moment, pierced by evil, one falls into a state of delusion. (27.14)
One should recognize that which is contrary to right thought as being of the nature of evil;
this evil of contrary conduct approaches the senses. (27.15)
Having first restrained the senses through most firm practice, this very meditation, when cultivated, leads to the state free from obscuration. (27.16)
When one is unable to exercise restraint over all the senses,
then the single sense of taste alone should be conquered in the desire to conquer them all.

When taste is conquered, desire is conquered; when desire is conquered, the senses are conquered. For one who has conquered the pleasures of the tongue and the genitals, what indeed remains that is unattainable? (27.18)
Formerly, from the breast of Brahmā as he desired to create, Dharma emerged in the form of a bull, possessing four feet in the form of the four Vedas and a beautiful appearance. (27.19)
O beloved, his two horns are knowledge and most intense dispassion;
truth and austerity are his pair of ears, while self-restraint and charity are his two eyes.
His tail was sovereignty, and the line of hair on it was the succession of merit;
all subjects touched by him became pure in essence.
Endowed with knowledge and dispassion, and devoted solely to the path of liberation, they beheld him; thereafter, the Blessed Brahmā created sin.
That evil, in the form of a buffalo and consisting of darkness among embodied beings, is ignorance, lack of sovereignty, lack of dispassion, and unrighteousness. (27.23)

Its four legs are indeed deceit and treachery, along with the two types of scriptural learning; its two horns are anger and delusion; the pair of ears are wrath and infatuation; and its two eyes are lust and greed. (27.24)
Avarice is its fierce tail, and the murder of a Brahmin is its head;
the drinking of liquor is its heart, and minor offenses (upapātaka) are its hips.

Touched by him, all creatures became devoid of strength (or, according to another reading, "defiled"), bereft of knowledge and dispassion, and exhausted by the performance of rites for the sake of desire. || 27-26 ||
Being utterly deluded, they became attached only to demonic states;
therefore, O beloved, one must thoroughly understand that [self] which moves within the body and the senses.
A wise person should practice right conduct so that his own intellect becomes radiant; for when the intellect is radiant, one indeed perceives all things with equanimity through it. (27–28)
While pleasures are present, seeing suffering, grief, fear, and so forth within them, one desists from them; and at that time, there is purity of the intellect.
His mind is not distressed by blame nor does it rejoice in praise; indifferent toward both enemies and friends, his enlightened intellect remains equanimous. (27–30)
Freedom from greed, faith in the scriptures, the desire for liberation, profundity, serenity, happiness through one's own self, and withdrawal from attachment to worldly society. (27–31)
A delight in solitary practice and the avoidance of hypocrisy and pride—wherever these qualities arise, one's intellect becomes brilliantly radiant. (27–32)
In this world, the supreme fruit of practicing right conduct is the purification of the intellect;
once the intellect is purified, one proceeds to the meditative absorption on the Arhats through effortless play.

O Goddess, a wise person, desiring to achieve purity of being, should avoid that which is corrupt according to the scriptures, corrupt in its inherent nature, or even corrupt by worldly standards. (27–34)

O Maheśvarī, one should always and in all circumstances perform the purification of the private parts, the purification of the feet, the purification of the hands, and fourthly, the purification of the mouth. (27–35)
O daughter of Śambhu, one who is impure from eating remnants should never touch the ritual implements;
having prostrated, one should enter the sacred space, and having prostrated again, one should depart. (27–36)
While standing there, one should not spit, chatter, discharge downward wind, or harbor indifference, fear, or anger. (27–37)
According to their caste, according to their knowledge, and according to their seniority or juniority,
they should sit there in that very manner, free from attachment and aversion.
One should not revile a maiden, a Brahmin, or a teacher in thought or speech; one should practice compassion toward all beings and must not harm anyone, my dear. (27-39)
One should endure all harshness by contemplating the impermanence of the body;
for the body, home, wife, kin, friends, wealth, and prosperity [are all transient]. (27-40)
One may see [forms] resembling dreams or lightning, but one should not become attached to them there;
for through the power of attachment to what is unreal, saṃsāra does not cease. (27.41)
Generosity, self-restraint, and compassion—this triad must never be abandoned under any circumstances.
One should not speak words that are untrue, for such speech is indeed death to one's own voice. (27.42)
The dead tongue is not fit for speaking of the qualities of the Supreme Lord;
nor should one ever cast a glance at the face of another's wife with a desire for enjoyment. (27.43)
The conception of being a woman would vanish within oneself; therefore, that is indeed a sin, like the senses of a newborn infant which are free from modification.
O Priyaṃvadā, even though he stands in the midst of a multitude of women, his mind is not divided;
his state as a friend remains firm and pure.
Even those who appear as men but possess the pure nature of women should be understood with certainty as beloved to the Blessed One. (27.46)

Those corrupted by women, those who have fallen from their commitments, those averse to meditation, the deceitful, the nihilists, those of evil conduct, the wicked, and those eager to go to the wives of others—[these should be avoided]. (27.47)
O Goddess, one should not seat those who are antagonistic, cruel-minded, devoid of faith and love, or engaged in improper conversation within the same row. (27–48)
One should never drink water from the same vessel there; likewise, one should avoid sharing footwear, clothing, beds, couches, seats, or dwellings.

One should certainly not act together with them, for otherwise there would be an onset of faults; [this applies] even with those who have not seen the person, O Goddess, or those residing in another land. (27.50)
O Beloved, one should not maintain association with those who delight in sense objects, even if they have come together through hypocrisy and deceit, during this festival of supreme bliss. (27.51)

Neither one who has not bathed, nor one whose feet are unwashed, nor one who is lacking in ritual purity, nor one agitated by fear, nor even one whose garments are unwashed, should ever enter a festive gathering. (27.52)
During the festival, one should engage in the singing of virtues and other such acts, as well as auspicious narrations of Kṛṣṇa’s stories;
one should not engage in worldly talk nor quarrel with one another. (27.53)
O Goddess, one should not speak of the vital points [of others], nor should one cause them distress;
rather, O Mistress of the Gods, one should contemplate with the intellect the identity of oneself with the other. (27.54)
When one's state is free from modification, then there arises an immersion in rasa;
therefore, one should direct the mind toward that great festival.
Some meditate with their eyelids closed tight;
others roar, having attained a great stature through the acquisition of weapons;
while others dance, their hearts and desires melted away by that aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
As if melting with devotion, [they were seen] by those emerging from the lotuses of their eyes. || 27-56 ||
Their intellects delighted by perceiving the state [of reality] through that meditation, they are serene,
their pure nature surging forth from the ocean of their own bliss;
the regions of their bodies are made variegated by the mantle of horripilation.
Those of various sectarian marks do not know this entire [truth]. || 27-57 ||
Whatever account occurs during a festival, whether good or bad, one should not reveal it externally as if it were forgotten from the heart. (27.58)
O Goddess praised by the gods, one should accept the offerings according to the distinction of their colors; furthermore, one should provide separate seats and vessels for each.

In this manner, they should bow to one another and perform this great festival of festivals on the birthdays of their own sons and wives, as well as on the day of the preceptor’s birth or its reversal.
On an auspicious day, during an abundance of prosperity, upon gaining profit, at the gathering of devotees,
as well as on the Vyatīpāta yoga, on the eighth lunar day, on the eleventh lunar day, and at the transit of the sun.

On a Sunday coinciding with the Puṣya asterism, on a Sunday coinciding with the Hasta asterism, during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, on the day of Kṛṣṇa’s birth, O Goddess of Gods, and likewise on the day of Rādhā’s birth; || 27-62 ||
Thus, on the days of the incarnations of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor,
on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the Blessed One assumed the form of a fish.
Then, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, he assumes the form of a tortoise;
and on the ninth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, Hari assumes the form of a boar.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, at the end of the day,
Nṛhari appeared, intent upon protecting his devotees.
O Daughter of the Mountain King, on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha,
Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, was born of Reṇukā.
O Goddess, on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, Vāmana was born from Kaśyapa by Aditi to accomplish the purpose of the gods. || 27-67 ||
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha and the Supreme Person,
was born of Kauśalyā for the purpose of slaying Rāvaṇa.
O Goddess, in the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, on the eighth day at the dead of night,
Kṛṣṇa appeared with the desire to accomplish the work of the gods.
On the second day of the month of Nabhas, Hari will become Balabhadra;
and on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, the Buddha will appear.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, Kalkī will appear;
especially on these and other meritorious days. (27.71)
O Goddess, one should perform the festival free from stinginess regarding wealth; for a festival is not constituted by mere edibles and foods, nor by the arrangement of flowers and such. (72)
Where there is an immersion in aesthetic flavor (rasa), they call that the supreme festival;
the mind becomes free from fluctuations and comes within the range of knowledge of the Blessed One.

In that festival of the Lord of the Gods, O Goddess of the gods, there will certainly be an immersion into the pure state of those whose sole essence is love (or, according to another reading, those who are unified in love and skilled in the *rāsa* dance); indeed, the gathering of people therein is of three kinds.
The first [creation] consists of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of those who are dear; the second is the divine creation (*devasarga*);
and the third, O Gautamas, consists of those known as the Vaiḍālinas who were cursed. (27.75)
There is no doubt that in this state, the immersion in aesthetic flavor (*rasāveśa*) within latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is pure;
likewise, among the gods—even those possessed of love for the Lord—there is the immersion in divinity (*devatāveśa*). (7.76)
Devoid of love, they are of wicked conduct, greedy for the wives and wealth of others;
they are backbiters, deceivers, cruel, crooked, and practitioners of sin. (27.77)
Devoid of proper conduct, wicked, shameless, and eager for quarrels,
they have fallen into a demonic state, reviling the meaning of the Vedas and the scriptures.
O Goddess, those who are indeed *vaiḍālins* are devoid of authority;
they are possessed by asuras—let what I have said be taken to heart. (27–79)
One should recognize each specific possession according to its corresponding behavior;
having thus understood these three types occurring during the great festival in Śiva, [one should act accordingly].
One should conduct legal affairs as is appropriate so that there may be no confusion;
[acting] according to what is fitting, at the proper time, with the right materials, and in a manner that is suitable. (27.81)
One should act thus, O Maheśānī; otherwise, one would fall.
This has been told to you, O Goddess; what more do you wish to hear? (27–82)
Therefore, I shall explain that to you in detail, even though it is a profound secret.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Śrīmāheśvaratantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. || 27-27 ||
Then, the twenty-eighth chapter.
Pārvatī said:
"O Mahādeva, speak again so that there may be the arising of devotion."
Whom should one serve as a guru, and how may the arising of knowledge occur? (28.1)
Śiva said:
"Well asked by you, O blessed lady; I shall explain it exactly as it is.
It must be guarded with effort and never shown to anyone."
This entire universe is seized by illusion, afflicted by various sufferings and fears, and scorched on all sides by the heat of impermanent existence. (28.3)
Seeing himself perpetually seized day and night by the serpent of the Staff of Time, he became dispassionate and constantly strove for the sake of his own auspicious liberation. (28.4)
O beautiful lady, one should take refuge in a true guru with a pure disposition;
for there are many gurus, like lamps in every house. (28.5)
O Goddess! Gurus who illuminate everything like the sun are difficult to find;
there are many gurus who merely plunder the wealth of their disciples. (28.6)
O Goddess, rare are the gurus who remove the suffering from the hearts of their disciples;
they are of pure lineage, pure-minded, pure in dress, and auspicious in appearance. (28.7)

Speaking what is auspicious, practicing what is auspicious, pure in disposition and himself clean, he knows the true meaning of the Vedas and Shastras and is free from attachment to the world. || 28-8 ||
Free from greed, of excellent character, endowed with compassion and courtesy, generous, dispassionate, virtuous, a knower of virtues, and affectionate toward his disciples. || 28-9 ||
Content with whatever comes to him, a refuge for others, free from anger, knowing the true meaning of his own established doctrine, moderate in speech, and beloved by the world. (28.10)
Having recognized such a guru—one who is pure, a dispeller of doubts, overflowing with love for Kṛṣṇa, and a showerer of the nectar of mercy—[one should serve him]. (28.11)
Carrying fruits, flowers, and other offerings in his hands, he should go toward the Guru; having reached the Guru's residence, O beloved, he should bow down at its threshold.

O Goddess, by the command of the true guru, having entered that house preceded by circumambulation of the right foot, she should prostrate like a staff before him at his command. (Note: There is also a reading "tat" for "tam.")
O Lord, ocean of compassion, deliverer from the sea of saṃsāra!
I have wandered through the thicket of saṃsāra, which is crowded with various ascetics. (28.14)
O ocean of compassion, lift me up—I whose heart is utterly wretched, who am devoid of all means of accomplishment, and who am submerged in the mire of ignorance. (28.15)
I have come to you for refuge; you are my protector, a treasure-house of compassion.
O Lord, bring about the cessation of my worldly existence without delay.
Thus entreated by his guru, that lord, a treasure-house of compassion,
[spoke] regarding the brahmin who had previously been tested for one year, O beautiful lady.
O Goddess, one should awaken a Kṣatriya who is afflicted by separation in two years, a Vaiśya in three years,
and a Śūdra in four years.
If the *jīva* is merely a mental impression (*vāsanā*), then it must be understood as such in every respect;
if it is dream-like, then it must be abandoned, because its qualification [for spiritual practice] is reversed. (28.19)
O Goddess, O sinless one, I have previously explained the examination by means of characteristics;
if one were to bestow the awakening upon a living being who has not been examined, [the result would be contrary]. (28.20)
One should not recognize him as a guru, nor would he possess even the latent impression (vāsanā) [of being one], if his thought is: "Having taken wealth from my disciples, may I be happy. (28.21)
One should not recognize him as a guru; he is merely a rogue.
Those who assume the outward appearance [of a teacher] are hypocrites intent on acquiring wealth and sustenance. (28.22)
They delude all people while appearing as those who possess knowledge;
therefore, O Goddess, a teacher must indeed be examined in every way, even by a disciple.
If, due to ignorance, a disciple should perceive his teacher as being devoid of the required characteristics, he should abandon that teacher at that very moment and take refuge in another. (28.24)
Just as a bee, greedy for fragrance, goes from flower to another flower, so too a disciple, greedy for knowledge, may go from one guru to another guru. (28.25)
One should abandon a friend who does not know one's secrets, and an unfaithful woman;
one should abandon a teacher who lacks self-restraint, has evil associations, and is devoid of knowledge. (28.26)
While the five musical instruments resound and the Brahmins recite, and likewise while the women sing, the Guru should awaken the disciple. (28.27)
At the outset, the skillful guru should purify the body of the disciple; for one whose body is unrefined is in no way fit [for initiation]. (28.28)
Having summoned him who has performed his ablutions, one should place him before oneself—
seated on an auspicious seat, clad in white garments, and free from impurity.
O Īśānī, one should awaken that self-consciousness (ātmacaitanya) in the lotus of the heart in the form of a lamp-flame, and then one should unite it with one's own self.
Then, O Supreme Goddess, one should contemplate the fourteen worlds within his pair of feet, and the elemental beings within the region of his *liṅga*.
One should contemplate the remaining principles within the lotus of the heart;
one should also contemplate the qualities of Nāda and Bindu in the region of the throat. (28–32)

Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa, the Lord of Prakṛti, within the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), O Goddess of the Gods, one should offer those oblations in their proper sequence.
One should offer oblations in the region of the *liṅga* for the fourteen worlds;
one should offer oblations for the elements situated in the region of the *liṅga* within the principles (*tatva*) in the heart.

One should dissolve the principles (tattvas) located in the heart— or according to another reading, "those which are in the heart"— into the *bindu* and the *nāda*, and then, O Goddess, into the consciousness at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), within the partless Supreme Brahman.
Having offered the qualities of *nāda* and *bindu*, one should contemplate the dissolution of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*);
then, O Supreme Goddess, one should awaken the disciple to that which is free from proliferation.
At that time, among the castes such as the Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, there was no one who was a god, nor a Gandharva, nor an Asura, nor even a serpent. (28–37)
You are not the body, nor are you the burner [of the body], nor likewise the senses or the mind;
you are considered to be neither the vital breath, nor the intellect, nor the ego-sense.
This entire phenomenal world is perishable, yet it is reflected within the imperishable;
the desire to see the imperishable arose for the purpose of beholding the play of Brahman.
His beloved had a desire to behold the play of the Imperishable;
from that, a longing arose, and she produced ignorance within Brahmā. (28–40)
Entering the egg of delusion, the witness beheld a world appearing in a dream;
there, in Vṛndāvana, his beloved was delighted by the rāsa-līlā. (28–41)
Now that your beloved Kṛṣṇa has vanished, you have gone from sorrow to even greater sorrow;
you have wandered aimlessly in many ways through this darkness of time and illusion.
You are the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the perfect Supreme Self;
awakening from this dream within your heart, take refuge in your own true nature as His beloved.
Having become invisible, and having gradually cast off this unwanted body of illusion—
which is both perishable and imperishable— you shall return once more to your own Lord.

O beautiful one, listen as I describe the method for those holy ones who possess the knowledge of Brahman and have tasted the essence of the bliss of Brahman—the method for the creations of Brahmā. (Note: In some manuscripts, these verses 45–54 are not found between verses 44 and 55. 28–45.
The lineage is said to be the bliss of consciousness; indeed, the true Guru is the bliss of Brahman.
The topknot is declared to consist of knowledge, and the sacred thread is of the nature of the imperishable syllable.
A young maiden, supreme devotion, service to the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), and exclusive devotion to her husband are declared to be the means of accomplishment. (28–47)
Vṛndāvana is eternally liberated and known as the bliss of divine play; the couple-name is to be recited, and it is remembered as the mantra of ascending excellence (tāratamya). || 28-48 ||
The supreme goddess is the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), and the god is the eternal Brahman; the hall (śālā) is said to be Goloka, and the door above is thus described. (28–49)

Self-realized (or, according to other readings: well-realized, subtle realization; some also read *svasaṃvedya*), it is taught as the fruit consisting of eternal abiding. It is the divine city of Brahman, the abode described as higher than the highest. (28.50)
The feet of the true guru are the supreme field that effects all purification;
the sacred ford known as Yamunā is contemplation characterized by divine love. (28.51)
The Śrīmad Bhāgavata is declared to be the wonderful essence of all that is heard;
its seer is said to be Mahāviṣṇu, and its knowledge is of the nature of the waking state. (28–52)
The Kula known as Ānanda has been attained and is proclaimed in the eternal abode; the oral tradition (sampradāya) is the bliss of consciousness, manifested through innate joys.
Thus has been declared the manual known as Puruṣottama;
thereafter, O auspicious lady, one should proceed with the means of accomplishment for the sake of attaining the Self.
O Supreme Goddess, having thus awakened consciousness within him, the Guru should establish it once again by means of the gaze of divine vision.

Remembering that [the breath] has descended through the path of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) into that [place], one should thereafter establish the sound (nāda) and the point (bindu) in the region of the throat. (28.56)
One should place the principles (tattvas) in the lotus of the heart, and the five elements in the liṅga; thereafter, one should establish the series of worlds (bhuvanāvali) in the region of the feet.
Having thus consecrated the Virāja fire, one should then impart the mantra;
O Dear One, prior to the instruction of the mantra, one should worship the Guru.
Having given away all his possessions as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), he indeed becomes one who has fulfilled his duty;
or else [he may give] half of that, or half of that again, or even half of that half.

One should satisfy the guru with devotion by means of wealth, grain, clothing, and so forth; likewise, one should give ornaments, garments, and other gifts to others according to one's ability. (28–60)
Then, O Goddess, having prostrated on the ground with the eight limbs [of the body] like a staff,
he should bow to his own guru, and the guru should raise him up.

Having seated her again by his side, he should instruct her in the various varieties of amorous play (*līlābheda*). O beautiful one, these varieties of amorous play must indeed be learned from the mouth of the Guru.
Then, remaining in solitude after solitude, one should meditate upon them;
when the state of endearment toward the Buddha arises, then one has accomplished what was to be done.
Thus has been told to you, O Goddess, that which is more secret than the secret;
in brief, O Great Goddess! What more do you wish to hear? (28.64)
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the Śrī Nāradapañcarātra, within the Śrī Māheśvara Tantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī. 28.28.
Then, in the twenty-ninth chapter,
Pārvatī said:
"O Maheśāna, tell me that King of Mantras, O Maheśvara."
By the mere hearing of which, the fruit of all mantras shall be attained. || 29-1 ||
Śrī Mahādeva said:
O Goddess of the gods, this great king of mantras shines as most secret;
even by reciting it but once, all sins are dissolved. (29–2)
I have previously recounted to you seventy million great mantras;
among them, many Śrī Kṛṣṇa mantras have been proclaimed for you. (29–3)
O Maheśānī, in former times, when I had entered the Rāsa-līlā in the form of a cowherd, these mantras were spoken; however, this one was concealed by me therein. (29-4)
Because it is a secret, I did not speak of it; yet you ask about it again.
This must be guarded by you as well; it should never be given to anyone under any circumstances.
O beloved, having caused [the mantra] to be written down, one may give the mantra, but one must not teach it orally;
by doing so, one incurs the sin of killing a thousand Brahmins.
O Goddess, if an outburst of love should arise when the latent impression has been definitively determined, only then should one teach; otherwise, one is a slayer of Kṛṣṇa. (29.7)
O beloved, every ritual procedure should be performed except for the imparting of the mantra;
then, when the time has matured and [the disciple's] fitness has been tested, one should instruct the mantra. (29.8)
Listen, I shall proclaim the mantra with an attentive mind.

The first vowel is *a*; the fourth long vowel is *ī*, joined with the half-measure dot (*bindu*), forming the seed-syllable of space: *āṃ*, meaning "I am space. First and fourth, followed by space: 29–9.
After that, the seed-syllable of Vāyu; after that, the seed-syllable of Agni; then the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, and after that, the seed-syllable of Bhū. || 29-10 ||
"O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Supreme Bliss, one should say, 'I am indeed dear to you.
Having said, 'Please accept me,' one should then say the two words, 'Show [yourself]. (29.11)
One should say "awaken" (prabodhaya) as the second part, and then say "delude" (moha).
Having uttered "remove" (apākuru) twice, this great mantra ends with "namas. (29-12)
O Dear One, it is composed of forty-nine syllables;
O Great Goddess, the first seed-syllable is the Lord, the imperishable Supreme Self. (29-13)
Therefore, creation consists of the phonemes and unfolds from the letter *ha* as its end;
through its dissolution in reverse order, that very [letter *ha*] alone remains.
O Maheśvarī, because it is infinite, because it is the reality of the Self, and because it is all-pervasive, there is no dissolution anywhere for that Self of the phonemes, O Beloved. (29.15)
The fourth vowel is *tanmāyā*; indeed, having ascended above, she has attained the state of a sprout.
Thereafter, O Goddess, she became *jñānaharā*, the deluder of the universe. (29.16)
Through the union with the central point, she indeed became the form of emptiness;
within that emptiness, the lower line is the form of the sprout of the world.
Indeed, through union with the half-moon (ardhabindu), she consists of the power of yoga-illusion (yogamāyā);
thus, by means of this triad, her three qualities (guṇatraya) are to be known.
When the source of the universe appears as a reflection within the stainless Supreme Self, it indeed then manifests in the form of a single, uniform essence. (29.19)
Through the union of the three corners, she consists of the triad beginning with Brahmā;
she is the essence of the three worlds and likewise the essence of the three Vedas. (29–20)
She is the essence of will, knowledge, and action; she takes the form of the three times;
she is the embodiment of fire, moon, and sun; and she is the form of all triads. (29.21)
For she should be known as descending from the Supreme Self with her face turned downwards;
and when she becomes upward-facing at the time of dissolution, she is like a flame of fire.
In the state of emptiness, the lower line takes the form of the sprout of the world;
and that which the proponents of Tantra call the Great Principle (mahattattva) is precisely this. (29.23)
But the ego (ahaṅkāra), situated within the lines and conjoined with the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of those qualities, is to be known as threefold; from it, the elements were born. (29–24)
O Maheśvarī, the five syllables that denote those [five elements], beginning with the letter *ha*, are seen at the beginning of the King of Mantras. (29–25)
Ākāśa resides in the letter *ha*, and its deity is Sadāśiva;
its quality is sound, as well as the sense of hearing and the object of hearing—the quarters of space, O beautiful one. (29–26)
In the syllable *ya*, O Goddess of the lords of gods, is Vāyu and also Īśvara;
the sense of touch, the tactile organ, and the object of touch, the tree, are likewise present, O Goddess. (29.27)
O Goddess, in the syllable *ra* there is fire; likewise, form is the eye and the sun.
It should be understood that what is to be seen is like a jewel within a casket. (29.28)
In the syllable *va* reside water, Viṣṇu, taste, the sense organ of taste, the object of tasting, and Varuṇa as the presiding deity; thus it is established. (29–29)
In the letter *la*, O Goddess, the earth element (*pṛthivītattva*), Brahmā, smell, the nose, the object of smell, and the two Aśvins are established as the presiding deities. (29–30)

Thus, O Īśvarī, the causal function of the five elements has been described; this is the seed (bīja), and its effect (kārya) has been told to you as that which they call by the name "the perishable" (kṣara). (29–31)
The letter *A* is the supreme Brahman—immutable, all-pervading, and eternal; it is called the unsurpassed, undifferentiated portion of consciousness. (29–32)
This mantra is remembered as having a form that transcends syllables, yet it consists of all remaining phonemes;
therefore, oh, this leader of mantras is of the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss.
O Dear One, because it brings about reflection, universal knowledge, and protection from the perils of saṃsāra, a mantra that has attained perfection is so called. (29–34)
Having known the crest-jewel of mantras, one is liberated from all doubt;
once the king of mantras is realized, nothing further remains to be known. (29–35)
O Supreme Goddess, this verbal form of the one whose body is supreme bliss—this crest-jewel of mantras—has been proclaimed by me to you. (29–36)
Though it is inexpressible from the perspective of ultimate reality, it has nevertheless been told to you;
yet it must be guarded with great effort, like the pregnancy resulting from a lover's union with one's own mother. (29–37)
Those of deceitful intellect who perceive the Great Mantra as being composed of [ordinary] syllables—
all of them go to the hells for as long as the dissolution of all beings lasts.
Those lowest of men who behold a person reciting mantras—even their sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin and others, are destroyed. (29–39)

Even those who have been most wicked throughout millions of kalpas, and who are perpetually devoted to sin, are purified through contact with the reciter of the mantra; of this there is no doubt. (29–40)
O Goddess, when the wish-fulfilling gem has been obtained, what is the use of other accumulations of wealth?
Likewise, when the king of mantras has been obtained, what need would there be for other means of accomplishment? (29-41)
This knowledge of the meaning of the mantra indicates the established conclusion of the mantra;
for one who constantly contemplates this in the mind, their latent impression (vāsanā) is purified. (29.42)
Having abandoned the veil of illusion bound to the body and the senses, let the latent impression of discernment manifest before one like a reflection. (29.43)
This majesty of the mantra has thus been proclaimed by me to you.
What else do you wish to hear? Tell me that now, O beloved; I shall speak it. (i0 pā0) 29-44.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Māheśvara-tantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. || 29-29 ||
Now begins the thirtieth chapter.
Pārvatī said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, I desire to hear [more] once again."
The direct accomplishment of the mantra, by performing which it becomes complete in all its parts. || 30-1 ||
Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess of the lords of gods, to the practice of the king of mantras.
Its seer, O Goddess, is remembered as the Supreme Self, Puruṣottama. (30.2)
Its meter is known as Anuṣṭubh, and its deity is Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
"I" (Aham) is the seed-syllable, "Namaḥ" is the power, and its application is for the purpose of propitiation. (30.3)
Having placed the Sage upon the head, the Metre upon the circle of the face, the Deity upon the heart, one should place the Seed-syllable upon the pair of feet. (30.4)
One should place the Śakti on the region of the hips; the Niyoga is in the hollow of the hands.
Having thus performed the Nyāsa of the Ṛṣis and so forth, one should then proceed with the Varṇanyāsa.
Then one should place the seed-syllable on the head; one should place *māyā* on the forehead;
one should place the seed-syllable of space (*vyoma*) on the pair of ears, and then the seed-syllable of wind (*samīraṇa*).
O beloved, one should then place the fire-seed (RAṂ) on the skin,
the water-seed (VAṂ) on the tongue, and the earth-seed (LAṂ) on the two nostrils.
One should place the syllable Śrī at the region of the throat and the syllable Kṛ at the heart;
one should place Ṣṇa and Paṃ on the pair of breasts, beginning from the left, O Supreme Goddess.
One should place the syllable *ra* and the syllable *ma* in the two sides of the belly, starting from the left;
likewise, one should place the syllable *na* and the syllable *da* on the two hips.
One should place the syllable *te* on the linga, and the two syllables of *priyā* on the two thighs;
likewise, O Goddess, one should place the two syllables of *smi* on the pair of knees.
O Goddess of gods, one should place *maṃ* and *gī* upon the pair of shanks;
one should apply the pair of syllables *kuḥ* and *rvī* to the pair of heels.
One should place the syllable *da* and the syllable *śa* on the two foreparts of the feet;
likewise, one should place the syllable *pra* and the syllable *bo* on the two soles of the feet.
One should place *dhaṃ* on the fingers themselves, and *yaṃ* at the tips of the fingers; then, from the palms up to the knees, one should again place two syllables of the *prabhu*.
One should place two syllables of the color of smoke from the knees up to the navel;
one should place the syllable *mo* at the navel and the syllable *ha* in the stomach.
One should place the letters *ma* and *pā* on the pair of shoulders; one should place the letter *ka* on the pair of armpits;
and one should properly place the two letters *ru* on the two arms and the two cheeks. (30.15)
Having assigned [the mantra] to the crest (śikhā) with "namas," one should assign the entire [mantra] as the pervasive (vyāpaka).
Thus, by this assignment, he becomes one who bears the form of the mantra within his body. (30.16)
Having assumed a supramundane body, one should go to that state through meditative absorption;
O beautiful one, I shall explain that method, even though it is well-guarded.
One should meditate on the body as having color and form, for those [bodies] are composed of the five elements;
one should dissolve each effect into its respective causal elements. (30.18)
One should contemplate the earth-element (pṛthvī-tattva) from the feet up to the knees.
I shall now briefly declare the phonemes consisting of the earth-element. (30.19)
The fifth, the sixth, and the thirteenth—this triad of vowels is the first syllable after the space (ākāśa). (30.20)
The eighth among the objects of touch, as well as the thirteenth, and those that are cool—
these are proclaimed to be the qualities of the earth element.
The letters ṛ, ṝ, au, gha, jha, ḍha, dha, and bha are remembered as belonging to Varuṇa;
one should meditate on them as residing in the water-element from the knees up to the waist. (30.22)

One should meditate on the letters *i*, *ī*, *e*, *kha*, *cha*, *ṭha*, *tha*, *pha*, *ra*, and *kṣā* as having the form of fire, situated within the element of fire from the waist up to the throat. (30.23)
O beloved, the letters a, ai, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, sa, and ṣa are said to be the Maruts;
one should contemplate them as consisting of the element of air, extending from the throat to the region of the eyebrows.
One should contemplate the sounds ḷ, ḷ, aṃ, aṅ, añ, aṇ, an, ama, śa, ba, ha, nā, bha,
sā as being composed of space, situated from the middle of the eyebrows up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
One should effect the dissolution of each respective phoneme into the causal syllable;
having abandoned the gross form consisting of the elements, one then proceeds to the subtle form consisting of sound. (30.26)
He is the embodiment of the Śabdabrahman, the cause of all causes;
he is established within the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus.
O Dear One, one should meditate solely on the partless syllable *A* within the belly;
O Maheśvarī, that *A* is the space of the belly, and within that space of the belly resides the *dahara*. (30.28)
She should remember the previously experienced *rāsa*-pastimes and the pastimes of Vraja, thinking:
"I am the beloved of the Blessed One, who can assume any form at will. (30.29)
O Supreme Goddess, one should remember [the form] of Kṛṣṇa with a mind brought under control by firm practice alone; one should not think of anything else at all. (30.30)
Then, by that very same path, one should abandon even the body of sound,
[reaching] the supreme abode beyond sound, the great ocean of the bliss of rasa.
It was filled with various kinds of games and arts, resounded with the cries of diverse birds,
and made the quarters of the sky resonant with the humming of wandering bees.
Then, having attained self-luminosity, one should contemplate that essential nature,
which is endowed with fresh youth, enchanting, and fond of love.
It was resplendent with lotus-feet beautified by tinkling anklets,
its feet smeared with lac-dye, and it possessed a girdle of jingling small bells.
Her body was exceedingly large due to the weight of her high breasts in the bloom of fresh youth;
her sprout-like fingers were radiant with a multitude of rings upon them.
Beautiful with various ornaments, adorned with garments from Kauśāmbī, his chest radiant with pearl necklaces and flashing with the luster of glittering gems.
His eyes were like arrows from the curved brow-bow of Kāma;
his forehead shone with a pearl-ornament and was radiant with a saffron tilaka.
His limbs were anointed with divine sandalwood paste, he was adorned with garlands of celestial flowers,
and he shone with a tilaka of excellent jewels gleaming upon the region of his forehead.
Having meditated thus, one should remember one’s own divine body as being among a group of female companions;
having meditated with an undivided mind upon Kṛṣṇa situated in the midst of that group. (30–39)
There she should entreat that husband, whose face was beautiful with a smile:
"O Lord of my life, I am yours; protect me from manifold sufferings. (30-40)
O Lord, exquisite with supreme bliss, I have forgotten you;
I have experienced a dream-like play crowded with a multitude of various sufferings.
"A great deal of time has passed without you, O Supreme Person;
while deeply attached to my body and home, I have wandered much in dreams. (30.42)
In some places in human form, or in the form of a god;

in some places in the form of a gandharva or a serpent; or in some places in the form of an animal. (Such a state of the creations of Brahmā never occurs; however, this is merely a prayer, or rather, it should be understood as a prayer for the sake of living beings by the wise. 30–43.
Indeed, I have caused this self to move within a dream created by illusion;
now I am one who has accomplished her purpose, for the illusory form of the dream has vanished.
"O Lord, look with a compassionate eye; everything has been seen by us without you.
Having thus entreated her husband, she should prostrate at his lotus-feet.
She was raised up by him and embraced again and again, and the nectar of his lips was bestowed upon her even as the circle of her friends looked on. (30.46)

Being gazed upon by her friends with feigned curiosity as they looked at one another, she was likewise gazed upon by her friends with feigned curiosity while she moved through all ten stages of the eternally blissful pastimes. (30.47)
And in the valleys of shining mountains composed of topaz,
and especially upon the vast peaks of mountains of sapphire and ruby.
In the seventy sacred bathing places (tīrthas) of the Yamunā, where various trees grow, and which are adorned with paved floors shining with jeweled pavilions; || 30-49 ||
For she was led by her beloved through various designated pleasure-gardens, overflowing with the blissful rasa of great divine play in each and every place. (30.50)
Having arrived at the jeweled floor shining with sixteen pillars,
she stood before Kṛṣṇa as he sat in the midst of a circle of his companions.
Thus consoled by her lord of life, who showered the nectar of his words, O Goddess, [she remained] until the mind became steady through such concentration. (30.52)
One should practice these līlās for that long, and in this way the self becomes purified.
Thus, O Goddess, I have explained to you the mantra, meditation, and so forth.
In brief, O Great Goddess, what more do you wish to hear?
That I shall declare to you, O lady of excellent vows, under oath.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the Śrī Nāradapañcarātra, within the Śrī Māheśvara Tantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī. || 30-30 ||
Then, the thirty-first chapter.
Pārvatī said:
"Tell me the method of service by which the Lord himself may be pleased."
How should worship be performed, and what is the nature of the ritual practice? || 31.1 ||
Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the ritual worship and other practices.
Having risen during the fourth watch of the night while still upon your bed, O lady of excellent vows— (31-2)

One should meditate on the Guru at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), possessing a luster white as camphor, with two eyes and two arms, and clad in white garments and anointed with white unguents. (31.3)
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship the Lord with these five offerings consisting of the five elements; one should then remember the Self as being absorbed in Him.
One should contemplate oneself as having become washed, stainless, and pure, with the stream of water from his feet falling upon one's own head. (31.5)
Salutation be to that Guru, who is the very embodiment of the chosen deity, whose nectar-like speech destroys the poison known as saṃsāra. (31.6)
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the god Sadāśiva;
the Guru alone is the supreme reality (Brahman). Salutations to that venerable Guru.
Having prostrated with the pair of mantras, one should contemplate [the deity] dissolved within the heart;
thereafter, one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, who is engaged in playful pastimes, within the lotus of the heart.
O Goddess, one should worship him as before with the five types of offerings;
then, O sweet-spoken lady, with hands joined in reverence, one should pray to that Lord.
"I am yours, O Lord; you are my husband, O Master.
I have been led astray by you, O Lord, onto the path of the dense forest of illusion. (31.10)
"O Lord, lead me to your side; separation distresses me.
I have no other refuge; therefore, do what is appropriate. (31.11)

Having thus prayed to her husband, who is reddened by a mass of light, the Goddess should contemplate her own body and then offer salutation, O Beloved. Then, having prayed to the earth, she should place her right foot [upon it]. (31-12)
O Goddess whose girdle is the ocean, whose breasts are the mountain ranges, O Consort of Viṣṇu, salutations to you; forgive my touch of your feet.
Then, O beautiful one, she should go outside the village for the purpose of voiding excrement.
Having advanced from the distance of a single arrow-shot across the ground without weariness, he covered the earth with grass and veiled his head with his garment. (31.15)
One should keep the earth and the water vessel within the span of one's own hand;
furthermore, one must not look at the sun, the quarters of the horizon, or cows.
One should perform the cleansing of the penis with three applications of earth, and five applications of earth should be applied to the anus, O beautiful lady of the gods. (31.17)
One should perform purification in this manner so as to remove both odor and residue;
in that very process, seven applications of clay should be made to the left hand.
Having returned to his own home in silence, he should cleanse his hands, feet, and other limbs;
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, seven applications of clay should be made to the left hand.
In that same manner, seven [applications] are prescribed for both hands;
likewise, five auspicious applications of clay should be given to each foot. (31.20)
Then, O Dear One, one should wash the mouth with twelve mouthfuls of water;
thereafter, having performed the ritual sipping (ācamana), one should employ the tooth-stick.
One should clean one's teeth with a twig originating from the Jambu, Udumbara, or Badarī tree, or even one produced from the Apāmārga.
O beloved, one should never touch the teeth with wood that is unknown, pierced by insects, burnt in the forests, or otherwise forbidden. (31.23)
Grant me long life, grant me progeny, wealth, knowledge, and happiness;
O Lord of the Forest, you are entreated by me: grant me the perfection of speech forever.
Having consecrated a wooden stick twelve times with the root mantra, the knower of mantras should wash it and consume it before the sun appears.
One should perform the cleansing of the teeth while facing the northern direction;
O beloved, one should not spit or discharge anything while facing the sun.
