Having removed the impurity from the tongue and washed the wooden tooth-stick, the knower of mantras should then cast the stick away in a secluded and pure place, O Dear One. (31.27)
Then, O Goddess, one should wash the face with water produced by the mantra;
one should discard twelve mouthfuls of water without forgetting the root mantra.

Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and having paid homage to the Sun, O Dear One, one should proceed while meditating upon him; thereafter, one may go to a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), or otherwise, one should remain at home without attachment.
Having filtered and purified the water which has been placed in a clean vessel,
one should devoutly invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas) from the solar orb into it.
O Goddess of the Suras, having meditated upon that eight-petalled lotus,
one with a firm mind should invoke Kṛṣṇa, who has gone to his beloved, into the pericarp.
One should worship with water-offerings or even with mental services,
mixed with the nectar flowing from the pair of his feet.
O Goddess, having realized that water to be the manifest form of consciousness itself,
whose nature is the bliss of knowledge, one should then sprinkle it three times upon the head.
One should perform the *mauśala* bath upon the head with other water;
thereafter, O lady of excellent hips, one should bathe with the previously consecrated water.
Then, having meditated that Śrī Kṛṣṇa is dissolved within the heart,
one should sip water (ācamana) and wipe the body with the divine Lord’s mantra-purified water, O Goddess.
Having put on the garments, one should then enter the temple;
standing outside the sanctum of worship, one should apply a tilaka with the earth from Gopikā.
One should perform the wearing of the discus and other marks, and one should wear a garland of *tulasī*.
Without the *tulasī* garland and without the wearing of the discus and other marks [there is no benefit]. (31–37)
He is never fit for recitation, meditation, or worship;
rather, having gratified the gods and the ancestors, he should thereafter bow to the guardians of the directions.
One should meditate on everything as consisting of Kṛṣṇa and abandon the sense of duality;
for, O Goddess, it is said that saṃsāra consists essentially of the state of duality.
Having bowed to the threshold, he should enter the hall of worship with his right foot foremost and remove the faded garlands and other offerings.
One should awaken the Lord while He is asleep with beautiful songs and auspicious sounds.
The most excellent image is the mental one; then there is the stone image originating from the Gaṇḍakī river. (31–41)
O beloved, one should worship the image made of gold, silver, stone, wood, or even clay, on the full moon day of Caitra, with auspicious offerings.
He offers the *argha*, water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*);
then, touching water, he performs the bath, puts on a garment, and finally offers clothes and ornaments. (31–43)
Then there is the looking into a mirror, followed by fragrant flowers;
then incense produced from agaru, a lamp, and indeed the food offering (naivedya).
Water for drinking, water for sipping, water for rinsing the mouth, and thereafter a hand-cloth; then betel, anointment, and then the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and so forth.
Song, instrumental music, as well as dance, praise, and circumambulation; the offering of handfuls of flowers, prostration, and likewise the full-body obeisance with eight limbs. || 31-46 ||
One should worship the beloved of the vital breath with these ritual services.
Worship is considered to be of two kinds: that which involves flower garlands and that which is without them. (31–47)

That worship which is properly performed with divine flowers born of the mind and captivating fragrant substances by those who are devoted is called *anirmālya* (that which is not discarded). || 31-48 ||
As soon as they are born, flowers are naturally smelled by the five great elements, as well as by the sun and the moon.
And by living beings such as bees and others, using only flowers— of this there is no doubt— that worship, together with the floral remains (nirmālya), bestows divine enjoyments and liberation.
Through charming materials for worship produced from villages, forests, and so forth, a small fruit may be achieved from a flower that has been smelled; it is not so from a mental [offering]. (31.51)

Therefore, because it is unavoidable and because there is another means as well, O Goddess, one should worship with external substances for the sake of purifying the intellect—[according to another reading: "from that purification of the intellect"]. || 31-52 ||
Furthermore, the worship of Kṛṣṇa is threefold: superior, inferior, and middling.
That which is performed with all ritual implements (or, according to another reading, sacrificial implements) is the most excellent of the superior.
Worship performed with materials obtained as they come is called middling;
worship performed with leaves, flowers, and water is designated as inferior. (31.54)
First, having performed the mental [worship], one should then proceed with the external;
having completed it up to the lustration (nīrājana), one who has conquered the senses should perform the recitation (japa).
With a rosary made of beads produced from *tulasī* wood, one should recite [the mantra] a hundred or a thousand times;
one should perform that recitation at all three junctions of the day.
One should prepare a seat for the recitation and worship made of a variegated woolen blanket, or of silk, or of cloth, or even of leather or cotton. (31.57)
A seat made of cane, palm leaves, or darbha grass; or one fashioned from bamboo, stone, wood, the earth, grass, or young shoots. (31.58)
The practitioner of mantra should avoid a seat that bestows poverty, disease, and suffering;
in this manner, O Supreme Goddess, one should worship Kṛṣṇa every day.
O moon-faced one, a householder does not attain auspiciousness either in this world or the next through mere knowledge alone, without recitation, worship, and other such practices. (31.60)
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, recitation of mantras, straightforwardness, forbearance, fortitude, moderation in food, faith, and generosity. (31.61)
Dispassion, discernment, tranquility, faith, self-restraint, as well as the desire for liberation, discrimination, and likewise the composure of the self. (31.62)
O Supreme Goddess, for those who accomplish this perfection of means, knowledge that pacifies poverty shall arise; of this there is no doubt. (31.63)
O beloved, the state that certainly produces no affliction for any living beings whatsoever through speech, mind, or action is truly designated as "non-violence" (ahiṃsā). || 31-64 ||
Furthermore, the truthful description of things exactly as they have been seen or heard is called "truth" by the virtuous; it is the means for attaining Brahman. (31.65)
O Priyamvadā, even the non-taking of grass and such from another is this limb of non-stealing, which is eternal for the attainment of Brahman. (31.66)
In all circumstances whatsoever, the renunciation of association with women through action, mind, and speech is declared to be celibacy (brahmacarya).
O Śivā, compassion is said to be the pursuit of the eradication of suffering upon seeing the suffering of others, regarding it as one's own. (31.68)
In all worldly dealings, the absence of crookedness in all actions of mind, speech, and body toward everyone is known as straightforwardness (ārjava). (31.69)
O Supreme Goddess, forgiveness should be practiced toward all who have been helpful at all times and in every way, with conduct as if toward one's own kinsmen. (31.70)
O beautiful lady, they declare that fortitude (dhṛti) is the absence of vain longing for objects already acquired and the presence of steadfastness even amidst sufferings. (31.71)
For one whose mind is healthy, the meal should consist of only a fourth part of what is fit to be eaten,
and it should be free from excessively pungent, bitter, sour, or salty flavors.
That which is beneficial, pure, and pleasant is called moderate diet;
faith in what is declared by the Vedas and other scriptures is termed orthodoxy (āstikya). (31.73)
Having meditated daily upon the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) within the mind with the intention of offering everything to Him,
whatever gift is given to a worthy recipient— that is called true giving.
Even among the many objects of experience, from Brahmā down to the level of stationary beings, the loathing of them as if they were vomit is the means for attaining dispassion (*vairāgya*). (31.75)
The constant renunciation of latent impressions regarding the wives and houses of others, and devotion directed toward supreme bliss—that indeed is called tranquility (śama). (31.76)
Devotion to the words of the Nigamas and Agamas is proclaimed as faith;
it is the restraint of the senses that wander among the pleasures of sense objects. (31.77)
O Goddess, self-restraint is indeed the cause for attaining Brahman;
having realized that worldly existence is fraught with fear, one should practice renunciation, which is the complete [remedy] for even a tenth part of separation. (31.78)
O Goddess of gods, that state of seeking liberation has been described for one who desires liberation:
"Who am I? How did this come to be? Who indeed exists as its creator? What is the material cause here? Such is this inquiry. (31.79)
There is nothing whatsoever that constitutes the material cause of phenomenal manifestation other than Brahman;
therefore, this entire phenomenal world is Brahman itself, extended by ignorance. (31.80)
"Brahman alone bears all names and various forms, as well as all actions in their entirety"—thus the Śruti has proclaimed. (31.81)
Just as there is blueness in the sky, as there is water in a desert,
and as there is the notion of a person in a tree stump, so too is the universe [superimposed] upon the conscious Self.
Just as water alone manifests fully through waves and billows, and just as copper appears in the form of various vessels, so indeed does the imperishable Brahman manifest as the universe.

Therefore, having restrained the mind that was wandering in the manifold world of conceptual proliferation within the Self, and being endowed with the aforementioned means of attainment, he returned to his own state as a friend. || 31.84 ||
By worshipping her own husband, Puruṣottama, who eternally delights in the bliss of divine play, with undivided intelligence, she shall attain union with him once again. (31.85)
Thus, O Goddess, the characteristics of that propitiation have been told to you in brief, O Maheśānī; what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the Śrī Nāradapañcarātra, within the Śrī Māheśvara Tantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī. || 31-31 ||
Now begins the thirty-second chapter.
Pārvatī said:
O Lord of Gods, O Blessed One, O Śambhu, O Dhūrjaṭi, you who are affectionate toward your devotees!
This supreme crest-jewel of a great mantra has been heard by me.

By the mere knowledge of whom one's own latent impressions (vāsanā) are purified by themselves, others also attain purification by themselves through association with those who associate with him. (32-2)
O God, what man, though bound by the various nets of the fetters of karma with their diverse fruits, could obtain this king of mantras? (32-3)
Neither woman nor man exists in any way from the perspective of name and form;
that Brahman which is to be attained as a woman is Kṛṣṇa, whose very body is bliss. (32.4)
And according to the Śruti, the essence (rasa) exists in the form of both the enjoyer and the enjoyed;
yet there is no absolute difference between the two, O Lord, for their distinction is inherent. (32.5)
If it lacks its objective support (ālambana) and other factors, the aesthetic flavor (rasa) itself cannot be established;
for that which cannot be accomplished without something else is not that thing at all, nor anything other than it. (32.6)
Nevertheless, it plays incessantly with its two parts, the enjoyer and the enjoyed;
for the part that is the enjoyed consists of suffering, while the part that is the enjoyer consists of immortality.

The relationship of inseparable concomitance exists between suffering and happiness; the separation of the subjective experiencer and the objective object of experience serves to establish the nature of suffering. (32.8)

If the arising of torment occurred for the wives of Kṛṣṇa during their separation from him, then their purpose would have been fulfilled; it was not while they remained under the rule of prohibitions.
But if, when separation is known, no heat arises in the heart, then success is swiftly attained through the recitation of the Cūḍāmaṇi mantra, and not otherwise. (32.10)
Therefore, O Śambhu, tell us specifically the ritual service (puraskriyā) for this crest-jewel, the king of mantras, so that he may be restored to life. (32.11)
No satiety arises in me from drinking the nectar of your speech;
blessed is the pair of my ears, drenched in the nectar of Brahma’s play.
Today my parents are blessed, for I have become their daughter,
a recipient of your grace as you speak these words in private to Brahmā.
Fie on his lineage! Fie on his wealth! Fie on his learning! Fie on his spotless fame!—if his mind should not be absorbed in reflections upon Brahman. (32.14)
The lifespan in this world is a hundred years; half of that is taken away by sleep, and likewise by childhood and old age, as well as by the afflictions of disease and the like.
Great fools, turning their backs on the glorification of Brahman, render it useless;
therefore, O Lord of Gods, tell us the story that destroys all sins.
O Śaṅkara, [I shall describe] the ritual procedure for the King of Mantras, endowed with its various forms, by the mere hearing of which the accomplishment of the mantra arises. (32.17)
Śiva said:
"O Goddess, daughter of the Lord of Mountains, you are blessed; this secret has been well asked.
It must not be told to just anyone, but it should be told to one who would give away everything he possesses."
Having properly received the mantra from the guru through service and grace,
one should awaken that supreme mantra by means of recitation, libations, fire-offerings, and other such rites.
In an empty house, on a delightful mountain, at a sacred ford free from worldly attachments,
in a garden, at a seat of the Siddhas, or likewise at Puṣkara for the practice [of yoga].
Whether on the bank of the Narmadā, on the Vindhya mountain, or at any auspicious place, success arises swiftly for one who recites the king of mantras. (32.21)
One who has conquered the senses, conquered anger, and conquered the mind; one who is firm in his vows, endowed with steadfast dispassion, and free from the egoism of the body. || 32-22 ||
Compassionate toward all beings, turning away from harming living creatures, free from fear, anxiety, and the like, and devoid of attachment and aversion. || 32-23 ||
Having abandoned all concern for the body, the home, and so forth, with a tranquil mind,
one should be constantly devoted to the meditation on the mantra and always intent upon the meditation on the Divine Play (līlā).

By abandoning the threefold association with women, constantly maintaining the meditative posture (*dhyānamudrā*), observing silence, bathing at the three times of day, keeping the body pure, and wearing white garments; || 32-25 ||
One who is engaged in the duties of the castes and stages of life, full of faith, free from malice, devoid of reviling gods, Brahmins, or cows, and abandoned by greed; || 32-26 ||
Endowed with such qualities, one should perform the preliminary rites for the mantra;
one should mentally designate a field for coming and going. (32.27)
One should scatter mustard seeds, purified by a hundred-fold recitation of the mantra, in all directions;
seeing them resembling blazing fire, the Vināyakas flee.
Then, O beloved, one should drive stakes of *khadira* wood into the ten directions;
thus pinned down, the obstacles do not approach, having seen the sacred field itself secured by the stakes.
One should not go outside by transgressing the boundary of the sacred field out of delusion;
for some beings, consisting of pure darkness, are obstacles to one's spiritual welfare.
One should avoid indifference, fear, anger, sleep, and drowsiness;
one should subsist on milk, fruit, or food obtained through alms. (32–31)
One should provide for one's bodily sustenance with bulbs, roots, fruits, leaves, and likewise with food obtained unasked, in such a way that there is no agitation of the senses.
But if there is a corruption of the sense faculties, the practitioner perishes quickly, even while practicing all the paths of Dharma with the desire for spiritual accomplishment. (32–33)
There is no other obstacle as great as the corruption of the senses;
therefore, one should conduct oneself with vigilance for the sake of guarding the senses. (32–34)
"The senses and the mind, O Goddess, must not be neglected; this is my conviction.
By neglecting them, people are destroyed and wander about in various ways. (32–35)
Although I have withdrawn from sense objects and have conquered desire and pride, I do not neglect the senses; for the creation of Māyā is delusive. (32.36)
O Goddess, who indeed has not been slain by the powerful enemies that are the senses?
Even Indra, the protector of the three worlds, acted as a paramour toward Ahalyā. (32–37)
The Moon was appointed to Tārā, the wife of Bṛhaspati;
and Bṛhaspati, a poet learned in the Vedas and Vedānta, was likewise appointed to Bandhū’s field.
Even though Daśānana was a devotee of mine, he was captivated by Sītā, the wife of Rāma;
these and others too were destroyed by their senses. Therefore, one should not place trust in them.
Therefore, it is my view that one should conquer [the senses] by restricting one's food;
one should keep one's nails and hair short and wear washed clothing.
He should sleep on the ground or on a bed made of kusha grass during the nights;
O Goddess, he should wash his garment whenever it becomes loose around the waist.

While engaged in recitation (japa), one should not speak with those who have fallen from their status, with outcaste laborers (karmacāṇḍālas), nor even with those who are outcastes by birth (jāticāṇḍālas), nor with barbarians (mlecchas), the lowest castes (antyajas), or those of mixed caste (saṅkaras).
When the time of twilight has passed, one should indeed arrange for the sustenance of the body;
however, O Goddess, one should not perform the recitation (japa) either deficiently or excessively day after day.
In conversing with a low person— [where "low" refers to one other than a Yavana]— or likewise in conversing with a Mleccha, O Goddess,
one should perform an expiation by means of a thousand recitations.
He who abandons his bed when half a watch of the night remains, and who sleeps while drowsy and indolent once the thousand-rayed sun has risen; || 32-45 ||
Recitation incurs defects, and success becomes distant;
therefore, O Goddess, one must remain vigilant day after day. (32-46)
When weary from recitation, one should meditate; when weary from meditation, one should recite again. Endowed with both recitation and meditation, the knower of mantras attains success swiftly.
One should not recite the mantra while wearing a single garment, nor while distracted by many clothes;
one should avoid all enjoyments such as oil, betel, areca nut, and the like.
One should abandon crookedness of speech, mind, and body in every way; one should not cause anyone any agitation by word, nor should one dwell upon anything unwholesome. (32.49)
One should never gaze at the sporting of animals with the eyes;
one should not look at a naked woman, nor touch anything inauspicious. (32.50)
Until midday, one should recite the king of mantras with undistracted mind;
thereafter, being composed, one should meditate upon the divine play (līlā) with the mind.
One should perform the fire oblation (homa) every day with a tenth part of the recitation (japa);
or else, having recited up to one hundred thousand times, one should perform the homa.
Or at the conclusion, O Ambikā, one should offer oblations as far as possible;
one who possesses faith and is not overly fickle should mutter the mantra a hundred thousand times for each syllable.
But when it has begun, O Goddess, the mind becomes exceedingly agitated;
anxiety, grief, fear, distress, bad dreams, and the like arise. (32.54)
Then, maintaining fortitude, one should steady the mind through the intellect;
thus, when three hundred thousand recitations have been performed by one whose mind is solely intent on meditating upon the Divine Play (Līlā).
All obstacles flee and all sins are consumed by fire;
for one who is free from obstacles and cleansed of sin, the mind becomes perfectly serene.
O Goddess of gods, when the mind is serene, there is the vision of deities and other beings in dreams. (32–56)
O beloved goddess, even when entreated for the sake of boons, one whose mind is not at all greedy should perform five hundred thousand recitations of the mantra of the gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas.
He becomes invincible, like a blazing fire manifest before one's eyes;
when ten hundred thousand recitations are accomplished, even the celestial maidens entreat him.
"You are our master and we are your maidservants; show us favor, O you who are devoted to compassion, until you pierce through the sphere of the universe and depart for your own abode. (32.59)
Therefore, remain in heaven for now, having been served by us;
there lies the Nandana grove, adorned with the excellences of all seasons.
The celestial river has golden steps, is adorned with jeweled pavilions,
is crowded with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, and is filled with rows of golden lotuses.
Where nectar is the food and the King of the Gods is the protector, those skilled in ritual action pray for the world of the gods through sacrifices. (32.62)
"Therefore, adorn for yourself heaven, which is adorned by the thirty gods.
Even though he was thus being enticed, the minister remained firm in his mind. (32–63)
One should cause them to hear the higher [teaching], remaining unperturbed and free from curiosity;
for there is neither heaven nor hell, neither liberation nor bondage.
Just as it appears in a dream, so it does not please me in the slightest;
therefore, as I have told you, all of you should go to the abode of the gods.
Upon hearing these words of his, those fifteen hundred thousand women departed, despondent, once the great mantra had been recited.
Then, O beautiful one, the Siddhas arrive together with their supernatural powers (siddhis),
including entry into the netherworlds (pātāla) and the abilities of hearing and seeing from afar.

They undoubtedly demonstrate various kinds of supernatural attainments (siddhi), such as entering the bodies of others, moving with the speed of the mind or the wind, the perfection of magical sandals and ointments, and the alchemical transformation of mercury and minerals. (32–68)
And when the previously mentioned words have been spoken, they proceed not before that time;
this occurs when twenty lakhs of the Cintāmaṇi-mantra have been recited.
O beloved, when the Cintāmaṇi has been recited twenty-five hundred thousand times, all branches of knowledge and various scriptures flash forth.
O Goddess of gods, she directly perceives the cosmic egg as being of the nature of the Imperishable;
and having entered within the cosmic egg, O beloved, she beholds Virāj.
When thirty lakhs of recitations have been accomplished, O Goddess of Devas, one beholds in meditation the flawless Nārāyaṇa, all-pervading and facing every direction.
With hands and feet extending everywhere, with ears and eyes everywhere,
possessing many heads and crowns, and crowded with many ornaments.
However, by virtue of the reverence shown in reciting the mantra thirty-five hundred thousand times,
one may behold the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa with one's own eyes, even without meditative concentration.
When one recites the mantra four million times,
one shall then see a person lying upon a couch composed of Brahman.
By the merit of reciting [the mantra] forty-eight hundred thousand times,
even one who remains under the influence of delusion and sleep may behold the splendor of the City of Brahmā.

O Queen of the Gods, in the ocean of nectar extending for many yojanas, on the island of jewels in the city of Brahmā, resides the eternal Vṛndāvana. (Note: An alternative reading is *nityavṛndāvanasthite*.)
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne situated in the center of a palace of gems,
his left side embraced by his consort and surrounded by a circle of female companions.
One should behold the Supreme Person as if seeing him directly before one's own eyes in meditation;
thereafter, there arises a fever of intense longing, which constitutes the fruit [of that practice].
And at that time, O Maheśānī, all observances—whether performed or unperformed—are brought to completion by virtue of the very nature of the absence of well-being. (32.80)
Thus, O Goddess, has been told how the arising of heat occurs.
In brief, O Great Goddess, what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the Śrīmāheśvaratantra, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, within the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. || 32-32 ||
Then, in the thirty-third chapter, the Goddess said:
"Well spoken is the wonderful preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) of the King of Mantras."
O Īśāna, speak further; the state of heat (tāpa) is extremely difficult to attain. || 33-1 ||
O You who are affectionate toward Your devotees, I am desirous of hearing that [devotion] by which, when experienced, the full flavor is perfectly experienced. 33-2.
Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, to this supreme secret which you have asked; I shall tell it to you.
The Vedas have proclaimed that Brahman is the essence of rasa and the enjoyer of rasa.
O Daughter of the Mountain, the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) was declared by you to be the foremost of sentiments;
it is proclaimed to be of two kinds, consisting of union (saṃyoga) and separation (vipralambha). || 33-4 ||
Now, only the aesthetic sentiment (rasa) consisting of separation exists;
its experience must be cultivated, for that alone is the supreme fruit. || 33-5 ||
As long as there is no arising of heat and no deception is established, tell me, O lady of noble vows, how can there be experience of that? (33.6)
She who remains indifferent to the pleasure of union, yet is separated from her beloved—only she, and no one else, shall ever experience such torment. (33.7)
These ten stages occur when the torment of separation arises;
O Mistress of the Gods, I shall describe them to you—listen with a one-pointed mind. (33-8)
Likewise, longing, reflection, and remembrance, O beloved;
then agitation, lamentation, stupor, and even madness. (33.9)
The chanting of his virtues and death with fever are recorded as [the stages];
O Goddess, in the most intense separation, there occurs the tenth state.
Just as a prince, by fate dwelling in the forest with forest-dwellers, O beloved, comes to regard himself—though he is helpless—as being nothing other than a forest-dweller; (33.11)
All qualities such as sovereignty, valor, and fortitude have vanished;
he is wretched, of base intellect, dull-witted, and subsists on the flesh of animals. (33.12)
Seeing someone who has fallen into self-negation, one should awaken him:
"You are not the son of a forest-dweller; you are in every way a prince. (33.13)
Why indeed do you yourself, wretched and of base intellect, harm living beings?
Where are your virtues such as heroism and fortitude, and where has your sovereignty gone? (33.14)
"Abandon this natural weakness and resort once more to your own true nature.
Having heard these words of the authoritative teacher, he cast off his nets, snares, and other such gear.

Having mentally resolved upon the attainment of sovereignty, let his mind become agitated; with a heart swollen [the root text reads *ucchūna*] with desire, let him be one whose lineage is ruined by longing. (33.16)
Likewise, O Goddess beloved of Kṛṣṇa, having attained a body through latent impressions within this world imagined by delusion, she is agitated by the sense of "mine" regarding that body.
With the quality of bliss concealed, wretched, and possessing a miserable and dull intellect, she exists like a living being and lives by harming other beings. (33.18)
Through the grace of Puruṣottama, the true Guru should awaken her:
"You are not a worldly woman, nor are you a man in any way. (33.19)
Furthermore, you do not strive for your own true self under the guise of being a Brahmin or any other caste;
abandon in vain the delusion of "mine" regarding the body and home, as well as egoism. (33.20)

Of the Lord who is beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which is the seed of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*); of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is perfect and even transcends the imperishable (*akṣara*). || 33-21 ||
You are beloved, O Supreme Bliss, established in the state of supreme bliss;
O lady of excellent limbs, abandon through various means this Māyā which is intent upon the identification with the body. 33-22.
In the midst of a beautiful jewel-island within the ocean of nectar,
[there was a place] resplendent like ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons.

It was most wonderful, surrounded on all sides by thousands of palaces belonging to her female companions, and encircled by walls adorned with jewels, pearls, and other precious things. (Variant reading: "Abandon Māyā, who is intent on contemplating her own true nature. 33-24.
The jewel-palace, five yojanas in height, stands outside the cosmic egg; there, O lover, is your auspicious pleasure-dome.
Remember your own sport with your husband at the seventy sacred bathing places of the Yamunā, amidst the interior resonant with the humming of swarms of bees among full-blown lotuses. (33.26)
Surrounded by her female companions, she ascended a boat adorned with jewels and pearls upon a great lake, which was graced by glittering jeweled steps.
How can you, through delusion, forget yourself as you play—that delightful being yoked to a thousand horses and radiant with the splendor of a hundred wheels? (33.28)
On all sides, with networks of small bells and interiors adorned with jewels and pearls,
they made all the quarters of space resonant with their own tinkling sounds.
Resembling the pomegranate flower, it was fashioned upon the protective fender,
shining manifoldly with beautiful golden jars.
It was beautifully adorned on all sides by groups of women who were dancing, singing with great enthusiasm, and laughing while making others laugh.
With the quarters of the sky illuminated by the moonlight of your pearl canopy, mount the chariot with your beloved and remember your own pleasure-garden excursion. (33.32)
Once, in a most beautiful garden on Mount Puṣparāga, which was filled with flocks of various birds and adorned with garlands of land-lotuses, || 33-33 ||
It was surrounded on all sides by many high pavilions with paved floors,
and the quarters of the horizon were made fragrant by the abundance of the scent of divine flowers.
In the delightful Candraprabha lake, crowded with beautiful lotuses,
there were ten thousand flights of stairs made of gold and set with pearls.
In various places, they were beautified by pavilions atop paved floors,
adorned with four pillars made of great jewels and radiant with archways.
While the trees were shaken by the wind arising from the wings of falling birds,
the divine collyrium from the eyes of her circle of companions fell as they descended from heaven.
With sandalwood paste trickling from their limbs, with saffron fallen from their breasts, with pollen falling from lotuses, and with flowers carried by the wind; || 33-38 ||
How has the blissful delight in the sport of water been forgotten now, in that place with its various divine waters and sands of jewels and pearls? (33–39)
In the divine Mahāpadma forest, extending for a hundred thousand yojanas in every direction,
which was filled with swarms of bees descending due to the sweetness of its fragrance.
In the midst of a jeweled pavilion one yojana in height and breadth,
the interior of the sky was overspread by masses of pollen carried by the wind,
serving as a pleasant abode for the clamor of many flocks of birds.

How is it that you have suddenly forgotten all those sports performed by your beloved, which were the very essence of all delights, and are now tormented as if you were dead? How can you remain clinging to this face of illusion, which is false and consists of delusion? (33–42)
Just as there is the perception of musk in mud, the delusion of a moon in salt, the mistaken notion of a gem in a fragment of glass, and the perception of water in a desert; 33–43.
In the same way, those of dull intellect, through delusion, perceive sugar in gravel, stones, and the like; for such indeed is your [perception] as well.
No one has ever attained prosperity through silver found in a mother-of-pearl shell;
nor has any king become renowned for having obtained a kingdom in a dream. (33–45)
No one has ever attained satisfaction by drinking the water of a mirage;
if you desire eternal happiness, abandon this entire delusion.
Without the removal of delusion, without self-possession, without detachment from sense objects, and without contentment and straightforwardness; || 33-47 ||
Without extremely intense dispassion, without service to a true guru, and even without humility, faith, and instruction in the scriptures; || 33-48 ||
The superimposition of the body, produced by delusion, would not cease in any way;
however, the superimposition of the body ceases once the confusion of delusion has been removed.
The forgetting of one's own nature, which is like a reflected image, is called delusion (moha).
The latent impression (vāsanā) residing in that delusion is perceived as being like a living being (jīva). (33-50)
No living being exists as anything real, like the moon in water;
and the nature of the moon in water is just like the moon in the sky. (33.51)
In the very same way, the beloved ones remain within their own abode in the form of latent impressions (vāsanā);
just as qualities such as trembling and so forth are perceived in a reflection. || 33-52 ||
Pleasure, pain, and so forth, arising from delusion, are described as residing within the latent impression (vāsanā);
for you, there is neither pleasure nor pain, as these are merely the unfolding of delusion alone.
Therefore, having understood your true nature from both the scriptures and the guru, abandon delusion and attain your own innate bliss, O you who are closed in love.
Thus, when one has been sprinkled with the nectar-like words of the true guru, having extinguished the painful flames of the poison of the serpent of delusion; (33-55)
May she possess longing for the Lord of Supreme Bliss;
I have described this longing—now hear its nine other aspects. (33–56)
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Māheśvara-tantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī. || 33-33 ||
Now begins the thirty-fourth chapter.
Śiva said:
When a desire has arisen, from that, thought proceeds.
Supreme bliss, the supreme self, the best of persons—he is dear to me. || 34-1 ||
I, however, his beloved Vāsanā, enveloped by delusion, having entreated Puruṣottama for the sake of beholding the play of a child, [have come here]. (34.2)
Immersed in the ocean of delusion, difficult to cross and shrouded in darkness, all my knowledge has been cast away and I have become one who has forgotten my own self. (34-3)
Overwhelmed by delusion, I wander here and there, possessed by the superimposition of a body, thinking:
"This is my mother, this is my father, and this is my uterine brother. (34.4)
Sons, grandsons, friends, kinsmen, and those of the same lineage—out of a sense of "mine," or rather, out of vain longing and futile delusion, they have embraced me who am utterly deluded. (34–5)
In the worlds seen in a dream, there is neither the hated nor the beloved;
whether [an object] belongs to another or to oneself, delusion alone is indeed the cause.
Henceforth, I have no concern for those who are dear to me, nor even for those who are unpleasant;
there is only one who is truly dear—the Lord—but he has been forgotten by me.
Then what need is there for other causes of suffering that exist only in a dream?
Therefore, what means should I employ by which I might attain joy? (34.8)
I do not see anything in this world, nor even in the Vedas and Vedāntas, by performing which my beloved husband might become easily attainable to me. (34.9)
A husband is not obtained through ritual action taught by the Vedas;
for the fruit of ritual actions is declared to be heaven alone, which is perishable. (34.10)
Neither by gifts, nor by asceticism, nor by great hardships at sacred fords, nor by fasts, vows, and recitations that purify the mind; || 34-11 ||
"How may my husband Kevalānanda come under their control?
He cannot be brought under control by mere knowledge, for that leads only to liberation. (34.12)
In this world, detachment is the armor for a person to protect their knowledge;
for if there were no arising of knowledge, and if there were only detachment, [it would be insufficient].
Even so, it dissolves directly into Prakṛti; yet what of it?
For even Yoga reaches its ultimate limit only upon the vision of one's own Self. (34.14)
In the Purāṇas and Itihāsas, devotion is highly extolled;
yet that too is declared to be a limb of knowledge—how then can the Lord be attained through it? (34.15)
There is no one at all who can speak of the means for attaining what is dear;
what shall I do, where shall I go, and before whom shall I speak? (34.16)
Just as someone wandering in a forest, utterly deluded by a *piśāca*, is tormented by hunger and thirst day and night, his resolve having collapsed; (34.17)
He was greatly terrified by venomous serpents, wild beasts, tigers, and boars;
likewise, he was distressed by gadflies, mosquitoes, and predatory animals.
Desiring to go to the hermitage, I am lost on the path; what shall I do? Who will lead me to my destination, for I am wandering through the forest paths? (34.19)
What shall I do? Where shall I go? And before whom shall I speak?
This forest is devoid of people and filled with many trees and creepers.
Performing various actions such as these with a distracted mind, he remains thus; likewise, anxiety arises even regarding his speech. (34.21)
Just as one immersed in thought does not see anything even while seeing everything,
so too is the latent impression of friends submerged in the essence of thoughts concerning their beloved.
Thought itself, through the state of agitation, then becomes transformed;
for one whose mind is agitated, nothing whatsoever leads to joy. (34.23)
In the separation from one dearer even than life, what indeed could be pleasant, such that the self might find rest for even a moment or attain composure?
For all the functions of the senses arise together like bubbles shimmering in water.
Having taken it up and cast it aside, the anxiety of separation from what is dear prevails. || 34-24 ||
With her inner being agitated by a state of anxiety,
neither ornaments nor garments, nor beds, seats, food, or sacred learning are pleasing to her.
Or whether it be a place for bathing and so forth, or a world, or a forest.
From here for a moment, or from there for a moment;
for a moment in the house, or for a moment on the bed; likewise, having come outside or inside for even a mere moment—
Being of an agitated nature, one shall not find peace. || 34-26 ||
Just as one who is dispassionate is no longer subject to ritual injunctions, nor does he incur fault regarding actions performed or left undone—
even when there is a failure in his state of spiritual agitation.
There is no application of obligatory or occasional ritual acts. || 34-27 ||
O Goddess, when that agitation born of separation from the beloved arises,
then for women nothing whatsoever is to be performed according to the Vedas—
not penance, pilgrimage, yoga, vows, observances, or any ritual acts.
Thus it was concluded, for their minds had indeed ceased to be concerned with the body.

O Goddess, that agitation which arises in us, the lords of the world, during separation from Śrī Kṛṣṇa and from our beloveds, is difficult to attain even for us; how much more so for mortal men? (34.29)
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter in the Śrī Māheśvara Tantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. 34.34.
Then, in the thirty-fifth chapter, the Goddess said: "O Lord, when detachment has arisen, there should be a limit to the practice for the sake of knowledge."
Even there, regarding the limit of the means of accomplishment, that agitation which was spoken of by you— || 35-1 ||
Just as one who is dispassionate, O Lord of Gods, has no authority over ritual actions, so too, O God, even one who is distressed shall not be authorized for ritual action. (35-2)
The reason you have stated for why the intellect does not have the body as its object is this:
my mind is troubled by this; I do not have a clear understanding. (35.3)
The body is composed of the elements and is unstable; latent impressions belong to Brahman alone.
To whom, then, would transmigratory existence apply? Who here possesses the authority for ritual action? (35.4)
When an action is being performed, who here is the enjoyer of its fruit?
How could that [fruit] belong to the body, which is impermanent and insentient? (35.5)

If, O Śaṅkara, it is the latent impression (vāsanā) that experiences the fruits of actions here, then the loss of what has been done (kṛtanāśa) would follow, as well as the acquisition of what has not been done (akṛtābhyāgama). (35.6)
For if an action is performed by one, how can it be experienced by another?
And tell me, O Lord, what is the cause of the gradations in latent impressions (vāsanā) and the body, and so forth? (35.7)
Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess of gods, I shall answer your most excellent question, by the mere hearing of which the notion that the body is the self is destroyed. (35.8)

But on the path of knowledge, O Goddess of gods, detachment is the limit of practice for those whose minds are colored by the passion resulting from the habitual tendencies of various previous births. (35–9)
The mind of living beings indeed runs outward toward sense objects alone;
for there would be happiness in a desired object, while in an undesired one, it becomes like suffering. (35.10)
The ego conceives of everything, such as pleasure and pain;
when consciousness is practiced, everything that was contained within the ego is perceived [as distinct from it]. (35.11)
Just as the quality of trembling and so forth is seen in the moon reflected in water,
even though this is merely a matter of perception, it nevertheless does not cease.
O Śivā, I shall tell you the method to dispel that misconception, through the power of the means perfected over many lifetimes. (35.13)
O Goddess of the Gods, detachment approaches one whose mind is pure;
due to the absence of passion and other such afflictions, the ego-sense ceases with regard to sense objects. (35.14)
The mind should not run hither and thither among sense objects;
because of the absence of passion, hatred, and the like, it does not grasp at pleasure or pain. (35.15)
Indeed, agency and enjoyership are seen in the ego (ahaṅkāra);
O beautiful one, the gross body is the substratum of the subtle body (liṅga). || 35-16 ||
O Pārvatī, he who performs other actions with the gross body seized by egoism would indeed be bound by them.
For the body is proclaimed to be merely the locus of experience;
yet when the ego is superimposed upon it, that ego is then superimposed upon the conscious Self. (35.18)
Just as the redness of a hibiscus flower appears when superimposed upon a crystal, so too, O Dear One, does the ego-sense appear when superimposed upon the pure reflection of consciousness. (35.19)
And having veiled the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), it shines forth by itself, just as the space within water shines forth having veiled the space within a jar. || 35-20 ||
Happiness, suffering, fear, anger, delusion, and likewise envy;
merit and demerit, virtue and vice, as well as knowledge and ignorance. (35.21)
Everything pertaining to the ego-sense does not belong to the reflection of consciousness anywhere;
nevertheless, due to the superimposition of identity, it is perceived as being in the Self alone. (35.22)
O Goddess, just as [redness] appears in a pure and stainless gem, so too are all insentient dharmas that are not the Self eternally and entirely [unreal]. (35.23)
Having realized this, one attains dispassion even toward the realm of Ābhāsvara;
due to the absence of passion and other afflictions, the mind no longer pursues sense objects. (35-24)
O beloved, when the mind is stainless and free from attachment to sense objects,
one's own Self shines forth through meditation, just as one's own face appears in a mirror.
Even when the mind has dissolved into that abode of hundreds of transformations, the yogi becomes established in samādhi, wherein no sorrow exists. (35.26)
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Śrīmāheśvaratantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. || 35-35 ||
Now the thirty-sixth chapter.
Śiva said:
"O friends, by their respective delusions, they were led into a dream of the Supreme Self."
Therefore, O Maheśvarī, the gross bodies are composed of the elements. (36-1)
They know them in their general nature; likewise, their subtle bodies are of that same kind.
The causal self is delusion, which exists separately within each of the latent impressions (vāsanās).
The latent impression (vāsanā), delimited by that [consciousness], has as it were attained the state of being a living soul (jīva);
because it is impelled by the power of will (icchāśakti), even that delusion (moha) consists of aesthetic flavor (rasa).

O Goddess of the Gods, saṃsāra does not belong to latent impressions (vāsanā), nor to delusion (moha), nor likewise to the Self (ātman); rather, O Goddess, it is the subtle body (liṅga) that undergoes saṃsāra.
Since he is proclaimed as an illusory manifestation born from Nārāyaṇa, the delusion of his female companion is merely produced from a portion of his will and bliss. (36-5)
Therefore, this cycle of existence belongs to the ego-maker (ahaṅkṛti) and never to anything else;
both agency and the state of being an enjoyer belong to the ego-maker alone.
Delusion regarding latent impressions (vāsanā) is the cause of that perception; through the identification with the gross body, the ego (ahaṅkāra) expands. (36–7)
Having become the range of all the senses and the accomplisher of all actions,
one is thus bound by their fruits in various ways in every birth.
When it is superimposed upon the latent impressions (vāsanās), the latent impression becomes identified with it;
likewise, when the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti) has attained a state of identity [with it], the latent impression becomes so as well. (36.9)
The latent impressions (vāsanās) of those female companions who are embodiments of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), as well as their nature of bliss, are mixed with egoism (ahaṅkāra). (36-10)
Having reached the door of Nārāyaṇa reflected in the Imperishable, there arises a twofold state of activity—internal and external—as in a dream. (36-11)
The inward-turning state is internal, while that which goes outward is external;
yet, O Goddess of Gods, through the inward-turning state, there is the bliss resting in the ego. (36-12)
Through the very mouth of Nārāyaṇa, it attained manifestation within the immutable one (kūṭastha), just as a great lake is filled by a thousand streams. (36.13)
The fragrance of the fully blossomed lotus, beautiful in form, is pleasing;
yet, O Goddess, one who is filled with thousands of latent impressions (vāsanās) mixed with egoism may experience what is called "counted bliss" (gaṇitānanda), even if it is full of joy. || 36-14 ||
But that external function of the ego, O beautiful one, which perceives the universe as if it were outside, by that [function], O Śivā, it consists of the "this" (idam). (36.15)
The ego, the seed of the universe, reflected within the latent impressions (vāsanās), displays the entire world just as a mirror shows [its reflection] to its friends. (36.16)
Thus, O beloved, the two of them—remaining as immovable pillars in secret—experienced this most difficult feat together with their circle of friends, like the play of children. (36.17)
Just as the moonlight spreads across a mass of waves,
so does the latent impression of beloved ones pervade the various manifestations of ego.
O Maheśvarī, just as moonlight is perceived when the mass of waves has subsided,
so too is latent desire perceived when it has subsided.
O beautiful one, for that purpose, you should seek refuge here with the true guru, [saying]:
"I am your beloved, O Kṛṣṇa, the perfect Supreme Self. (36-20)
"You have undoubtedly come here for the sake of observing the play of children; how is it that you remain fearless while submerged in the ocean of phenomenal existence? (36.21)
Sons, grandsons, wealth, grain, the body, the home, clothing, and so forth—all this is obtained like a dream; having abandoned it, take refuge in your own true nature.
Why do you incessantly weary the reflection, submerged as you are in delusion?
You are the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of beloved things; you are not considered distinct from those beloved things themselves. (36.23)
The weariness of you who are dependent on the ego-sense would be like that of one dependent on a reflection;
therefore, having awakened suddenly, awaken your own true nature.

This body of yours, composed of the five elements, is indeed superimposed upon me; it is because of it that you falsely identify yourself as "I am a woman," "I am a man," "I am dark," or "I am fair. (36.25)
Taking this "thisness" as the oblation, which is fashioned by the creation of "not-this," offer it into the fire consisting of your own true nature and attain bliss. (36.26)
Having struck down this extremely fierce enemy of yours in the courtyard of the root-I-ego with the sharp sword of mindfulness, become happy. (36.27)
When the latent impression (vāsanā) has been thus correctly awakened by the Guru,
it gradually attains a state of agitation through yoga, as if reaching dispassion (vairāgya).
One immediately abandons egoism even toward one's home, body, and senses, once the identification with the body has dissolved and one's own Self is firmly realized. (36.29)
Having reached the state of separation known as *udvega*, which consists of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*),
there then arises the experience of the bliss of the *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) sentiment.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter in the Māheśvara Tantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. || 36-36 ||
Now, the thirty-seventh chapter.
Śiva said:
"Indeed, for a yogin who is dispassionate, the mind becomes intent upon meditation."
Likewise, with right mindfulness well-arisen, the mind is devoted to its play.
In this way, mental service is perfected, and not otherwise;
therefore, service should be performed both internally and externally until mindfulness arises. (37-2)
But without mindfulness, O Goddess of gods, one should abandon external service; otherwise, one incurs sin and may even become lost from the path. (37-3)
O Goddess of the gods, the very state of mindfulness is said to be the root of the mental [practice].
When the mental [practice] arises, external service ceases. (37–4)
Service to the beloved is the beloved's duty, as long as there is activity of all the senses;
when there is an absence of activity of all the senses, that [service] proceeds as a mental one. (37-5)
When the mind becomes immersed in the ocean of the nectar of divine love, external service no longer occurs due to the absence of activity in the external senses. (37–6)
That mental [consciousness] proceeds when there is the arising of a state of mindfulness;
therefore, I shall explain mindfulness—listen with a one-pointed mind. (37.7)
When mindfulness is indeed arising, the mind, devoid of discursive reflection, plunges into its play like an elephant tormented by the heat.
And when one plunges the mind into the great river of Brahman’s play,
all mental fluctuations— even those directed toward the home and the self— dissolve away.
When the mind has plunged deep and entered the great ocean of the nectar of the bliss of divine play (līlā),
there is neither "this" nor "that," neither pleasure nor pain.
She knows that her mind is attached right there. || 37-10 ||
Then one should remember that ocean of the nectar of bliss, with its unrestrained and surging rows of waves,
beautiful with ripples illuminated by the sprouts of the radiance of jewels shimmering within on all sides.
It was delightful with the flight of flocks of birds such as peacocks and cranes emerging from its golden peaks;
it was crowded with many herds of young deer running here and there, and it measured ten million yojanas in extent.
Its central region was adorned by the radiance of many golden mountains and jewels resting in the water;
its banks were beautified by groves of *tālī* trees and beryl, and it resounded with the songs of warbling birds and the sound of mango trees.
He was uprooting the darkness born of the dense groves of palm trees with gems situated on the banks, which,
by their shimmering light illuminating the quarters of the sky, seemed as if they were stealing away the splendor of both the sun and the moon.
With its high banks adorned by [palaces] that mock the full moon surpassing even the city of Alakā,
it possesses the splendor of one bewildered by the presence of many moons.
Shaming even the sky with its shells. || 37-15 ||
And remember that island of jewels, which, emitting filaments of rays rising from within it,
surpasses many tens of millions of moons and suns.
O Maheśvarī, [the state that is] a mass of consciousness and bliss. (37-16)
It was endowed with nine auspicious divisions made of the nine precious gems,
consisting of nine levels, variegated, and adorned with gardens.
Measuring fifty million yojanas in length and breadth, it is exceedingly beautiful;
with four lines drawn across and upwards, it is divided like nine compartments.
The middle section consists of ruby and is the ground of bliss;
its eastern portion is established as being made of topaz.
There, one should indeed contemplate with the intellect the ground consisting of consciousness and bliss;
in the southeast, there is the ground of dispassion, fashioned from vajras.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should contemplate the supreme fragment of Mahāmārakata in the right [hand], wherein the ground of great satisfaction shines forth. (37.21)
In the southwest (nairṛta), one should contemplate the section where the ground of love (premabhūmikā) resides;
it is set with coral gems and is supremely radiant with light.
In the west, O Goddess, is the ground for enjoyment adorned with sapphires,
made of indranīla gems, and filling the interior of the sky with its radiance.
In the northwest, one should recollect the Khaṇḍa that rests upon the ground of knowledge;
in the north, one should contemplate the Khaṇḍa whose interior is fashioned from Gomedaka gems.

O Dear One, one should constantly remember that place where the most enchanting Prakāśabhūmikā shines, and where the Mahāmauktikakhaṇḍa situated in the northeast shines, as well as where the Ratibhūmikā shines.
O Goddess of the gods, daughter of the mountain, I have told you that those seven earths measure fourteen hundred thousand yojanas; understand this, O beloved of the mountains. (37-26)
The stage consisting of consciousness and bliss is proclaimed to be exactly that much;
the ground of bliss extends for twenty-two hundred thousand yojanas. (37.27)
One should remember that Brahma-pura, supremely radiant with light, shines there eternally in the form of the pericarp where Vṛndāvana is situated.
In the midst of that, O Goddess of the gods, there is a palace constructed from a single jewel,
radiant with the light of many millions of suns and moons risen simultaneously.
In some places blue, in some red, in some black, and in some white—
one should contemplate one's own glorious abode as consisting of the ten stages (daśabhūmi).
Surrounding the temple is a row of palaces belonging to the wives of Kṛṣṇa;
O Goddess, each individual palace measures half a yojana in extent.
His own wonderful palace was two and a half yojanas in height,
protected by ten walls adorned with magnificent gardens.
One should remember its revolutions as being six thousand yojanas;
this sūtra extending from south to north is two thousand [yojanas]. (37.33)
One should meditate upon the Mahāpadma forest surrounding one's own abode, extending in all directions with the same dimensions as the sūtra running from east to west.
O beloved, one should remember the supreme Blue Mountain (Nīlādri) at the junction of the planes of Light (Prakāśa) and Bliss (Ānanda), measuring ten thousand yojanas in height.
O Goddess of the gods, he has three wonderful peaks:
Candragaura, Candracūḍa, and beyond that, Mahācandra. (37–36)
On the great peak, white as the moon, there is a great lake named Candra,
extending for a hundred yojanas and adorned with moon-like steps.
The quarters of the sky were made resonant by the humming of buzzing bees,
and the swarms of six-legged insects were enchanted by the fragrance of the groves of blossoming lotuses.
It was adorned by flocks of swans situated in the midst of herds of female swans, and it was exceedingly charming due to the warbling of birds with variegated plumage. (37–39)

One should contemplate, with a continuous stream of mindfulness, that temple of the bliss of the eyes, filled with the nectar of joy, and beautified by the splendors of the gardens situated on its banks.
Once, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, sported there solely with his mistress,
who was attended by thousands of female companions.
The five lakes, whose waters are the nectar of supreme bliss, pay homage to the moon-crested Lord;
they are made festive by thousands of golden jeweled stairways.
They were constantly beautified by groves of golden lotuses that, being repeatedly stirred by the wind, perpetually perfumed the very ends of the quarters.
O Goddess of the gods, the Blessed One sometimes sports there with throngs of women; one should also remember Mahācandra as the king of gardens. (37–44)
The trees had broad leaves and were exquisite with their golden branches;
they were rich with foliage of blue lapis lazuli and wore garlands of pearl clusters.
With *kadamba*, *aśoka*, *punnāga*, *mālatī*, *bakula*, and *arjuna* trees; with *bilva*, *pāla*, *tamāla*, *hitāla*, and *pārijātaka* trees. (37–46)
Adorned with ketakas, campakas, and those kalpa-trees,
one should, O Goddess, visualize in its center a vast jeweled pavilion,
supported by a hundred golden pillars and with its interior inlaid with pearls and gems. (37–37)
It was resplendent, with four gates and seven stories, free from all defects;
at each gate there were two paved courtyards, and for every courtyard there was a long pond.
In its long ponds, bees were busily occupied with shimmering golden lotuses;
it was enchanting, with jeweled pillars gleaming upon its paved floors.
It was radiant with the splendor of its central region, which shimmered with svastika patterns formed by coral, sapphire, ruby, pearl, lapis lazuli, and emerald.
It was graced by the warbling of parrots, pigeons, and swans,
and it shone with radiant archways adorned with gold, lapis lazuli, and pearls.
Adorned on all four sides by a magnificent row of great palaces, it was wondrous;
once, the Blessed One, having mounted a brilliantly shining chariot here, [remained].
O Maheśvarī, she approaches with thousands of female companions for the sake of play,
having performed various musical sounds in a most beautiful garden.
Then, surrounded by her female companions, she should immediately enter the pavilion;
thereafter, all those who are their attendants shall perform worship for them.
Divine palaces, shining on all sides with jewels,
resound with the strings of lutes and drums as those eager for fame sing his glory.
With the functions of their senses immersed in the mass of bliss from that song, the male and female deer of the garden, as well as the parrots and cranes, [became motionless]. (37.56)
Cuckoos, pigeons, and peacocks speaking with honeyed voices seemed to silence their own calls, as if they were merely figures in a painting, O Śivā.
With words even sweeter than the essence of nectar and imbued with the sentiment of humor, they cause laughter both while laughing themselves, toward their beloved and their mistress as well. (37.58)
On one occasion, thousands of them, having taken the side of their mistress, requested Kṛṣṇa to play the game of blindman’s buff.
Then, once the binding of their eyes had been performed, they made a wager:
"If indeed you do not know [the answer], then, my dear, you shall be defeated. (37.60)
"Give her your own clothes and ornaments without distressing your heart;
that beloved will make you appear charming in form. (37.61)
Having ascended your throne and declaring, "I am Kṛṣṇa," let her command you: "Friend, dance before me! (37-62)
"Then you must certainly perform a dance, as it were, like a woman;
for while you dance without hesitation, we ourselves shall indeed sing. (37.63)
"Or if you do indeed know [the way], let even your beloveds do so.
Having thus made them take this oath, those beloved women surrounded their beloved.
Then a certain friend of Indirā, having arrived from behind in haste,
bound his pair of eyes with her own pair of lotus-like hands.
When Kṛṣṇa was seized by her hair, he said, "You are beautiful.
Then Indirā, smiling, released his pair of eyes and spoke to her friend.
"Why do you speak in vain, saying 'O lord of my life, I have been defeated'?
I am not Sundarī by name; I am your beloved known as Indirā. (37.67)
"Therefore, casting aside shame, deliberate upon the wager.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"I was not actually defeated; do not be deluded by the thought that I was unaware."
O Indirā, I have always held the delusion that you are Sundarī;
yet, in my beloved Sundarī, there constantly flashes the delusion that she is Indirā. (37.69)

"Having perceived that there is not even the slightest difference between you [the Goddess] and Indirā, either in name or in form, I spoke the word 'Sundarī' in a moment of deluded intellect; please take this which I have said into consideration. (37-70)
Having heard the words of her beloved, Indirā spoke these words again.
Indirā said:
"O Lord, oh, how great is this artifice of yours! (37-71)
"O Lord, even though I know that [the words] 'Indirā' and 'Sundarī' have issued from your mouth, how can I believe them? It is like an atheist accepting the meaning of the Vedas. (37.72)
"Regarding women, jests, rogues, and threats to one's life, speech may speak untruth; this you surely know, O sir. (37.73)
For our trust rests in what emerges from the mouth, not in what resides in the heart;
just as for an atheist, direct perception is the authority, but not verbal testimony.
Therefore, if you intend to make your own word true,
cast aside shame and quickly give back the garments and ornaments.
If you are not independent, what can we do? You are the master, yet you yourself are not independent; for what conviction can there be in you who fears the loss of your wager? (37.76)
Therefore, having again determined within your own heart what is beneficial and what is harmful according to reason, do as you wish.
Having heard Indirā’s words, which were exceedingly bold yet endowed with cleverness in the assembly of her friends,
she smiled and immediately took off her own ornaments and garments and gave them to her.
He gave a garment of great blue hue, a golden-colored lower cloth,
a saffron-colored turban, and earrings adorned with pearls.
His supreme uṣṇīṣa-jewel shines with millions of throbbing moons;
his radiant neck-ornament is set with divine pearls.
She wears a garland made of the nine precious gems, blazing with variegated rays, which makes her heart-lotus appear as if it were dappled with many colors. || 37-81 ||
A pair of bracelets inlaid with rubies, pearls, and gems;
and a most beautiful ring for the nails, adorned with golden lotuses.
A pair of beautiful armlets with interiors inlaid with wish-fulfilling gems, and a most lovely fourfold necklace with a ruby shining at its center.
It emulated the throat-bells of the intoxicated elephant of the God of Love;
it was encircled on all sides by shimmering blue diamonds and other gems;
and with the tinkling sounds of tiny bells, it possessed a golden girdle that was beyond compare. (37–84)
The rings, situated amidst the shimmering mass of light from the gems, spread the suspicion that they were streams of beauty flowing from the guise of her fingers.
The high-minded Kṛṣṇa gave him two divine, well-rounded bracelets for his feet, adorned with jewels, as well as whatever other ornaments he possessed.
Then he fashioned for her a captivating attire:
a turban was placed upon her head, and a pair of earrings were set upon her ears.
He placed a beautiful garland, resplendent with nine gems, around his neck; likewise, he fashioned bracelets upon both his wrists. (37-88)
He placed a pair of armlets upon his two arms, four upon the lotus of his heart, and fashioned a captivating golden girdle around his waist.
Then Hari placed rings upon his fingers and fashioned ornaments for his limbs; he gave him a great, divine staff inlaid with gems and pearls.
Having seated his friend named Indirā upon the jeweled throne,
Kṛṣṇa danced and manifested beautiful emotions.
Assuming the form of a woman and as if deluding them with his illusory power, while he danced with enthusiasm, O beloved, some women sang. (37.92)
Mādhvī, arrogant with the overflowing pride of youth, struck the mṛdaṅga drum;
Āsāvatī, like a flash of lightning, played the vīṇā lute.
Suprabhā, a literal wave of loveliness, and Nistulā, both intent upon playing the flute, became the two keepers of the rhythm.
Some made sounds with their mouths, intent on clapping their hands;
others, overwhelmed by the sentiment of laughter, cried out loudly, "Victory! Victory! (37.95).
Sumukhī, Lalitā, and the others exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! while others, immersed in curiosity, gazed upon the lotus-face of Kṛṣṇa.
Wandering about, intoxicated by the sweetness of her beauty, she was unrestrained.
Then, at the conclusion of the play, a female companion assuming the form of Kṛṣṇa rose from the throne and approached with palms joined in reverence.
The beloved fell at her husband’s feet; having raised up that friend, he embraced her for a long time with love and kissed her lotus-like face. (37.98)
She adorned Kṛṣṇa once again with those ornaments and garments;
then, all having mounted the chariot, they went to their own palace with their beloved.
His beloved wives surrounded their beloved, who was seated upon a lion-throne on a floor resplendent with sixty-four great pillars.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter in the Śrī Māheśvara Tantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. || 37-37 ||
Then, the thirty-eighth chapter.
Pārvatī said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Supreme Ruler, saluted by gods and asuras!"
This narrative is exceedingly meritorious and is praised as being sweeter than nectar.
Nevertheless, O Lord of the gods, for one whose mind is intent on hearing, the satisfaction born from drinking the nectar of your speech does not reach its full measure. (38.2)
The joy born from hearing the sacred narrative is not seen even in liberation;
who, then, would waste their own life through delusion by forsaking it? (38-3)
Indeed, those unfortunate ones are of wicked intellect and devoted to evil conduct, by whom this true narrative—the nectar for the ears—has not been obtained even for a moment. (38.4)
The three and a half crore holy places, the sages, and the deities of the mantras will certainly all come there when the discourse on the stories of Kṛṣṇa takes place. (38–5)
Therefore, I have been favored by you, whose very nature is compassion, as you have related this delightful narrative of Kṛṣṇa, who is the embodiment of bliss. (38.6)
Speak again, O Lord of Gods, of the story that brings joy,
whose ground is adorned by rows of sixty-four great pillars.
O Maheśāna, if you have favor toward me, tell me this: having empowered these [goddesses] with love and being united with them, what did he do? || 38.8 ||
Śiva said:
Listen, O Pārvatī, O fair-eyed one; I shall speak that which I have been asked, by the mere hearing of which the highest delight is born.
Having come from the peak of the Blue Mountain to his own abode, the Supreme Being beyond the supreme sat upon a jeweled lion-throne adorned with the nine gems.
Seated in a circular formation around the lion throne,
they gazed upon their beloved with joy, their lotus-like eyes wide open.
To him who was full of bliss and whose desires were fulfilled, golden women there attended with joy according to the royal rites of service. (38.12)
The parasol of Mithilā was held aloft—white as the luster of the autumn moon, adorned with pearls and gems, and captivating with its jeweled handle. (38.13)
The noble and high-minded Candralekhā attended upon him by waving yak-tail fans with golden handles inlaid with rubies.
Holding in her hand a peacock-feather fan adorned with pearls set in a crescent-shaped mount and illuminated by golden threads, Citrā touched [the king].
Holding in her hand a mirror that resembled the orb of the moon, adorned with gold and variegated with jewels, Ānandamañjarī stood there. (38.16)
Taking betel-leaf rolls mixed with fragrant substances in a jeweled vessel, Madanamañjūṣā stood there. (38.17)
Holding in her hand a jeweled vessel that extended for a hundred yojanas and was filled with divine sandalwood, Bhuvanamālinī stood there.
Holding a golden *bhṛṅgāra* pitcher filled with water, its handle fashioned from pearls and set with rubies, Ratnarekhā stood before him. (38.19)
Holding a handkerchief as white as the rays of the autumn moon and adorned with a string of pearls, the playful woman stood before him.
Taking up the divine enjoyment of bliss, situated in a golden vessel and endowed with various delicious flavors, Mādhurī stands on the right. (38.21)
Standing in the north-eastern corner, Sundarī remained there to praise those playful words which Puruṣottama spoke here.
Mādhvī was captivated by the sound of the mṛdaṅga drum; the virtuous Āśāvatī by the lute; and likewise, Vidyullatā was exceedingly moved by the resonance of the strings. (38.23)
With his flute-playing, he possesses a graceful form that is a wave of loveliness; through the terminology employed for the sake of diversion, he is the stage of aesthetic passion. (38.24)
Skilled in the arts of love and full of passion,
those highly fortunate women approached Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, with their amorous charms.
Then they performed various kinds of playful acts, abounding in the sentiment of humor;
at the conclusion of those, having addressed their beloved, they asked him with great eagerness.

The friends said: "O Lord, O best of men, you are dear to us and we are dear to you; let there be that love which belongs to those who share mutual affection and is not produced by external conditions. (38.27)
If this affection were produced by external conditions, then its true nature would not be established;
therefore, you ought to explain to us accurately the state of those who possess such love. (38.28)
O Beloved, our incomparable love for you alone shines forth—beyond the reach of words, caused by extreme passion, and free from all ailment. (38.29)
How can we women grasp that which is conditioned by sound?
Therefore, we are never capable of making it manifest. (38-30)
This shines forth as something to be known by oneself; how can we describe it with words?
O Supreme Person, let there be that love for you which exists within us. (38.31)
"Are we more, equal, or less? How shall we know, O beloved?
You yourself must tell us by word; for we are those who discern degrees of excellence. (38.32)
Even among all the friends, their disputes regarding the nature of their respective loves are pacified upon hearing of your love. (38-33)
Having heard their words, the Supreme Self, Puruṣottama,
knowing that it was not possible for his speech to be manifested through the activity of words, spoke these words out of love.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O ladies, what has been spoken by you is exactly so; there is no doubt.
This love is to be known by oneself; it cannot be expressed by words for one who speaks. (38–39)
O friends, it may also be characterized by delightful and charming emotions; love consists of passion (rati), and I am that very passion, which is the aesthetic flavor (rasa). 38-36.
Therefore, love centered on Me must be understood here in every respect;
for who knows My true nature, or who even desires to describe it? (38-37)
The learned Vedas describe [the nature of time] through negation;
how then could others—miserable beings whose very forms are limited by time—possibly know it? (38–38)
This love for my true nature is not an object of words;
therefore, even I am unable to describe it—what then can be said of another? (38-39)
Having thus responded to them, Puruṣottama took the mirror standing before him and presented it to them, facing them directly.
Then, as the women were looking at their lotus-like faces in this mirror given by their beloveds with affection, a very great reflection arose within them.
The vision of the Self has been presented in order to speak the answer to the question regarding love. How indeed is it understood what has been indicated by this? (38–42)
Does the Lord, like a clear mirror, express His own love toward us? Is He the reflection and we the original object, or is it the other way around? (38–43)
Or rather, just as a form is seen in a mirror exactly as it is, so too has it been indicated that my likeness should be like [his] love. (38–44)

Is it not possible that, for the purpose of dispelling the notion of difference between love [and its object] and to indicate their unity, the form [of the beloved] might become like a reflection of itself? (38–45)
Thus, to his circle of friends who were submerged in doubt, he, the one higher than the highest, said: "This reasoning of yours reveals my own intention. (38-46)
Not even the slightest difference between you and me exists;
"I am you" and "you are I"—this is my beloved conviction, O dear ones. (38–47)
"A mirror has been held before you for the purpose of indicating non-duality";
with these words, which produced great joy, he gladdened them. (38–48)
Śiva said:
Having heard these most beautiful words, they were all thus delighted; overcome by the force of their great joy, [they gazed] upon the lotus-face of Kṛṣṇa.
Grasping their chins with their thumbs and forefingers, they—having cast aside all shame—kissed them with supreme affection, making soft sighing sounds. (38.50)
Some embraced him, while others praised him, saying:
"O Lord, this is worthy of you, that you act for the benefit of those who are dear to you. (51)
Thus spoke other female friends, their hearts pierced by love. In the meantime, there was an excellent woman named Sundarī.
Preceded by a smile, Sundarī, proud with love, spoke these words:
"O ladies, although this proposal of yours is agreeable to my beloved," (38-53)
Nevertheless, there remains a residue of reasoning that has not been revealed by my beloved; and even by you, through your own intelligence, that supreme [truth] has not been understood. (38.54)
When her beloved asked, "What kind of love do you have for me?", she showed him her own reflection; there I shall describe the intention of the beloved. (38-55)
Just as one correctly perceives one's own true nature in the mirror of the self, in the absence of that [mirror], the experience of one's own true nature does not arise at all. (38-56)
In that same way, this very nature of mine, consisting of aesthetic flavor (rasa) as sung in the Vedas, is fully experienced by me when it rests upon the vessel of my beloved. (57)
Otherwise, there would never be any experience of my own true nature;
just as the sun, having drunk up moisture from the earth, pours it down again as rain. (38-58)
Likewise, having drunk me— the essence of the beloved— and being filled with that state of being,
they bring joy to me alone, who am composed of the very essence of condensed rasa.
"O friends, this matter has also been indicated by means of the pretext of the mirror.
Having heard these words of Sundarī, her friends were greatly amazed. (38–60)
The Blessed One, whose self is full, approved of the meaning of what she had said.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O Sundarī, your name is truly meaningful; it is dear to me. (38–61)
"You are dearer to me than my own life-breaths; indeed, you alone are my everything.
O virtuous lady, I am subject to you, bound by the noose of love. (38–62)
What was spoken by you has been spoken by me; what was seen by you has been seen by me.
O virtuous lady, that which was accepted by you has indeed been accepted by me as well. (38.63)
"There is no difference between the two of us; he who makes such a distinction is a sinner.
Having heard these words, which were so dear and spoken with affection, those beloved women—
They experienced supreme joy, for they were no longer despondent in the absence of their mistress.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrīmāheśvara-tantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī. || 38-38 ||
Then the thirty-ninth chapter.
Pārvatī said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, expert in divine knowledge!"
This story, which is exceedingly wonderful and difficult for the living to encounter, has been told to you. (39.1)
O Lord of Gods, in this creation the gods and dānavas appear;
they also come into existence in the world of men by their own will. (39.2)
The gods are endowed with forgiveness and straightforwardness, possessed of compassion and courtesy;
they have conquered their senses and subdued their anger, and are free from hypocrisy and envy. (39-3)
Free from greed, virtuous in conduct, and endowed with faith and devotion;
desirous of knowledge, firm in their practice, and contemplators of the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras. (39-4)
O Mahādeva, even for them this reality is very difficult to attain;
how much more so for those who possess the nature of Dānavas and whose souls delight in harming others?
[This is for] the nihilists, the rogues, the wicked, and the evil-minded;
for those who revile the meaning of the Vedas, and for those who consider the body and such things to be the ultimate goal. (39.6)
Of the Vaiḍālikas whose minds were corrupted by the curse of Akṣapāda, of the Saugatas and Bauddhas, and of those who adhere to the doctrine of the Digambaras. (39.7)
For the Jains, the Mādhyamikas (or as some read, the Jain-Mādhyamikas), and the wicked-minded Cārvākas—
who have abandoned the Vedic scriptures— liberation is nowhere renowned.
