O Dhūrjaṭi, that third creation consisting of latent impressions (vāsanā) which was described by you—that for the sake of which this instruction on the knowledge of reality exists—[is now explained]. (39.9)
"But my conviction is that I have achieved my purpose through hearing alone;
attainment has its domain in the relationship [between the teacher and the taught], and never otherwise. (39.10)
Therefore, O Lord, the joy of hearing [this] is exceedingly dear to me;
for the joy of hearing is unattainable by wicked-souled ones who are seized by sin. (39.11)
Therefore, I wish to hear it, if you think it right to speak;
for there is no one equal to you, an ocean of the nectar of compassion. (39.12)
"O Mahādeva, as for what you said— that all those wives of Kṛṣṇa attained supreme joy except for their dejected mistress— " (39.13)
In this regard, O God of gods, Lord of the world, a doubt has arisen within me;
O Master, tell me truly the cause of Svāminī’s distress. (39.14)
Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the cause of the Mistress’s weariness;
the pastime consisting of the binding of the eyes was performed upon the peak of the Blue Mountain. (39-15)
Thereupon, her beloved, abandoning the name Indirā, called her Sundarī. To that, Indirā spoke these words: "I am not Sundarī. (39.16)
"O leader of my life, I am Indirā herself, your beloved.
Then Kṛṣṇa spoke these words while the women were listening. (39.17)
O Indirā, my delusion that you are Sundarī has been constant for all time.
Even though I know you are Indirā, by virtue of a mind wandering in error, I have uttered the word "Sundarī"; please take this which I have spoken into consideration. (39-18)
Having heard these words, which were full of respect for Sundarī,
her mind became somewhat troubled in the midst of the circle of her friends.
For the affection of a beloved man is indeed equal toward all these [wives];
by what reason, then, is there greater love for the beautiful one? (39.20)
And among all my friends, I alone am the most excellent woman; has anyone been born superior to me in beauty and other such qualities? (39.21)
Having thus reflected within her own heart, which was filled with love, the mistress remained with a concentrated mind and concealed what was within her heart. (39.22)
Then, having come from the peak of the Blue Mountain to the palace of jewels,
Puruṣottama remained there, surrounded by his beloveds.
There, when her dear friends had made their inquiries, he presented a mirror;
taking the mirror, her friends rejoiced as they examined themselves within it. (39.24)
By her own intelligence, Sundarī also composed herself according to the mind of her friend;
hearing that she was thus composed, Puruṣottama became pleased. (39.25)
Manifesting his own love, he then spoke these words:
"O virtuous one, your name 'Sundarī' is truly meaningful and dear to me. (39.26)
"You are dearer to me than my own life, for you are indeed my everything;
I am dependent on you, O virtuous lady, bound as I am by the noose of love. (39.27)
That which was spoken by you has been seen by me as it was spoken; that which was seen by me has been seen by you.
O virtuous lady, that which was accepted by you has indeed been accepted by me as well. (39.28)
"There is no difference between us; he who makes such a distinction is a sinner"—having heard these and other words indicative of Sundarī’s love. (39-29)
Raising the creeper of her brow, her eyes slightly clouded,
and her lower lip quivering, the mistress spoke with her neck turned.
This Sundarī, the beloved of Sundara, is the foremost among thousands of female companions; what purpose do we serve, given our deficiency in both virtue and beauty? (39.31)
If Sundarī alone is his beloved, how can those who are not beautiful be dear to him?
Yet these beautiful-eyed women, who resemble her, have become dear to this handsome-faced one. (39.32)
Having thus uttered this indirect speech (vakrokti) before her friends,
she suddenly rose and went into the interior of her own pleasure-chamber.
Then the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa dispatched a messenger named Kalāvatī in order to dispel the displeasure of his beloved.
Skilled in the business of diplomacy, she spoke with a smile; she was adept in elegant speech, steadfast, and discerning in the art of logical argumentation. (39.35)
Then, having gone to Kalāvatī and seen that Mānavatī,
he found her alone in secret, staying in her own beautiful pleasure-chamber.
Just as a physician checks the force of poison through the application of various mantras,
he checked the force of pride by means of novel applications of speech.
"O virtuous one, even more than [your own] life-breath—O beloved, how can this be appropriate?
You are like the very life of your husband, and your husband is like your own life. (39.38)
Even the entire circle of your friends is like the senses belonging to an embodied being; you are like the very self of your beloved—where, then, is there any occasion for pride on your part? (39)

O Pūrṇānanda, O you whose desires are fulfilled, O most beloved of speech—when you are present, it is not fitting for a man to speak [harshly], just as one would not address a messenger who is deceitful and wicked. (39–40)
From the quivering of your bimba-like lips, from the knitting of your eyebrows, and from the redness of your cheeks, your heavy resentment is clearly perceived. (39–41)
With hot sighs from inner torment, you burn your sprout-like lower lip;
in vain do you wither your creeper-like body with the fire of pride.
The momentary separation from my beloved is unbearable; since one might live even without beholding the lotus-face of the dear one, death is better than that. (39–43)
Although there are many thousands of female companions,
my heart delights in you alone, just as the moon’s light delights in the night-blooming lily.
O proud woman, a husband who is worthy of respect must always be addressed with words resembling nectar by his beloved; he should be honored by joining one's hands like soft lotuses in salutation.
Furthermore, whether his speech is pleasing or displeasing, it should never be taken to heart by virtuous women. This is their duty.
Good conduct has been taught by me; why do you abandon it and suffer in vain? (39–45)
O proud lady, what is the use of speaking much? Act according to my word so that your beloved, who is tormented by intense pride, may turn toward indifference.
Therefore, placing faith in my words, go to his presence;
otherwise, through delay, this pride will reach its ultimate limit. (39-47)
Now that you have departed, your beloved has suddenly become overcome with distress; he currently remains devoid of any inclination for the pleasures of laughter or play. (39–48)
"Indeed, O beloved, I have been sent by my dear one solely to summon you;
if you command me, O lovely one, I shall bring him here this very moment."
Śiva said:
Having heard Kalāvatī’s words, the mistress, slow-moving due to her pride,
descended slightly from the peak of the mountain of her pride and spoke these words.
The mistress said:
"O dear Kalāvati, I have never shown pride;
hearing of the greatness of Sundarī’s virtues has caused me distress. (39-51)
O Kalāvati, if my beloved should think only of one beautiful woman adorned with virtues, then what indeed would be the need for us? (39–52)
Thinking thus, I have risen and come to this secluded dwelling;
may the virtuous beloved of the virtuous and beautiful Sundarī be happy. (39–53)
Kalāvatī said:
"O virtuous lady, you should not be so insistent toward me, for I am a simple-minded leader [of women].
There are four types of leaders, distinguished by their own specific characteristics. (39–54)
The *anukūla* (favorable), the *dakṣiṇa* (liberal), the *dhṛṣṭa* (bold), and the *śaṭha* (deceitful) [are the four types of heroes].
One who observes the vow of a single wife is declared to be the *anukūla*. (39–55)
Even though his mind is fixed on another woman, he never abandons his affection and respect for the former; and such a man is the *dakṣiṇa-nāyaka* (the liberal or versatile hero). || 39-56 ||
"You alone are my everything; no other beloved woman is dear to me.
He who speaks thus in her presence but acts otherwise in her absence is a rogue (this is the implied meaning). || 39-57 ||
One who, having been discovered in his transgression, takes oaths while acting with concealed intent—
one should know such a crooked man as a leader known by the name "the rogue" (śaṭha).
Even when guilty of a fault, one who is free from apprehension feels no shame when being struck; even when his faults are manifest before his eyes, he who speaks falsely is called audacious.
Thus, among these four types of heroes, O wise lady,
your beloved is described as the *anukūla* (favourable) and the *dakṣiṇa* (courteous).
"He is not deceitful; he is bold. Why do you distress your heart in vain?
When this was said, she was filled with wonder and spoke again to Kalāvatī.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter in the Māheśvara Tantra, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, within the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. 39-39.
Then, in the fortieth chapter, the Mistress said: "O Kalāvati of great wisdom, regarding that which you have spoken concerning the Beloved;
The Mistress said: "O Kalāvati of great wisdom, regarding that which you have spoken concerning the Beloved; [I shall explain it to you]."
It appears to me as if contradictory, for it is indeed characterized by contradictory marks. || 40-1 ||
One who observes the vow of having only one wife is celebrated as "Anukūla" (Favorable);
one who has many wives but is impartial toward all of them is known as "Dakṣiṇa" (Generous).
O virtuous lady, how can these two exist in a single leader? It appears almost incredible; if you know the reason, please tell me. (40.3)
Kalāvatī said:
Listen, O Mistress; I shall declare the auspicious answer to your question, by the mere hearing of which you will attain well-being. (40-4)
Once, my beloved went to the Puṣparāga mountain to sport, having ascended a divine palanquin resplendent with golden jars. (40.5)
Adorned with various archways set one above the other,
it resounded with the cries of swans, pigeons, parrots, cuckoos, and cranes.
It shone with the variegated splendor of the nine gems, moved at will with the speed of thought,
was a hundred yojanas in extent, and was an abode of various pleasures and delights.
When the golden central jar has been placed and set upon it,
she illuminates the sky with jewels as white as the radiance of ten million moons.
Seated within that most excellent celestial chariot, Puruṣottama shone like the moon amidst the stars, surrounded by twelve thousand companions.
The celestial chariot of the dark-complexioned women, which moved according to their will,
fell upon the peak of the Flower Mountain, moving sideways, upwards, and downwards.
There, the river named Candraprabha was filled with nectar; it featured stairs made of gold and was adorned with golden lotuses. (40.11)
To the south of that [mountain] there is an exceedingly beautiful lake,
renowned by the name Pañcanada, extending for a hundred yojanas.
It was bound together by long, divine staircases made of gold, their interiors inlaid with seven hundred jewels arranged one below the other.
It was adorned here and there with clusters of beryl lotuses, ruby lotuses, and the playful alighting of swans.
In that regard, O beautiful woman, remember those various sports you performed with your own husband, distinguished by whether they took place in water or on land. (40.15)
There, my beloved, surrounded by all his friends in the lake,
was struck by rains falling from all sides and fled.
Then he quickly ascended the pavilion for resting by the lake;
all his beloved wives, having emerged from the lake, returned there to him.
Then he suddenly fell once again into the water of the lake;
having emerged from the deep waters, he went to some secluded spot in the wilderness.
He remained alone, concealed within the dense thickets of many groves;
meanwhile, all his beloveds wandered here and there, searching for him.
Searching there, I went into that dense thicket and beheld Kṛṣṇa, exceedingly beautiful, standing there dissolved [in meditation].
There, O fair-browed one, seeing me approaching, my beloved,
full of curiosity, smiled and stopped me by pointing his forefinger at the tip of his nose.
Priya said: "O Kalāvati, you who are skilled in the arts, women are searching for me;
they do not see me here, and therefore they wander about in confusion."
"You too, O Kalāvatī, remain right here with me;
staying in private, I shall engage in amorous play with you. (40.23)
Having been addressed thus, I remained there, honored with great respect;
there my beloved engaged in various kinds of sports together with me.
Then, O beautiful lady, I asked a question concerning my beloved: "There are four types of lovers; among them, which one are you? (40.25)
Then the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa spoke the answer to the question;
O blameless lady, I shall relate that to you exactly as I have heard it.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Favorableness and courtesy—these two qualities exist in me;
elsewhere they would be contradictory, but in me they are clearly non-contradictory."
O Kalāvati, I am the essence itself, manifest and solidified in form;
know me to be its first part, and my beloved mistress to be the second. (Variant reading: "the supreme. [40.28]
No difference exists between us two, whose natures are that of the enjoyer and the enjoyed;
my self is called the Mistress, and my Mistress’s self is indeed myself. (40.29)
There is no person other than me, nor is there any woman superior to my mistress;
since he does not delight in being alone, rasa is therefore divided into two.
Through the divisions of male and female forms, I, as rasa, manifest myself;
one may not even truly touch Lakṣmī, who consists of the bliss of Brahman. (40.31)
Therefore, O lotus-eyed one, I am favorable toward you as your leader;
I shall tell you in what manner I am also devoted to you. (40.32)
Just as a multitude of rays radiates from a priceless jewel, yet that [radiance] is not distinct from the gem when investigated; so it is here. (40.33)
O Kalāvati, those friends are indeed the very forms of the arts of the Mistress herself;
there is not even an atom's worth of difference between the bathing Mistress and her friends.
Therefore, in all these [energies], I abide as the liquefied essence;
yet externally, having become solidified through them, I am intent on play.
Even while playing with all of them, I am overwhelmed by love for my mistress;
therefore, O Kalāvati, I am the right-hand one, for I am indeed the leader.
Even here, upon investigation, there is no contradiction of favorable conditions;
for the metaphorical application of the two kinds of difference sometimes occurs in relation to me. (40.37)
Thus, O proud lady, that which was asked by you has been told by me exactly as it was spoken by my beloved himself with his own mouth. (40.38)
And at the conclusion of their questions and answers, those beloved women, searching about,
saw him hidden within a dense bower and approached with great haste.
Then, accompanied by her beloved, she came into your presence;
you already know all of this, for which I have now stated the specific details. (40–40)
Therefore, O proud lady, pride toward your beloved is not fitting;
even joy itself appears joyless without you. (40–41)
Therefore arise and adorn his side, O wise lady;
for, O passionate one, we are not able to behold our beloved when he is separated from you. (40–42)
Having heard this display of scholarship and cleverness employed by Kalāvatī, she, with a joyful countenance, spoke these words: [40-43]
The mistress said:
"O Kalāvati, O highly wise one, your pride has been dispelled by my words;
nevertheless, you understand the inner conventions of proud women (or, as another reading has it, 'of beautiful women')."
"If I were to come of my own accord, my respect [for you] would vanish;
therefore, my beloved, taking me by the hand, may you lead me away happily. (40–45)
Thus addressed by her, the friend reached the presence of her beloved;
seeing her with a joyful countenance, the beloved also rejoiced greatly. (40–46)
Thus ends the fortieth chapter in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Śrīmāheśvaratantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī. 40-40.
Then, the forty-first chapter.
Pārvatī said: When Kalāvatī, the messenger of her beloved, arrived in the presence of her lover, [what occurred?]
What happened there after that? Tell me that, O Maheśvara.
Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess of gods, I shall tell you a divine story centered on aesthetic flavor (rasa),
the joy arising from hearing which is not found even in liberation.
Seeing the messenger Kalāvatī, whose lotus-like face was radiant with joy, her beloved spoke as if smiling, while the other women listened. (41.3)
O Kalāvati, skilled in the arts, what was said by that beloved wife?
Like nectar to a thirsty man, those words of hers have brought me satisfaction. (41.4)
O Kalāvati, you are a conduit for the nectar of the treasury of immortality;
water me, who am embraced by the vine of my friend, like a wish-fulfilling tree.
Kalāvatī said:
"O Lord of my life, your beloved remains today maintaining her pride;
though I have gone to her and repeatedly awakened her with many kinds of words. (41-6)
Having ascended the peak of the mountain of pride, she somehow spoke to me:
"O beloved Kalāvati, never have I ever displayed pride. (41.7)
Hearing of the greatness of Sundarī’s virtues causes me distress, for my beloved considers Sundarī alone to be an abyss of excellence. (41.8)
"There is no service for him to be performed by us who are devoid of virtue"—speaking thus with various words such as these, that high-minded woman [addressed them]. (41.9)
Indeed, she has been gratified by me as well with words endowed with reason;
having abandoned her anger, she now longs for you, her beloved, to take her hand.
"This is the innate nature of women; therefore, O Lord, act accordingly.
Considering Kalāvatī’s words to be true, the Supreme Being, though delighting in the Self, approached her presence for the sake of pleasing her. (41–11)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O dear, virtuous one, it is not fitting for you to show anger toward me, who am innocent;
for because you are my very self, all my friends are as dear to me as you. (31.12)
Just as waves do not exist apart from water, and just as sparks do not exist apart from fire, so too, O friends, you are never separate from me. 41.13
Whatever love for all of them revolves within me, though it manifests in many ways, ultimately culminates in you alone. (41.14)
"By this word of truth, I entreat you again and again: come to our secret appointment. Having said this, he took her hand. (41.15)
With her mind filled with longing as her husband took her hand,
she cast sidelong glances like arrows, her lower lip curved into a smile.
Kissed and embraced with love by her beloved, she was quickly raised up;
her arms were placed upon the shoulders of her beloved, while his arms were raised upon her own shoulders. (41.17)
Having come together at their own appointed place, they sat down as before;
seeing him joined with his beloved, her friends attained the highest joy.
At the conclusion of their laughter and play, her beloved spoke to her as if smiling:
"My dear, I wish to make a request if you have the desire to hear it. (41.19)
Know that it is indeed unspeakable; nevertheless, I shall tell it to you, lest you should at some time be submerged in the ocean of delusion. (41.20)
Therefore, this Sundarī herself shall deliver you;
whenever you sink into the ocean of great delusion, she will be your deliverer at that very time—of this there is no doubt. (41–21)
Since I have realized that all my friends will cross the ocean of delusion by relying on her alone, this beautiful woman is dear to me.
"The reason for your excessive love for Sundarī has been clearly ascertained. Having heard these gentle and affectionate words, they were all filled with wonder. (41.23)
All of them, including the mistress and the beautiful Sundarī,
honored her with words pleasant to hear, as if with flowers.
Like sandalwood trees naturally cool and beautiful by their very nature, [the sages] were likewise;
yet the ascetic Kāla was a burner whose heart had been utterly consumed by the blazing fire of passion.
Then, after a very long time had passed, when Sumaṅgalā was born, she was like lamps whose grace destroys the blinding darkness of pride.

"This Sumaṅgalā conceals the interval between those who dwell in the absolute abode—which is both situated within the syllables and transcends the syllables—because of her presence in the space of the heart of the Imperishable. For even the Imperishable Brahman, whose mind longs for the vision of her who dwells in the bliss of Brahman, finds it difficult to enter her own abode; how then could she proceed there? Thus indeed do the feet of those who know the essence of the bliss of Brahman declare. Then the circle of friends, possessed by her, requested their beloved's desired object, being informed that "this is a most grievous sorrow" and that they had been entreated thus.
Deluded by their own desires and powers, they did not follow the words of instruction.

When the Rasa indeed sports by resorting to the petal of separation, then Sumaṅgalā—whose gait is favorable to that Rasa—deludes [the senses] (variant reading: "Sumaṅgalā, whose gait is favorable to that time, deludes [the senses]"). || 41.28 ||
Then Priya said to her friends, "Listen to my words; for though I was being restrained by you from this disastrous desire," (29)
"O friends, you have not yet turned away from being intent on persistence—[the variant reading is *āgrahamedurāḥ*].
Do not look upon childish play consisting of manifold sufferings for much longer. (41.30)
"You will forget me there; what more need I say?
Nevertheless, this Sundarī shall indeed deliver you from that darkness. (41.31)
Having been thus addressed and having correctly explained the definitive conclusion, all her friends were filled with joy upon hearing these affectionate words. (41.32)

Immersed in an ocean of serene bliss and enchanted by her power, they perceived a delay regarding the fruit; thus, eager once more to pray, they said: "O Beloved, if you desire our welfare, then fulfill our desire! (an alternative reading: "then grant what we wish"). Whenever they spoke thus, the Beloved fulfilled their heart's longing.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter in the Māheśvara Tantra, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, within the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. 41-41.
Now, from here on, I shall proclaim the forty-second chapter; listen to what is presented, O beautiful one!
Having heard this, O beloved, various divine sports will take root in the heart.
At the junction of the two lands of Santoṣa and Ānanda stands the supreme Puṣpādri,
extending for ten thousand yojanas, vast and filled with manifold wonders.
Consisting of various minerals, glorious, and adorned with diverse gems,
that preeminent mountain has three radiant peaks.
The Pāvamāna peak is most delightful, and it is distinguished by the name Vibhrāja;
on that Pāvamāna summit, Hari eternally sports.
Even for the mistress and Kṛṣṇa, who were constantly engaged in play, there was a great outpouring of sweat from their bodies due to fatigue. (42.5)
There lies that most beautiful lake, filled with those waters,
measuring one hundred yojanas in extent and radiant with jeweled stairways.
It was crowded with lotus groves beautified by wandering bees,
and its sandy banks were adorned by flocks of birds with golden wings.
From that lake issued forth the river named Yamunā,
possessing unfathomable waters, deep, and terrifying with its many whirlpools.
Falling from the Pāvamāna mountain onto the summit of Viraja,
which rises a hundred yojanas high and possesses caverns resounding with the roar of waterfalls, that river flows on.
Having flooded the stage of contentment and the stage of slight detachment, [one reaches] the stage consisting of consciousness-bliss and the stage of slight bliss. || 42-10 ||
Flooding the stage of delight (ratibhūmi), she proceeds to the stage of illumination (prakāśikā).
Indeed, between the stages of illumination and bliss (ānanda) lies the great lake.
It was three hundred thousand yojanas in circumference,
as deep as the ocean, and beautiful with stairways made of jewels.
Filling [the world] once more, she emerges from that state and proceeds to the stage of knowledge;
having flooded the stage of enjoyment, she goes to the ground whose nature is love. || 42-13 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain, having flooded the earth consisting of love, she dissolved into the ocean of nectar;
[this occurred] from the two petals of the one who delights in aesthetic essence (rasa).
One should contemplate the Yamunā as being merely its own flow, through non-difference from that [consciousness].
The ocean of bliss arising from contact with the breeze of the Yamunā perpetually fills the immutable, enumerated bliss. (42-15)
Kṛṣ� liquid form of the Supreme Brahman—by what could one compare Yamunā, whose very essence consists of the waters of the bliss of rasa? || 42.16 ||
In the region of Gomeda, the current of the Yamunā extends for one yojana;
there, the water is as clear as if it were drunk, resembling nectar. (42.17)
On both its banks were vast paved terraces,
radiant with pavilions featuring pillars made of various precious gems.
And they were covered with bowers of creepers filled with humming bees and blossoming flowers;
O Goddess of Gods, there were four hundred thousand [great and radiant ones], blazing with a multitude of splendors. (42–19)
Above and below them stood birds with variegated wings;
some moved through the groves, while others remained within the pavilions.
Some, standing within the paved courtyard, sang with sweet voices;
its entrance consisted of diamond fragments extending for ten yojanas in measure.
There, auspicious water resembling the foam of milk is seen;
its current is of that very same extent, and its two banks are paved with stone slabs.

All of them were variegated with gold inlay, adorned with jeweled svastikas, possessed four gates, and featured archways made of pearls. (Variant reading: "possessed four gates and various archways made of pearls.")
They were provided with jeweled pavilions, radiant with pillars of gold, and furnished with seats enriched with diamonds,
pearls, and corals.
There, by means of the sweet warbling of birds whose very nature is the bliss of aesthetic flavor (rasa), which shower forth a multitude of joys for the ears, one attains happiness. (42.25)
In that region made of topaz, which is the ground of the nature of consciousness and bliss,
the dark river Yamunā shines as it enters with its white waters.
Extending for a measure of one hundred yojanas,
those broad channels have stairs made of gold and rubies and are filled with blossoming golden lotuses.
The water was turned tawny by the mass of pollen falling from the lotuses,
while the banks were festive with the constant clamor of swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks.
Shining with the glittering luster of jewels situated within it, its extent is one hundred yojanas less one. (42.29)
The ground of bliss, pervaded by the foot of the earth of consciousness,
lies within the boundary of the banks of the Yamunā, which traverses the plane of bliss.

O Īśānī, one should remember the seven sacred fords (tīrthasaptaka), which are the refuge of the essence of divine play, as well as the forests on the boundaries of the banks of the paths where the waters descend. (42.31)
The second forest is named Cāndramasa, and the second [grove] is Nīlakānana; the third is called Puṣpadanta, and the fourth is Ānandakānana. || 42-32 ||
The fifth is named Hemakūṭa, the sixth is Tārakūṭaka, and the seventh is called the forest renowned as Gāruḍa. (42–33)
And in the Cāndramasa forest, O Goddess, there shines a great banyan tree named Cāndramasa,
its leaves gleaming like lapis lazuli.
Then there was a lotus-red gem with eyes, adorned with the expansive luster of its fruit, and possessing clusters of pearls hanging from the tips of its matted locks of golden sprouts. (42.35)
Through the graceful movements of swaying the branches where he has made his divine bird-dwelling,
he causes the inner self to marvel at the sight, like a dancer.
With the beauty of their beaks concealed by fruits and their leaves concealed by foliage, they were made manifest only by the words "Great King" or "Kṛṣṇa. || 42.37 ||
And flocks of parrots produce a divine speech, sweet as honey, filled with various musical notes and words, which stirs great curiosity.
Beneath it shines a ground of moonstone gems,
exquisitely beautiful with a mass of radiance rising from the unbroken moonstones.
In which [forest], friends, hanging from its long branches and swaying in playful motion,
embrace one another on the ground through their reflections.
When the excellent floor of rubies shone like a water-basin,
supported by four golden pillars adorned with pearls and lapis lazuli.
Above, it was shaded by the canopy fashioned from sun-crystals;
its edges were covered by branches spreading out in all directions over the ground.
Beneath a wish-fulfilling vine at the foot of a banyan tree, rich with divine shoots and flowers, upon a supreme jeweled lion-throne. (42–43)
The Supreme Person remains there, having come for the sake of sport;
his circles of female companions stand upon a floor of rubies extending ten thousand yojanas.
Laughing and causing others to laugh with their divine play and curiosities, they sing with melodious voices the stainless glory of their Beloved alone. (42–45)
O Goddess of the gods, twenty-four thousand attendants of that place reside here in this great garden, according to their number. (42–46)
O Pārvatī, their palaces were brilliant white with jeweled doorways,
featuring thresholds of coral and surrounded on all sides by groves of banyan trees.
O beautiful one, there are delightful seven-storied mansions arranged in two rows;
an equal number of them shine forth in the center, provided with walkways.
With groups of female friends mounted on swings hanging from the palaces arranged in rows one after another, they suddenly come together in mutual collision;
singing, they repeatedly embrace one another with their hands joined in a circle. (42–49)
This lunar grove is encircled by a golden wall,
and its golden gate shines facing toward the Yamunā.
At the doors stood two pavements made of jewels and gold, positioned to the right and left;
they reached up to the splendor of great pavilions adorned with four pillars and shimmering gems.
From there, the Yamunā river is to be reached by way of the staircase;
the stairs number two thousand two hundred and ten.
With rubies, sun-stones, lapis lazuli, coral, moonstones, emeralds, pearls, sapphires, hessonite, topaz, diamonds, and gold. || 42-53 ||
Again and again, by means of these successive steps and surrounding pavilions arranged one below the other, one properly reaches the Yamunā river.
There, well-fashioned boats adorned with jewels and gold drifted here and there,
their silken banners fluttering in the wind.
Among his friends arranged in many groups of boats, the Supreme Person,
situated in the central boat, shone brilliantly, accompanied by three others.
The Mistress stands on the left side, her garments having the luster of a pomegranate flower;
both Indirā and Sundarī are in front, on the right and left respectively.
Indirā belongs to the dark fortnight; she is beautiful, the supreme mistress, amidst laughter, playful pastimes, sports, disputes, and states of aesthetic flavor (rasa). (42–58)
Therefore, this Indirā is the manifest mistress, dearer than life to her lord;
and she, Sundarī, is indeed Kṛṣṇa’s beloved, dearer even than his own life.
In this way, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, sported at his own will in the moonlit forest with his friends who delighted in the joy of play.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter in the Māheśvara Tantra, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, within the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. 42-42.
Then, the forty-third chapter.
Śiva said:
"O Goddess of the gods, once in the Blue Garden (Nīlodyāna) as well, Puruṣottama..."
Accompanied by thousands of female friends, she comes and sports with the faces of her mistresses. || 43-1 ||
The blue ground was fashioned from unbroken slabs of ruby,
interspersed here and there with pearls, diamonds, lapis lazuli, and coral.
Where there are ponds filled with nectar, garlanded with golden lotuses, featuring ornaments of coral and flowers, and pavilions made of shimmering creepers. (43.3)
Attendants stationed on levels arranged one above the other made the forest region resound with the sound of lutes and drums.
Adorned with jewel ornaments blazing like rays of light and lightning, they, who are experts in various arts and flavors, sing their praises together in unison. (43-5)
There are twenty-four thousand attendants at that place,
and their palaces shine brilliantly, arranged in two rows all around.
In the midst of that ground, O Queen of the Gods, is an unsurpassed palace of play,
fashioned from jewels that surpass a mass of light from ten million moons.
It was resplendent with rows of shining golden pillars in the four directions,
and it was adorned by figurines placed upon each pillar.
The door-panels, gates, and archways were fashioned with pearls and coral,
while swans, pigeons, and parrots made their homes upon the wall-crevices.
Like disputants desiring victory, they cast words at one another;
captivating both mind and ear, these words bring delight to the circles of their female friends.
On all four sides of the palace courtyard were vast paved floors,
along with pavilions and watchtowers, and hundreds of pillars made of precious gems.
In those [gardens], auspicious lotus-pools overflow with water, creating a rising tide;
their waters are beautifully perfumed by the fragrance of the flowers of the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa). 43-12.
Where dancing girls, experts in the art of drama, perform their dances, and where the tinkling sounds of their anklets are heard throughout the groves. (43.13)

Grown near the paved courtyard are four excellent *jambu* trees; their branches extend a hundredfold in width like the banners of the forest. (Verse 43-14) [This verse 43-14, "Grown near the paved courtyard are four excellent *jambu* trees, contemplating hundreds of branches here in the forest like a gambler," is found in ancient manuscripts composed in the Āryā meter.
Their branches spread out a hundredfold, like the banners of the forest. (Verse 43-14)
Women mounted on swinging cradles, shimmering with golden chains fastened to the branches,
delight the peacocks with the deep resonance of mṛdaṅga drums passed from hand to hand;
they cause their garments, resembling masses of lightning, to cast flickering halos of light.
They bore faces and eyes shimmering with smiles, agitated by the confusion of coming and going.
Surrounded by a wall shining with sapphires,
the Supreme Person sports in the most delightful blue garden.
Facing the Yamunā, its great gate shines forth,
with door-panels fashioned from moonstone and adorned with jeweled arches.
To the right and left of the door are two equal golden pavilions,
featuring four gates and canopies fashioned from jeweled pillars and vajras.
Then, by way of the stairway path, the Yamunā river is to be reached;
there are two thousand one hundred and ten steps.
On this stairway as well, there are numerous paved courtyards situated on both the left and right sides, enriched with the splendor of jeweled pavilions. (43.20)
Sometimes, at the conclusion of their water-sports, groups of female friends stay here;
there stands a high, square, and spacious jeweled altar.
Upon the spacious terrace was a paved floor adorned with jewels;
it had four golden pillars as its gates and a pavilion embellished with pearls and gems. || 43.22 ||
Upon the altar, two petals arose like golden leaves,
adorned on both sides with clusters of rubies.
Above the pavilion, its branches spread out, laden with flowers;
some of them extended into its beautiful central area.
There, O Goddess, is a lion-throne, stainless as the rays of ten million moons,
presided over on its two sides by Indirā and Sundarī.
Sometimes the lotus-eyed Lord Kṛṣṇa stays there and plays with those female companions, having performed his festive rites.
Then he remembered the divine and wonderful forest named Puṣpadanta,
where delicate rows of vaidūrya creepers shine resplendent.
With their minds rendered bewildered by the greed for the outpouring of fragrance from the creepers,
the bees run hither and thither like those afflicted by illusion.

There, a pomegranate tree named Puṣpadanta flourishes, possessing the beauty of rubies as its flowers and leaves as radiant as lapis lazuli. (Note: In this passage, the word *vaiḍūrya* is found everywhere, and not *vaidūrya*.)
There, the ground shines forth, made of pure crystal;
free from dust, it flows with nectar, and its trees appear as mere reflections.

Entering the forest filled with masses of luster from beryl leaves and colored by the radiance of ruby flowers, the peahens dance, their minds suspecting them to be clouds charged with lightning. (43.31)
Beholding the clusters of seeds from split-open pomegranates, women of intense passion hold up mirrors to see whether or not they resemble their own teeth.

With its crown extending ten thousand *yojanas* and its branches covering the surface of the earth, its great arms were bent down by the weight of the beauty of its fruits, shoots, and flowers. (43.33)
Delighting in listening to the songs of many flocks of birds, beneath which shines a magnificent floor made of gold. (43.34)
Adorned with a jeweled pavilion richly beautified by pillars of young shoots,
Puṣpadanta has his flowers used as an ornament for the circle of his companions.
As if appointed to the sovereignty over this forest, he shines resplendent amidst a golden pavement set with jewels of lapis lazuli. (43.36)
O Goddess, that great lion-throne upon which Kṛṣṇa sits appears as if clad in blue garments, even though he wears white raiment. (37)
All her friends as well, seated upon a succession of sapphire lion-thrones, shone as if they were wearing blue garments. (43.38)
Observing the extreme mismatch of their ornaments and garments, the female friends laughed among themselves,
clapping their hands like lotuses for one another, even though they were dear to their own kin.
Twenty-four thousand attendants of those places dwell there, devoted to service for the women of Kṛṣṇa. (43–40)
There, female attendants serve [him] with celestial flowers, garments, and ornaments, with divine fragrant unguents, and with the essence of celestial bliss. (43-41)
When her friends were indeed deeply attached to the pleasures of various games with their beloved, then one played upon a mṛdaṅga drum and another upon the sound of a lute.
Some, having ascended to their own houses all around, gratified her from afar with sweet lutes, dances, songs, and other such performances.
O Pārvatī, by the manner previously described, their palaces shine on all sides in two rows, with a pathway running through their centers.
Surrounded by a wall shimmering with lapis lazuli gems,
the Supreme Person sports in the great garden Puṣpadanta.
Facing the Yamunā, his great gateway shines,
with its doors and arches fashioned from rubies.
Thence, one must proceed to the river Yamunā by way of the staircase;
and the steps are as many in number as there are divisions of the letters of the alphabet.
To the right and left of the door were two very beautiful paved courtyards,
provided with pillared pavilions and adorned with archways of pearls and rubies.
At the conclusion of the water-sports, Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by his female companions, stays for a moment on the paved courtyard and then proceeds to his own abode. (43–49)
Thus ends the forty-third chapter in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Śrīmāheśvaratantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī. || 43 ||
Now begins the forty-fourth chapter.
Śiva said:
One should then remember the Forest of Great Bliss (Mahānandavana), which is frequented by all the seasons.
It was resplendent with the beauty of clusters of bowers formed by various flowering creepers.
There, the divine ground is made of gold and variegated with the nine precious gems;
the central altar-platform measures one and a half yojanas in length and breadth.
It is square, made of divine jewels, with its interior reddened by masses of light;
in its center, O Goddess, is a paved courtyard measuring half a yojana.
With silver, gold, diamonds, moonstones, pearls, corals, emeralds, lapis lazuli, sapphires, rubies, sun-stones, and gomedas; || 44-4 ||
O Pārvatī, having pulled the thread situated in the middle from south to north, which is adorned with rows of pillars arranged all around,
one should place the eastern central point below and the western central point above.
In this way, the four corners are smeared with the luster of sapphire;
at each corner, a wish-fulfilling tree and creeper shine above the four corners. (44–6)
It was thick with divine fragrance spreading for a hundred yojanas,
and its bees were enchanted by the scent of divine coral-flowers.
At the eastern gate, two pillars made of ruby were set up, upon which flower-stalks swayed in contact with a gentle breeze. (44.8)
Two pillars of great sapphire are situated on the south,
while two pillars of great diamond-jewels are fashioned in the western direction.
To the north, a pair of lapis lazuli pillars was indeed fashioned;
a pavilion constructed of refined gold was arranged upon them.
There, pearls shine both inside and out like clusters of stars,
possessing a luster that surpasses the radiance of many millions of moons and suns.
In the center of the altar, water-jars resplendent with jewels shine forth;
beneath the pavilion, in the middle portion, is a supreme lion-throne made of gems.
O Goddess of the gods, when Kṛṣṇa occupies the central seat, there is a succession of lion-thrones all around him, worthy of the residence of his beloveds.
Around the railing shine creepers made of various jewels:
*mālatī*, *mallikā*, *yūthī*, *jāti*, *candana*, and *pāṭalī*. (44.14)
The kadamba, pārijāta, āmra, bakula, arjuna, and kesar; the ketakī, campaka, aśoka, nīpa, aśvattha, vaṭa, and others. || 44-15 ||
Dense with jeweled canopies and adorned with flowers and sprouts, their branches swayed playfully in the wind as birds perched upon them. (44.16)
O beloved, the divine trees in the Mahānanda forest shine forth, thoroughly satiated by the flood of nectar flowing from the Ratnakulyā stream.
There are twenty-four thousand attendants at that place;
their divine residences shine all around, O beautiful one. (44.18)
I pay homage to Mahānandavana, the sole city of the bliss of aesthetic flavor, which is encircled by a great rampart fashioned from vajras. 44-19
Facing the Yamunā, its gate is made of ruby,
radiant with the simultaneous brilliance of many rising young suns.
O Īśānī, the two pavements that appear beautiful on the outside have four doors, four pillars, and serve as the ground for the manifestation of splendor. (44.21)
Then, one should proceed by way of the staircase to the Yamunā river;
thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should remember the great Hemakūṭa forest.
There, the ground is made of gold and is crowded with golden trees;
in its center are two golden pavements and four golden pillars.
The glorious [city], extending for half a *gavyūti*, was adorned with pavilions made of gold;
its attendants numbered twenty-four thousand. (44–24)
Their divine houses, equipped with golden furnishings,
shine all around the pavilion like masses of lightning.
O Goddess, the entire space between the palace and the pavilion was completely covered on all sides by hundreds of orange trees.
It was served by fragrant breezes scented with elā, lavaṅga, and kāśmīra,
provided with pavilions of grapes, and radiant with citron vines.
It was adorned with bandhūka, hayamāra, and lavalī flowers,
and surrounded by karṇikāra, kunda, campaka, and sandalwood trees.
The quarters of the sky were made resonant by the cries of various flocks of birds,
while the warbling of the cuckoos was surpassed by the great exuberance of supreme bliss.
Where flocks of peacocks were dancing, where intoxicated bees were humming, where herds of deer were running about, and where trees were being leaped upon by bounding monkeys. (44.30)
Enclosed by a golden wall, it stood like Mount Hemakūṭa;
it was the great garden of Hemakūṭa, adorned with golden gate-towers.
Then the river Yamunā descended by way of the staircase, shining with its two outer sides resplendent with golden pavement.
And then one should remember the wonderful forest named Tārakūṭa,
where the incomparable ground, composed of sapphire, shines brilliantly.

With *kadamba* trees resembling wish-fulfilling trees, with *pārijāta* trees whose abundant fragrance attracts swarms of bees, and with flowers possessing rows of sprouts shimmering in the breeze, the assembly hall shines exceedingly, as if filled with virtuous men.
With *jambīra* trees, *nimbuka* trees, as well as *kovidāra* and *arjuna* trees;
with *śrīparṇa*, fresh mangoes, *panasa* (jackfruit), and *dakula* trees as well. || 44-35 ||
It was adorned on all sides by *nāga*, *puṃnāga*, and *mandāra* trees, as well as by *āmalakī* trees,
which were decorated with unfading flowers.
I bow to Tārakūṭa, which is encircled by a rampart of Tāras;
its attendant deities number twenty-four thousand. (44.37)
O Goddess of the Gods, their divine houses, with their lofty star-studded floors,
shine on all sides like the petals of a lotus.
Facing the Yamunā, his lofty gateway shines;
outside that gateway, two courtyards are resplendent.
It is supported by four pillars made of silver and adorned with golden cords;
from there, one must proceed by way of the staircase to the Yamunā river.
Then, O Maheśānī, he remembered the wonderful Garuḍa forest,
whose ground was fashioned from heaps of Garuḍa-gems.
There, O Goddess, within the space of a cubit, there is a square fashioned from jewels;
on its eastern and western sides are two moonstone gems.
Marked by two rubies on its southern and northern sides, with their faces kissing one another, it was set within a house of pure gold. (44–43)
In this manner, O Goddess of the Gods, sets of four corners shine everywhere at intervals of one cubit upon the grounds of emeralds belonging to Garuḍa.
At the four corners of which even land-lotuses exist,
by the masses of their pollen-dust the sky is turned crimson.
Situated in its center shines the glorious Maṇikya-maṇḍapa,
radiant with the beauty of pillars made of sun-stone gems and leaves of sapphire.
In its midst was a long oblong pool, garlanded with golden lotuses,
its interior made resonant by the humming of bees intoxicated by the scent of their fragrance.
Even when pearls fall upon a ground of rubies,
they do not delight the cakravāka birds, who are deceived by the suspicion that they are merely guñjā berries.
Surrounding the pavilion from afar, plantain creepers shine brightly, their trunks embraced by rubies and their leaves shimmering with lapis lazuli.
Swans, resembling the foam of cow-milk, perched upon the trunks of plantain trees;
blended with the luster of their leaves, they were not discernible even in the slightest degree.
With their kanda-stalk breasts trembling from the mass of leaves shaken by the wind, they were a delight to the mind and eyes through the play of flocks of warbling birds. || 44-51 ||
The plantain trees there shine as if they were dancing;
twenty-four thousand female attendants serve at that place.
Outside of that, the palatial mansions with their central courtyards shine in two rows,
possessing glittering jeweled doors and courtyards resplendent with gems.

Outside of that, O Queen of the Gods, shine the great gardens, creepers, and trees; they are shaken by the impact of the wind, and bees, greedy for fragrance, hover about them. [Alternative reading: "The seven notes of your song are sung by the bees hovering about, greedy for the scent. 44-54.
With peacocks, deer, cakravākas, swans, kāraṇḍava ducks, cuckoos, parrots, pigeons, curlews, cranes, and also hārilas; || 44-55 ||
It was frequented by monkeys, rabbits, boars, cātaka birds, sparrows, various other winged creatures, and kulaṅga deer.
May this garden named Gāruḍa, constructed with walls of pearls and serving as a refuge for extraordinary beings, destroy the dullness of my intellect. (44–57)
Facing the Yamunā, his great gate shines forth,
beautiful with a ruby threshold and sapphire door-panels.
Outside the great gate, there were two wonderful paved courtyards,
featuring pillars of gold and coral and adorned with golden pavilions.
Where the excellent women, residing there, sing and dance,
they are endowed with skill in the arts of playing the lute, the drum, and other musical instruments.
Then the Yamunā river is to be reached by way of the stairs;
O Priyaṃvadā, the number of stairs is everywhere exactly as previously stated.
O Goddess of the gods, for the sake of sport, Puruṣottama comes to these places, surrounded by his companions, in a celestial chariot radiating moonlight. (44–62)
Once, Hari, mounted upon a chariot yoked with a thousand horses,
stood in the midst of a gathering of his friends, proud with the love for his divine play.
There are sixteen thousand great divine chariots;
among them, there are sixteen principal ones, which I shall name for you—listen! (variant reading: *śṛṇu*) || 44-64 ||
Candraka, Bhadraka, Manojava, Mahājava, Javamālin, Maṇiskanda, Rociṣmat, and Bhadrasenaka.
Meghanāda, Mahānāda, Candragaura, Visarpaṇa, Nīlacakra, Kuraṅgāhva, Svarṇanemi, and Vibhāvasu. || 44–66 ||
All these [elephants] were yoked to a thousand horses, adorned with golden garlands,
and filled the quarters of the sky with the sound of tiny bells.
Some clouds, with blue-colored coverings and rows of scattered pearls, shine like masses of shimmering stars.
Some, with dark-blue coverings variegated with streaks of gold and radiant with the flashing of lightning, put to shame the beauty of the clouds.
Some, with red-colored armor and adorned with pavilions of diamonds,
put to shame the sky at sunrise, which is filled with hundreds of twilight clouds.
Other excellent chariots as well, with sounds as deep as thunderclouds,
shine with circles of radiant jewels in the divine forest called Muktika.
To the right of the pavilion shining in the courtyard of the great palace, sixteen chariots stand; those horses are in their stables. (44.72)
They also possess divine celestial chariots, vast in extent according to their own desire, and furnished with various couches, seats, assembly halls, and courtyards.
Adorned with canopies of pearls, radiant with pillars of jewels,
and featuring courtyards variegated with gems that rival the light of ten million moons.
The mansions shine with jewels fashioned by the hands of statues gleaming upon rows of gem-studded pillars, as if they were rows of lamps.
Indeed, there are eighteen thousand excellent celestial palaces;
among those, there are eighteen that are most preeminent and radiant.
The Unmādana, the Sudhāsyandin, the Candraka, the Śatacandraka, the Tuṅgabhadra, the Manoyāna, and the Mahānīlaudañcana.
Vajrakūṭa, Kalāsāra, Cārucandra, Prabhāruṇa, Hemakakṣa, Prabhāpūra, and Puṣpagandhamanāvila. || 44-78 ||
Citradhvaja (or Citrakūṭa, as an alternative reading), Vajrakūṭa, and so forth—these eighteen are recorded;
they are established as those called Śivika upon the most excellent grounds of the celestial palaces (vimāna).
Having thus flooded both the ground of consciousness-bliss and the ground of [ordinary] bliss,
that river indeed enters the lake situated at the junction of light and bliss.
Emerging once more from Lake Sarasa, it flows toward the light;
then, measuring one hundred yojanas, it flows toward the west.
Having flooded the stage of knowledge (*jñānabhūmi*), they proceeded to the stage of enjoyment (*bhuktibhūmikā*);
then, having flooded the stage of love (*premabhūmi*), they entered the western ocean.
Between Ānanda and Bhukti lies the great mountain of rubies (Mahāmāṇikya-parvata),
resplendent with the brilliance of ten million rising suns, and measuring one hundred yojanas in height.
The four rivers originating from his hips flow into the Yamunā,
while the white Suṣumṇā enters the ocean of nectar through the head.
All those rivers, known by the name Nimlocā, carry nectar;
once, he sports there, which resounds with the sound of waterfalls.
Seated upon an excellent celestial chariot crowded with thousands of female companions,
the Blessed One, Puruṣottama, [dwelt] in the delightful mountain valleys.
And thus, the Supreme Person, Kṛṣṇa himself, who is the very embodiment of aesthetic flavor (rasa), plays day after day with manifold pastimes that consist of that same flavor. (44.87)
All this has been told to you, O beloved, even though it was not asked,
because at the time of the emergence of the state of remembrance (smṛti), this is for the benefit of the women of Kṛṣṇa.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Śrīmāheśvaratantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī. || 44 ||
Then, in the forty-fifth chapter, Śiva said:
"Furthermore, O Great Goddess, one should remember the auspicious splendor of the Brahmā-stalk."
It stands in the form of a staff, extending from the Anandavana grove of the Brahmā-nāla. (45-1)
O Great Goddess, on the very path within the precincts of one's own abode,
starting from the gate of the gateway (gopura) up to the tenth enclosure wall, || 45-2 ||
O Brahman, the stalk is said to be twenty yojanas [in height];
on both its sides, O beloved Goddess of Devas, there are one hundred and sixty palaces with paved floors on the outside. (45–3)
Enclosed by various ramparts and containing various circular gardens,
it is reached from the Brahma-nāla by entering through various gates.
O Sovereign Lady, at the entrance of each successive wall, there are two gates on the left and right of the Brahma-nāla, radiating an intense, reddish light.
Enclosed by golden walls were great groves of campaka trees,
resounding with the cries of many birds and thick with abundant fragrance.
The campaka buds, possessing the luster of molten gold, shine like lamps situated in a windless place, having been abandoned from afar by the bees. (45.7)
There, divine campaka creepers shine in great numbers, brilliant with blossoms that imitate the full autumnal moon.
In the groves of the Campaka gardens, fourteen thousand female attendants dwell, having made their abode in celestial palaces.
Sometimes Śrī Kṛṣṇa plays there, surrounded by his female companions,
like the full autumnal moon in the midst of a host of stars.
Within that, O Goddess, one should visualize a forest filled with wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas),
surrounded on all sides by great vaidūrya and śāla trees.
Rejoicing in the fragrance of the flowers of the wish-fulfilling tree, the bees do not look for any other scent, just as those whose desires are fulfilled do not seek anything else.
With their intellects captivated by the delicious taste of the flowers from the wish-fulfilling trees, these householders here seal their own speech as if they were knowers of reality. (45.13)
Just as a pearl fallen upon ground fashioned from great emeralds,
so is the intellect of a devotee of darkness, though it may be radiant with the sprout of love.
Possessing the splendor of Madhu and Mādhava, with his noble arm resting upon the shoulder of a woman,
he is the glory of his dwelling adorned with flowers, and is embellished by ornaments and amorous grace.
There, that springtime, whose essence is rasa, moves continuously,
overwhelmed with love within the pathways of the great groves of kalpa-trees.
He possesses the charming grace of the curved creeper-like eyebrows that serve as the bow of Kāma;
he is clad in garments reddened by saffron and is expert in casting sidelong glances.
Gray with heaps of the pollen of divine flowers and with smiling faces,
they made their dwellings in celestial palaces within the groves of the Kalpa garden.
Thirteen thousand female attendants dwell here;
sometimes the lotus-eyed Lord Kṛṣṇa is present in this place.

Delighting in the pleasures of the spring festival, he wandered through the grove whose essence is aesthetic flavor, enchanted by the amorous charms of his beloveds, foremost among whom was Indirāsundarī. (45.20)
He was as if drunk from all sides by the goblets of his beloved’s sidelong glances,
and as if showered from every direction by floods of flowers released by her friends.
She herself rained down showers of flowers upon her friends,
while her eyes were agitated by the humming of bees intensely attached to the fragrance of her mouth.
He was firmly embraced around the neck by his mistress, who held a lotus in her hand;
and he was sprinkled with saffron-water emerging from water-jets by his beloved wives full of affection, so that he appeared like the god clad in yellow garments (Viṣṇu).
Like an elephant with female elephants, he who is greedy for pleasure takes delight in diversions endowed with manifold flavors, his curiosity being aroused by them. (45.24)
Within that, one should recall a divine grove of Mandāra trees,
surrounded by a rampart made of radiant divine coral and jewels.
It rests upon a ground shining with great sapphires, where peacocks dance constantly, suspecting them to be clouds. (45.26)

Just as bees whose minds are dissolved in the nectar of the Mandāra flowers forget all other blossoms when they are saturated with the essence of Brahman, so too do those absorbed in the nectar of the Mandāra forget other flowers.
Where Rākā, accompanied by the full moon, dwells eternally;
where only Kuhū is found, stationed at the beak of the cuckoo.
Rows of bees, greedy for the gentle fragrance of the *mandāra* flowers, do not wish to go anywhere else, like supplicants greedy for gifts. (45.29)

In whose left side dwells the summer season, languid with intoxication, wandering through the Mandāra grove, radiant with the beauty of oyster shells and pure splendor; (an alternative reading: "the summer season, with its scorching eyes"). 45.30.
In the groves of the Mandāra gardens,
twelve thousand female attendants dwell, having made their abode in celestial palaces.
Once, for the sake of sporting in a grove of mandāra trees, she rose from the root-ground by way of the path to the western gate, accompanied by throngs of women. (45.32)
The lotus-eyed one enters; eager for pleasure, he sports;
the Supreme Person, whose nature is desire, is a master of the great arts of love. (45.33)
Then, one should visualize that inner garden consisting of *pārijāta* trees,
surrounded on all sides by a palace of great rubies.
Its ground was fashioned from moonstone (candrakānta), making it exceedingly beautiful,
where the rays of the moon, upon contact, were reduced to droplets of nectar.
Where the paved floors were mostly adorned with pavilions shimmering with jewels,
resounding with the humming of swarms of bees buzzing within the groves.
The lakes were adorned with thousands of shimmering golden lotuses possessing a thousand petals, with pairs of sporting swans, and with trees scented by their fragrance. (45.37)
With their masses of petals completely covered by motionless bees, they gaze intently with eyes devoid of blinking. (45.38)
Eleven thousand female attendants dwell there, having made their abode in divine palaces within the groves of the Pārijāta forest.
"Perhaps the Blessed One will come here at some time with his circle of female companions, his mind longing for the pleasure of sporting in the Pārijāta grove. (45-40)
Indeed, his friends adorn Kṛṣṇa, who is seated upon a jeweled pavement near a lake, with garments, ornaments, and other items—specifically, with saffron-dyed (kausumbha) ones. (45.41)
With necklaces, earrings, armlets, bracelets, and towering crowns;
with turbans, bodices, waistbands, and beautiful upper garments. (45.42)
The Blessed One, his splendor enhanced by flowers, was moving amidst the circle of his friends,
holding a divine flower-made staff in his lotus-hand.

With the edges of her knitting brows quivering as if vomiting forth true love, she seemed to shower her circle of friends with lotus-eyes; [in another reading: she seemed to shower the bees that were the eyes of her circle of friends]. (45.44)
Adorning his friends with flower-garlands plucked by himself, he, who was skilled in playful movements, laughed while making everyone laugh. (45)
With his fame being sung, he delights in singing within the grove grounds; one should remember that garden of yellow sandalwood situated therein. (45–46)
Her own gate-towers were fashioned from the great gem gomedaka,
and she was radiant with the rays of floors shimmering with pure crystal.

In the reflecting pools of the rows of trees, which were adorned with ranks of sprouts quivering in the breeze, birds repeatedly performed the act of pecking with their beaks, mistaking them for ripe fruit. (45–48)

In some places, birds perceiving the illusion of their own reflections upon the surface of the crystal ground, their minds filled with the suspicion that they were flocks of birds of their own kind, repeatedly cry out their respective notes loudly and incessantly. (45–49)
Wandering through the forest upon crystal ground shimmering with the brilliance of yellow sandalwood,
the birds— seated on nests formed by branches swaying in the breeze— chatter like a group of eminent scholars.
The jeweled pavilions, constructed with gems, shine all around with the intense radiance flashing from their jeweled floors;
their delightful interiors are attended by parrots, cuckoos, bees, swans, and cranes. (45–51)
Filling the sky with its loud and boisterous laughter, adorned by beautiful women standing upon the firm clouds,
this very king of seasons known as the rainy season shines forth, its eyes rolling with intoxication.

In the circles of forest thickets, millions of insects, resembling deep blue jewels, wander about, their luster acquired from the darkness created by the formation of clouds that rumble softly and faintly. (45–53)
O Śivā, within the groves of yellow sandalwood trees, ten thousand celestial residences for female attendants shine on all sides, their courtyards graced by the beauty of blazing fire-seeds.
Here too, Kṛṣṇa plays, surrounded by his mistress and other female companions, with various playful diversions and the delights of jesting and the like. (45–55)
Within that, one should recollect a divine and most enchanting garden, adorned with groves of lapis lazuli creepers, a delight to the eyes. (45–56)
Wherein, from the reflections of coral upon the lapis lazuli trees,
a certain splendor arises that serves as a cause for delighting the lotus-eyes.
It was adorned with a divine rampart fashioned from sun-crystal gems (*sūryakānta-maṇi*),
and its ground was constructed of flawless ruby stones (*māṇikya*).
With its floors of rubies struck by the reflections of sun-stone gems, it produces a delusion as if the dawn has already arisen; oh, how marvelous! (45–59)
In groves of beryl trees, having made their abodes in divine palaces,
nine thousand attendants of that place are said to dwell.
Within that, one should visualize a divine enclosure of great pearls,
surrounded by a wall of shimmering topaz.
It was covered by great pearl necklaces that shone like *māṇikya* flowers;
and upon the creepers there were clusters of divine lapis lazuli that gleamed brightly.
Its ground was flooded with rays shining from great, radiant vajra-jewels,
and it was enchanting with the echoes of birds singing in its groves.
With his inner being immersed in the flood of the beauty and grace of the Goddess of Fortune, he had jasmine and *mālatī* flowers as his ornaments and his very attire. (45–64)

There, the autumn season itself, whose lotus-face is beautified by a smile and which is as pale-white as the luster of the campaka flower, wanders about in the form of aesthetic flavor (rasa). || 45-65 ||
O Queen of the Gods, eight thousand female attendants dwell there, completely surrendered to the delight of sporting in the world of the Pearl Bower.
Even here, the lotus-eyed Lord Kṛṣṇa plays,
eager for the delight of sporting in the assembly of his circle of friends, headed by Svarūpā.
Within that, O beloved, one should meditate upon a divine grove of coral trees,
completely concealed on all sides by a pavilion of emeralds.
Its surface was adorned with ground fashioned from emerald stones,
and it was filled with coral trees resplendent with clusters of pearls.
There, the winter season moves about, attended by the two women Sahasā and Sahasyā (the latter being the variant reading for Sahas), and intent upon performing playful sports.
In palaces and mansions made of jewels situated within groves in coral gardens,
seven thousand female attendants dwell.
Within that, one should visualize a divine garden, radiant with sun-crystal gems and with creepers, flowers, and sprouts, shining like ten million suns.
It was arrayed with halls of moonstone shimmering like ten million moons,
and its ground was paved with a multitude of divine coral gems.
Adorned by the two young women, Tapas and Tapasyāśrī,
he rejoices day and night in the bliss of experiencing their very being.
There, they should resort to the cool season, [approaching him] as he wanders about, overwhelmed by passion;
while they themselves, intoxicated with desire, sport within groves of sun-stones.
O Goddess of the gods, six thousand female attendants dwell here;
sometimes Puruṣottama comes here for the sake of sport with his companions.
And having approached his mistress, while sporting, he even causes her to sport;
at the end of that, he should remember a divine and captivating garden, resounding with bees within groves of thickets formed by clusters of ruby-like creepers. (45–77)
Its interior was illuminated by various wish-fulfilling gems set within the ground, and it shone with many pavilions featuring jeweled floors situated amidst groves.
The interior of the sky was filled with the rising splendor from the rows of jewels on the glittering door-panels,
making it appear as if a multitude of rainbows had risen on all sides.
In some places, the surging rays of light from groves of blue lotuses seemed to smear the edges of the quarters with the darkness of dense clouds.
There, the peacocks, with joyful hearts, dance incessantly,
spreading their plumage as if suspecting the gathering of clouds.
It was filled with the clamor of parrots, pigeons, cranes, and cuckoos;
it possessed the splendor of ten million moons and moonlight, and was free from hundreds of creeping vines.
It was adorned by herds of leaping deer, wild boars, gavayas, rabbits,
ruru deer, musk deer, and yak-cows.
Therein lies the vow of the *cintāmaṇi* canopy, resplendent like many suns,
where five thousand jeweled pavilions have taken up their abode.
Attendants dwell there, richly adorned in divine and elegant attire, capable of manifesting aesthetic sentiments and emotional states, and skilled in the art of service and hospitality. (45.85)
Within that, one should contemplate the great, divine forest of lotuses,
extending for a hundred thousand yojanas, filled with the humming of intoxicated bees.
Making the sky appear as if covered by a canopy of pollen driven by the wind,
it was variegated by the guise of bees wandering in pursuit of its fragrance.
In the midst of the Great Lotus Forest, one should remember a single jewel-palace,
adorned with the magnificent splendor of sixty-four great pillars.
The first is the Ground of the Root; the second is the Ground of the Confusion of Intellect; the third is the Ground of Enjoyment; and the fourth is the Ground of Dancing. (45.89)
The fifth is called the bedchamber, and the sixth is the celestial mansion;
both the seventh and the eighth are described as the pleasure-pavilion grounds.
The ninth is Dūralakṣā, and the tenth is Candrabhūmikā.
These ten stages of one’s own abode have been declared;
in this [abode], the person who is the concentrated essence (rasa) dwells together with his beloveds. (45–45.91)
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Śrīmāheśvaratantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī. || 45-45 ||
Then, the forty-sixth chapter.
Śiva said:
Thus constantly remembering the great glory of her own abode, she—
Gradually, O Goddess, it causes the latent impressions to pass away day by day.
O beloved, if this state of separation called "remembrance" occurs, then your own abode would become ascended upon the path of memory.
Otherwise, for one who is meditating upon the great ocean of the nectar of the divine pastimes, the mind turns away from it, repeatedly breaking off in the midst of the process. || 46-3 ||
Know this: as long as this state born of separation has not arisen, one will not be able to perform service that is purely mental. (46.4)
As long as the arising of the state of mindfulness persists, so long shall there be the two types of service:
the internal and likewise the external; neither of these two is ever [to be practiced] exclusively.
Through service, the mind directed toward that [Lord] gradually becomes absorbed in His divine play;
O Supreme Goddess, it attains the state of constant remembrance (smṛti) in due course. (46–6)
O Goddess, when the state of memory arises, the mind, through its various mental desires, becomes agitated and attains the stage known as "lamentation. (46–7)

O beloved, incoherent speech (*pralāpa*) is said to be that which occurs without prior conscious intent, when the mind of one whose heart is fixed upon objects such as the playful dalliances of a lover [is distracted]. (46-8)
Delight yourself now in this beautiful forest with the love of a lover;
you, my beloved, have been found by me at long last. (46.9)
O Maheśvarī, such various conversations as these proceed when, from time to time, the contemplation of the body arises in the midst of them. (46–10)
Your speech, which flows with aesthetic essence, is ever like a stream of nectar, uniquely capable of extinguishing even the most intense torment.
Your form, capable of causing the ocean of bliss to overflow, is like the essence extracted from the churning of the great ocean of beauty belonging to millions of bodiless gods of love.
O Beloved, the beauty of your smile is as radiant as moonlight, more capable than anything else of tearing asunder the mass of darkness that is great suffering. (46.13)
"O Lord, how could this [world] proceed in such a contrary manner?"—such are the words that proceed in the hymn to the qualities. (46.14)

Thereafter, O Goddess of gods, the state of *ādhyā* (mental longing), which brings the mind under its own power and consists of the condition of separation (*vipralambha*), gradually proceeds. (46.15)

The inner mind, scorched by the fire of long-standing suffering and seized by mental anguish, emits streams of tears externally, as well as trembling from labored breathing and other such symptoms. (46.16)
O Goddess of the gods, when there is separation from the lord of one's life and no attainment of union, a state known as "madness" arises. (46.17)

O Goddess, the condition known by the designation "insanity" (unmāda) is recognized through symptoms such as labored breathing, the shedding of tears, distress, trembling, and scratching the ground. (46.18)
Then, O Goddess, as the heat born of separation arose,
she was overwhelmed by lassitude and delusion, uttering only the sound "huṃ."
Devoid of inquiry, her lower lip dried up by her sighs;
her facial expression discolored, her body had become emaciated. (46.20)
O beloved of existence, O Goddess of the lords of gods, there may sometimes arise a state of insensibility—a death not born of physical injury—due to the instability of even one's fortitude. (46.21)
O Goddess of the gods, when the body is scorched by the flames of the fire of separation from one's own Lord, a period of existence takes birth that is of the nature of death. (46.22)
Thus, O sinless one, these ten states of separation have been described to you; they manifest within the aesthetic sentiment (rasa) of love known as *vipralambha* (love-in-separation). 46.23.
Even though a single state arising from separation may occur,
nevertheless, O lady of beautiful hips, there shall be an experience of aesthetic flavor (rasa).
O Goddess, as long as even a single state born of separation has not arisen, so long the experience of aesthetic flavor (rasa) does not occur anywhere.
Even after knowing of the separation from one's beloved, if there is no arising of [the appropriate] state,
then the recitation of the Cūḍāmaṇi mantra must be performed for the sake of purification.
O Goddess of the Suras, when that mental transformation called *bhāva* arises, that very *bhāva* assumes the state of separation (*viraha*) upon failing to attain [the object]. (46.27)
When the beloved Supreme Bliss is known, yet remains unattained here,
the mind undergoes a transformation characterized by an extraordinary state known as *bhāva*.
When the mind has become free from the impurities of many births, it no longer attains that state of non-existence by which separation could arise. (46.29)
To remove that impurity, one must certainly perform recitation, service, worship, and so forth for a long time for the sake of pleasing Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (46.30)
Whenever Puruṣottama beholds one with a gracious glance, having become favorably disposed, then the dawn of separation occurs.
Thus, O Great Goddess, I have explained to you in brief the description of the ten states; what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Śrīmāheśvaratantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. || 46 ||
Then, the forty-seventh chapter.
Pārvatī said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear how Kṛṣṇa becomes pleased."
O Lord, even without recitation, without service, and even without worship— || 47-1 ||
Tell me now the means by which Kṛṣṇa may become pleased;
otherwise, O Lord of the gods, the goals of human endeavor will not be accomplished. (47-2)
Śiva said: "Excellent, Pārvatī! Your question is well-posed; listen with attention.
O beloved, even without recitation, without service, and even without worship—"
I shall tell you the means by which Kṛṣṇa may become pleased;
yet even that is not accomplished without this hymn, even through practices such as recitation and service. (47.4)
For the Blessed One, the noble-souled Supreme Person, is fond of fame;
service consisting of right conduct is for the sake of attaining success through recitation and absorption in Him. (47-5)
Praise brings about grace; therefore, I shall speak a hymn to you:
[O Goddess] who dwells upon a beautiful island of jewels situated in the midst of the ocean of nectar.
In that place, which consists of nine divisions and is adorned with the nine gems,
one should contemplate in its center a beautiful and unsurpassed palace of jewels.
In that place, which shines all around with charming forest garlands,
one should contemplate a beautiful, most enchanting paved floor.
It is resplendent on all four sides with sixty-four jeweled pillars;
there, upon the lion-throne, one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes are like lotuses. (47–9)
Resplendent with a crown inlaid with priceless jewels and shining earrings,
with a beautiful smile upon her lotus-like face, she is attended by a host of female companions.
Having thus meditated upon Him, whose left side is embraced by His consort and who is the embodiment of supreme bliss, one who has well-conquered the senses should then recite the hymn of praise.
I bow down to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the lotus-petal-eyed one, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, who moves among the circles of his friends, the highest of the high. (47-12)
To him whose form is the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), whose nature is perfect bliss, whose eyes are as red as a lotus, and who embodies ten million Cupids; || 47-13 ||

To Him whose form is the source of the Vedas and other scriptures, whose essential nature is that which is known through the Vedas, and who initiates His own divine play which is beyond the reach of speech and mind; || 47-14 ||
Salutation to the Pure One, the Full, whose activity of qualities has been cast aside;
to the Indivisible, the Partless, whose form is unobscured.

To Him who is the great ocean of the states of union and separation, whose universal form consists of the aspect of existence, and who possesses the imperishable form of the aspect of consciousness; || 47-16 ||

To the one whose essential nature is a portion of bliss, who is of the form of existence, consciousness, and bliss, whose form transcends all limits, who is without support, and who is the witness; || 47-17 ||
To him who is far removed from the proliferation of illusion, who dwells upon the Blue Mountain (Nīlācala), and who engages in playful sport upon the mountains of rubies and topazes; 47-18.

To Him who is the inner controller in the form of consciousness, whose nature is the bliss of Brahman, who is beyond the path of the means of valid cognition, and whose form cannot be grasped by the means of valid cognition. || 47-19 ||
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the source of auspiciousness, who is free from the impurity of illusion;
who is both the perishable and the imperishable, yet distinct from both the perishable and the imperishable.

Salutations to the one whose form transcends the fourth state (turiyatita), who possesses the form of the Supreme Person (Puruṣa), whose essential nature is the Great Desire, and who knows the true meaning of the principle of desire. || 47.21 ||
Salutations to you, O ocean of mercy, who sport in the ten divine pastimes, who traverse the seven sacred fords, and who are filled with the essence of playful enjoyment.
And for the arising within the hearts of devotees scorched by the fire of separation, he has manifested his own bliss and rendered liberation fruitless. (47.23)
To the one who tears asunder the veil of the great darkness of delusion regarding duality and non-duality;
to the unchanging witness of the creation and dissolution of the universe. || 47-24 ||
To the Lord who is himself without a lord, to him by whom all karma has been cast aside,
to the sun for the darkness of worldly existence, to the one who took away the life of Pūtanā.
To him whose mind is filled with the waves of the playful pastimes of the *rāsa-līlā*, and who alone knows the various nuances of the emotions within the lotus-eyes of the Queen; 47.26.
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the creator, whose nature is absolute bliss;
salutations to that very Self, who is the sprout of joy for the heart of his mistress.
O Lord, protect me with compassion—I whose soul has wandered manifold times through the forest paths of saṃsāra, and who am tormented by the mental anguish of separation from you. (47.28)
You alone are my mother, father, and other circles of kinsmen; as for learning, wealth, lineage, and character, I possess nothing whatsoever apart from you. (47.29)
Just as a wooden woman moves by the instruction of a craftsman, so do I move about, O Lord, lacking independence through you. (47.30)
"You ought to protect me, who am destitute of all means of accomplishment, turned away from the practice of dharma, and fallen into the ocean of worldly existence. (47.31)
