O Lord, O ocean of compassion, protect me, who am situated upon this machine of illusory wandering, agitated both above and below, and unaware of my own secret sign. (47.32)
O you who are devoted to compassion, lift me up—I who am deluded, perceiving what is not beneficial as beneficial, trusting in a place of danger, and sleeping when I ought to be awake. (47.33)
O lotus-eyed one, I am terrified that my internal continuity of past and future existences might become severed and turn away from you. (47.34)
Lead me, who am indeed addicted to drinking the waters of the ocean of the salt of illusion, to the proximity of the nectar-ocean that is your presence; do not delay.
O Lord, having encountered the pain of separation from you, how shall I show this mocking face, out of shame at the fact that I still live? (47.36)
"O Lord of my life, even in separation from you, I maintain my vital breaths;
does this great impropriety not cause me shame here? (47.37)
What shall I do? Where shall I go? Before whom shall I speak?
Mental states arise and dissolve like waves in the ocean. (47.38)
"I am distressed by suffering and wretched; there is no one other than you who can destroy my pain.
O Lord of my life, having understood this, do as you wish. (47.39)
Then, with palms joined in reverence, one should bow again and again to Kṛṣṇa.
This secret has been declared; it must not be spoken, O Daughter of the Mountain King. (47–48)
O Goddess of gods, for one who thus praises [Thee] three times a day with senses subdued, the Lord Himself appears within that person's mind in the form of love. (47–48)
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Śrīmāheśvaratantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. || 47 ||
Then, the forty-eighth chapter.
Pārvatī said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Protector of the world, Ocean of Compassion!
This excellent and highly meritorious narrative has been related by you.
I have been favored by you, my Lord, who are compassionate in soul;
for this secret of Brahman, O God, has been made manifest. (48.2)
Beyond this, O Lord of Gods, there is nothing further to be known;
nevertheless, I wish to ask: who, having drunk the nectar, attained satisfaction? (48.3)
In connection with the King of Mantras, your service has been described;
O Lord of Gods, how the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the women of Kṛṣṇa are perfected. (48-4)
For those dear to Kṛṣṇa, there is indeed nothing superior anywhere to the practice of *dharma*;
nevertheless, O Lord, you have even indicated some form of worship for us. (48-5)
O Lord of Gods, by what rite is it performed, when, and by whom?
Tell me this, O learned one, for you are great and compassionate toward the distressed. (48–6)
Śiva said:
"O beloved, you are blessed, you are blessed, you are blessed; you delight my mind as the sun delights the lotus with its radiance by answering my questions."
Therefore, I shall tell you about your worship, even though it is most secret;
service alone is said to be primary, while worship is called secondary. (48–8)
If one is unable to perform service, one should worship Puruṣottama;
that which you ask me, O beloved, I shall explain to you. (48.9)
O Goddess of gods, having risen in the morning and meditated upon one's own Guru at the *brahmarandhra*,
one should worship that Supreme One with the five mental offerings.
Then, one should meditate upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa together with His Mistress within the lotus of the heart—
He whose lotus-face is serene and who sports with the multitude of His beloveds.
Then, O Dear One, having performed the worship as before according to the rules of ritual practice, she should request his permission with her hands joined in the *añjali* gesture. (48.12)
I know the Dharma, yet I have no engagement in it; I know the non-Dharma, yet I do not desist from it.
I have entered the dense darkness of illusion and, through negligence, have fallen into the blind well of the household. (48.13)
Whatever I shall do, whether auspicious or inauspicious, I do it all without independence;
therefore, O beloved Lord, forgive me for everything as I follow the course of worldly existence. 48-14.
Then, O Goddess, having received permission and requested the ground as before, one should perform the ritual for the evacuation of waste and the cleansing of the hands, feet, and so forth. (48.15)
O Goddess of the lords of gods, as before, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth;
and having performed the ritual bath, either at a sacred ford or in one's own home, as previously described. (48–16)
Having gone near the house of worship and taken his place on the prescribed seat,
he should apply a tilaka mark upon the temple of Hari with auspicious substances such as saffron.
O Dear One, Brahmā is situated on the left line, and Hari is in the middle;
therefore, one should not smear the central region with [the paste].
One should not apply a forehead mark after looking at it in a mirror, in water, or in oil;
for whatever has been done is seen as undone when reflected in a mirror or similar surfaces. (48.19)
O Maheśvarī, one should perform the wearing of the mudrās and other symbols in their proper places;
first, one should place the Kaumodakī mace upon the region of the forehead.
One should place them one by one on the left side and likewise on the left breast; similarly, one by one or two by two on the pair of arms, with a spirit of devotion. (48.21)
One should place five wheels in the abdomen and three wheels in the heart;
then, O Goddess, one should apply two wheels on the right side.
One should join three [marks] on the right breast, carry two on the right arm,
and place a pair of wheels at the base of the right ear.
Likewise, one should place the *cakra* once each on the region of the throat and the left arm;
O Goddess, there shall be only a single *śaṅkha* placed upon the left cheek.
Likewise, one should place one [syllable] on the left side, two on the left breast,
know three on the left arm, and likewise two on the left ear.
Having placed two [marks] on the lower lip with auspicious cowherd-mud, one should likewise place a single mark on the right arm; in this manner, one should duly apply the conch-marks.
One should place two lotus mudrās on the left and likewise on the right;
one devoted to worship should wear the name-mudrā on all the limbs. (48.27)
Without wearing a garland of *tulasī* and without bearing the mark of the weapon, no one shall attain perfection; this word of mine is indeed the truth. (48.28)
Pārvatī said:
"If one should perform worship and other rites without wearing the insignia of weapons, he would not attain success in this world; my mind is utterly bewildered by this. (48.29)
Since Kṛṣṇa, whose very form is rasa, does not bear any weapons, why indeed would his beloved herself carry the weapons of Viṣṇu? (48.30)
"Whosoever is devoted to whichever deity, he bears that deity's weapon;
yet there is no purpose [in this], nevertheless it is commanded by you. (48.31)
Therefore, a doubt has arisen within me; my heart trembles like one pierced by a thorn.
O ocean of compassion, extract it, so that I may attain certainty. (48.32)
Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare that which you ask me;
by the mere hearing of which the mind becomes free from doubt. (48.33)
One should constantly contemplate non-duality and not contemplate the state of duality;
through the constant contemplation of duality, saṃsāra does not cease. (48.34)
One who is proficient in the state of non-duality does not perceive saṃsāra at all;
therefore, he who perceives through the state of non-duality truly sees. (48.35)
O Maheśānī, for one who perceives distinctions such as "this is Brahmā," "this is Hari," or "this is Rudra," there is fear caused by Time (Kāla).
The phenomenal world (prapañca), from Brahmā down to the lowest immobile beings, is merely Brahman;
the Vedic statement that "there are two Brahmans" must be due to a distinction made for the sake of divine play (līlā). (48.37)
"It is one alone without a second; otherwise, it would be contradictory.
Therefore, O Goddess of Gods, duality is merely an illusion; of this there is no doubt. (48-38)
The duality of the moon may be perceived due to the limiting condition of water;
by removing the limiting condition of water, the non-duality of the moon is revealed. (48.39)
Likewise, duality even within Brahman is manifested through ignorance;
when ignorance is dispelled, however, the non-duality of Brahman remains as it truly is. (48–40)
For one who perceives the oneness of Śiva, Hari, and Brahmā, there is no contradiction in wearing weapons and sectarian marks. (48–49)
For those engaged in their own spiritual welfare, while relying on the creation of darkness (tāmasa-sarga), other defects and obstacles, residing within the mind, cause them to fall away. (48.42)
And they all fled at the sight of the Vaiṣṇava weapon, as if agitated by the blazing flames of a fiercely burning fire. || 48-43 ||
Brahmā, residing within the limiting adjunct of sentient beings, is Viṣṇu;
even his weapons, upon being seen, cause all defects to flee, just as elephants flee upon seeing a lion. (48–44)
For indeed, by entering your mind in another way, they cause you to abandon devotion;
therefore, O beloved, the wearing of weapons and emblems is in every respect necessary.
Seeing him whose body bears the marks of the discus, sinful beings are struck with fear;
those states consisting of passion and ignorance never touch him at any time.
Those heretics who, for the sake of pleasing the world, bear the marks of weapons such as the discus and other emblems, fall again and again into the hells. (48-47)
Therefore, one should carry the weapons as an ancillary part of worship;
by worshipping thus, one attains perfection, unattached to the faults of sin and the like.
Then, having performed the worship of the door, one should enter the sacrificial hall,
striking the ground three times with the left heel and clapping the hands three times.
Having dispelled with divine vision the beings situated in the intermediate space and those dwelling in heaven,
and having requested the earth [for permission], he should sprinkle the seat according to the ritual rule.
Having sipped water and tied his topknot with the root mantra, the preceptor— assuming the attire of a woman, being handsome, and with his mouth containing betel— should perform the worship.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Śrīmāheśvaratantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī. || 48 ||
Then, in the forty-ninth chapter,
Śiva said:
"And having dissolved the elements, beginning with earth, into Brahman,"
And having generated them again in sequence, one should then visualize the purifiers.
Having thus performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should again establish the vital breaths (prāṇas).
Then, having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the fifty Mātṛkās, one should thereafter perform the placement of the seer (ṛṣi) and the other [limbs].

Then, having performed the placement of the syllables of the root mantra with a concentrated mind, one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes are like lotuses, within the lotus of one's own heart. (49.3)
O Dear One, one should visualize a crown of divine jewels upon the head;
or else, one should meditate on an uṣṇīṣa having the luster of a pomegranate flower. (49-4)
Adorned with pearl earrings shimmering with priceless jewels, and with a highly radiant, circular crest-jewel bound upon his head. (49.5)
It was as if reproaching the orb of the rising full moon;
its beautiful uṣṇīṣa was encircled by a divine garland of pearls. (49.6)
Exceedingly beautiful with the splendor of the waves of the milk-ocean, shining with the luster of set jewels, and clad in spotless garments. (49.7)
Wearing an upper garment that shone like a fresh rain-cloud, radiant with hanging pearl-strings that gleamed like blossoming sprouts at its edges.
His two hands were resplendent with bracelets, armlets, and upper-arm ornaments,
and he was adorned with the weight of necklaces made of lapis lazuli, pearls, and rubies.
He was repeatedly warding off bees, intoxicated by the scent of his divine body-unguents,
by the circling of his playful lotus.
Scattering the moonlight of his pearl-like teeth from his smiling face,
he bewildered his beloved with the playful knitting of his brows like a mango blossom.
Her lotus-face was graced by dark, curled, and beautifully glossy locks of hair;
her forehead-region was enchanting, shining with a sandalwood tilaka mark. 49-12.

One should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa within the lotus of the heart—his face filled with betel, his body possessing the luster of a campaka flower, and eternally sixteen years of age. (Note: *vārṣikyam* is an alternative reading.)

O beloved, one should recollect his mistress situated on his left side, possessing the beauty of the playful grace of her creeper-like eyebrows, which are like the curved bow of the god of love. (49.14)
Resplendent with a row of teeth that have become sprouts of the bliss of aesthetic flavor,
her eyes destroy the fierce pride of fish, lotuses, and wagtails.
Her nose was adorned with a jasmine bud, and she was decorated with ornaments of shimmering pearls;
her forehead ornament was beautified by a dangling string of pearls. || 49.16 ||
Marked by a musk tilaka shining upon her moon-like facial orb, and enchanting with a pearl necklace rolling upon the slope of her cheeks. (49.17)
With the radiance of their safflower-colored garments spreading upwards and downwards,
they made the expanse of the sky appear as if filled with vermilion.
She bore breasts that were dark as blue clouds, variegated with gold-worked settings shimmering with pearls and gems. (49.19)
The ground was strewn with clusters of pearls and other jewels dangling from its edges,
and she wore a beautiful dark blue lower garment that resembled a golden thread.

I meditate in my heart upon the venerable Mistress Śrī, whose beauty is enhanced by necklaces of gold, pearls, and gems; whose conch-like throat is illuminated by a jeweled collar; and whose lotus feet resound with ruby anklets. 49-21.
Then, one should worship those two with divine mental offerings.
Having offered the food oblation (naivedya) to the Lord, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite;
then, having visualized a square great sacrificial pit (mahākuṇḍa) in the Mūlādhāra, [one should proceed].
O Dear One, one should offer oblations there— consisting of desire, anger, and so forth— into that which blazes with the fire of consciousness, fashioned by the fourfold self.
One should offer desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy, along with unrighteousness, falsehood, and ignorance, as oblations into the fire of knowledge.
Having meditated upon himself as the very essence of latent impressions (vāsanā), his nature defiled by desire and other passions that have been burnt away,
and having found a moment of leisure, he should offer water for sipping (ācamana) to these two.
Having mentally meditated on those two while they eat, and having given them water once more,
one should offer a roll of betel leaf and recite [the mantra] with devotion according to one's ability.
Having thus completed the internal worship, one should commence the external worship;
one should draw the worship-diagram on a cloth or on a plate made of gold or silver.
O Maheśānī, having first fashioned a hexagon upon copper [or] upon [wood] produced from the śrīparṇī and sandalwood trees, one should pierce the śakti with fire.
Thereafter, one should construct an eight-cornered figure; hear from me the method for doing so. First, one should draw a square, straight-lined and beautiful. (49.30)
O Pārvatī, having drawn a line from the upper part of the eastern line, O Great Goddess, [draw another] from the middle part according to the sequence of dividing the joints. (49.31)
O Pārvatī, drawing a line from the middle of the eastern line,
O Great Goddess, and following the sequence of dividing the joints from the center,
one should pierce through the southern line and extend it slightly outward.
O Supreme Goddess, having drawn the line of Dakṣa extending upwards, [32]
One should bring the western direction as before, leading it outward;
having drawn that [line], one should lead it to the head of the northern line.
O fair-eyed one, having drawn back that [line] which was previously spreading outward,
one should place it upon the eastern line and join it with its tip.
Having fashioned this eight-cornered figure, one should encircle it with a circular line;
then one should draw the twelve-fold yantra with its attached root-petals.
Above that, O Goddess, one should draw a circle resembling the full moon;
one should then construct three squares, beautiful with four gates.
Having established the seat of worship (pūjāpīṭha), one should then perform the worship;
O Goddess, one should prepare the general water offering (sāmānyārgha) according to the general procedure.
O Goddess of the gods, having drawn a square with water on your own left side and having worshipped it with unbroken grains (akṣata) treated with red sandalwood paste and perfumes; 49-38.
There, having established the support, one should worship the fire-mandala;
O beautiful one, having placed a conch or some other vessel there.
There, one should worship the solar disc together with its constituent parts (kalās).
Having filled it there with pure water mixed with sandalwood paste, perfumes, and other offerings. (49–50)
There, having invoked the sacred bathing places (tīrthas) and pierced the solar disc, one should consecrate [the water] eight times with the root mantra using flowers and other offerings. (49–51)
Having consecrated the conch and the fish with fragrant water and rendered them immortal, one should display them;
by this very procedure, one should prepare the water for the feet (pādya) and the respectful offering (arghya).

Having thus consecrated the vessels— the bell-metal vessel for the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and likewise that for the water for sipping (ācamanīya)— one should commence the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā).
The Tortoise, Ananta, and Varāha, as well as the Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Space, are the supporting powers (ādhāraśakti) for the Frog. (49–44)

The ego (ahaṅkāra), the principle of greatness (mahattattva), primordial nature (prakṛti), and likewise the spirit (puruṣa); then the island of jewels (ratnadvīpa), the stalk of Brahmā (brahmanāla), and the forest of wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadrumavana). || 49-45 ||
O Īśānī, from there is the Mandāra garden, then the Pārijāta forest,
the Haricandana garden, and the grove of Vaiḍūrya trees.
Then there is the divine forest of pearls, the grove of coral trees,
the garden of sun-stone trees, and thereafter the forest of rubies.
And there is the Mahāpadma grove and the unsurpassed Maṇigṛha;
beyond that is the pavilion with sixty-four jeweled pillars.
O Goddess, on its four legs are the jewel-throne’s supports:
Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya, in order starting from the southeast direction.
Having thus performed the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭha) and having formed the mudrā for invocation,
one should meditate with an undistracted mind upon Kṛṣṇa together with his Mistress.

Meditating that [the deity] has entered his heart, he offers the flower, accompanied by water and unbroken rice grains, as a great light consisting of aesthetic rapture (sāmarasya) through the gateway of the eyes.
Having cast [the deity] upon the King of Yantras, one should perform the placement of the vital breaths (prāṇanyāsa).
Then, O Pārvatī, one should display the mudrās beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).
A wise person should offer water for the feet using only the water from the vessel for the feet; likewise, one should offer the arghya at the head using only the water from the vessel for the arghya.
Then, having prepared the madhuparka, one should offer the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka).
After that, having offered flower-oil, one should show the jeweled sandals (maṇipādukā).
O Goddess, having offered a bath with divine waters, garments studded with jewels, ornaments and the like, and then the application of divine perfumes; 49–55.
With *campaka*, *karavīra*, *ketaka*, and *bakula* flowers; with lotuses, *jātī* blossoms, *mālatī*, and *mogarā* as well. (49–56)
One should worship the deity seated upon the king of yantras and offer incense according to the prescribed rite;
thereafter, one should present a lamp that destroys the darkness of ignorance.
One should place a lamp on the right and an oil lamp on the left;
one may offer a lamp using either of these two according to one's preference.
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship the three kinds of gurus on the left side:
Karuṇānanda, Yaśas, and Taruṇānanda. (49–59)
And Bhuvanānandanātha—one should worship these three above;
likewise, O Supreme Goddess, in the second row, below those. (49–60)
Then one should worship Madana, Mohana, and Mandra;
as well as Mandara, Śaṅkara, Tāmra, one's own guru, and likewise that guru's guru.
O Maheśānī, one should worship the six Gurus and their Gurus below that;
the space between the practitioner (sādhya) and the seeker (sādhaka) is called the East. (59–62)
Beginning from the prepared eastern direction, one should perform worship everywhere;
O Goddess, one should likewise worship Sundarī and Indirā within the six corners.
Āhlādinī, Ānandā, Aruṇā, Karuṇāvatī, Śyāmā, Anaṅgā, Anaṅgarekhā, Surangā, Vyañjulī, and Rati.
One should worship Balākī and Kesarāṅgī in the southeast corner (vasukoṇa).
Next, I shall describe to you the worship in the twelve petals. (49–65)
Forty leaders of the hosts are proclaimed as three groups of three;
for each leaf, one should worship two [leaders] who are eternally by the side of the Mistress. (49–66)
Mālatī, Mādhavī, Nandā, Subhadrā, Rucirānanā, Puṣpāvatī, Ratnarekhā, Padmavṛndā, and Vilāsinī. || 49-67 ||
Mandāramadhurā, Mādhvī, Mañjanādā, Kalāvatī, Śṛṅgāralatikā, Vṛndā, Pramodā, and Madhumālatī. (49–68)
Kiśorī, Kusumānandā, Rasakulyā, Prabhāvatī, Āśāvatī, Viśālā, Nistulā, and Nīlakuntalā. (49–69)
Vidyudvarṇā, Nimnanābhi, Virajaskā, Vihāriṇī, Rāgiṇī, Raṅgalatikā, Ratnāvatī, Padmāvatī, Padmagarbhā, Padminī, and Pikasvarā. (49–70)

O Supreme Goddess, one should worship that which is situated beyond the external manifestation—the immutable, all-pervading, eternal, and undecaying; the indivisible Being-Consciousness-Bliss. (49–71)
Resplendent with earrings of shimmering rubies like a row of dark clouds,
he was like the sacrificial fire itself, illuminated by the flame of his divine jewel-encrusted crown.
Wearing a pearl necklace and possessing four arms, his garments are as red as the rising sun;
he is supremely radiant, shining with a mass of light like the rays of ten million moons.
Through its opening and closing, it causes the emergence and dissolution of the cosmic egg;
it is the substratum for the delusion of the world, just as mother-of-pearl is for the illusion of silver. (49.74)

Through superimposition and negation, that which is the object of knowledge for the wise—which, though non-existent even by its own being, appears as if existent, conceptualized through name and form—[is thus established]. (49.75)
The seven-year-old [child] was accompanied by the five-year-old Ramā;
he was most excellent, adorned with a magnificent garland variegated with the nine jewels.
Outside of that, O Goddess of the Suras, in each of the four gates,
one should worship Puruṣa, Prakṛti, Kāla, and Yajña, starting from the east and moving counter-clockwise.
And outside of that, in a square, one should worship Vāsudeva and the others,
who wear crowns and earrings and possess forms dark as rain clouds.
Then, one should worship those [deities] with four arms shining with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, even within the square outside of that.
One should perform the worship of the five elements in sequence from Agni up to Īśāna;
one should fully worship the subtle elements (tanmātras) from Īśāna up to Vāyu.
One should worship the five organs of action from Nairṛti up to Vāyu, and the five [organs of] knowledge from Nairṛti up to Agni. (49–81)
Outside of that, at the locations of the gates, one should worship in the order starting from the east:
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛti, and the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa).
One should worship Pavana, Dhanada, Rudra, and Brahmā above;
likewise, one should worship Ananta below, and there itself the weapons together with their mounts.

Having worshipped [the deity], O Goddess, one should then offer the food offering (naivedya), consisting of an excellent vessel provided with a stand and filled with various kinds of eatables and foods. (49–84)
Having sprinkled [the object] with ordinary water and offered flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and so forth,
one should then consecrate it as nectar by means of the cow (dhenu-mudrā) while reciting the root mantra eight times.
One should offer the five breath-oblations while displaying the *grāsamudrā*;
then, having presented the vessel of water, one should hold a cloth between [oneself and the deity].
Having praised the Lord with ancient and vernacular hymns while He was eating,
and having meditated upon Him, one should know that He is satisfied and remove the covering of the cloth.
Having offered water for rinsing the mouth, O Īśānī, and having removed the oil from the hands of the Supreme Lord with various kinds of fragrant powders; 49–88.
Thereafter, one should perform gargling and cleanse the mouth with camphor;
having washed the hands and feet, one should then worship the hand-garments.
Then, at the conclusion of the Prasanna-pūjā, one should offer a roll of betel (tāmbūla-bīṭikā) mixed with nutmeg, cloves, and camphor, and interspersed with powdered areca nut and lime. 49-90.
Having offered prayers and placed the pair of sandals before Śivā,
one should then perform the *nīrājana* ceremony with lamps for her as she is seated upon the lion-throne.
One should fashion nine, seven, or five [mounds], square in shape and auspicious in appearance, raised four finger-breadths high, using slightly cooked, well-ground flour. (49–92)
Then, having offered a parasol, a fly-whisk, a peacock-feather fan, and likewise a mirror, one should perform circumambulation and prostration.
Having performed song, dance, and so forth, one should gratify the Supreme Lord.
Thus, O Goddess, the supreme procedure for worship has been told to you. (Variant reading: ...the supreme procedure for worship has been told to you. || 49-94 ||
But when the mind is serene, one should perform worship with a concentrated mind;
O Supreme Goddess, there is no restriction regarding the time for this.
Thus has this been told, O Goddess, which was asked by you, O fair-eyed one;
in brief, O Great Sovereign, what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Māheśvara-tantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. || 49 ||
Now begins the fiftieth chapter.
Pārvatī said:
O God, O Lord, O Maheśāna, O Three-eyed One, O Master of the World!
I have also heard the supreme and great rule for worship.
O Śaṅkara, regarding the worship of the Immutable (Kūṭastha), you have indeed described his meditation as all-pervading, eternal, unmanifest, and indivisible. (50-2)
If that [Brahman] is indeed indivisible and all-pervading, why has it not entered into bliss? To maintain that it exists only in the play of absolute bliss is contradictory. (50.3)
O Lord of Gods, if this is not accepted, its all-pervasiveness is contradicted;
for [the Self] is of the nature of knowledge, immutable, bliss, and the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). (50.4)
O Lord of Gods, O Sovereign of the Suras, knowledge and bliss are mutually opposed;
yet when knowledge free from duality arises in the women of Kṛṣṇa— || 50-5 ||
Then, O Lord, because of the state of non-distinction, the aesthetic flavor (rasa) would cease to exist;
for how could knowledge that produces a semblance of rasa be applicable there? (50.6)
O Lord, what is the status of attributes such as being indivisible and all-pervasive in that [reality]?
My mind is greatly distressed by the desire to understand this. (50.7)
Śiva said:
"Well asked by you, O blessed lady, is that which is desired by those seeking knowledge;
hearing which, at that very moment, their desire for further inquiry ceases. (50.8)
O Goddess, the immutable is all-pervasive, while the effect is that which is pervaded; thus it is established.
Nowhere is the effect all-pervasive, nor can the cause be something that is pervaded. (50.9)
That which has limited function is the pervaded (*vyāpya*), while the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is otherwise;
and the relationship of pervaded and pervader exists even between the immutable (*kūṭastha*) and bliss (*ānanda*). (50–10)
I shall explain the distinction therein; listen, O lotus-eyed one, to that which is pervaded by a minute particle of the essence of desire, yet is immutable and of the nature of knowledge.
For this very reason, it is celebrated as "Bliss" by hundreds of scriptural texts;
for although it exists as immutable and undivided, O beloved, it is so designated. (50.12)
Like the lunar orb on the new moon night hidden within bliss, the portion of desire is yet undivided, whole, immovable, and eternal. (50.13)
Pervading everywhere, O Goddess of gods, she is manifested in her own essential form;
this play, consisting of consciousness and bliss, is said to arise from the state of being a portion of Kāma. (50.14)
O Goddess of excellent complexion, this was experienced by the Vedas in the past during the dissolution of Prakṛti; therefore, it is called the "Pastime of Goloka. (50.15)
Pārvatī said:
What is that *līlā* (divine play) like which is experienced through the Vedas? How can the Veda, being composed of sound, be capable of experiencing aesthetic rasa? (50.16)
"Tell me this, O Blessed One, if it may be appropriate for me.
Śiva said: "Listen, Pārvatī; I shall answer your most excellent question. (50.17)
When the period of reabsorption (pratisañcara) has arrived, that all-pervading Lord Brahmā, the Master of Creatures, does not exist;

nor do the sun and other luminaries, the planets, constellations, oceans, rivers, mountains, trees, and medicinal herbs; at that time, neither the gods, the Daityas, nor humans, nor the directions remain.
Neither Gandharvas nor Rākṣasas, nor the best of Munis, nor Yakṣas, nor Siddhas, nor Uragas [could do so]. (50.18)
When all that was created by the Ordainer—both the stationary and the moving—had perished, nothing remained;
yet he who remained was the all-pervading Lord, free from destruction, the immutable, the one Supreme Person.
Then the Vedas, their minds filled with wonder, entered into that all-pervading Lord who dwells within them, like Brahmā himself.
Then, having reflected in their hearts, they praised in secret him who is beyond the range of speech and mind.
The Vedas said: [As it is stated in the *Bṛhad-Vāmana Purāṇa* regarding the words of Brahmā to Bhṛgu and others:
"In former times, I performed austerities for sixty thousand years in order to obtain the dust from the feet of the women of Nanda’s cowherd settlement. (50.1)]
"Even so, I have not obtained even the dust of their feet.
Having heard these words of Brahmā, Bhṛgu then spoke respectfully.
Bhṛgu said:
"Even those like you grasp the dust from the feet of the Vaiṣṇavas;
there are many such Vaiṣṇavas in the world, such as Nārada and others. [50.3]
You alone are the one Self, the ancient Person, eternal, immutable, possessed of infinite qualities, and free from worldly desire.
We do not know where you abide or where you have gone; we have come to you, the Supreme, for refuge. (50.20)
Since even you accept the dust from the feet of those gopīs after they have left [their homes], I have a doubt in this matter; tell me, O Lord, what is the reason for that? (50.4)
Then Brahmā, having reflected upon an ancient narrative and the most wonderful secret of all the Vedas, spoke to Bhṛgu.
Brahmā said:
O son, those beauties of Vraja are indeed the Śrutis;
neither I, nor Śiva, nor Śeṣa, nor even Lakṣmī is equal to them anywhere.
In the past, when the primordial dissolution had arrived and the manifest had entered the unmanifest,
only Brahman remained— the pure consciousness alone, beyond time and māyā, the imperishable.
The world consisting of the bliss of Brahman, known as pervasive Vaikuṇṭha, exists within the absolute Imperishable; it is devoid of qualities and is without beginning or end. (50.8)
The imperishable Brahman, the supreme, the highest abode of the Vedas;
the dweller in that world, praised by the Vedas residing there, he who is higher than the highest. (50.9)
Satisfied by their long eulogy, he spoke these words to them in their absence:
"I am pleased; speak, O wise ones, whatever boon is desired in your hearts. (50.10)
The Śrutis said: O Acyuta, the forms beginning with Nārāyaṇa have been known by us;
all this is Brahman with attributes (saguṇa), yet we have no perception of them as substantial entities.
That supreme form which is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and beyond the reach of speech and mind, which we recite as "Brahman," is indeed not known [by us]. || 50-12 ||
"O you who know the ancient lore, show us that form which those here call 'pure bliss' alone, if indeed a boon is to be granted to us. (50.13)
Having heard this, he showed him his own world, which is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti),
consisting solely of the bliss of pure experience, imperishable and immutable.
There is a forest named Vṛndāvana, rich with wish-fulfilling trees,
abounding in enchanting groves, and endowed with the pleasures of all seasons.
There is the mountain named Govardhana, endowed with beautiful waterfalls and caves, composed of jewels and minerals, glorious, and crowded with flocks of excellent birds.
There flows the Kālindī, the best of rivers, with its pure waters, its two banks bound with jewels, and teeming with swans and rows of lotuses. (50.17)
There, amidst a multitude of cowherd girls intoxicated by the savor of various amorous sentiments, stands Acyuta in the form of a youth situated in the midst of that group. (50.18)
Having thus shown it, he said: "O observers of vows, what may I do for you?
This world of mine has been seen, which is why there is no higher boon."
The Śrutis said:
"O You whose beauty is like ten million Kandarpas, upon seeing You, our minds have undoubtedly attained the state of amorous longing and are agitated by passion. (50.20)
"Just as the cowherd women dwelling in your world worship you, considering you their lover out of the nature of desire, so too has a desire arisen within us. (50.21)
The Blessed One said:
"Your noble desire is difficult to attain and difficult to accomplish;
yet, being fully approved by me, it shall surely come true."
When the future Virañci arises and exerts himself for the sake of creation,
upon reaching the Sārasvata Kalpa, you shall become gopīs in Vraja.
On earth, in the land of Bhārata, within my district of Māthura,
in Vṛndāvana, I shall become your beloved in the circle of the Rāsa dance.
Having obtained from me, through the practice of lovers, a very deep, firm, and all-surpassing affection,
you shall all indeed have fulfilled your purpose.
Having heard this and reflected for a long time upon the form of the Blessed One, the cowherd women reached the appointed time and, having become gopīs, went to Hari.
Whether woman or man, by regarding Keśava as their husband and placing him within their hearts, they attain the goal of the Vedas; of this there is no doubt. (50.27)
By merely attaining the dust of their feet upon the eternal ground of Vṛndāvana,
and through the longing for that, alas, [even others] attain the state of the gopīs.
Therefore, O sons, I have truly desired the dust from the feet of the women of Nanda’s cowherd settlement, for they are indeed the personified Vedas.
Having heard these words of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin,
the sages became completely devoted with their whole being to Śrī Gopījanavallabha.
And it is said in the thirty-first chapter of the Sanatkumāra-saṃhitā, where the illustrious Mahādeva said: "O Brahmins, is all well with you regarding Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the gods?"
Meditation, yoga, austerity, and the Vedas are the eternal means of skillful action.
I shall explain clearly that for which you have come;
however, O sages, this secret has never been revealed by me anywhere before.
And this which is being told is great, a secret more secret than the secret;
listen, O tigers among sages, for you are eager for the abode of Kṛṣṇa. (50.3)
Vṛndāvana is supremely meritorious, the purifier of all purifiers;
it stands outside of all worlds, self-supported and radiant. 50.4
Clad in pure garments, beloved, and seated comfortably there, that couple sports, surrounded by their friends such as Lalitā and others. (50.5)
Furthermore, it is stated in the twenty-second chapter of the Sanatkumāra-saṃhitā that Sadāśiva said:
"The non-dual primordial [reality] of Vṛndāvana is called Vṛndānandana."
In the second [kalpa], the supreme Mathurā-maṇḍala was produced by the instruments.
There is no other holy place equal to that, nor indeed is Vaikuṇṭha itself; what else can be said, O Sage? For the multitude of other holy places is like a blind well. (50.7)
The Mathurā-maṇḍala is beautiful, the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Therein lies the lovely Vṛndāvana, extending for five yojanas.
And those mortals who, knowing reality and seeing reality, renounce their lives in the forest, attain the auspicious and meritorious state. (50.9)
In the northern and southern regions, an extent of two yojanas is said to exist,
where by mere remembrance, accomplishment (siddhi) will certainly and surely come to pass.
And on this earth, the site of Vṛndāvana was fashioned for the sake of attaining the perfection of the individual soul (jīva-siddhi),
in a way that cannot be suddenly achieved on any other ground, even in the most excellent [of places] like Vṛndāvana itself.
Having completely renounced the state of a householder as well as the multitude of all sacred pilgrimage sites, the attainment of that state occurs before long and with ease. (50.12)
More secret than the secret [from the Vārāhasaṃhitā], this secret is the cause of supreme bliss;
it is the most auspicious secret among the most wonderful secrets. (50-13)
O Goddess, it is the most difficult among all things difficult to obtain, the deluder of all, composed of all powers, and hidden within all the scriptures. (50.14)
The supreme Satvata station, the exclusive favorite of Viṣṇu,
is the eternal place named Vṛndāvana, situated above the mundane egg of the universe.
The eternal, imperishable bliss and sovereignty of the fullness of Brahman is present there;
Vaikuṇṭha and other realms are but portions of its portions, whereas Vṛndāvana itself exists on earth as that very essence. (50.16)
Whatever sovereignty belongs to Goloka is established in Gokula;
and whatever majesty belongs to Vaikuṇṭha is manifested in Dvārakā.
O Goddess, that supreme sovereignty of Brahman which has its eternal abode in Vṛndāvana is specifically the Māthura region in the center of Vṛndāvana. (50.18)
The woman was Lakṣmī and the man was Viṣṇu; they became portions of portions [of the Supreme]. There, in the form of a youth, he is eternally a personification of bliss. (50.19)
In the infinite millions of cosmic eggs, which are the locus of infinite threefold qualities (guṇas),
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are but infinitesimal fractions— parts of parts of a crore— of His power.
And it is said in the *Gotamītantra*: "Goloka is above all of that; and above that Goloka, Govinda himself, the incomparable leader, sports in supreme bliss. (50.21)
And it is said in the Vārāhasaṃhitā: "That form which is eternally the Lord of Vṛndāvana in the divine forests... (50.22)
The lord of Vraja, the sovereign of the Sātvatas, the sole beloved life-breath of Vraja.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Abode, the Supreme Form, the two-armed Lord of Gokula, the Lord of Vṛndāvana, the sole cause of the attributeless [Brahman]. (50.24)
Some say that the single cause, the fullness of Brahman, which consists of the rows of moonbeams from his fingernails, is that very ray— the imperishable Brahman whose nature is consciousness.
Truth is difficult even for the lords of yogis to attain and is beyond the reach of ordinary men;
yet the wise declare that Mahāviṣṇu is but a minute fraction of a fraction of it.
And it is said in the thirty-fifth chapter of the Sanatkumāra-saṃhitā, where Sadāśiva said: "The fourth portion of Kṛṣṇa was born in the house of Nanda."
He was seen by Vasudeva and worshipped under another name.
"Just as Viṣṇu has four arms, so too is there another person; he too is to be meditated upon as four-armed"—thus was he deluded by delusion. (50.28)
Droṇa was Nanda, and Yaśodā was that illustrious one;

from their union was born the portion of Kṛṣṇa who bore the form of Kṛṣṇa. For this very reason, he is called the son of a cowherd, the offspring of the cowherds, and the son of the gopīs. || 50-29 ||
They performed that great *rāsa* dance,
which caused wonder even to the sages and was difficult for the hosts of deities, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others, to comprehend.
[50–30] Thus [end] those deeds and those qualities of yours here, O Lord.

O Lord, all those infinite beings have now perished; they no longer exist. Some are slain, some have departed—where indeed have those creatures gone who were the eaters of the sacrifice, led by Brahmā? (50.21)
Those gods such as Purandara and others, who might consume the sacrificial offerings given by us in the ritual, do not exist anywhere;
for they would grant desirable objects of the mind without ceasing.
They too have gone to destruction; we do not know where they are.
Bearing the names of Brahmā, Īśa, and Nārāyaṇa, you yourself— though beyond the qualities (guṇas)— perform creation, destruction, and preservation by means of the three qualities.
You create humans, Daityas, and gods. || 50-23 ||
Salutations to the one whose form is immutable; salutations to the infinite Creator;
to the one whose nature is both the pervaded and the pervader, and whose form is both the signified and the signifier.
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful, who is devoid of qualities yet the soul of qualities;

who is distinct from both the existent and the non-existent [variant reading: whose form is the manifestation of the existent and non-existent]; who is the cause of the manifestation of the existent and non-existent; salutations to Him whose worldly activity proceeds from His will, and who is delight. (50.25)
This entire world has arisen in You and is dissolved in You, just as a bracelet exists in gold;
that which exists at the beginning and at the end must exist as reality in the middle as well, even though it appears as non-existent.
O Lord, this composition of words from us appears to you like the ritual of lighting a lamp for the purpose of illuminating the orb of the sun; it is, as it were, fruitless. (50.27)
Therefore, be gracious, O Blessed One; accept our favor.
We are born from you, the Vedas are rooted in you; how then can we praise you? (50.28)
Thus praising the imperishable Blessed One, the Vedas remained with their hearts both startled and moistened— [the variant reading *cakitārdramānasāḥ* is preferred], their hearts covered in awe;
for they were present at the Great Assembly known as Prākṛta.
Then there appeared in the sky a beautiful cow. || 50-29 ||
Listen to these pleasing words of the All-pervading Lord;
choose a boon from me, for when I am pleased, even the Vedas are attained. When the Supreme is gracious, what is there that cannot be obtained?
And there is no eternal existence, neither in this world nor in the next.
The Vedas said: "What other boon is there that is superior, which we should praise, and beyond which nothing else exists here in this world?"
Whatever supreme reality exists here,
if you are pleased, grant us the vision of it.
We constantly describe your many forms; for although they are known in their particulars, they have indeed been seen by us many times. (50.32)
They manifest and dissolve within you, the absolute one who is devoid of qualities;
therefore, show me today that Self of yours which transcends all qualities.
While the Vedas were thus praying in many ways at that time,
Līlā, renowned throughout Goloka, suddenly manifested herself.
There appeared a most enchanting river, its banks of great jewels shimmering and its sands like water-pearls,
beautified by golden lotuses.
A garland of waves of the nectar-water of the profound depths. || 50-35 ||
That Vṛndāvana is endowed with multitudes of excellent trees— wish-fulfilling cintāmaṇi and kalpa-pādapa trees—
as well as śālas, tamālas, taralas, and kadambas.
With rose-apple, mango, fig, banyan, pipal, and so forth. || 50.36 ||

It was filled with *kapittha*, *bilva*, *āmalaka*, coconut, *aśvattha*, and betel-nut trees, as well as groves of plantains and other captivating trees such as the *aśoka*, *pāṭīra*, and excellent *pārijāta*. (50.37)
It was surrounded by many delightful groves and endowed with the dwellings of cows, cowherds, and cowherdesses;
its trees, their sprouts made to dance by the winds, seemed to be vomiting forth a mass of bliss.
A forest appeared there, teeming with flocks of various birds, and not far away stood Govardhana, the best of mountains. (50.39)

Endowed with the excellences of all seasons, variegated by various minerals, its golden peaks shimmering, and cooled by cascades of nectar—seeing that, they were struck with wonder: "Is this a dream, or a delusion of the mind? (50.40)
Doves cooing with sweet sounds, black swans, ducks,
ruddy geese, cuckoos, and other such birds—
multitudes of winged creatures as enchanting as the *sāraṅga* and peacock.
They stood praising him, like hosts of Apsarases [tasthurvane] or like groups of bay horses [harigaṇā]. || 50-41 ||
He whose form is dark like a dense cloud, whose eyes are like full-blown lotuses, whose brows and cheeks shine with a crown and armlets;
who has a beautiful nose and a handsome face, who holds a sounding flute in his hand, who is adorned with a peacock feather crest, and who is clad in yellow garments. (50.42)
Then they beheld the son of Nanda, the Lord whose very form is bliss, wandering in that forest which is bliss itself;
he was moving in the midst of a great multitude of cowherd women, his beautiful form radiant with the three-fold bend of his body.

Beholding Him— whose body shines with the radiance of ten million suns, who dispels the pride of ten million moons, whose form possesses the splendor of ten million manifest Cupids, and who has the profundity of ten million oceans— that treasure-house of loveliness, suddenly attended by Rādhā standing at His side, O Gopikā,
You were struck with wonder by His constant and supreme love. (50.44)
One gopī, with a *camara* in her hand, fanned her beloved; another stood motionless in front of him, having formed a hollowed cup of her two hands.
Another, having arranged a row of lamps made of clusters of jewels in a vessel, performed the function of a lamp by holding it before the faces of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
One girl, beholding Kṛṣṇa’s dark face, became as if fixed in a painting;
another, seizing Kṛṣṇa’s hand and placing it upon her heart, stood there with joy;
and yet another, joyfully and tenderly grasping his pair of feet, placed them upon her own head.
Another, intent on chanting the glories of Kṛṣṇa, dances while holding cymbals in her hands. || 50.46 ||
Thus, beholding Kṛṣṇa in Vṛndāvana— immersed in the rasa of divine love and standing in the midst of the assembly of gopīs— the Śrutis simultaneously offered their salutations.
Then, being pleased, he said to them: "Choose from me an auspicious boon;
you have indeed beheld this abode known as Goloka."
The Śrutis said:
"We do not choose any boon whatsoever that is perishable and seized by Time;
O Lord, if You will grant one, then bestow Your grace upon us. (50.49)
Just as the cowherd girls, your beloveds, sport with you, so too does our mind become agitated by a desire for amorous play. (50)
Fulfill our heart's desire in that manner;
beholding one as beautiful as ten million Cupids, we are unable to remain still. (50–51)
Having heard what was spoken by the Vedas, Acyuta, in the form of a youth,
spoke with a smiling face while the gopīs were listening.
This desire is as difficult to attain as a flower in the sky; though it is true according to the Vedas, no one who relies on their own human intellect can achieve it. (50–53)
Perceiving his own self as one of beloved form, and thinking "I am my beloved," he approaches me with a body ablaze with the most intense flames of the fire of separation.
Until this very day, this realm known as Goloka has not been attained by anyone, even by those well-versed in the Vedas, nor by following the path described by me.
Nevertheless, you have been addressed by me, the Giver of Boons, for the sake of granting a boon;
yet my word shall never, at any time or in any place, prove false.
And when the four-faced Brahmā comes into being during the Padma Kalpa,
within the world-system created by him, there shall be the auspicious Maṇḍala of Mathurā.
There, the divine Vṛndāvana shall become the abode of aesthetic rasa;
there, this very pastime of Goloka will descend in every respect. (50–58)
And there my own primordial form shall arise with my beloveds; you too, moreover, shall abandon your male state. (50–59)
O women of Vraja, you shall become beautiful damsels possessed of amorous passion;
even there, you will be enchanted by the bliss of hearing the sound of the flute. (50–60)
When you have transcended your own boundaries and arrived at the circle of the rāsa dance,
then you will undoubtedly have your desires fulfilled.
Having spoken thus, Acyuta, appearing in the form of a youth, vanished.
Then, after some time, during the Padma Kalpa, when the four-faced Brahmā had appeared—
When his first *parārdha* had passed away after he was born,
this divine play arrived in the midst of his second [parārdha].
Having divided themselves into twelve thousand distinct forms,
they attained the state of beloved consorts and stood in the midst of the circle of the *rāsa* dance.
"Through association with the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, they became fulfilled;
thus I have told you everything that I was asked, O fair-eyed one. (50–65)
The immutable heart is directly known as Goloka;
there, Puruṣottama, a portion of Kāma, sports with the gopīs.
This [consciousness] is always manifest in the immutable Supreme Self;
however, consciousness remains concealed in the Puruṣottama (the Supreme Person). || 50-67 ||
O Śivā, who is capable of reaching the further shore of the ocean of the nectar of the rasa-līlā? Know that what has been described by me is merely a glimpse of its direction.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Śrīmāheśvaratantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. 50-50.
Now begins the fifty-first chapter.
Śiva said:
"O Pārvatī, listen; I shall now explain another method to you."
By the mere hearing of which, auspicious contemplation arises. || 51-1 ||
O lady of excellent complexion, those ten stages have been described by me;
the fifth is called Śayanīyā, and on it he sleeps even during the nights. (51-2)
Adorned with a shining pavilion raised upon a golden handle, variegated and sparkling with the rays of glittering jewels; provided with comfortable, radiant divine cushions;
covered by cloths shimmering with many pearls and gems at the edges; and perfumed by the fragrance of flowers that delight the mind and possess a divine scent. (51–3)
Upon a couch— the very seat of pleasure— excellently canopied with shimmering pearls, stuffed with swan-down, brilliantly illuminated by the high radiance of clusters of sparkling gems,
and attended by his supreme mistress who was intent on the various delights of amorous play.
At night, the Lord, whose essence is aesthetic flavor (rasa), sleeps in the bliss of an intense festival of love. || 51.4 ||
Surrounded on all sides by the sounds of lutes, drums, and the sweet melodies of song within their pleasure chambers,
her friends attend upon her beloved at the close of night.
They are skilled in the task of awakening the beloved lord who is dearer than life.
She has limbs of gold, a beautiful face, and a sweet voice; her countenance is smiling.
She is the creeper of bliss, Vṛndā, the multitude of friends, and she who is free from sorrow.
Citraprasthā, Vicitrāṅgī, Candraghaṇṭā, Vibhāvarī, Mañjumodā, Vidhumukhī, Ratnadantī, and Madālasā. (51.7)
Lāvaṇyalaharī, Līlāvatī, Lāvaṇyamantharā, Lalitāṅgī, Kāmavatī, Puṣpiṇī, and Puṣpadantikā. || 51-8 ||
Hasantikā, Haṃsagati, Puṣpaveṇī, Marullatā, Muditā, Modinī, Śyāmā, as well as Muktāvatī and Rati. || 51-9 ||
Hāriṇī, Hariṇī, Haṃsī, Vihansī, Haṃsakuṇḍalā, Aruṇāṅgī, Raṅgaraṅgā, Rasaraṅgā, and Kumudvatī. (51.10)
Kuṅkumāṅgī, Kundahāsā, Candrahāsā, Caritriṇī, Ānandamañjarī, Mandrā, Padmavṛndā, and Jvalantikā. || 51-11 ||
Kundadantī, Ratnakalā, Jayinī, Svarṇamekhalā, Pulindinī, Hemavarṇā, Hariṇākṣī, and Ratipriyā. || 51-12 ||
Padmakośā, Bhṛṅgarāvā, Gāyanī, and Madamantharā—these sixty-one companions were appointed for the task of awakening him. (51.13)

Behold Him at dawn, who has just arisen; whose creeper-like eyebrows are raised by His long eyes like lotuses; whose smiling bimba-lips shine from the beautiful lotus-face blooming with a yawn; whose incomparable limbs possess a splendor like a lotus bud shimmering when stirred by the wind, as He gazes with a glance that rolls slightly from the end of sleep upon the circle of His friends. (51.14)

In a vessel adorned with shimmering gold and radiant with spotless gems— a most auspicious object— those lovely female friends, emitting the soft and charming tinkling of their bracelets, performed the lustration ceremony for their beloved, who was as beautiful as ten million Cupids, using auspicious lamps of precious jewels. (51.15)
Thereupon, suddenly placing the *Añjanāmañjarī*— which brings joy through passion—
and a mirror into the stainless lotus-hand of the King,
she said: "Behold this lovely face of your beloved, as beautiful as a lotus."
"Behold this beautiful place, its splendor enhanced by the dark mango trees," [the reading *sukṛtijanakṛtaśri* is also found in the i0 manuscript]. || 51-16 ||
Having placed his two lotus-feet, upon which jeweled sandals were set,
upon a resounding jeweled footstool, that handsome one performs the rite of cleaning his teeth.
When the procedure for cleaning the teeth was undertaken, the two women known as Mandrinī and Surasā were present;
Mandrinī held auspicious water, while the other held a clean cloth in her hand. (51.18)
Then Madanamañjūṣā, having placed it in a worthy vessel, presented it mixed with the powder of lavali, camphor, cardamom, and betel nut. (51.19)
Then, having tasted betel and being exceedingly pleased at the request of her circle of friends,
she ascended two sandals radiant with jewels.
He proceeds facing toward the bath-house. || 51-20 ||
Adorned with canopies of jewels and pearls, perfumed by rows of its own incense-smoke,
and filled with the fragrance of garlands of flowers from the wish-fulfilling tree—
The sky was made resonant by the humming of wandering bees.
It was attended by a host of ready female attendants and many dancing troupes of performers;
it was made charming by the echoing resonance of various resounding musical instruments and songs.
Having approached the radiant bathing pavilion where a multitude of jeweled figurines are fixed upon the pillars,
the Lord ascends the precious throne brought forward and presented by Bhāmā.
Having removed his charming collection of ornaments and having caused each of those to be placed upon the hands of his beloveds,
he was then honored with the lustration ceremony by means of the ornaments offered by his most excellent wives.
It shines as if with hundreds of lamps, with the radiance of its splendor. || 51-24 ||

He performed an anointing with delightful aromatic substances mixed with the powder of saffron and turmeric, along with *yakṣakardama*— which, according to Dhanvantari, consists of camphor, agallochum, musk, saffron, and sandalwood, and is called by the name "Great Fragrance"— as well as with cardamom and other charming perfumes. (51–25)
Having brought scented oil contained in a jeweled vessel, Manojava performs an anointing upon her limbs, even though they are naturally fragrant.

O friends, they bathe their beloved with waters scented by clusters of flowers, enriched by the great fragrance of musk and yakṣakardama paste, rivaling nectar, and rising from the frontal globes of elephants as bright as the autumnal full moon— globes adorned with golden jars variegated with pearls and gems. || 51-27 ||
Smiling-faced, like a digit of the moon, with the sweet song of birds,
she is the garland of unions [or the garland of auspiciousness], the joy of love, the bliss of the universe, and adorned with beautiful earrings.
Tejovatī, Hemagarbhā, Taruṇī, and Tapanāvatī—these twelve are declared to be the principal [rivers] for the rite of bathing. (51.29)

Gopīnasvācchaśuci, with her body adorned by fine earrings, brings delight to her beloved as she gently wipes him dry with a clean, pure cloth. (Variant reading: *proñchayati* / *prīṇayati*) || 51.30 ||
Having cast off her bathing garment, she wears a hip-cloth offered by Tejovatī, beautiful with the hue of saffron. (51.31)
Mounting a pair of sandals, the supreme Lord approaches the pavilion of ornaments very slowly, surrounded by his beloveds.

Seated upon a crystal throne within a pavilion whose interior was filled with the arrangement of Indra’s bow, its golden floor inlaid with jewels and shimmering with masses of upward-radiating rays, [he stood] amidst the celestial canopy.
Lalita’s tresses were being combed by her lover with the tip of a comb,
while she was perfumed by the smoke of burnt black agalloch incense.
Here, the fragrance of the lotuses perfumes [the air].
Then Anaṅgarekhā placed upon his head a magnificent turban, intensely red with a flood of vermilion,
its edges adorned with strings of pearls.
She fastened upon the front of her turban a border fashioned of gold, adorned with a network of pearls, featuring a ruby in the center and a sapphire at the tip.
Shining with many pearls and gems, having voluntarily taken up her own swan-shaped earrings,
she made her two ears appear like ornaments emitting a mass of lightning-like luster.
A necklace made of the nine gems, as well as a neck-ornament (graiveya), a pendant hanging from the heart-lotus, and likewise a four-fold ornament; || 51-38 ||
A pair of armlets on the two arms, bracelets, bangles, and finger-rings;
a girdle-string set with shimmering gems—this is great wealth. (51.39)
The excellent white garment, glistening and charming, was as if variegated by the mass of rays emerging from her ornaments; it was a fine cloth that served as a veil for her sighs.
A most beautiful upper garment, glossy like a fresh rain-cloud,
its four edges shimmering with priceless pearls and gems.
She indeed arranged many divine ornaments upon the body of her beloved, who had attained the wonder of amorous adornment.

Thus, having adorned himself with erotic finery and surrounded on all sides by groups of female companions holding musical instruments in their hands, he proceeds to the pleasure grounds while being sung to. (51.43)
In the kitchens dwell his beloved attendants, such as Lalitāṅga and others, who are fortunate, youthful in form, and numbering one hundred. (51.44)
Seated upon a golden throne, Puruṣottama remains there,
holding a pure golden vessel with a base that is exceedingly wide.
Around him, a thousand golden vessels were placed,
and within them were set various kinds of smooth and heart-pleasing enjoyments.
In front of her is rice that creates the illusion of a cluster of jasmine buds;
to her left is *āḍhaka* rice with green gram, along with abundant ghee from buffalo milk,
soup, cakes, *hayaṅgavīna*, and shining cooked foods such as plantains.
With pearl-sweets, pūlikās, śikhariṇī, and māṣa-rice mixed with curd; || 51.47 ||
Milk mixed with fire-hot sugar placed in a jeweled vessel,
as well as milk-rice (pāyasa) and ghee mixed with sugar,
adorned with the reflection of the full moon, sweet, sour, and bitter—
It possesses various flavors, the essence of mango, honey, and cow's milk.
Combined with well-cooked kushmanda, vṛntāka, paṭola, bimbī, śimbī, sukauśātakī, sūraṇa, and other such vegetables, which have been thoroughly cooked over a mild fire;
[The food] was thoroughly perfumed with asafoetida, black pepper, and other such fragrant substances.
While the four kinds of food were being served,
Ānanda and Ānandamaya also ate;
all his dear ones surrounded him on every side.
Laughing, they ate from their own bowls.
Then, at the conclusion of the meal, she, with her limbs purified, offered water for sipping (ācamana) to Kṛṣṇa from a golden pitcher upon a jeweled pedestal to his right.
For the purpose of removing oiliness, he gave auspicious fragrant powders,
as well as tooth-sticks and pieces of camphor like fragments of the moon.
At the conclusion of the rinsing of the mouth and the sipping of water, having mounted a pair of sandals with a betel-roll containing saffron, preceded by the five musical instruments— || 51-53 ||
All the goddesses, headed by Svāminī, showered pearls upon Kṛṣṇa, who had entered another seat and was the embodiment of supreme bliss.
In a square golden vessel adorned with pearls and various gems, accompanied by auspicious offerings such as *dūrvā* grass and curds,
and provided with auspicious jewel-lamps that cast steady flames—
They perform the lustration ceremony for their own Lord, who is free from desire.

Then the Supreme Lord, experiencing the joy of the erotic, the comic, and the marvelous sentiments out of compliance with his beloved, rested there for just a moment and proceeded to the ground known as the bed. (51–56)
Being sung to by beloved women with soft instrumental music and the like,
he lies down fanned with a colorful fan by one holding a soft whisk in her hand.
Having arisen from sleep together with his attendants, he stood upon the dance floor at the lion throne, which was variegated by the rays of pure jewels,
and [enjoyed] the dancing and singing of his beloved’s playful charms and the like.
Seeing this, he was pleased; indeed, even his own satisfaction [was a cause for joy].

Mithilā held up a parasol, its orb radiant with the brilliance of a flawless autumn moon; [the reading *apasmāra* appears in another version]. Furthermore, ten thousand vessels of gems were filled with milk, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and ghee mixed with sugar, along with black gram cooked in oil.
Holding fans, beautiful sandals, chowries, mirrors, and other such items,
those previously mentioned attend upon the Supreme Being who is higher than the highest.
Then, having mounted a magnificent celestial chariot named Citradhvaja,
he departed with thousands of female companions for the lunar forest.
Sometimes in the Nīla forest, sometimes at Puṣpadantaka;
sometimes in Ānandavana, and sometimes also on Hemakūṭa.
Sometimes on the blue mountain called Tārakūṭa belonging to Garuḍa,
sometimes on the mountain of topaz, and occasionally also on the mountain of rubies.
In some place within a grove of *mandāra* flowers, in the interior of a forest of *pārijāta* trees,
in a garden of yellow sandalwood (*haricandana*), or in a grove of lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*)— [an alternative reading is "in a forest of *vaiḍūrya* gems"]— somewhere [he dwelt].
In a certain great forest of pearls, as well as in coral gardens,
in ruby forest-gardens, and likewise in great lotus forests.
Sometimes in a grove of campaka trees, and sometimes in a forest of kalpavṛkṣa trees,
Puruṣottama sports with manifold pastimes;
then, having descended from the moon by means of a highly effulgent celestial chariot...
Kṣaṇa (or, according to another reading, Kṛtakṣaṇa) stood for a moment in the pavilion situated before the great gate,
resting upon the ground supported by sixty-four great pillars.
At that very moment, deluded by desire, the women led by their mistress, filled with longing, entreated Kṛṣṇa as he sat upon the jeweled lion-throne.
All of that has been told by me to you previously, O lady of excellent complexion;
hereafter I shall speak further—listen with a one-pointed mind.
Just as they attend upon him in this manner with affection,
even so some remain busily engaged in serving their mistress and other such duties.
With lustrations, ritual baths, garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments,
as well as beds, seats, and betel, her female friends attend upon her.
Twelve thousand in number are those who attend upon her;
indeed, six thousand are devoted to the service of Kṛṣṇa.
Six thousand attend upon the Mistress for her service;
indeed, O Goddess of Gods, their groups number forty.
Their divine palaces number twelve thousand;
each one is endowed with a length and breadth of half a yojana.
O beloved, in each and every palace of each of his beloveds,
one hundred attendants are employed for the sake of service.
O beautiful lady, outside the area of your beloved’s palace, there are separate mansions for each of the groups of female attendants, arranged in that very same order.
Measuring half a yojana and slightly more than that,
they were endowed with width and length, possessed three stories, and were radiant.
The beloved celestial mansions are of various colors and forms,
exuding the nectar of the moon and originating from moonstones.
Some were black and white, some red, some black and red,
some red and black, and some white and red.
Some were white, some red, and some were reddish-white; likewise, some were smoky-colored, some black, and some were smoky-black.
O Goddess of the gods, this sequence applies to all the palaces;
O Goddess, in each individual mansion there is a long bathhouse.
Equipped with various implements and a canopy of divine jewels,
it was an ornamented chamber, a single great pavilion with a magnificent jeweled floor.
To the east of the hall of ornaments, however, is the temple of perfumes and ointments;
it is enriched with various kinds of fragrances and equipped with many ingenious arrangements. (51–83)
O Goddess of the gods, the kitchen is situated in the southeast corner,
while the assembly hall, resplendent with divine seats, is in the northeast.
Thus, O sinless one, has been described your dwelling in the palace of Kṛṣṇa’s beloved;
for Kṛṣṇa himself is the essence of liquefied rasa, whose very nature consists of his beloved.
Manifesting himself, he sports with his beloved groups in every mansion;
yet in the palace of the Sovereign Lady, he remains solely in a state of intense concentration.
Without the Mistress there is no Kṛṣṇa, and without Kṛṣṇa there is no Mistress;
O Goddess, they do not remain apart for even a moment, for otherwise the aesthetic flavor (rasa) would be lost.
Here, there are jewels and pearls, flowering creepers and trees, and various kinds of minerals such as coral, gold, and silver. (51.88)
O Goddess, the sun and moon, beasts, birds, and the winds, as well as the various categories of food—namely, that which is chewed, eaten, licked, sucked, and drunk—are indeed manifold. (51.89)
Having realized that the distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, as well as the knower and the knowable and so forth, is nothing but *rasa* itself, one is never again deluded.
O Supreme Goddess, there the reckoning of time does not exist;
nor do the rising and setting of the sun, the moon, or the stars occur. (51.91)
For although states such as rising and setting are perceived,
know this, O Pārvatī, to be solely for the sake of distinguishing the different moments of the divine play (līlā).
O virtuous lady, this which I have spoken has indeed been well heard by you.
O Goddess, this secret of all the Upanishads must not be told to anyone.
This is the Māheśvara Tantra, the most excellent among all tantras,
which is endowed with the definitive determination of the *rasa* (taste/essence), as it was heard by me in meditative absorption.

By this it is known that because of the extreme secrecy of this tantra, not even its name has been revealed anywhere in [the other] tantras; for it is my opinion that the Haṃsamāheśvaratantra deals with a different subject matter. Today, I have revealed to you that which was hidden even from my two sons.
Indeed, those possessed of latent impressions (vāsanā) are satisfied upon hearing this virtuous narrative. (51–95)
Do small wells ever swell like the ocean by means of moonlight?
Only lions are satisfied upon hearing a song, not donkeys. (51.96)
Therefore, O Maheśvarī, one should speak only after careful examination; one should not reveal it hastily to anyone who is merely faithful, but only to one who is peaceful and of noble birth.
Let it be given to one who is disciplined, grateful, and pure in action;
but not to one devoid of faith and devotion, nor to the ungrateful, nor to the evil-minded. (51.98)
To one devoid of devotion to the guru, to one who delights in dialectical reasoning, to one whose mind is unrefined, and to one who speaks with perverted intent; || 51-99 ||

To one who acts solely for the sake of worldly gain, who prides himself on the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras, who is hypocritical, extremely wicked, and whose mind is overwhelmed by sense objects; (51.100)
O Goddess, the meaning of this Tantra, which is supremely wonderful, must not be given under any circumstances;
there is nothing in the three worlds by giving which one could become free from debt. (51.101)
O Goddess of the gods, this entire essence of the Lord has been revealed by me to you; beyond this, nothing remains to be known.
Therefore, having thoroughly understood this secret of the wives of Kṛṣṇa,
O beautiful one, become yourself immersed in supreme bliss.
Beyond this, O Goddess of gods, there is nothing further to be asked;
that which I constantly meditate upon in my mind has now been revealed to you. (51–104)
Having spoken thus, Śambhu then remained silent and fixed his mind upon the great ocean of his own immeasurable divine play.
Like an ocean with waves of smiles, his body covered in horripilation and his eyes beautiful,
the Lord of the gods, the Lord of Umā, became an ocean of compassion.
Seeing Śaṅkara thus immersed in a flood of bliss,
Pārvatī worshipped him with the ritual of all the services.
Prostrating herself like a staff, saying "I have achieved my purpose," she praised Śaṅkara, the unsurpassed treasury of compassion, once again. (51.108)
O Lord, you are yourself the teacher and the preceptor of all sciences;
may mantras, yantras, and the like be effective only for those who possess devotion unto you. (51–109)
Having spoken thus, Pārvatī, having fixed in her heart the playful sport she had described,
attained supreme bliss, marked by tears of joy and horripilation.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Śrīmanmāheśvaratantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā. || 51 ||
The total number of verses from the beginning is 3060.
Thus ends this Śrīmāheśvara Tantra.
